adam-broomberg-oliver-chanarin.html.lead_html: Adam Broomberg and Oliver Chanarin turned their experience in magazine editing and reporting into work about how photographic meaning is produced after the shutter is released. In The Day Nobody Died, they used the military embed system to transport photographic paper into a war zone; War Primer 2 pastes Google images into an existing book; People in Trouble... enlarges the selection stickers left by archive editors; and Spirit is a Bone lets facial-recognition technology generate portraits. Permission, selection, publishing, search, and identification become photographic material.
adam-broomberg-oliver-chanarin.html.thesis_html: Since the 1970s, Martha Rosler and Allan Sekula had argued that the meaning of a photograph is produced through captions, journalism, institutions, and economic conditions of use as well as through what appears in the frame. Broomberg and Chanarin, having worked as both magazine editors and photographers in the field, built those problems into the production of the work itself. Military permission became the condition for transporting photographic paper; an archive editor’s circular sticker became a cropping device; Google images were layered onto Brecht’s book; and facial-recognition software was made to generate portraits. They shifted the site at which photographic “truth” was contested. Instead of restricting doubt to the image, they turned military authorization, editorial selection, existing books, search engines, and facial recognition into material, making visible the procedures through which photographs acquire the status of evidence.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Meeting in South Africa, Then Moving from COLORS Editors to Collaborative Artists

Adam Broomberg and Oliver Chanarin were friends before they became an artistic duo. According to an interview with Art on the Underground, they met in Wupperthal, South Africa, later became close in London and lived together, and eventually worked on the magazine COLORS*20. A conversation in BOMB likewise describes friendship and editorial work as preceding the collaboration, followed by their departure from COLORS and the production of their own editorial and commercial photography*23. They did not form around an abstract idea of deliberately combining two viewpoints. They became collaborative artists after years of sharing reporting, editing, and image selection. Later, they emphasized a process of argument and counterargument about the work and weakened individual ownership of photographs to the point that who pressed the shutter became unimportant*20. That history is directly connected to their later emphasis on selecting, sequencing, and assigning meaning to images rather than privileging the photographer’s single “decisive” exposure.

After Rosler and Sekula—Treating Captions, Institutions, and Circulation as Conditions of Photography

Long before Broomberg and Chanarin, photographers and critics had challenged the evidentiary authority of documentary photography. MACBA’s Universal Archive places Martha Rosler, Allan Sekula, and others within a 1970s critique arguing that the testimonial value of photographs is not automatic and must be understood through text, institutions, and economic conditions of use*21. For Broomberg and Chanarin, this was not an abstract theoretical problem because they had worked as both editors and photographers at COLORS. In the BOMB interview, they describe the unease of seeing photographs made through specific encounters with people pass into agencies or other publications, severed from the relationships in which they were made and given new explanations and uses*23. Their response was more specific than the general claim that “photographs lie.” Each project isolates a concrete procedure through which an image comes to function as evidence: what the military permits a photographer to see, which frame an editor chooses, how a museum classifies an object, or what a search engine ranks first. Their reductions, appropriations, and substitutions are necessary because they keep these procedures from disappearing outside the frame.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
The Day Nobody Died—Not Photographing War, but Leaving Material That Was There

In 2008, Broomberg and Chanarin joined the British Army as embedded artists in Helmand Province, Afghanistan, carrying a fifty-meter roll of photographic paper instead of making conventional war photographs. Their official text explains that on days when significant events occurred, they removed roughly seven meters of paper from its box and exposed it to sunlight for about twenty seconds*5. In the Cleveland Museum of Art’s The Day Nobody Died II, no people or explosions appear; only an abstract field of color remains*6. Yet the paper itself traveled through the military supply system into the war zone and physically received the light there. The work preserves photography’s indexical claim that something was “there” while withholding the dramatic scene through which viewers might feel they have understood the war.

Treating the Military Embed System as Part of the Photographic Apparatus

The color fields of The Day Nobody Died cannot be separated from the military logistics that carried the photographic paper into the war zone. Bringing a large box into the embed required inspection, transport, escort, and compliance with military rules; the logistics of production therefore made the embed system itself part of the work. In a conversation with Conscientious Photography Magazine, the artists explain that their research into embedding led them to focus on a structure in which the military could control photographers’ movement and what they were permitted to photograph, with embed rules sharply restricting images that could serve as evidence of conflict*15. The Guardian likewise presented the project as a critique of photojournalism’s incorporation into political, military, and economic systems*7. Refusing the dramatic image of war is therefore not an aesthetic preference for abstraction. It is a way of making visible the gap between the ideal of a photographer freely recording truth on location and the institutional conditions that actually govern access.

War Primer 2—A Photobook for “Reading” Existing War Images

The official archive for War Primer 2 reproduces pages and exhibition views of the work*11. The artists overlaid low-resolution images of the “war on terror,” gathered through Google searches and other online sources, onto pages from the English edition of Bertolt Brecht’s War Primer. MoMA describes the book as a critique of the political economy of conflict imagery, using contemporary screen images against Brecht’s combination of Second World War press photographs and short poems*2. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation identifies the work as the recipient of its 2013 Photography Prize*4. Forma likewise emphasizes the publication’s use of an existing photobook structure to bring historical war imagery into collision with contemporary internet images*16. Here searching, selecting, printing, and layering replace the taking of new photographs as the central work of the photographer.

Making the Traces of Archival Selection into the Work

People in Trouble Laughing Pushed to the Ground grew out of research into roughly 14,000 contact sheets from the Northern Ireland conflict held by Belfast Exposed. Belfast Exposed identifies the colored circular stickers left by earlier editors to mark possible selections as the project’s starting point*12. Broomberg and Chanarin removed those stickers and enlarged the small circular areas that had been hidden underneath. Their official archive reproduces the resulting “dots” works*13. Frieze argues that this procedure refuses to treat the archive as a neutral repository, bringing traces of past selection, reporting, and political use into the meaning of the photograph itself*14.

sections.title: Key Works, Photobooks, and Institutions
sections.body_html:
Fig.—Museum Classification and Photography’s Empiricism

In the 2007 book Fig., museums, colonial collecting, ethnographic classification, and the language of explanatory display become objects of critique. In an interview with Seesaw, the artists explicitly identify the empiricism embedded in figure numbers and museum language as a concern*3. Since the nineteenth century, photography had also served scientific and administrative systems that classified people and objects as “types.” The book therefore examines how display cases, illustrations, captions, and photographic description produce the authority of knowledge. An interview with Photoparley likewise shows the pair’s attention to the histories of classification and institutions behind the assumption that photography transparently explains its subject*19.

Holy Bible—Layering Disaster Images and State Violence onto an Existing Bible

For the 2013 Holy Bible, Broomberg and Chanarin placed photographs selected from the Archive of Modern Conflict onto pages of the King James Bible and marked passages of text with red lines. TIME describes the book, developed through their research on Brecht, as addressing relationships among disaster, violence, state power, and photography*17. Lisson Gallery’s announcement of a reissue of War Primer 2 likewise situates both books within the history of the photobook and the critique of war imagery*18. Pasting photographs onto an existing authoritative text unsettles the conventional relation in which an image simply illustrates or verifies a written account; text and image instead destabilize one another on the page.

Spirit is a Bone—Photography Without a Human Photographer, Toward Machine Vision

Spirit is a Bone uses facial-recognition technology developed for Moscow’s public-surveillance system. Its portraits are not made by subjects posing for a photographer; a machine extracts faces as data, producing what the artists call “non-collaborative portraits.” Aperture discusses the work through a shift in photographic history from evidence and record toward surveillance and prediction*8. GRAIN’s exhibition material likewise presents the conversion of faces into three-dimensional data as a meeting point between portrait photography and technologies of state and police identification*9. The artists’ text The Bone Cannot Lie extends this inquiry into the history of biometric systems that turn the body into measurable evidence*10. The power attached to photography does not disappear when a photographer no longer presses the shutter; the work shows that it can instead become automated.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Permission, Selection, Publishing, Search, Identification—Making the Production of Image Authority Visible

Describing Broomberg and Chanarin as artists who “investigate image infrastructures” can sound abstract, but each project identifies a precise mechanism. The Day Nobody Died uses the British military embed system and supply chain to carry photographic paper into a war zone. People in Trouble Laughing Pushed to the Ground enlarges only the areas hidden beneath the circular stickers with which archive editors marked possible selections. War Primer 2 layers images obtained through Google searches onto the pages of an existing book. Spirit is a Bone lets facial-recognition software in a public-surveillance system generate portraits. Photoworks also traces how the artists developed from editorial work at COLORS toward photobooks, archives, and political imagery*22. Their contribution therefore concerns more than the choice of subjects in documentary photography. They made permission before the photograph, selection afterward, placement on the page, search ranking, and machine identification visible as materials that help produce photographic meaning.

Collaborative Authorship and Distance from the Authority of the Individual Photographer

Their institutional critique is inseparable from the fact of collaboration. According to their conversation in BOMB, they met and became friends in South Africa before moving through Fabrica and editorial work at COLORS into joint artistic production*23. In the Art on the Underground interview, they explain that working as a pair slows the decision to press the shutter and creates time to discuss why a photograph should be made at all*20. Collaborative authorship does not guarantee objectivity because two people are involved. It functions as a production condition that prevents one photographer’s intuition from becoming the final justification for an image. That structure corresponds to works in which photographic paper, existing books, archive stickers, search results, and facial-recognition systems—elements other than the authorial eye—help determine the image. Their official archive records that the collaboration, which lasted twenty-three years, formally ended on February 20, 2021*1.

aglaia-konrad.html.lead_html: Aglaia Konrad has photographed architecture and urban change in Beijing, Cairo, São Paulo, Tokyo, and other cities with a 35mm camera, later developing the images through photobooks, photocopies, silkscreens, and wall-based installations. Through Iconocity, Japan Works, and Umbau, this page examines how an urban archive assembled through travel connects modern architecture with informal additions, transportation, and quarrying.
aglaia-konrad.html.thesis_html: Konrad expands the basic unit of architectural photography from a finished image that explains a single building to groups of images whose order and scale continue to change in books, on walls and windows, and in moving-image works. Her 35mm archive brings high-rise housing, street-level additions, transport infrastructure, quarried stone, and buildings after completion into proximity. These comparisons reveal how modernization proceeds at different speeds and under different material conditions from place to place. The roughness of reproduction, enlarged halftone dots, images transmitted through windows, and the viewer’s route through the gallery all enter the structure of the work. Photographs of architecture act physically on walls and passageways, allowing the same production process to address both the viewpoint that classifies cities and the exhibition space that produces meaning around images.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
From a Mountain Village to Vienna: Learning to See the City through Film and 35mm

Konrad grew up in a small mountain village near Salzburg and moved to Vienna at nineteen. She worked during the day and went to the cinema at night; later criticism has described the changing buildings, roads, and flows of people on screen as an education in seeing the city.*1 Moving from a rural environment to a metropolis provided an early basis for understanding architecture as an environment that appears fragmentarily before a moving body, rather than as a completed object viewed from a fixed position. By the time she pursued research at the Jan van Eyck Academie in the 1990s, this experience had developed into a method of traveling through Beijing, Cairo, São Paulo, and other cities to photograph how modern architecture was used, extended, and absorbed into surrounding transport systems under different social, economic, and topographic circumstances.*2

Konrad has identified portability, economy, materiality, and freedom of movement as reasons for choosing analog 35mm photography.*3 A small camera lets her move between a vehicle, the street, and building interiors, attending to additions, signs, construction work, and peripheral equipment with the same care given to the façade of a celebrated building. Her process emphasizes returning with many negatives and rearranging them through copying, enlargement, and sequencing for each exhibition and publication, rather than deciding on a single conclusive view at the moment of exposure. The ability to collect images while moving and compare cities afterward gives the 35mm format its necessity within the work.

Urban Expansion since the 1990s and Architecture after Completion

Since the 1990s, high-rise housing, transport networks, redevelopment, and informal additions have advanced simultaneously in global cities. Konrad photographs dirt, renovation, vegetation, provisional structures, and surrounding roads alongside recently completed architecture. Even buildings shaped by similar design principles take on different forms of use in Beijing, Cairo, and São Paulo, according to local materials, migration, climate, and regulation. Her sustained movement among cities adds the time of extraction, construction, occupation, and alteration to a view that would otherwise fix a building as the architect’s completed work. *4 *5

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
An Archive Re-edited through Exhibition Space

Konrad’s archive functions as more than a repository searchable by place and date. It is a working resource whose internal relations are remade for each exhibition. Photographs from different cities, periods, and scales sit beside one another, so the meaning of an individual image changes through neighboring photographs, height, size, and the route through the gallery. The photobook Elasticity similarly takes the form of a visual essay that “installs” the personal archive inside a book according to its own rhythm.*6 Rearrangement, more than classification, becomes a procedure for reading urban structure.

Konrad mounts images on windows, enlarges them across entire walls, carries them around corners, and brings moving images and printed matter into close proximity. She has explained that images dealing with architecture should respond to the material and formal dimensions of the exhibition site.*3 A monumental photograph near an entrance, reflective glass, and a copy that dissolves into halftone dots at close range alter the viewer’s route in tangible ways. Exhibition space becomes a site of production that shapes both the meaning of the image and the body’s experience of seeing it.

Quarries and Modern Architecture within a Chain of Resources

In the quarry series, Konrad leaves the finished architectural form and turns toward the geology and labor from which stone is extracted. The Secession exhibition Autofictions in Stone connects stories of stone, mining, movement, and architecture through photography and spatial construction.*7 When modern architecture is viewed as formal beauty, the origin of its material is easy to overlook. By linking urban façades and quarry cuts within the same archive, Konrad treats architecture as a process of cutting the ground, transporting matter, and stacking it into place, as well as a cultural sign.

How Reproduction and Enlargement Expose the Circulation of Architectural Images

Alongside prints made from negatives, Konrad uses photocopiers, silkscreen, coarse enlargement, and wallpaper-like printing. Successive reproductions lose tonal range and detail, turning architecture from an information-rich record into particles and contours that occupy a wall. In FOMU’s Umbau, the same image changes scale in response to columns, passageways, and monumental walls; up close it breaks into halftone dots, then resolves into a building again at a distance.*8 The rough surface turns the cultural circulation of architecture through magazines, advertising, and design documents into a bodily experience of viewing distance in the gallery.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Japan Works: Comparing Use and Traces of Occupation across the Page

Japan Works brings together housing, schools, hotels, temples, high-rises, stations, bridges, classrooms, stairs, and furniture across color and black-and-white images, exteriors and interiors.*9 Each spread links different uses, periods, and scales, giving celebrated architecture and everyday equipment the same rhythm on the page. Alongside styles associated with individual designers, the reader follows buildings as they are occupied, altered, and connected to transport and vegetation around them. As an IACK review observes, the binding and spread of the book operate like a small, portable exhibition wall.*10 Editing unlike buildings and traces of use into proximity enables comparison without erasing differences of place, making the photobook a second site that gives the archive new adjacencies.

Umbau: Treating the Exhibition as a Renovation

FOMU’s Umbau looked back across the long-term archive without fixing the work in chronological order, rearranging the venue as though it were being renovated.*8 The title, meaning “conversion” or “rebuilding,” joins photographs of altered cities and buildings to a form in which image size and position are reconstructed for each site. Large prints, sequences of small images, books, moving-image works, and reproductions enter the field of vision at different speeds. Viewers assemble comparisons as they walk instead of following a single explanation of one city.

In books, the time of turning pages, the connection across a spread, the quality of paper, and the repetition of images produce a different form of urban movement from the wall. A review in Glean examines the centrality of books, cities, archives, and spatial thinking to Konrad’s work.*1 Just as an exhibition changes its arrangement from venue to venue, the book functions as a small architecture that redesigns the order of images.

Her early urban surveys relied heavily on black-and-white photography, while later work makes active use of color. A Glean/HART review of Umbau notes that color connects building materials, signs, vegetation, and provisional structures through a different rhythm, altering the familiar appearance of the archive.*11 Older black-and-white negatives and newer color images appear side by side in exhibitions, foregrounding relations produced by present editing over a chronological account of the city.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Adding Multiple Positions of Observation to the Representative View of Architecture

Architectural photography often aligns horizontal and vertical lines and summarizes a building from the position that makes the design intention most legible. Konrad’s images include objects protruding from windows, later signs, parked cars, additions, and shadows from neighboring buildings, then jump in the next photograph to another point in the same city. A review of Iconocity in De Witte Raaf likewise argues that the urban situation and the method of display must be read together.*12 Fragments gathered in motion and the order imposed afterward both become forms of urban knowledge, without converging on one representative image of a building.

Joining Urban Research and Exhibition Design in One Process

Movement through a site, archiving, reproduction, enlargement, photobook editing, and installation in the gallery form one production process. The “rebuilding” named by Umbau also describes the remaking of architectural images in relation to an exhibition space. FOMU placed this transformation of architectural and urban processes into photographic installation at the center of the exhibition.*8

When photographing works by well-known architects, Konrad includes items taped to windows, additions, dirt, cars, and surrounding buildings, recording how occupation changes architecture after completion. An exhibition at Museum für Gegenwartskunst Siegen paired Konrad with Armin Linke as artists concerned with the complexity of architecture and society.*5 The building appears as the preservation of an author’s intention and as part of a city continually updated by many people and institutions.

Reading the Specific Differences of Cities through Comparison

Across many cities, similar forms of high-rise housing and roads begin to repeat. Konrad’s sequences also retain differences in terrain, material, additions, and use. Published in 2021, Japan Works mixes building types and interiors, presenting architecture in Japan through several uses and temporal layers.*13 Comparison becomes a procedure for examining institutional and everyday differences that remain between superficially similar images, not a conclusion that fixes their common features.

The 2023 exhibition WHAT MAD PURSUIT brought Konrad together with Armin Linke and Bas Princen to reconsider photography as a medium that records and transforms reality while acquiring a physical presence on the walls and pathways of the exhibition.*14*15 In Elasticity, the personal archive is reconstructed through book sequence and repeated exhibition; in Autofictions in Stone, photographs linking quarrying, stone, and architecture extend across the surfaces of the gallery.*16*17*20

The jury statement for the Camera Austria Award valued the archive produced through urban research across the world as an apparatus for analyzing and historicizing cities, beyond its role as documentation. Seen alongside her sustained attention to metropolitan infrastructure and spontaneous additions since the early 1990s, Konrad’s photography accumulates the time through which cities are revised by society, rather than illustrating buildings as isolated objects.*18*19

alexander-gardner.html.lead_html: Gardner, born in Scotland, broke from Brady's organization during the Civil War and published Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the War (1865–66) with individual photographers named throughout — a principled assertion of authorship in documentary photography that the Smithsonian would later call the work of "America's first modern photographer."
alexander-gardner.html.thesis_html: Through his records of the Civil War, Gardner brought the notion of the photographer's individual authorship into documentary photography. By making visible the names of photographers that had been absorbed under Brady's studio imprint — crediting eleven individual operators in his 1865–66 Sketch Book — he made one of the first institutional attempts to attribute photographic making and responsibility to specific people. His public exhibition of the Antietam dead showed that photography could mediate the reality of the battlefield to civil society, and the controversy over the staging of “Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter” inscribed the question of photographic testimony and ethics into the history of the medium.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Alexander Gardner was born in 1821 near Glasgow, Scotland. He emigrated to the United States around 1856 and became manager of Mathew Brady's Washington, D.C., portrait studio. When the Civil War broke out, he was attached to General McClellan's staff to copy maps and charts, then moved into battlefield photography*1.

He left Brady in November 1862 and set up his own studio, taking much of Brady's experienced staff with him. In 1865–66 Gardner published Gardner's Photographic Sketch Book of the War, two volumes containing 100 albumen silver prints. Unlike Brady, who suppressed individual photographers' credits, Gardner specifically named all eleven contributors — a principled assertion of authorship in documentary photography*2.

After photographing the carnage at Antietam in 1862, Gardner produced at Gettysburg one of the most debated photographs in the medium's history: "Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter" (1863). Subsequent research has established that the body was moved, the stone-wall position was staged, and the rifle leaning against the rocks was a prop*3.

In 1865 he was the only photographer permitted to document the execution of Lincoln's four conspirators on July 7. After the war he was appointed chief photographer for the Kansas Pacific Railroad (1867), documenting westward expansion through Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona. He died in 1882*4.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The core of Gardner's practice is the introduction of individual authorship as a concept in documentary photography. Under Brady's organization, the photographer's name was subsumed under the studio brand; who had actually made any given photograph was not publicly known. Gardner changed this deliberately. The Sketch Book credits each photograph by name of photographer and caption writer — an early institutionalization of the idea that a documentary photograph carries the personal testimony and responsibility of an identifiable individual*5.

The Antietam dead photographs mark a turning point in the history of war photography. Exhibited in October 1862 at Brady's New York Gallery as "Brady's exhibition," these photographs gave American civilians their first visual encounter with battlefield corpses. The New York Times reported that "Brady has brought the terrible reality of war to our doors" — the photographer was Gardner, but the credit was Brady's*6.

The staged-body controversy around "Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter" (Gettysburg, 1863) is the foundational case study for debates about documentary authenticity. The evidence suggests the body was moved from elsewhere, the position was composed, and the rifle was placed as a prop. This problem — the photograph as simultaneously record and construction — is positioned at the center of the fundamental argument about what documentary photography is*7.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
The Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery, in its 2015–16 retrospective "Dark Fields of the Republic," called Gardner "America's first modern photographer," crediting him with injecting a sobering realism into American visual culture*8.

The Getty Museum calls the Sketch Book "the first published collection of Civil War photographs"*9, and the Metropolitan Museum writes that "it was Gardner who actually executed" the grand idea of an epic Civil War documentation that Brady had conceived*10.

The western survey photographs Gardner made from 1867 to 1869 — covering Kansas, Colorado, New Mexico, and Arizona — are valued as an important archive of nineteenth-century American expansion, and they situate Gardner's practice in a documentary tradition separate from, and as significant as, his war photography*11.

alexander-rodchenko.html.lead_html: Russian and Soviet Constructivist who presented everyday objects as a new vision for post-revolutionary society through extreme angles and diagonal compositions. He worked across photography, graphics, photomontage and design, becoming central to Soviet print culture and visual education.
alexander-rodchenko.html.thesis_html: With steep angles and diagonal compositions, Rodchenko captured everyday objects from unfamiliar viewpoints and presented photography as a new vision fitting a post-revolutionary society. Crossing photography, graphics, photomontage and design, his practice presented the very choice of viewpoint as a formal and social act, and he became central to Soviet print culture and visual education.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Alexander Rodchenko was born in St Petersburg in 1891 and studied art in Kazan and Moscow. *1 From around the time of the revolution, he worked as a Constructivist practitioner across painting, sculpture and graphics, making the search for new visual forms for a new society a central concern. *2 In the 1920s he began using a camera, and photographs of Moscow's architecture, sports, bodies and streets taken from extreme angles began appearing in Soviet magazines and posters. *3

His relationships with Soviet Constructivist groups and the magazine LEF (Left Front of the Arts) formed the context in which his photographic practice connected to state propaganda culture. *4 He worked throughout his life in Moscow, producing across diverse media — painting, photography, advertising, book design and stage design — until his death in 1956. *5 MoMA and Centre Pompidou both position him as a central figure in Constructivism and photographic modernism, and retrospectives and collection presentations continue. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The revolution of viewpoint and extreme angles

The defining feature of Rodchenko's photography is not the novelty of the subject but the revolution of the viewpoint. *7 Stairs, telephones, athletes, architecture and streets are taken out of the horizontal line of sight and seen from above, below and diagonally. This converts the subject from mere documentation into visual training for perceiving the new society. Smarthistory's analysis of At the Telephone examines how Rodchenko uses the bird's-eye view to transform everyday objects into new compositional entities. *8

In the Constructivist context, photography was simultaneously an artwork and a tool for publication, advertising, political education and collective visual culture. Rodchenko's extreme angles function not merely as style but as a way of breaking the bourgeois fixed viewpoint and seeing the post-revolutionary body and city dynamically. *9 However, this formal innovation also connected to state propaganda, and evaluation needs to take account of the tension between avant-garde radicality and institutional use. *10

Photomontage, design and Soviet print culture

Rodchenko also left important practice in photomontage. Combining photographs, text and graphics in a single image, he produced new media forms that integrated vision and information. *11 MoMA's Object:Photo archive of the Ten Years of Soviet Photography exhibition is an important resource for understanding the institutional context of 1930s Soviet photography. *12

Comparing him with Moholy-Nagy, both claimed the new vision, but where Moholy-Nagy organised experiments in light and perception within educational and design institutions, Rodchenko used photography within Soviet print culture, posters, photomontage and revolutionary public space. *13 From this comparison one can see that even within modernism, the political conditions were different. *14

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: MoMA, Centre Pompidou and the Getty all place Rodchenko at the centre of Constructivism and photographic modernism. The evaluation recognises not only the boldness of his formal choices but the way he anticipated the twentieth-century media environment in which photography connects to magazines, advertising, the state and education. *15 The AIC, Guggenheim, Metropolitan Museum and SFMOMA also hold collections. *16 His relationship with the Soviet regime is not treated as simple admiration but as the process through which an avant-garde becomes institutionalised, and a multi-layered evaluation continues that includes both formal innovation and the problem of political use. *17 Contemporary photographic history research has accumulated detailed analysis of how Rodchenko's extreme angles and photomontages circulated through the multiple channels of advertising, propaganda and education. He continues to be a primary reference for thinking about the political functions of photography within twentieth-century visual culture, and for understanding how Constructivist visual language spread across national boundaries.

amalia-ulman.html.lead_html: In Excellences & Perfections (2014), Amalia Ulman used her own Instagram account as the site of a performance that unfolded over several months. Combining selfies, hotels, meals, lingerie, captions, hashtags, and intervals between posts, she successively played a young woman newly arrived in the city, a woman using sexual appeal to pursue upward mobility, and a woman recovering through wellness culture. The work did not simply test whether individual posts were true or false. As similarly toned photographs of the same person accumulated over time, an invented life began to read as a record of lived experience*4. Through Instagram’s interface and users’ responses, Ulman showed how gender, class, consumption, and expectations placed on young women artists enter that process of reading*10.
amalia-ulman.html.thesis_html: Since Cindy Sherman, staged photography had shown within a single frame how costume, makeup, and composition construct images of femininity. Ulman recognized that a finished photograph was insufficient for social media, where a person becomes credible through months of posting history. On an existing Instagram account, she performed three female personas and made selfies, text, geolocation, posting intervals, and comments part of the same work. She shifted the unit of staged photography from the single image to the entire account, revealing how looking at photographs and judging the account holder’s life proceed together. This shift marks her specific contribution to the history of staged photography.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Ulman was born in Argentina in 1989, grew up in Gijón, Spain, and studied at Central Saint Martins in London. Her official website presents net art, photography, performance, video, and film as a continuous body of work, tracing concerns that run from Excellences & Perfections and Privilege to Sordid Scandal and El Planeta*1. At its center is the way class, appearance, consumption, work, and the body are used to assign value to people. Speaking about Los Angeles, she has described her interest in how people edit their lives for others and how class differences become visually apparent while moving through the city*19.

When Excellences & Perfections began in 2014, Instagram was shifting from a service for sharing everyday photographs into a platform for continuously promoting one’s life, body, tastes, and profession. A photograph’s credibility no longer depended on the depicted event alone. Earlier posts, follower counts, geolocation, captions, hashtags, and the spacing of posts combined to produce the sense of a coherent life*4. Instead of describing this system from outside, Ulman fed scripted posts into the account she already used*7. The work had to occupy the same space as ordinary posts in order to test which photographs viewers accepted as records of real life*14.

This decision also addressed a situation in which the work and appearance of young women artists are evaluated together. In a public discussion organized by Rhizome, Ulman asked how women artists are expected to look and behave, how we consume images, and how images consume us. To examine how displaying her own body could become publicity, sexual evaluation, and career management at once, she needed a platform where appearance and popularity were quantified, not simply a gallery wall*20.

sections.title: Core Ideas and Methods
sections.body_html:
Why Did the Work Have to Be Performed on Instagram?

Ulman was not testing whether viewers could detect retouching in a selfie. On social media, a person’s identity takes shape as the same figure repeatedly displays similar places, language, and habits. A staged photograph shown in an exhibition would announce itself as fiction from the outset*6. Excellences & Perfections withheld its status as an artwork and unfolded at the pace of ordinary Instagram use*10. Months of mirrors in hotels, meals, flowers, lingerie, tears, treatment, and exercise allowed followers to fill the gaps between photographs and assemble a life story themselves*12.

Why Use Familiar Female Archetypes?

Ulman has explained that she chose types viewers already recognized so that the structure of the experiment would remain legible. The narrative moved through three stages: the innocent young woman arriving in the city, the woman pursuing advancement through consumption and sexual appeal, and the woman returning to a healthy life after a breakdown. These were less private confessions than plots already circulating through Tumblr, fashion advertising, gossip media, and wellness culture*6. Because the photographs were familiar, followers could infer romance, income, occupation, and mental state from limited information*8. The work exposed how those inferences relied on shared models of femininity and class*13.

Los Angeles supplied practical conditions for the performance. Ulman has described it as a city shaped by the fashion industry where she could inhabit another persona without repeatedly running into acquaintances. Hotels, cosmetic surgery, beauty culture, fitness, and luxury retail also provided settings in which the body and consumption signify social mobility*5. She chose the city for more than its visual style: it allowed her to sustain an invented life in real locations over time*19.

What the Comments Revealed About Judgment

Followers’ responses were not reactions added after the work; they helped form the persona as the performance unfolded. The innocent young woman, the sexually self-styled woman, and the woman restored to health drew different forms of praise, concern, and condemnation. Ulman later said that audience response also influenced the development of Privilege*5. Comments and unfollows recorded more than the fact that viewers had accepted a fiction. They preserved, in concrete language, judgments about which forms of behavior were acceptable for a young woman in relation to her body, pregnancy, success, spending, and recovery*14.

From Feminist Performance to Social Media

Performing images of femininity has a history in staged photography and feminist performance, including the work of Cindy Sherman. Ulman moved this method from the completed single image to a public account updated as part of daily life. In Sherman’s film-still photographs, costume, makeup, and composition compress a feminine type into one frame*2. In Ulman’s work, continued posting, text, geolocation, and viewer response build the persona*3. Tate’s inclusion of the project in Performing for the Camera helped situate it within the history of performance for the camera, beyond the novelty of the internet platform*17.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Excellences & Perfections, 2014

The work unfolded on Ulman’s own Instagram account from April through September 2014. Selfies, photographs of restaurants and hotels, flowers, clothing, food, pole dancing, images staged to suggest breast surgery, apologies, and posts signaling recovery appeared in the sequence of the three personas*4. Because actual experiences were mixed with staged events, deciding whether each photograph was true or false does not explain the work as a whole*6. Credibility arose from the familiar sequence of the posts and the apparent development of the person over time*10.

Posts, Captions, Time, and Interface

In this work, photographs cannot be separated from captions and hashtags. Short texts suggested romance or states of health; geolocation supplemented signs of lifestyle; gaps between posts encouraged viewers to imagine breakdown and recovery*4. The medium therefore included Instagram’s chronological feed and profile page, not simply a collection of selfies*7. Rhizome’s Webrecorder preserved the structure of the interface, demonstrating what disappears when later exhibitions extract the photographs from the platform*11.

Privilege, 2015–16

In Privilege, Ulman used a corporate office setting, an exaggerated version of herself, pregnancy, a pigeon named Bob, and inexpensive decorations to address work, the female body, class, and political language. Pregnancy supplied a nine-month temporal structure, while another character signaled the presence of a script. By offering clearer signs of fiction than the earlier work, Privilege shifted the question from making viewers believe to examining how they participate in a performance they already recognize*5. The choice of cheap, easily reproduced props reflected both economic necessity and the standardized commodities that construct corporate environments*9.

Archives and Exhibition

Social-media works change as services alter their features, redesign interfaces, or remove accounts. In Excellences & Perfections, photographs, captions, comments, profile information, and posting order formed a single structure; saving the images alone could not preserve the work’s progression. Rhizome’s Webrecorder captured Instagram’s screen and interactions, including display formats later lost through redesign*4. At the same time, archiving raised questions about the privacy of commenters and about who owns memory produced on social media*11. Preservation became a new editorial act: a decision about which screens and responses should remain in the public record*21.

In the later video work Sordid Scandal, Ulman examined how family history, rumor, archival footage, and the authority of a narrator shape fact, extending the question beyond online personas. Her feature film El Planeta follows an impoverished mother and daughter who use clothing and behavior to present a different life, tracing the gap between economic circumstances and the self shown to others*15. Although the medium shifted from Instagram to moving images, the question remained: who speaks, and which fragments are accepted as evidence of a life?*22.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beyond the “Hoax” Reading

Excellences & Perfections was often described as an Instagram deception or prank. Yet the conclusion that photographs can lie was already familiar from the histories of staged photography and digital manipulation. Ulman relied less on sophisticated compositing than on ordinary hotels, meals, lingerie, self-help language, and regular posting to make fiction feel routine*7. Followers did not accept a single photograph unconditionally*14. They followed familiar conventions for reading other people’s daily lives on Instagram and built a consistent persona from repeated images and texts*18.

Class, Consumption, and the Body of the Young Woman Artist

The three personas in Excellences & Perfections convey narratives of upward mobility as well as differences in taste. Hotels, cosmetic surgery, brands, and healthy food appear as means of managing the body and converting attractiveness into capital. Ulman has discussed her interest in the pleasures of consumption, its physical and emotional costs, and the class differences made visible in Los Angeles*19. To address how young women artists are judged through appearance and behavior alongside their work, she staged that system of evaluation on a platform where her own appearance could be appraised as a commodity*20.

How Social-Media Photographs Acquire Credibility

Ulman’s place in photographic history cannot be explained simply by her early use of Instagram. She made the credibility of a photograph depend on posting order, text, profile information, and exchanges with followers in addition to optical recording*3. Where staged photography completes a role within a single image, Ulman sustained an account long enough for a persona to emerge and recorded viewers’ judgments in the comments*16. As Rhizome’s preservation project demonstrates, conserving the work for the future requires preserving posting order, the former interface, captions, and responses along with the photographs*21.

an-my-le.html.lead_html: In Viêt Nam, Small Wars, 29 Palms, and Events Ashore, An-My Lê used a large-format camera to photograph memories of the Vietnam War, historical reenactments, Marine Corps training, and the global operations of the U.S. Navy. Working at a remove from the decisive moments of combat, she made the preparation, performance, and afterlife of war in landscape and history her subject.
an-my-le.html.thesis_html: War photography has often concentrated front-line wounds and explosions into decisive moments. Lê expanded its field to include training before a conflict, reenactment after it, films, monuments, and memories of home. Her point of departure was her return to Vietnam in 1994, when she discovered that the homeland she had carried in memory no longer matched the place before her. Photography allowed her to hold the details of the present landscape together with the past that failed to align with them, without resolving an exile's memory into a single verbal account. Through the detail and deliberation of the large-format camera, she gave equal descriptive weight to people, equipment, sky, vegetation, and distance, presenting war as a system through which a society imagines, prepares, repeats, and remembers conflict. Lê extended war photography from evidence gathered at the front to the long duration accumulated in landscapes and institutions.

sections.title: From Memories of War to Landscape Photography
sections.body_html:
Why Photography? Holding Exilic Memory and the Present Landscape in the Same Frame

Lê grew up in Saigon and fled the country with her family in 1975, later settling in the United States as a political refugee. She studied biology at Stanford University, moved toward art after taking photography courses, and received an MFA from Yale University in 1993*2. When she returned to Vietnam in 1994 after an absence of about nineteen years, she realized that the memories sustained during exile did not correspond to the country before her. She has recalled that an exile's memory, cut off from direct access to its culture, had proved unreliable; after returning, she repeatedly revisited the same places with a large-format camera*24. She was encouraged to photograph the effects of Agent Orange and sites associated with the war, but concluded that such subjects would reduce the conflict to familiar signs and predetermine the Vietnam she was trying to find*23. In Viêt Nam, she photographed rice fields, rivers, cities, labor, and leisure, examining how personal memory, regional histories, and postwar daily life occupied the same terrain. Art21 likewise identifies her return as the starting point for comparing a remembered homeland with postwar life through landscape*3。

. Photography did not serve here as proof that memory was accurate. Lê has observed that photographs are tied to truth while also remaining fictions constructed through framing and distance*23. A verbal account of home can smooth over the discrepancies between memory and the present landscape. A photograph can retain rice-field labor, vegetation, buildings, and distant views as concrete facts of the present while leaving their relation to the past unresolved. As the record of her Harvard lecture suggests, repeated visits with a cumbersome view camera created room for childhood, war, and older histories to appear contingently within a single landscape*24. The return thus became a way of measuring how far memory had drifted from a real place, instead of an act of recovering an intact homeland. From there, Lê moved beyond her own memories to examine how American culture remembers the Vietnam War through cinema, news photography, and reenactment.

The Large-Format Camera: Describing War Through People, Terrain, and Institutions

Lê chose a large-format camera to step away from the speed that turns war into immediate news and to observe people, military machinery, terrain, sky, and vegetation as a single spatial field. She has explained that the view camera records minute information on a large negative and describes an experiential space in which even the air between objects can be sensed*23. She experimented with more mobile cameras, but found that they could not hold the multiple layers of time, distance, and memory present in the landscape, and returned to the cumbersome large-format camera*24. Setting a tripod and taking time to examine composition and focus shifts attention away from chasing an event toward watching what prepares war and which terrain makes military action possible. As SFMOMA notes, Lê treats landscape itself as a site where war is prepared, performed, and remembered*5. The camera's slowness is inseparable from this subject: it leaves soldiers, the land that enables training, equipment, vegetation, light, and the photographer's position at the same level of resolution. Art21 places the work between documentary and staged photography because the realities she photographs have already been constructed through military exercises, reenactment, and preexisting images of war*2。

sections.title: Photographing Reenactment, Training, and Logistics
sections.body_html:
Small Wars: The Vietnam War Performed by Others

Small Wars (1999–2002) photographs Vietnam War reenactments staged in American forests. The participants do more than imitate historical events. Through equipment, assigned roles, terrain, and memories shaped by film and news photography, they produce scenes that look recognizably like the Vietnam War. As a condition of being allowed to photograph, Lê was also asked to participate and played the role of a Viet Cong soldier*21. Because the positions of photographer, refugee with personal memories of the war, and reenactor overlap, the series settles into neither an outside ethnographic observation nor a private act of remembrance. The Museum of Contemporary Photography explains that she avoided shocking combat reportage and photographed places where war is psychologically anticipated, processed, and relived*6. Quiet woods, smoke, weapons, and ambushes share the same tonal register, making the landscape itself the stage on which an image of war is produced.

29 Palms: Military Training as an Image of War Before Combat

29 Palms (2003–04) follows Marines preparing for deployment to Iraq and Afghanistan at a training ground in the California desert. In MoMA's Infantry Platoon (Machine Gunners), soldiers and a machine gun occupy part of the frame, with a vast expanse of arid land extending behind them*7. The activity is real military work, yet targets, mock villages, and role-play anticipate a future battlefield. Lê has explained that black and white separated the images from contemporary color news coverage and connected the exercise to a longer image history that includes the Vietnam War and nineteenth-century war photography*4. In Mortar Impact, the explosion becomes a dramatic center while the scale of the terrain also relativizes its force*8. The series avoids reducing its subject to a choice between military heroism and antiwar critique. It describes the combined system of training, imagination, technology, and environment that makes war possible.

Events Ashore: The Navy's Global Reach in Color

For Events Ashore (2005–14), Lê accompanied the U.S. Navy and photographed exercises, transportation, relief work, scientific research, and humanitarian operations across all seven continents. Aperture's photobook presents the many forms through which military power becomes present worldwide in disaster response, diplomacy, logistics, and technical assistance as well as combat*14。《Suez Canal Transit, USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, Egypt is a five-part work that presents a massive aircraft carrier, the canal, and the surrounding land as one continuous field of vision*10. Her earlier black-and-white photographs linked memories, reenactments, and exercises associated with the Vietnam War to earlier war photography. Events Ashore addresses an active contemporary navy coming into contact with different climates, cities, waters, and civilian activities. Lê has said that she initially felt like “a black-and-white photographer taking color pictures,” before learning to use color psychologically and descriptively*25. The gray of ships, blue water, uniforms, relief supplies, and local vegetation preserve the specific relations between military activity and each environment instead of compressing the armed forces into a single symbol. The move to color shifted the emphasis from layered memory toward a description of the present in which military power, diplomacy, resources, and labor operate simultaneously.

Silent General and the Recurrence of History

Silent General brings together Civil War monuments, film production, borderlands, environmental disasters, protest movements, and the political spaces of the capital in a sequence of chapters. Its title comes from Walt Whitman's Specimen Days, and the work favors a structure in which the past recurs in contemporary places over a linear chronology*11. MoMA's Fourteen Views places photographs from Vietnam, France, Louisiana, and elsewhere across a monumental continuous surface, producing a fractured view of history that differs from nineteenth-century panoramas designed to make military victory visible at a glance*1. The series, shown at Marian Goodman Gallery, likewise treats the legacy of the Civil War and contemporary politics as arrangements embedded in land*19。

sections.title: Major Works and the Structure of the Medium
sections.body_html:
Dong Thap: A Landscape Where Memory and the Present Do Not Coincide

Dong Thap, Southern Vietnam (1994) views riverside vegetation and human activity from a distance, offering few direct markers of war. The Met identifies it as a photograph made after Lê's return and describes its memory-like or dreamlike quality*9. The lack of explicit information does not erase history. It preserves, in detailed photographic form, the experience of seeing one's conviction that one knows a homeland collapse before the present landscape. Lê's engagement with war imagery begins here, and the impossibility of directly recovering the past remains central to her later photographs of reenactment and training.

29 Palms: Disturbing the Military Sublime from Within

29 Palms presents desert, mountains, nocturnal flashes, and armored vehicles as a grand visual field. Such beauty can make military power seductive, and Lê has consistently addressed the problem of aestheticizing war, including in her Art21 discussion of the series*4. At the same time, soldiers and vehicles often appear small against the expanse of the terrain, and the fiction of training remains visible. Scholar Bogumiła Kowalczyk has analyzed Small Wars and 29 Palms in terms of invisible violence haunting the American landscape*17. The work's critical force lies less in eliminating beauty than in asking viewers to recognize the moment when beauty and military domination become intertwined.

Reading the Series Through Photobooks and Exhibitions

The 2005 photobook Small Wars brought Viêt Nam, Small Wars, and 29 Palms together in three sections, establishing a structure through which return, reenactment, and predeployment training could be read as one problem. Prix Pictet's artist profile similarly describes the trilogy as roughly a decade of work on the myths and memories of war*18. The Carnegie Museum of Art's 2020 exhibition On Contested Terrain assembled more than one hundred works from seven series to consider landscape photography, military imagery, and diaspora together*11. MoMA's 2023 exhibition included video, embroidery, and sculpture alongside photography, showing how images of war circulate through cinema, journalism, decorative forms, and exhibition space*1。

sections.title: Reception, Criticism, and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
The Risk of Beautifying War and the Function of Distance

Lê's precise large-format photographs and balanced compositions can render military exercises and weapons visually compelling. The artist herself has repeatedly examined this risk as a problem of “aestheticizing war”*4. In an Aperture interview, she discusses the relation among memories of Vietnam, the confusion of war, and memories made accessible through photography*13. Her distance can soften the immediacy of suffering, yet it also prevents a single casualty or explosion from standing in for history. Land, labor, institutions, and the war films already present in viewers' memories return to the field of vision. Lê's selections for The Met's Artist Project, in which she interprets other artists' images of war, landscape, and power, further show that she understands her own work within a long visual culture*22. The New Yorker identified the way conflict becomes embedded in physical and psychological terrain through reenactment, training, and film sets as a central concern of the MoMA retrospective*16. When Lê says that photography is equated with truth but that every photograph is also a fiction, she is not arguing for the fabrication of events. Framing, distance, light, access, and the sequence of a series shape what counts as war; the ethical task is to make that construction perceptible rather than conceal it*23。

War Photography Beyond the Front Line

Lê's historical position rests on more than the paradox of addressing war without photographing a battlefield. She treats a reenactors' forest, a predeployment desert, naval supply routes, monuments under removal, film crews, and protesting students as connected sites that produce images of conflict. In a conversation with The Brooklyn Rail, she calls herself a landscape photographer and places military intervention within longer histories of violence*15. The Carnegie Museum of Art catalogue describes her work as connecting the landscape tradition with the complexities of war*12. MoMA's organization of the work from Viêt Nam to Silent General through the structure “Between Two Rivers” likewise evaluates it as an art of movement and opposition in which multiple places and histories act at once, instead of as a chronological account of individual wars*20. Lê demonstrated that war photography can address training, logistics, environment, media, and memory—the systems that sustain conflict—as well as evidence from the front. The purpose of working away from the battlefield lies in bringing what she has called “universal history, personal history, and cultural history” into view at the same time within a single terrain*24。

ana-torfs.html.lead_html: Ana Torfs is a Belgian artist who combines existing language—trial records, plays, films, diaries, and colonial documents—with actors’ faces, slide projections, moving images, subtitles, and sound. Focusing on Du mentir-faux, Anatomy, and Displacement, this page examines how history is read when testimony and face, original text and translation, or photography and memory fail to coincide.
ana-torfs.html.thesis_html: Conventional documentary and legal records often make photographs, testimony, and captions reinforce one another in identifying the same event. Torfs deliberately loosens those bonds. She has actors speak other people’s testimony and distributes faces, voices, subtitles, and documents across different parts of an installation. Photography then becomes more than an illustration that confirms testimony; it becomes a site for examining whose voice speaks, in which language, and through which institutions testimony acquires meaning. Her key shift lies in constructing a mismatch between lucid faces and precise words; the images themselves remain visually clear.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Communication Studies and Film/Video—Learning Language and Image in Parallel

Torfs was born in Mortsel, Belgium, in 1963. She studied communication studies at KU Leuven from 1981 to 1986, then film and video in Brussels from 1986 to 1990*22. Her official biography traces a long engagement with perception, memory, representation, and the construction of images across photography, moving image, slides, text, sound, and tapestry*1. The DAAD Artists-in-Berlin program likewise places the relation between the human figure, photography, and text—and the gap between reality and perception—at the center of her work*3. This educational background encouraged a method in which photography is rarely treated as an isolated visual medium. Language directs what an image means, while moving images alter the duration through which language is encountered.

Archives, Reenactment, and Moving-Image Installation After the 1990s

As Torfs’s work developed in the 1990s, contemporary artists were increasingly editing existing documents, films, trial records, and historical materials into works meant to be read in exhibition space. WIELS describes her use of found texts and images to explore the interplay among language, representation, translation, and visualization*2. MACBA similarly situates her work around the transmission of memory and history and the gap between words and images in photography and moving image*4. MUAC adds another dimension, approaching her work through the difference between seeing and thinking one knows, while stressing how language produces knowledge and has historically participated in colonial systems of naming and classification*25. Within this field, the archive is less a neutral container of past facts than a site whose meanings change according to who classifies, translates, and reenacts them. Torfs’s later Displacement, which breaks Roberto Rossellini’s Journey to Italy into slide photographs and sound, can therefore be understood as an inquiry into what remains and what is lost when an existing narrative moves between media*24. Generali Foundation describes the work as a “photographic remake” of Rossellini’s film, placing this separation and reconstruction of film, photography, and sound within Torfs’s sustained study of text and image*23.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Du mentir-faux—Separating Testimony from Faces in the Trial of Joan of Arc

Du mentir-faux is an important early work based on the trial records of Joan of Arc, placing questions and answers from the testimony alongside staged black-and-white portraits and slides. The official work page explains how actors take the place of historical witnesses, unsettling the expectation that a document provides direct access to “truth”*5. A related publication shows Torfs approaching Joan less as a national symbol than as an embodied individual caught inside an apparatus of power*6. The photographs themselves are not obscure. Faces are sharply rendered and the words derive from historical documents. Their pairing is artificial, however, exposing how the credibility of testimony depends on who is understood to be speaking and whose face is seen.

Anatomy—“Dissecting” the Rosa Luxemburg Case

For Anatomy, Torfs researched legal records concerning the 1919 murders of Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht in the military archive in Freiburg, then combined moving-image testimony spoken by twenty-five actors with seventeen projected slide portraits*7. The official publication shows the same event fragmenting across different witnesses’ viewpoints, with language refusing to resolve into a single objective account*8. Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen notes that although the work is staged in an anatomical theater, the object supposedly being “dissected” never appears on screen. The viewer must connect the testimony mentally, assembling an image of historical responsibility from partial accounts*9.

Keeping Voice and Face Out of Sync—Slowing Down the Reading of a Photograph

In Dia’s Approximations/Contradictions, twenty-one performers sing songs from Hanns Eisler’s Hollywood Songbook, with three different versions presented through portrait-like framing*10. Dia’s materials show how the work begins in research and produces multiple readings among music, subtle facial expression, and historically charged lyrics*11. For Torfs, photography and moving image do not function as illustrations that deliver information quickly. By weakening the synchronization among voice and face, subtitle and image, document and performance, she creates a duration in which viewers cannot simply move on with the feeling that seeing has amounted to knowing.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Parrot & the Nightingale—Columbus’s Journal, Plants, and Translation

The Parrot & the Nightingale, a Phantasmagoria takes Columbus’s journal as a point of departure and brings together repetition, translation, plants, and colonial classification. The official page situates the work against the history of a Cuban botanical garden, sugar plantations, and slavery, while showing a structure in which image and text never fully explain one another*12. In the subsequent TXT (Engineered by), words associated with colonialism, trade, slavery, and exploitation move through space, treating language itself as a material carrier of history*13. Photography here does not primarily present colonial “evidence.” It tests what becomes visible when contemporary photographs of plants and places are placed beside inherited vocabularies from the past.

Echolalia—Expanding Repetition and Translation into Exhibition Space

Torfs’s WIELS exhibition Echolalia brought together slides, sound, photography, moving image, silkscreen, and tapestry, organizing different supports so that words and images acquire altered meanings with each repetition*2. The accompanying publication likewise resists reducing the work to a single medium, offering a way to read translation, historical voices, and citation as forms of echo*14. Understanding Torfs’s photographs therefore requires attention to more than the individual image: neighboring text, projection order, delayed sound, and the viewer’s movement all shape the moment at which a photograph appears evidentiary. The title Echolalia itself refers to the repetition of heard speech. Citation in Torfs’s work does not simply preserve an original source; it becomes an event whose meaning changes when moved into another voice, medium, or historical moment.

Why Photography? Because It Can Sit Between the Theatrical Body and the Written Archive

In a BOZAR interview, Torfs speaks in detail about beginning film studies in Brussels in 1986, collecting fragments from existing texts and bringing them back to life through voices, and allowing associations to crystallize slowly through a lengthy production process*15. The Dutch Art Institute emphasizes her use of reproducible media to build language and visualization, interpretation and translation, into the structure of the work itself*16. Photography can stage a figure as theater does, while still carrying the look of a “trace of fact” associated with legal records. That dual capacity makes it especially suited to Torfs’s concerns. A still image also keeps a face present after a spoken voice has passed. Viewers must repeatedly decide whether they trust what was said or the face that remains.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Reading Torfs as an Artist Who Reworked Photographic Evidence

ARGOS records Torfs’s work since the early 1990s as a precise construction of photography, slides, sound, moving image, and print that begins in literary and historical sources*17. Its materials for ANATOMY describe an installation that separates the testimony of twenty-five actors, seventeen black-and-white slide portraits, and English interpretation into distinct layers, using display to make clear that language can never be wholly objective*18. Seen from this perspective, Torfs’s place in photography history is more specific than that of an “archive-based video artist.” She breaks down the authority that photography assumes when it appears to show history, separating it into voice, subtitle, performance, and translation. The silence of photography and the duration of testimony produce a stronger tension because they are kept apart. The viewer receives documents while also occupying the position of an editor who compares fragments and constructs a provisional historical account. Because no conclusion arrives from outside the installation, the acts of reading and judging become part of the work.

Reception and Reach—Making Reading Central to Viewing

The exhibition text for Pori Art Museum emphasizes the analytical structure of Torfs’s work and the layered narration produced by photography, writing, and projection*19. A University at Buffalo Art Galleries guide discusses When You Whistle, It Makes Air Come Out as an example in which breathing sounds and text derived from Piaget create a gap between bodily sensation and linguistic understanding*20. Torfs was also included in Photo Art, a survey of international photography in the twenty-first century, confirming her place within a period when photography expanded from the autonomous print into installation*21. Her work does not make answers difficult simply for the sake of opacity. It keeps visible the translators, witnesses, editors, and viewers whose labor always mediates access to historical fact. In that sense, she connects the act of looking at photography with the act of reading.

anders-petersen.html.lead_html: Anders Petersen began photographing at close range in black and white while spending time at the Hamburg bar Café Lehmitz in the late 1960s, sharing everyday life with its regulars. From the 1978 photobook Café Lehmitz through projects made in prisons, care homes, psychiatric institutions, London’s Soho, and the global City Diary series, he has repeatedly stayed in specific places and photographed from within relationships built over time. This page examines Christer Strömholm’s influence, Petersen’s habit of returning photographs to the people he photographed, and the relation between physical proximity, the printed image, and photobook editing.
anders-petersen.html.thesis_html: Postwar European subjective documentary already had two important precedents before Petersen. His teacher Christer Strömholm developed long relationships with trans women around Place Blanche in Paris and allowed those relationships to remain part of the photographs.*16 Ed van der Elsken edited the bohemian life of the 1950s Left Bank into the photo-novel Love on the Left Bank, a book Petersen later described as something like a “school” for him as a young photographer.*17 At Café Lehmitz, Petersen spent years returning to the same bar, was photographed by the customers as well as photographing them, and eventually covered its walls with roughly 350 prints that those depicted could take home; intimacy was built through shared time and the exchange of photographs.*6 Nan Goldin, from the 1980s onward, organized an already existing circle of friends and lovers into an autobiographical diary. Petersen entered bars, prisons, care homes, and psychiatric hospitals from outside and built relationships through extended stays.*19 Close range, flash, and dense blacks grew out of this method of staying and exchange.
