sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Christer Strömholm

Petersen entered Christer Strömholm’s photography school in Stockholm in 1966 and, around the same time, helped found Saftra, a group oriented toward socially critical reportage.*1 At Place Blanche in Paris, Strömholm maintained long friendships with trans women and made photographs from shared life without classifying “unusual people” as categories observed from outside. Foto Colectania has presented Les Amies de Place Blanche and Café Lehmitz together as teacher-and-student series, emphasizing empathy, sustained involvement, and photobook sequencing as shared concerns.*16 Moderna Museet likewise places Strömholm’s school in relation to Otto Steinert’s teaching of Subjektive Fotografie and identifies Petersen as one of the students who most clearly carried forward Strömholm’s subjective approach.*20 What Petersen inherited was less the appearance of dense black prints than the acceptance of the photographer’s own feeling and relation to the subject as part of the documentary situation.

Ed van der Elsken

Ed van der Elsken’s 1956 Love on the Left Bank edited youth, lovers, bars, and bohemian life on Paris’s Left Bank into a photo-novel centered on one character instead of a sequence of anonymous reportage. Petersen later described the book as a kind of “school” for him and spoke of learning the power of the photobook to build personal experience into a self-contained world.*17 Café Lehmitz has no fictional protagonist, but it is not simply an accumulation of single photographs. Embraces, fights, dancing, sleep, and exchanged looks are sequenced so that shared time in the bar becomes the unit of editing. From Strömholm came a way of forming relationships; from van der Elsken, the subjective chain of the photobook. Café Lehmitz joins the two in another form.

Café Lehmitz

From the period when Petersen began photographing at Café Lehmitz around 1967, the camera was not a one-way recording device. In his recollection, cameras passed from person to person in the bar; customers photographed one another, and the relationship began with Petersen himself also being photographed.*6 He returned to the bar whenever he was in Hamburg, sometimes sleeping in the kitchen, and photographed regulars, lovers, sex workers, sailors, and others who spent the night there.*6 The German Society for Photography describes the project as an early example of what would later be called “personal documentary,” foregrounding lived experience and the photographer’s relation to the people photographed.*4 The close-range images arose from remaining in the same place and sharing the acts of photographing and being photographed, not from first defining a “marginal community” and then approaching it from outside. At Café Lehmitz, the usual journalistic separation between photographer and subject becomes unstable. ROSPHOTO has described the series as a classic of subjective photography rooted in Petersen’s entry into the regulars’ everyday lives.*5

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
350 Prints on the Wall

Petersen did not wait until the Café Lehmitz photographs were finished and then take them exclusively into museums. He recalled covering the bar’s walls with about 350 prints so that the people in them could take whichever photographs they wanted.*6 In another interview he described photographing the bar’s people like a “family album” and said he did not want to separate the images from their lives.*7 This exchange means that the embraces, sleep, drunkenness, injuries, and nudity later seen in museums and books were made under circumstances different from a secret archive owned only by the photographer. Trust among participants and the gaze of anonymous viewers after publication remain separate questions. The ethical tension of Café Lehmitz lies in the coexistence of genuine intimacy during production and the possibility of voyeurism once the images circulate publicly.

Close Range and Deep Blacks

The Café Lehmitz photographs are known for deep blacks, coarse grain, bodies cut by the edge of the frame, and flash used at close range; Aperture describes them as bold, intimate black-and-white images produced through several years of immersion.*18 Petersen himself, however, locates the center of photography in being alive—with desire, dreams, and wounds—more than in a stylistic formula, and says an image must be believable to him.*8 The pictures followed years of returning to the same bar, being photographed by customers, and giving prints back. Isolated from that process, heavy black and proximity can turn the subject into a dramatic “outsider”; within the process, the photographer himself was also part of the conditions that made the image possible. The roughness of the photographs follows from bodily proximity and low light; it does not function merely as an accent on social marginality.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Institution Trilogy

After Café Lehmitz, Petersen spent extended periods in a prison, a home for older people, and a psychiatric hospital, producing Fängelse, Rågång till kärleken, and Ingen har sett allt. Nationalmuseum groups these works as an “Institution Trilogy” and emphasizes the time he spent in closed environments in order to come close to the people living there.*3 Petersen himself has connected these projects to “personal connections,” including the experience of entering a home for older people after his father’s death.*1 The photographs therefore do more than denounce institutions from outside. Personal fear and family experience become the points of entry through which he spends time inside and photographs ordinary relations there. Subjectivity and social record operate together: acknowledging why the photographer is present becomes part of the documentary method.

Editing the Photobook

Café Lehmitz was published by Schirmer/Mosel in 1978 and became a starting point for Petersen’s sustained use of the photobook. The ICP Library holds bibliographic records for the first and later editions.*10 The German Society for Photography lists the 1978 book among the publisher’s defining titles and describes its international circulation through the sequence of the book as well as exhibitions.*11 Petersen makes very large numbers of photographs, so the emotional relation created between adjacent images matters more than a single representative picture. In Dazed he has discussed editing from numerous contact sheets down to a few hundred photographs and the importance of building chains between them.*9 A BnF retrospective catalogue assembled roughly 300 works from the 1960s onward, while Nationalmuseum treats Café Lehmitz and the Institution Trilogy as continuous through both books and exhibitions.*12 Nationalmuseum identifies the desire to “come close” and a shared human condition as concerns sustained through changing locations by the way the photographs are edited into publications.*3

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Soho and City Diary

In Soho, photographed in London in 2011, Petersen again entered a specific urban district as he had at Café Lehmitz, while addressing the contemporary entertainment quarter on its own terms. MACK describes the commission as an immersion in Soho’s present.*13 City Diary mixes photographs from Stockholm, Tokyo, St. Petersburg, and other cities across time and place into a personal visual diary. Steidl records the project’s 2012 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Award and its later expansion into a seven-volume series.*14 The Hasselblad Foundation’s 2024 retrospective likewise organized six decades of photographs as a flow across time and cities, treating people, animals, bodies, and night as reflections of Petersen’s own life.*1

Intimacy and Voyeurism

Petersen’s photographs emphasize trust with the people he photographs, yet their images of drunkenness, nudity, wounds, and social marginality in strong contrast do not eliminate the possibility of a voyeuristic gaze from later viewers. ROSPHOTO has described his long-term immersion and solidarity as an “anti-voyeuristic” method.*5 A comparison with Nan Goldin shows that each photographer arrives at “intimacy” through a different relationship to the people photographed. Goldin has said that her relations with friends and lovers existed before the photographs, and she turned her own social world into the diary-like editing of The Ballad of Sexual Dependency.*19 Petersen also builds relationships first, but in Café Lehmitz and the Institution Trilogy he enters a specific place from outside and forms relationships through extended stays after entering from outside. Goldin’s work is autobiographical community photography; Petersen’s retains the ethical tension of how a photographer enters another community, leaves it, and later publishes the photographs. In 2003, he was named Photographer of the Year at the Rencontres d’Arles, and in 2008 he received the German Society for Photography’s Dr. Erich Salomon Prize.*15 In its award statement, the DGPh identifies the sustained approach to people and communities that begins with Café Lehmitz as a continuing feature of his photography.*2 In a Dazed interview, Petersen likewise places curiosity about his subjects and questions about himself within the same act of photographing, without reducing intimacy to a visual effect.*9

andre-kertesz.html.lead_html: Photographer who moved from Hungary to Paris and New York, finding private lyricism in everyday urban life and chance arrangements. He is recognised as a deep influence on the development of street photography and poetic documentary.
andre-kertesz.html.thesis_html: Kertész found a private lyricism in the everyday and the chance arrangements of the city, placing a personal gaze — neither reportage nor stylistic construction — at the center of the photograph. Built across repeated migrations, his way of looking prepared the path for later street photography and poetic documentary to take personal sensibility as their subject.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
André Kertész was born in Budapest in 1894 and began teaching himself photography as a young man. *1 He continued photographing during military service in World War One and, after the war, developed his photographic activity in Budapest. He moved to Paris in 1925, registering as a press photographer and working within an environment where modern art and photography intersected. *2

In Paris he photographed the artists of Montparnasse, published photographs in magazines, and produced works that would later be recognised as major achievements, including Satiric Dancer and Meudon. *3 He moved to New York in 1936, but his photographic vision was not immediately understood within the commercial magazine system, and his recognition as an artist took time to establish. *4 From the 1960s onward re-evaluation progressed, and his 1964 solo exhibition at MoMA was one of the important turning points. *5 After his death in New York in 1985, his photographs are held by the Getty, ICP, the NGA, the Metropolitan Museum and other major institutions. *6

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The edges of the everyday and chance arrangement

Kertész's photographs are constituted by finding chance arrangements at the edges of the everyday rather than reporting major events. *7 Streets, windows, shadows, stairs and domestic objects carry quiet tension depending on the angle and the time of seeing. His method involves a responsiveness not unlike later street photography, but rather than aggressive snapping he was searching for moments where private feeling coincides with the composition of the outer world. ICP exhibition materials record this approach as developed within the magazine and gallery culture of his Paris years. *8

In Satiric Dancer (1926), backlighting and floor reflections converge to transform the body into an abstract shape — a chance coincidence of light and form rather than a human snap. In Meudon (1928), a figure crossing a bridge, a distant train, and a tower-like shape in the sky coexist in the same frame at different distances and times. *9

The Paris context and migration

In Paris, Kertész worked within the networks of magazines, galleries and expatriate artists at a time when photography moved between journalism and art. *10 The Getty's Kertész: Of Paris and New York exhibition materials lay out chronologically how he organised everyday vision poetically while maintaining awareness of modern art. *11 After his move to New York, his recognition was delayed by the commercial magazine environment, and the gap between migration and reception has been incorporated into later photographic history research as an important context for his work. *12

Recognition as a precursor of street photography

Kertész is often discussed as a precursor of the "decisive moment," but this simplification warrants caution. *13 His photographs are certainly important for their sense of time before Cartier-Bresson, but the core of his work is not the dominating capture of the world — it is the lodging of private feeling in chance arrangement. MoMA's 1964 press release is a significant document that repositioned Kertész as an artist who had exerted a strong influence on younger photographers. *14 ICP exhibition records also evaluate him across multiple contexts — street photography, poetic documentary and the exilic gaze — from the Paris years to his late New York work. *15

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: The Getty, MoMA, ICP, the NGA, the AIC and Centre Pompidou all hold Kertész's work and position him as a photographer who made a major contribution to poetic documentary in modern photography. *16 Jeu de Paume, SFMOMA and the MFA Boston also hold related works. *17 Within photographic history, placing him at the intersection of modern urban poetry, magazine culture, migrant vision and private documentary allows the distinctive character of his work to become visible. His life between multiple countries, languages and cultures as a Hungarian-born migrant is inseparable from the distinctiveness of his photographic vision. *18 Kertész's re-evaluation accelerated after his 1964 MoMA exhibition, with a growing tendency to position him as a precursor of street photography and poetic documentary. For understanding the lineage of the "poetic snapshot" before Cartier-Bresson, Kertész remains an indispensable reference in photographic history education.

aneta-grzeszykowska.html.lead_html: Aneta Grzeszykowska erased only herself from family photographs in Album, restaged scenes from Cindy Sherman in Untitled Film Stills, and painted her skin black in Negative Book so that her body would appear white on the negative. In Selfie, pigskin stands in for the face and body; in Mama, a silicone doll assumes her likeness. Across these works, she tests what makes the “I” in a photograph legible as a person: the physical body, memory, authorship, or the photographic process itself.
aneta-grzeszykowska.html.thesis_html: From Album to Mama, Grzeszykowska turns the conditions that make a self-portrait possible into the subject of the work itself. In Album she removes herself from family photographs; in Untitled Film Stills she enters Sherman’s images; in Negative Book she adapts her body to the logic of the negative; in Selfie and Mama, skin and a silicone doll carry the signs of her identity. Working after Sherman’s model of staged self-imaging, each series asks whether memory, technique, resemblance, or family behavior is what makes an image read as “her.”

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Post-1989 Warsaw — The Raster Generation and the Photograph as a Manipulable Image

Grzeszykowska studied graphic design at the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw, graduating in 1999. Her early work moved among photography, video, and design and included collaborations with Jan Smaga, her husband and longtime collaborator, beginning with projects that translated interiors and architecture into images. Culture.pl places her among the “Raster generation,” which emerged as new galleries and critical networks developed after the collapse of the socialist system*12. In a 2025 interview, Grzeszykowska recalled that around the time she graduated, Raster began looking for young artists in Warsaw, making a full-time artistic career seem newly possible*16. After graduation, photography and video became her principal media, with digital editing, staged photography, film, and bodily replicas selected according to the needs of each work. Muzeum Sztuki notes that photography offered her unusually detailed control over both the production process and the final result*1. CAM St. Louis likewise centered its exhibition on the repeated appearance, disappearance, and substitution of the body across her photography and video*2.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Album — Removing Herself from the Life Story Constructed by the Family Album

Album (2004) digitally removes Grzeszykowska from more than 200 photographs accumulated by the artist and her family over roughly thirty years. The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw identifies it as an album assembled from family snapshots originally made as records of everyday life*3. Culture.pl describes the result as an autobiography in photographs without its protagonist: the artist disappears from a private archive extending from her birth to the time the work was made*13. The intervention extends beyond any single frame to the album as a sequence of birthdays, trips, meals, and group photographs that ordinarily tells a viewer, “this person lived within this family.” After the erasure, the gazes of others, the spacing between bodies, and the empty places remain, allowing her absence to be inferred from the relationships around it. Grzeszykowska later described Album as the first stage in a sequence of “losing myself” that continued through Untitled Film Stills, Negative Book, and Selfie*15. The work makes visible both the family album’s role in organizing evidence of a life and the author’s power to alter that organization.

Untitled Film Stills — Reworking Sherman’s 69 Images as 70 Color Photographs

Grzeszykowska’s 2006 Untitled Film Stills takes Cindy Sherman’s 69-part Untitled Film Stills as its point of reference and reworks it as seventy color photographs featuring Grzeszykowska herself. Art Collection Telekom records Sherman’s original as 69 images and Grzeszykowska’s version as 70*20. Raster notes that she matched compositions and makeup to the source images while sourcing backgrounds and clothing in contemporary Warsaw, completing the full series over the course of a year*10. In Sherman’s original, her body repeatedly becomes a woman who might have appeared in a film; MoMA discusses the works as images in which Sherman appears without classifying them as self-portraits*23. Grzeszykowska made the entire series, already established within art history, the object of reenactment. Discussing #54, Arsenal Gallery observes that as Sherman’s body disappears from the frame and Grzeszykowska takes its place, Sherman becomes more insistent in the viewer’s memory*19. Grzeszykowska later described a double erasure: she had “removed Sherman and put myself in,” yet viewers still recognized Sherman, which made Grzeszykowska herself harder to see*16. The series builds a self-portrait in which sitter, author, and remembered source image no longer align.

Negative Book — Making the Body Obey the Negative

Negative Book (2012–13) makes the analog photographic negative itself a condition of production. Grzeszykowska painted her skin and hair black and adjusted the tones of clothing and interiors so that her body would appear light on the negative. The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw holds works including #63 and #78 and publishes their material information as black-and-white photographs*4. The museum’s video Negative Process records the black-painted body being photographed, making the reversal between negative and print central to the production process*6. Art Collection Telekom similarly describes a series that imports photography’s rules of tonal reversal into scenes resembling ordinary family pictures, with the body itself altered to meet those rules*9. Raster’s photobook edits the procedure into a sequence of everyday situations, poses, and interiors*11. The distinction between manipulation performed after exposure in software and manipulation performed on the body before exposure becomes unstable; the stage at which the image is made becomes the subject of the work.

Selfie and Mama — Turning the Face into Skin, and the Mother into a Doll

In Selfie (2014), Grzeszykowska constructed fragments of her face and body from pigskin and photographed them. In the work held by the Centre Pompidou, precisely fabricated eyes, mouth, and seams in the skin meet the immediacy associated with the selfie in an unsettling way*7. For Mama (2018), she made a silicone doll in her own likeness and photographed her daughter, Franciszka, carrying, embracing, playing with, and burying this “mother.” The Museum of Modern Art in Warsaw holds fourteen works from the 2018 series*5. ArtReview recorded the series as twenty-five images when it was first shown and read the daughter’s play with the silicone figure as a reversal of mother-and-child roles*21. The review also connected that reversal around motherhood to Poland’s abortion law and the political conditions surrounding women’s bodies at the time*21. In a 2025 interview, Grzeszykowska emphasized that she, the actual mother, photographs from outside the frame, allowing viewers to begin accepting the doll as the “mother”*16. The silicone figure is recognized as the mother inside the picture while the artist remains on the camera side. Facial resemblance, the daughter’s actions, and the title attach the maternal role to the doll.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Digital Editing, Negatives, Skin, Dolls — A Different Process for Each Series

Grzeszykowska changes the process of manipulation from one series to the next. Album uses Photoshop; Negative Book uses film and the negative; Selfie combines pigskin sculpture with digital printing; Mama uses a silicone doll and staged photography. Art Collection Telekom describes a body of work spanning photography, film, books, and staged production while repeatedly returning to the body as material*8. A Frieze review likewise reads the work from Untitled Film Stills through Selfie as a movement between historical photographic forms and the physical substance of the body*17. What links the series is the repeated assignment of “her” identity to a different form, followed by a test of how securely that form can sustain the claim. In the photobook Negative Book, photographs that can be encountered individually on a wall enter the sequence of pages, allowing the inverted body to be read as moving through the time of everyday life*11.

Why Use Her Own Body? — The Most Controllable Model Becomes the Least Stable Subject

Grzeszykowska gives a practical reason for using herself as a model: it allows her to control the production in detail*16. With that statement in mind, self-portraiture becomes an experimental setup in which author, subject, and director can be concentrated in one person. In an interview with Contemporary Lynx, she describes Album, Untitled Film Stills, Negative Book, and Selfie as successive stages of “losing myself”*15. Erasure, entry into another artist’s image, inversion by the negative, and the fragmentation of skin form a sequence in which identity gradually separates from the body that can be most tightly controlled. Lyles & King likewise identifies the construction and erasure of the self, the gendered body, and combinations of artificial and organic matter as long-running concerns in her work*18.

sections.title: Citation, the Body, and the Reception of Self-Image
sections.body_html:
After Sherman — From the Body Performing a Role to the Body’s Absence

In the 1970s, Cindy Sherman used her own body in Untitled Film Stills to inhabit cinematic female types, exposing how images of women are produced through familiar conventions of film and photography. MoMA describes the series as an examination of images of women through roles such as the “career girl,” the vamp, and the lonely housewife*23. In 2006, Grzeszykowska made seventy color photographs referring to Sherman’s series, then shifted the carrier of the self-image toward the family album, the negative, pigskin, and a silicone doll. CAM St. Louis places the recurring appearance, disappearance, and substitution of the body at the center of her work in both photography and video*2. In Mama, the artist stands behind the camera while a silicone “mother” spends time with her daughter inside the frame. Grzeszykowska explains that the fact that she, the actual mother, remains outside the picture is what allows the viewer to begin accepting the doll as the mother*16. Sherman’s staged images locate the body as the site of role-playing. In Grzeszykowska’s later works, resemblance, titles, and family behavior can sustain a self-image even when the artist’s body is outside the picture. The question of self-portraiture moves toward the clues that make a person recognizable as themselves.

From Album to Mama — What Carries the Self Changes from Series to Series

In Album, the sequence of family photographs tells a life; in Untitled Film Stills, a familiar artwork helps identify the author; in Negative Book, the tonal logic of the negative determines how the body appears. Fragments of facial skin become a cue in Selfie, while a silicone doll performs that function in Mama. AWARE discusses this body of work through self-representation, the body, and critical approaches to images of women*14. Raster’s 2022 exhibition WAVE returned to Album: Grzeszykowska continued removing herself from family photographs extending beyond the birth of her daughter, while Skinformer rendered the bodily image as stitched skin*22. The methods change sharply from early digital erasure to recent artificial skin and dolls, yet each series isolates one basis on which a viewer recognizes someone in a photograph. Self-portraiture becomes a way to test, one by one, whether memory, authorship, the negative, skin, or family relations produce the recognition of a person as “herself.”

ann-sofi-siden.html.lead_html: Ann-Sofi Sidén is a Swedish artist working across photography, moving image, performance, and installation, with recurring subjects including surveillance, psychiatry, borders, care, and movement. Early works around QM and projects such as Who Told the Chambermaid?, Warte Mal!, 3 MPH, and In Passing combine recorded footage, performance, interviews, and the spatial structure of exhibition.
ann-sofi-siden.html.thesis_html: A conventional television documentary usually places multiple testimonies into a single edited sequence. In Warte Mal!, Sidén separates interviews filmed with the head held in a fixed frame, road-movie footage shot from a car, her own diary, and late-night observational footage onto different screens. No single channel is assigned the role of explaining the whole, and the artist’s own record appears as one channel among the others. The border town of Dubí is left as a set of differently positioned testimonies and recording methods instead of being resolved into one report.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Painting to QM, Moving Image, and Installation

Sidén was born in Stockholm in 1962 and studied in Berlin and Stockholm. She began in painting and, from the late 1980s, performed a mud-covered fictional figure she called Queen of Mud (QM), extending the character into public space, moving image, sculpture, and text*1.

QM does not settle into a fixed character symbolizing the artist’s inner life; her role changes from one situation to another. She enters department stores, the art market, psychiatry, and museums, exposing the classifications through which some bodies are defined as civilized and others as deviant. Magasin3 describes Sidén’s work as a cross-media practice concerned with vulnerability, control, and forms of violence that can remain inconspicuous*2.

By 1990, QM had already moved into performance and video around the Stockholm Art Fair. A 2002 Kunstforum essay looks back on these early works as crossings of everyday boundaries, civilization and wilderness, and institutional classification. Photography and moving image allowed Sidén to record QM’s incursions into different public spaces and institutions while drawing the act of documentation itself into the performance. *21

In 2001 Jan Estep published “Feral Children and the Queen of Mud” in New Art Examiner, showing that the QM works were already being discussed through cultural divisions between normality and abnormality and through questions of self-performance. The interest in questioning both the performing body and the observing camera is present from the beginning, so the later research-based works are not simply a turn toward documentary. *23

Using Surveillance Cameras and Television Documentary as Recording Methods

During the 1990s Sidén brought recording formats themselves—surveillance cameras, fixed cameras, and interviews—into her work. Moderna Museet presents her as an artist who investigates social exclusion, exoticism, and mechanisms of Western civilization through moving image and installation*3. The point of view from which a record is produced remains part of the exhibition, instead of disappearing behind an apparently transparent camera.

Camera position, the number of monitors, and the viewer’s movement through the installation all contribute to the work’s meaning. An e-flux exhibition on surveillance art places Sidén among artists addressing the complications of surveillance and photography*4. The position from which surveillance is watched is built into the exhibition structure as well.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Who Told the Chambermaid?—Exhibiting the Hotel as a Surveillance System

Who Told the Chambermaid? (1998) shows the hotel reception desk, corridors, storage rooms, and guest rooms across multiple surveillance monitors, combined with utilitarian shelving holding towels and supplies. Guests’ private actions and employees’ work spaces enter the same system, making the hotel service visible as an arrangement dependent on observation and control*5.

The fixed cameras in Who Told the Chambermaid? occupy positions managed by the hotel: reception, corridors, storage areas, and guest rooms. The Nordic Watercolour Museum likewise identifies surveillance cameras as an important motif in Sidén’s work*6. Guests, cleaners, and reception staff inhabit the same hotel but differ in what they are permitted to see and in their access to the monitors. The work centers on who places a camera where and who is made visible through it.

Warte Mal!—Keeping Borderland Testimonies from Closing into One Story

Warte Mal! (1999) turns interviews with sex workers, intermediaries, police, and customers in the Czech-German border town of Dubí into a multi-screen video installation. Moderna Museet’s 2003 material records an installation using sixteen VHS tapes. Sidén places footage from her stay, interviews, views filmed from a moving car, diary material, and late-night gatherings into separate moving-image formats*7.

In conversation with Robert Fleck, Sidén explains how a project that began with Amsterdam’s red-light district led her toward the process by which she expanded her research toward less visible forms of cross-border commerce*8. By keeping her own judgments and uncertainty visible, she resists fixing the people she interviews into a single image of victimhood or an exoticized scene.

In the same conversation, Sidén notes that a single-screen television documentary has a broadcast duration and an editing order that viewers follow. In Warte Mal!, she separates interviews filmed with the head held in a fixed frame, a road movie filmed from a car, diary material and still images, and late-night cinéma vérité into distinct formats*8. The refusal to merge these records into one sequence becomes part of the installation itself.

A 2004 Kunstforum review likewise connects Warte Mal! to the social conditions of movement, sex work, and the border between Eastern and Western Europe. By refusing to edit the material into a single narrative of accusation, the installation keeps visible the different positions of customers who can cross the border, women working there, police, and the interviewer. *22

Mixing Documentary and Fiction

Sidén’s early work QM, I Think I Call Her QM links material concerning the real psychiatrist Alice E. Fabian with the fictional QM in a film narrative. South London Gallery presented the film alongside an installation using Fabian’s diaries, recordings, documents, and measurements of her rooms*9.

An Artforum review examines how psychiatry, paranoid surveillance, and systems for classifying others are destabilized by the encounter with QM*10. The archival material is removed from the role of simply authorizing the fiction; the psychiatric expert can also become a subject under observation.

3 MPH—A Different Image of America at the Speed of a Horse

3 MPH (Horse to Rocket) (2003) is a multi-screen work filmed during a twenty-five-day horseback journey from San Antonio to NASA’s Space Center Houston. Its title refers to the horse’s average speed of three miles per hour*11.

Bilbao Fine Arts Museum describes the journey as connecting the western icon of the horse with the rocket of the space program*12. Towns, roadsides, and conversations that high-speed travel would pass quickly occupy long stretches of time at the horse’s pace. The slow pace of travel makes perceptible again distances and encounters that technological progress has compressed.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
In Passing—Baby Hatches and Systems of Care

In Passing (2007) concerns baby hatches that allow infants to be left anonymously. Across multiple screens, the work shows a young woman leaving a child and medical personnel receiving it. Bonniers Konsthall describes Sidén as an artist who enters social “cracks” and ethically difficult situations that resist easy narration*13.

The work juxtaposes the mother, infant, and medical staff moving through separate spaces and times. Care includes both protection and administration, and the moving image is never consolidated into the point of view of a single participant*14.

Barbara Thumm’s text describes In Passing as a narrative split across several viewpoints. The hospital side is filmed from an elevated angle close to surveillance footage, while the woman leaving the child is followed from a height closer to street level. Bodies connected to the same event are placed within different visual systems instead of being condensed into one image of the institution as simply good or bad. *24

My Country and the Repeated View from Horseback

For My Country (Somewhere in Sweden) (2010), Sidén traveled roughly 720 kilometers on horseback from Stockholm to Wanås, filming across Sweden. Moderna Museet describes the work as a continuation of 3 MPH and notes a reference to Paul Virilio’s thinking about speed and technology as forces of social change*15.

My Country (Somewhere in Sweden) records roads, settlements, stops, and conversations continuously from horseback at a steady pace. Where 3 MPH followed cities and the area around NASA from horseback in Texas, this work crosses Sweden, allowing changes in roads and inhabited landscapes to be compared at the same slow speed*15.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Showing the Conditions of Recording and Display Alongside Testimony

Sidén’s work exceeds the conventional category of “photographer.” Still and moving images enter the work as techniques of evidence, surveillance, identification, and field research. Museums including MoMA collect and present Sidén as an artist working across film, photography, sculpture, and installation*17.

Sidén’s photographs and moving images are never presented as self-sufficient “evidence.” Warte Mal! separates interviews, road footage, and diary material into different channels, while the QM works combine a psychiatrist’s records, audio recordings, measurements of rooms, and a fictional film. A Filmform essay looks back on Warte Mal! as a multi-screen work that grew from long-term research based in a hotel and emphasizes duration as part of Sidén’s method*18. Her distinctiveness lies in keeping these forms of material from being absorbed into the same explanation.

Keeping the Interviewer’s Position Inside the Work

Sidén’s subjects include mental illness, sex work, and infant abandonment—situations in which an image-maker can easily assume the authority to explain another person’s condition. A medical-journal review of the work using the real psychiatrist’s archive reads the boundary between exhibition and diagnosis as part of the problem*19. Placing Sidén’s own diary on a different screen from interviewees in Warte Mal!, and keeping different positions separate in In Passing, are concrete formal means of preventing the interviewer’s interpretation from becoming the final explanation.

Her reception at Wanås Konst and major museums reflects a body of work that extends beyond video installation into sculpture, public space, and movement*20. Larsen Warner describes Same Unknown in relation to Warte Mal!, Who Told the Chambermaid?, and In Passing as a multi-screen work stripped of dialogue and an explicit spatial setting*16. What each work separates and what it lets appear simultaneously changes from project to project.

Multi-Screen Form Does Not Reduce Testimony to One Editing Order

In Warte Mal!, witnesses, interpreters, roads, the hotel, and the artist’s diary occupy different screens and temporalities. In In Passing, the person relinquishing a child and the people receiving it are not folded into one viewpoint. Because no viewer can follow every screen at once, the material resists a single timeline or explanation and retains the position from which each image was recorded.

In Warte Mal!, interviews appear as fixed images of the speakers’ heads, movement becomes a road movie shot from a car, the artist’s judgments enter through the diary, and the night scene is kept in a separate observational register. There is no voice-over by the artist laid across all the channels; her position becomes one record among the others. Sidén uses multi-screen form to keep interviews, travel footage, diary entries, and late-night observation from being resolved into one final report.

annan.html.lead_html: Annan photographed the dense closes and tenements of Glasgow's old town before their clearance under the city's Improvement Act. Commissioned as administrative records, his photographs have since been reread as precursors to the documentary tradition and as testimony to the social conditions of industrial-era urban poverty.
annan.html.thesis_html: Within the institutional framework of a pre-demolition survey commissioned by the city's improvement authority, Annan organised the dense closes of Glasgow's old town into a systematic archive. His quiet, structural gaze — distinct from emotional indictment — holds a double character: grasping urban space as an object of improvement while simultaneously preserving its material weight, placing the work in the paradoxical position of an administrative record reread as testimony to urban poverty. This body of work opens, as a prehistory of documentary photography, the possibility that the record itself may exceed the intentions of the institution that commissioned it.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Thomas Annan was born in Cromartie, Scotland, in 1829 and established himself as a photographer in Glasgow. His work ranged across architecture, portraiture, and urban views, and he also undertook reproduction and publication work including a photographic record of the stained glass in Glasgow Cathedral.*1 In 1868 he was commissioned by the Glasgow Improvement Trust to photograph the areas of the old city subject to redevelopment, producing the series that would become The Old Closes and Streets of Glasgow.*2 The Getty exhibition text describes Annan as "a photographer who documented the social landscape and built environment of an industrial city for over twenty-five years," indicating that his practice was not limited to the old-city record.*3 He died in Glasgow in 1887.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The context of old-town documentation

To understand Annan's Old Closes it is essential to recognize that his client was the city's improvement administration and that the photographs were produced as administrative material for urban redevelopment. The Glasgow Improvement Act of 1866 drove a systematic program to demolish the closes — the dense alleyways of the old city — where cholera and typhus had repeatedly broken out, and Annan's photographs were positioned as a record of those streets immediately before demolition.*4 The scholarly book Thomas Annan of Glasgow: Pioneer of the Documentary Photograph, available through OAPEN, discusses Annan not as a minor local photographer but as one who documented urban change over an extended period, placing Old Closes at the origin of the urban documentary tradition.*5 The National Library of Scotland's exhibition situates the cultural position of Annan's photographs and photobook within the context of "Scotland and the Photobook," indicating the importance of distribution through the printed medium.*6

Duality of condemnation and preservation

What distinguishes Annan's photographs is a quiet, structural gaze quite distinct from the emotional accusation of social reform photography. The RISD Museum's entry for Close No. 37 High Street makes explicit that the wet-plate technique was required to photograph the dark alleyways and that the work was tied to the improvement plan for demolishing them.*7 Annan's photographs do register the material reality of urban poverty, but their compositional stillness and handling of spatial density set them apart from straightforward journalism or sensationalism.*8 Rather, his photographs carry a dual character: they comprehend the city as an object of improvement while visually preserving the weight of that space. The National Galleries of Scotland's feature on Annan describes The Old Closes and Streets of Glasgow as "the most celebrated work with continuing significance in Glasgow," indicating that this duality is at the heart of how the work is valued.*9

Cross-domain practice

Annan was not only a photographer of slums; he was also strongly connected to questions of architecture, publication, and graphic reproduction. The range of material documented by Glasgow Libraries (Annan Collection Loose Prints) shows that the archive he left encompasses not only photographs but a wide range of material connected to architectural, print, and publishing practice.*11 A Journal of Urban History article, "A Walk in Thomas Annan's Glasgow," analyzes his photographs from an urban history perspective, showing that they continue to be consulted for academic purposes such as tracing changes in street names, buildings, and spaces.*12 Individual close photographs such as Close #29 Gallowgate held by the High Museum of Art are in major North American museum collections, attesting to international reception within photographic history.*13

Critical reception

Later critical attention to Annan has concentrated on rereading The Old Closes and Streets of Glasgow as an early document of urban transformation, poverty, and publication photography. The Getty exhibition "Thomas Annan: Photographer of Glasgow" was an important opportunity for comprehensive reassessment of this work.*14 As collection records at the Met, MoMA, LACMA, and the Rijksmuseum demonstrate, the series has circulated internationally in the contexts of photobooks, graphic reproduction, and museum collections.*15 The Rijksmuseum's The Slums of Glasgow shows in its very title how the later reception has shifted, with photographs commissioned as administrative records being received as testimony to urban poverty.*16 The Art Institute of Chicago also holds The Old Closes & Streets of Glasgow, reflecting continued attention in North America.*17 The Rijksmuseum Bulletin has published discussion of Old Closes, showing that the photobook continues to be examined within both art history and photographic history.*18 The publication Thomas Annan: Photographer of Glasgow issued by the Getty Museum Store in connection with the exhibition serves as a focal point for scholarly reassessment.*19 The National Galleries of Scotland's most recent Biennial Review records a new acquisition of Annan's work, showing that his collection is continuing to grow in Scotland.*20 The Saint Louis Art Museum's Close, No. 75 High Street (Glasgow) illustrates the situation in which individual close photographs are distributed across institutions worldwide.*21 In photographic history, Annan can be understood not only as a precursor to Atget but, from a different angle than Jacob Riis or Eadweard Muybridge, as a pioneer who converted urban space into a photographic archive.*22

annie-leibovitz.html.lead_html: Annie Leibovitz is an American portrait photographer who began at Rolling Stone and later expanded her practice through Vanity Fair and Vogue, making people appear as charged scenes on magazine covers and in editorial features. Through John Lennon and Yoko Ono, the pregnant Demi Moore, Women, Wonderland, and Pilgrimage, this page traces how celebrity bodies, intimacy, fashion, and private memory become images shared as part of an era.

sections.title: Career and Background
sections.body_html:
Annie Leibovitz is difficult to contain within a single label such as "studio photographer" or "photojournalist." The National Portrait Gallery summarizes her career as beginning with her rise at Rolling Stone, where she became chief photographer in 1973 and photographed 142 covers before leaving a decade later; she then began working for Vanity Fair in 1983 and for Vogue in 1998*1. The International Center of Photography also notes that she published photo essays at Rolling Stone, including Richard Nixon's resignation and the Rolling Stones' 1975 tour, and that at Vanity Fair and Vogue she photographed actors, writers, musicians, athletes, politicians, business figures, and fashion*2. This movement across magazines was not simply a career of photographing famous people in different venues. It meant working across the institutions through which music, politics, cinema, fashion, advertising, photobooks, and museums make public images of people.

Her route into photography did not begin with a fully formed identity as a master portraitist. According to Hauser & Wirth, Leibovitz bought her first camera in the summer of 1968 while studying at the San Francisco Art Institute, and her early works include Bay Area landscapes and photographs made on the highway between San Francisco and Los Angeles*3. PBS's American Masters describes how she originally entered the school intending to study painting, discovered her interest in photography after traveling to Japan with her mother in the summer after her second year, and returned to San Francisco to take night classes in photography*28. Seen from this starting point, photography was not first a finished studio language for her. It was a way of receiving landscapes seen in motion and changes in vision experienced while traveling. The photographs she brought to Rolling Stone were tied to music, politics, movement, and the speed of reporting, and they formed the basis for the stance that remained in her later staged portraits: entering a scene while still keeping the distance of a photographer.

Rolling Stone mattered to Leibovitz in the early years because it was a place where photographs did not stand apart from musical and political events, but reached readers together with articles, covers, and the timing of publication. In an excerpt from Annie Leibovitz at Work published by Vanity Fair, she recalls that on the 1975 tour she tried to blend into the scene "like a chameleon" and become part of the subjects' world, while the camera also separated her from that world and reminded her that she was a photographer*23. What she sought, then, was not to arrange celebrities from outside the event, but to enter the time of a tour or assignment, stay close, and still retain a photographer's point of view. In a later interview, she said that when she began working at Rolling Stone she thought she was doing journalism, but gradually realized that she had a "point of view," and that following that point of view made the work stronger*24. The magazine gave that point of view a public form: not as a standalone print, but as an image connected to current events, music, and readers' memories.

Her later large-scale productions were not completely separate from these early experiences. Phaidon's description of Annie Leibovitz At Work presents the book as Leibovitz's own account of how photographs are made, covering photojournalism, studio work, dancers and athletes, writers, and the transition from film to digital*29. Her method, in other words, was not simply to make stars look spectacular. It grew from an accumulation of experiences in reporting, portraiture, bodily movement, collaboration, and technological change. Magazine work became one opportunity to compress those multiple experiences into a photograph that could reach a wide readership.

sections.title: Expression and Method
sections.body_html:
How magazine covers and pages change a portrait

In Leibovitz's photographs, the subject matters, but so does the place where the photograph appears and the audience to whom it is presented. Demi Moore's pregnant body, for example, did not appear as a private record; it became a star image seen by a national readership on the cover of Vanity Fair. Leibovitz herself recalled discussing with editor Tina Brown how to place a pregnant star on the cover*23. The Vogue shoot Alice in Wonderland was also a large-scale fashion story conceived by Grace Coddington, with Leibovitz making that world work photographically*27. It is therefore more accurate to describe her not as the person who "reassembled" the magazine page, but as a photographer who, in collaboration with editors and art directors, used bodies, places, clothing, and gaze to strongly direct how a person would be seen.

Once a portrait is placed on a magazine cover, it is received not only as a face or figure, but together with headlines, publication date, and the story that readers already know. The photograph of John Lennon and Yoko Ono was an intimate portrait of a couple, but it was also remembered as the cover of a Rolling Stone memorial issue. The photograph of Demi Moore was the body of a pregnant actor, but it also became a Vanity Fair cover that intensified Moore's star image after Ghost*6. In Leibovitz's portraits, the subject's appearance, the magazine's editorial context, and readers' memories overlap, turning a private person into a face of the moment. "Public image" here does not mean an abstract concept. It means the visual memory that readers share when they see a cover and recognize "this person at this time."

John Lennon and Yoko Ono: the last portrait becomes magazine history

Photographed on December 8, 1980, Yoko Ono; John Lennon is one of the key works through which many viewers enter Leibovitz's practice. The National Portrait Gallery explains that the image was made on assignment for Rolling Stone in the couple's Manhattan apartment, showing a naked John Lennon curled against the clothed Yoko Ono in a fetal posture, and that Lennon was murdered only hours later*5. The museum also notes that the photograph circulated worldwide as the cover of Rolling Stone and became an image of mourning for Lennon*5. The importance of the photograph lies not only in the fact that it was made just before a tragedy. It showed a male star not through strength or control, but through dependence, vulnerability, and intimacy. After his death, the cover folded that image into music history, magazine history, and the memory of mourning.

The American Society of Magazine Editors ranked the January 22, 1981 Rolling Stone cover first among magazine covers published since 1965*6. That status was not produced by the image's formal qualities alone. It came from the union of the time of the shoot, the subject's death, Rolling Stone's community of readers, and the cover's editorial role as a memorial issue. In Leibovitz's portraiture, what a person looks like matters, but so does where the photograph is read and which event it becomes attached to.

Demi Moore: the pregnant body and the celebrity cover

The 1991 Vanity Fair cover Demi's Big Moment, showing the pregnant Demi Moore nude, is another of Leibovitz's best-known works. Vanity Fair's official archive republishes the August 1991 article, confirms that Moore was pregnant with her second child at the time, and identifies the photograph as Leibovitz's*7. ASME placed the cover second in the same ranking and described it as a cover that further amplified Moore's star image after Ghost*6. The significance of the photograph lies in the way it placed a pregnant body not in a private sphere, but on a magazine cover as the public image of a Hollywood star.

Yet the image cannot be summarized simply as liberation. Vanity Fair itself describes its covers as often provocative and positions the Demi Moore photograph among its most recognizable covers*8. Showing a pregnant body instead of hiding it was important, but that body was also placed within the circuits of film stardom, magazine sales, and visual spectacle. The strength of Leibovitz's image lies in how celebration and commerce, bodily visibility and media staging, become inseparable on a single cover.

The photograph continues to be discussed because a pregnant body is made unstable within that cover. Michele Pridmore-Brown's essay treats Leibovitz's work through the lens of the consumption of motherhood*31. Imogen Tyler's essay likewise addresses celebrity, pregnancy, and subjectivity*32. Read through these studies, the Demi Moore photograph is more than a cover that "positively" displayed pregnancy. It marks a point at which a pregnant body could be seen simultaneously as a woman's body, a performer's marketable star image, and a magazine-generated public event.

Vogue and Wonderland: fashion as a stage for portraiture

For Leibovitz after Vogue, fashion was not merely a field for showing clothing. It became a tool for placing a subject into a role. Dresses, sets, locations, and props allow actors and models to appear not simply as people wearing clothes, but as figures in a film scene, characters from a fairy tale, or quotations from photographic history. In Phaidon's description of the photobook Wonderland, Leibovitz says that fashion has always been part of her work, but that photography comes first, and that photography is large enough to encompass journalism, portraiture, reportage, family photographs, and fashion*9. In a Vogue talk, she also described her work as mixing journalism, fashion, and portraiture, and said that she used "journalism and storytelling" in fashion assignments*25. Fashion, then, functions less as the display of products than as a stage that gives the subject a narrative role.

The distinctiveness of Wonderland is clearer when looking at individual shoots. Vogue presents the 1999 shoot with Sean Combs and Kate Moss as a crossing of rap culture and high fashion, the 2001 shoot with Ben Stiller as an homage to masters of fashion photography, and the 2003 shoot with Natalia Vodianova and Marc Jacobs as an Alice in Wonderland-like fantasy*11. Leibovitz herself has said that her first couture shoot was inspired by Helmut Newton, Richard Avedon, and Irving Penn, and that the concept for the 2003 Alice in Wonderland shoot came naturally because she knew the book well*25. This is why Hauser & Wirth describes her fashion photographs as drawing on visual references from literature, film, photography history, and art history*10. These references are not added as decoration. They create a doorway through which readers can immediately feel, "I have seen this story somewhere before." Leibovitz shows stars and models not merely as advertising faces, but as figures clothed in familiar narratives and memories from visual culture.

Women: a long project that refuses one fixed image of womanhood

Women is a major key for seeing Leibovitz's work beyond celebrity photography. Phaidon's description of the 2025 edition explains that the two-volume set includes more than 250 portraits of women made over more than thirty years, including dancers, actors, astronauts, artists, politicians, farmers, writers, CEOs, soldiers, and scientists*12. The point is not to present women as a single ideal type, but to place differences of profession, power, body, age, and media role side by side. Phaidon also notes that the book includes texts by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Susan Sontag, and Gloria Steinem, giving the project a structure in which portraits and writing overlap to ask how women are seen and spoken about in society*12.

The importance of Women lies in its refusal to reduce its subjects to a directory of "famous women." In book and exhibition form, the project makes differences in occupation, age, body, power, and visibility appear together. Stars appear alongside politicians, writers, scientists, and agricultural workers. This juxtaposition is best read not simply as an updated series of female representation, but as a long inquiry into how women become visible through photographs and texts, books and exhibitions, celebrity and social role.

Public commissions, private photographs, and portraits without people

For understanding Leibovitz after 2000, the exhibition and photobook A Photographer's Life, 1990–2005 is crucial. The National Portrait Gallery describes the exhibition as including more than 150 photographs, combining editorial assignments with private pictures of family and close friends, and presenting them together with Leibovitz's statement that she does not have two lives*13. The Brooklyn Museum also describes the exhibition as beginning there with more than 200 photographs, accompanied by a book of the same title and then traveling internationally*14. Here, public portraits of stars made for magazines and intimate photographs of Susan Sontag and family do not appear as separate genres, but as part of the same flow of time.

Scholarly interpretation has made this juxtaposition especially important. Catherine Zuromskis's essay "'All One Life'" analyzes A Photographer's Life, 1990–2005 through the complex relation between Leibovitz's influential celebrity photography and snapshot photography*30. From this perspective, Leibovitz's intimacy is not simply the result of getting physically close to a subject. A distance that resembles family photography or the snapshot passes through the institutions of magazines and photobooks, linking private-looking images to the public images of stars and writers. That tension makes her photographs difficult to reduce either to private record or to public portrait.

In Pilgrimage, Leibovitz moved even further away from faces, photographing Niagara Falls, Walden Pond, Yosemite, rooms and objects associated with historical figures, and other sites of memory. The Smithsonian American Art Museum describes the series as a new direction, different from the carefully staged portraits she made for magazines and advertising, and as a body of work made because she was moved by the subjects herself*15. The museum also explains that although no people appear in the images, they are in a sense portraits, including places and traces connected to Thomas Jefferson, Emily Dickinson, Georgia O'Keeffe, Pete Seeger, Elvis Presley, Julia Margaret Cameron, and Ansel Adams*15. If a place or object can carry the memory of a person, it too can become a portrait. Through this development, Leibovitz's work expands from images of faces toward an editing of cultural memory.

Archival sources further support this reading of Pilgrimage. NYU's finding aid for prints held by the New-York Historical Society describes the series as photographs made because Leibovitz was moved by the subjects, distinct from the staged portraits she made for magazines and advertising, and notes that it includes landscapes, interiors, and objects bearing traces of past lives*33. The Library of Congress likewise reports that for Pilgrimage Leibovitz photographed a draft of the Gettysburg Address and the glass-plate negative of Lincoln used for the five-dollar bill*34. Here portraiture shifts from the face to the objects and places that support personal and national memory.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
Leibovitz's photographs were first widely seen in the pages of Rolling Stone, Vanity Fair, and Vogue, and were later reconsidered through photobooks and exhibitions. ICP notes that her first two decades were gathered into the retrospective book and exhibition Annie Leibovitz: Photographs 1970–1990, organized by ICP and the National Portrait Gallery*2. But photographs that function powerfully in magazines do not necessarily operate the same way on gallery walls. In The New Yorker, Vince Aletti criticized some of Leibovitz's photographs as looking forceful on the page but often excessive and flat on the gallery wall; at the same time, he considered A Photographer's Life more interesting than earlier presentations because it mixed public assignments with private photographs, including those connected to Susan Sontag*16. This response shows how the meaning of her photographs shifts depending on where they are placed. In magazines they are attached to headlines and articles; in photobooks they are re-edited as a sequence of time; in museums they are viewed as individual works. That movement itself has shaped the reception of Leibovitz's work.

Recent criticism has also read her visual force from a different angle. Jörg Colberg's Photography's Neoliberal Realism discusses Leibovitz, Gregory Crewdson, and Andreas Gursky in relation to the way highly constructed photographs visualize beliefs and values shared in capitalist society*35. From this perspective, the more effectively Leibovitz turns fame, advertising, power, and desire into compelling scenes, the more urgent it becomes to ask what those images reinforce. Praise and critique arise together because her photographs have been made very close to the center of modern visual culture.

Leibovitz's position becomes clearer when compared with other magazine portraitists of the same broad tradition. Richard Avedon used a large-format camera, a white background, and exacting detail to produce a tense encounter between figure and viewer, and he understood the photograph not as a mere fact but as an "opinion"*17. Irving Penn, through his portraits for Vogue, photographed a wide terrain of twentieth-century culture while avoiding decorative backgrounds and placing subjects within restrained compositions*18. The National Portrait Gallery's chronology for Penn also shows that he worked on cover ideas as a staff member at Vogue and photographed the magazine's first color still-life cover in 1943*19.

Leibovitz connects to the magazine-portrait tradition of Avedon and Penn, but she did not move in exactly the same direction. Where Avedon stripped the background away and Penn gathered subjects into the order of the studio, Leibovitz added place, clothing, bodily posture, and references to literature, film, and art history, placing the subject inside a more narrative scene. In a Vogue talk, she said that she prefers location to the studio and, when asked whether place creates the story, answered that she would not work in the studio if she did not have to*25. In an interview with Crystal Bridges Museum, she also said that she is not good in the studio, prefers to begin with a subject's home or with a place that means something to them, and called location an "emotional tool"*26. Her staging, then, is not simply the addition of an elaborate background. It is a method for making a subject appear in relation to a place, a memory, and a story.

Leibovitz did not simply "elevate" commercial photography into art photography. Keeping close to her own statements, her work treats journalism, fashion, portraiture, and storytelling as interwoven, and uses series and locations as ways of seeing people*25. In John Lennon and Yoko Ono, an intimate bodily form became an image of mourning. In Demi Moore, a pregnant body became a celebrity cover. In Wonderland, actors and models are placed inside stories drawn from literature and photographic memory. Across these examples, Leibovitz does more than photograph people "as themselves." She uses place, clothing, body, story, and the conditions of magazine viewing to turn a person into an immediately legible scene. That clarity is the strength of her work. It is also where its risk lies: instead of critically dismantling fame and power, her images can make them even more attractive as modern myths.

annika-von-hausswolff.html.lead_html: Annika von Hausswolff is a Swedish artist who carefully stages bodies resembling crime-scene photographs, empty interiors, curtains, blinds, and furniture, extending these motifs across photography, sculpture, and installation. Through Back to Nature, Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire, and Alternative Secrecy, she examines how women’s bodies circulate as evidence or spectacle and how a sharply detailed image can intensify inference and prejudice.
annika-von-hausswolff.html.thesis_html: Von Hausswolff extracted the visual grammar of crime photography and used staged scenes to address gendered violence without photographing an actual crime or victim. Back to Nature places anonymous women face down in natural settings. In Hey Buster! What Do You Know About Desire, bodies, interiors, and furniture are rendered with the clarity of evidentiary photographs, while the name, date, and cause of the event remain absent. The images therefore readily connect to recurring figures of the female victim in crime reporting and film. In Esoteric Forensic and Alternative Secrecy, blinds, acrylic glass, and locked furniture enter the exhibition space, making display, concealment, and storage part of the work. A question about how crime images are made develops into a question about who can see what, and under which conditions, in the museum.
