sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
A 1990s Practice That Did Not Separate Architecture, Sculpture, Photography, and Publishing

Steinbrecher was born in Basel in 1963 and has been based in Berlin. A biography from the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin records his work across photographic installation, moving image, objects, sculpture, graphics, and artist books, as well as his participation in documenta X in 1997*3. HFBK Hamburg materials likewise document a career since the mid-1990s in which exhibitions and publications such as Prospekte, Farmpark-Box, COUCH, Baumann, and Gras developed in parallel*16.

His architectural training at ETH is an important background for understanding the later books and installations. Akademie Schloss Solitude records that Steinbrecher studied architecture at ETH Zürich, worked in the offices of Miroslav Šik and Hans Kollhoff, and served as an assistant at ETH from 1992 to 1994 while already making drawings, objects, photographs, and spatial installations*24. The parallel treatment of architecture, objects, and images begins in this period. Architectural experience with walls, circulation, and placement overlaps from the outset with the cutting out, sequencing, and repositioning of images. In the later books and archives, where an image is placed and what it is placed beside matters as much as what the image depicts.

Photography has a different role from sculpture or architecture in Steinbrecher’s work. It is easily reproduced, portable, available for cutting out, and capable of repeated insertion into new sequences. Les presses du réel describes his activity along two broad axes—architecture/sculpture and photography/publishing—and notes that the publications themselves function as autonomous works*5.

Couch Park: More Than 20,000 Images as a Working Foundation

Couch Park exposes a vast image archive that Steinbrecher assembled from newspapers, magazines, books, photographs, and reproductions. MoMA presented it as an open-studio-like environment in which more than 20,000 images—covering cities, bodies, nature, technology, sexuality, violence, and more—could be rearranged and related to one another*1. KW Institute for Contemporary Art likewise describes it as a “park of images” in which photographs, clippings, and reproductions are detached from their original settings and presented with equal intensity*2.

Why Collect and Arrange? Keeping Images Mobile Rather Than Preserved in Place

Steinbrecher’s image archive does not culminate in preservation. In a 2017 conversation, he says, “I like to categorize. It’s a game,” and explains that his rapid scanning of an older image collection was motivated, if anything, by a wish to “get rid of these images”*25. When the interviewer reframes this as preservation and archiving, the discussion turns to the same “attention to images” being directed toward everyday and purchased objects scattered around the studio*25. Collected images and objects remain working material that can be repeatedly classified, altered, and rearranged. The continual reconfiguration of more than 20,000 images in Couch Park reflects his refusal to fix the archive as a completed order.

Within this archive, the photographer’s name or the publication in which an image appeared does not determine its first reading. A photograph from a luxury magazine, an anonymous clipping, and one of Steinbrecher’s own images can acquire different meanings through adjacency. Treating photographs as images already circulating through society became a foundation for his later publications.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Making Photographs and Selecting Photographs Part of the Same Work

In Steinbrecher’s method, making a new photograph with a camera is not clearly ranked above finding, reproducing, and arranging an existing image. Material for Galerie Barbara Weiss’s Counter Images discusses his work as a practice of subtly estranging existing everyday objects and images through operations of imaging, reproduction, casting, imitation, copying, and doubling*4. Instead of rejecting originality as an abstract principle, he changes the conditions around an image through concrete operations.

Photography’s reproducibility allows the same image to move into books, walls, copies, and rephotographs. Each change of medium and adjacency alters its meaning. In Couch Park, collecting becomes exhibition; in HITS, the accumulation is transformed into page order. Reproducibility itself becomes a concrete condition for producing associations among images.

HITS: Turning Thirty Years of Collecting into a Sequence of Pages

HITS (2015) edits photographs, illustrated books, press and magazine images, archival material, and montages collected over roughly thirty years into a 169-page large-format book. Les presses du réel describes it as a book that presents the vast collection as an associative collage*6. University of Toronto Press Distribution likewise records the long-term collecting and editing behind a publication containing roughly 200 color illustrations*7.

With little explanation attached to individual images, the reader follows relations among forms, gestures, colors, and abrupt shifts of subject while turning the pages. Sequence, spread, repetition, and interval produce the relations among photographs. The registration of more than fifty related publications in edcat further indicates the centrality of publishing to Steinbrecher’s work*13.

Mondfotografie: Rephotographing the “Moon Photograph”

In Mondfotografie (2014), Steinbrecher collects existing photographs of the moon and places a finger in front of the lens while rephotographing them. According to Les presses du réel, this occlusion turns images of the full moon into dark crescent-like forms, producing a 46-page artist book about the act of reading a photograph*10. edcat also records the publication as a photobook issued by Edition Patrick Frey*11.

Steinbrecher manipulates photographs already circulating as images of “the moon.” An extremely simple intervention—a finger—changes the apparent lunar phase while leaving the photograph’s indexical character intact; only the interpretation is rewritten. A photobook exhibition at the Swiss National Library likewise presented the book as an example that reconsiders photography’s possibilities and explained the simulation of lunar phases with a finger*12. The subject is the set of conditions under which the same recorded image can be read as something else through a simple intervention and a change of context.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Superfundi: Building an Imaginary Territory from Hills, Trenches, and Graves

Superfundi (2007) sequences black-and-white photographs of hills, trenches, and graves in a magazine-like format. Les presses du réel explains that, while each image is a fragment of topography, their sequence creates a primitive, devastated “strange territory”*8. edcat records it as a 64-page artist book organized around Graves, Hills, Topography, and Trenches*9. The Centre de la photographie Genève published the book and co-published Stubborn Statue in the same year*14.

Through repetition of anonymous terrain, an imaginary geography comes to the fore more strongly than the identification of individual sites. As Le Journal des Arts records the exhibition of the same title at the Centre de la photographie Genève, the book and exhibition allow the same sequence to be experienced at different speeds*15.

Stubborn Statue: Reading Press Photographs Without Their “Information Value”

Stubborn Statue, made with Tomas Kadlcik in 2007, consists of photographs that the Keystone press agency did not distribute because they were considered to lack sufficient “information value” for newspapers. According to Art Metropole, the two artists selected these rejected candidates, removed captions from the images in the body of the book, and assembled them into a publication*28.

The book makes concrete the fact that the meaning of a press photograph does not reside in the image alone. Pictures that were useless to a news desk become, through a new selection and sequence, a strange chain detached from the task of explaining an event*28. The editing that discards a photograph and the editing that retrieves it for a book assign different values to the same material. The selection of existing images that continues in Couch Park and HITS is therefore tied not only to private collecting but to the institutional decisions through which mass media determine what counts as a useful photograph.

Making the Artist Book the Work Itself

The catalog of Edition Patrick Frey, publisher of Mondfotografie, lists both Gras and Mondfotografie as part of Steinbrecher’s sustained photographic publishing activity*17. Motto Distribution likewise treats Mondfotografie as an autonomous artist book in which existing images of the moon are rephotographed and transformed into new images*18. JRP Editions’ Minimalist Kitsch is a monograph bringing together concise interventions into sculpture, everyday objects, and images, showing that Steinbrecher’s method of changing meaning through minimal gestures extends beyond photobooks*19.

Artist as Publisher: Joachim Schmid, Céline Duval, and a Shared Contemporary Field

By the 2010s, collecting existing images and re-editing them as books was clearly recognized as a contemporary field spanning photography and publishing. At Friends With Books in 2015, Steinbrecher, Joachim Schmid, Céline Duval, and Elisabeth Tonnard were invited to the same panel on the “artist and author as publisher,” discussing strategies of image collection, sequencing, and publication*26. The following year, One Thousand Books similarly placed Schmid, who had worked with found photographs since the early 1980s, and Steinbrecher, who collects mass-media imagery and produces numerous printed works as autonomous pieces, within the same artist-book context*27. Both weaken the assumption that only the photographer who made an exposure can author a photographic work, but sculpture and everyday objects always remain active outside the book in Steinbrecher’s work. His distinctive approach to editing lies in the movement among page, object, and exhibition space, including works in which objects are placed on found photographs and rephotographed*22.

This extensive publishing activity is not a cataloging system for circulating finished works. The format of the book itself removes images from a fixed wall, allows them to be handled and seen in sequence, and makes them portable. Photography’s capacity for circulation is converted directly into artistic form.

Dissolving the Boundary Between Image and Object in the Exhibition

STAMPA’s artist materials summarize a long exhibition history moving among photographs, objects, installations, and publications*20. In Steinbrecher’s exhibitions, printed images do not simply line the walls; they sit beside sculpture and furniture-like structures, changing the viewer’s bodily position in relation to the image. Couch Park was both a place for browsing an archive and an installation, clearly showing his refusal to confine photography to a framed plane.

Books, Photographs, and Objects in the Same Exhibition Space

Steinbrecher’s photobooks do not function merely as records assembled after an exhibition. A 2013 Frieze review, noting that he had produced more than one hundred printed works including books, posters, invitations, and inserts, discusses exhibitions in which photography, moving image, sculpture, collage, and found objects enter into reciprocal relations with printed matter, almost as one another’s “appendages”*22. Placing found objects on found photographs and rephotographing them so that separate materials appear to occupy one physical space is part of the same refusal to fix the boundary among photograph, object, and page.

The Staatliche Museen zu Berlin exhibition UBER ALLES likewise placed artist books alongside film, photography, and sculpture and described a structure in which the exhibition’s graphic layout continued into a book*23. A book is both a reproductive medium and an object that is handled, sequenced, and combined with other things. For Steinbrecher, the meaning of a photograph is not contained within the print; it is continually revised by its placement on a page, in a case, on a wall, or beside another object.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Opening Photographic Authorship to Editing in the Age of Found Images

After the 1990s, photographs were increasingly read within a mass image environment that included newspapers, magazines, advertising, photocopies, and the internet as well as museum prints. Steinbrecher did not turn that environment into a topic to be explained; he incorporated collecting and rearrangement directly into the production process. In Couch Park, more than 20,000 images are organized by association rather than author name, while HITS turns thirty years of material into the rhythm of pages*1.

The photographer’s work here includes editing: selecting an existing image, deciding what will sit beside it, and choosing the medium through which it will be shown. edcat’s bibliography of Steinbrecher’s numerous artist books confirms that this has formed a structural basis of his work for decades*13.

Putting Reproduction and Rearrangement at the Center of Photography

Steinbrecher’s significance for photographic history lies in placing photography’s social circulation as a reproducible object at the center of production. In Mondfotografie, existing moon photographs become different lunar phases through rephotography; in Superfundi, photographs from separate sites become one imaginary territory through editing. Meaning does not end with the negative or the place photographed. It is revised through the copy, the finger, the page, the spread, and the exhibition site.

One reason photography remains useful to Steinbrecher is its ability to convert three-dimensional objects and places into thin, portable images that can be repeatedly redeployed as copies, rephotographs, prints, pages, and wall works. As Frieze records, his act of placing found objects on found photographs and rephotographing them so that separate materials appear to occupy the same space makes that portability especially clear*22. His architectural sense of space, the classification of archives, and the sequencing of artist-book pages all connect to a treatment of the image as an object whose position can be changed.

The more reproducible the image, the more exacting selection and sequencing become. Choosing which copy to use and in what order images will encounter one another becomes an artistic decision. Working across museums, photography centers, publishers, and bookstores, Steinbrecher extends photography from the individual print into an object of visual culture shaped by editing and circulation. In a history of photography after the 1990s told through archives and artist books, he can be situated as an artist who connects making photographs with reading images that already exist.

In Relation to Jeff Wall: The Constructed Single Image and the Edited Sequence

Comparing Steinbrecher’s 1990s work with contemporary photography clarifies where he places authorship. Frieze compares Farmpark (1997) at documenta X with Jeff Wall’s lightbox Milk (1984), since both inserted unexpected narratives into advertising space in Kassel, but notes a crucial difference: Wall meticulously constructed a single instant, whereas Steinbrecher used sixteen found images to build a chain of oscillations between similar and different, familiar and strange*21. Both present large photographs in public space, yet Wall concentrates authorial control within a single constructed scene while Steinbrecher disperses authorship across selection, sequence, and placement.

The contrast reflects a broader post-1990s expansion of authorship from taking photographs to selecting and editing existing ones. Frieze describes Steinbrecher’s work of the period as editing found photographs and his own images into sequences resembling “stories without plots,” then presenting them in vitrines and books*21, This provides a basis for reading Couch Park and the later books as a continuous editorial practice. Steinbrecher’s distinguishing feature is the treatment of photographing, finding, reproducing, and rearranging as artistic acts on the same level.

ernest-cole.html.lead_html: Born near Pretoria, South Africa, in 1940, Ernest Cole emerged from the Black journalism culture around Drum and, in House of Bondage (1967), linked mines, pass laws, commuter trains, schools, hospitals, and "For Whites Only" signs chapter by chapter. His photographs make apartheid readable not as a single symbolic event, but as everyday control embedded in labor, movement, education, housing, and public space. Recent republications, the recovery of unpublished chapters, and the publication of his American photographs have returned Cole to the intersection of South African photography, social documentary, and photobook history.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Ernest Cole was born Ernest Levi Tsoloane Kole on March 21, 1940, in Eersterust, near Pretoria, South Africa. After the introduction of the Bantu Education Act he left school, and because of financial difficulties he could not continue correspondence study; his first practical training came while assisting a Chinese studio photographer, and an old Yashica twin-lens reflex camera became his starting point*1. He later worked for the magazine Zonk, bought a Nikon rangefinder, and in 1958 sought work from Jürgen Schadeberg, the picture editor of Drum, who hired him as a design and production assistant*1. Around the same time Cole took a correspondence course with the New York Institute of Photography; with encouragement from the school's staff, his idea of documenting South African apartheid grew less as a single denunciatory image than as a photographic essay made from many connected scenes*1. The Fowler Museum explains that Cole was stimulated by the photo-essays of Henri Cartier-Bresson and, between 1958 and 1966, photographed miners, schools, whites-only parks and benches, young men arrested without passes, and commuter trains*2. In Anna Hutchinson's biography for South African History Online, Cole encountered Cartier-Bresson's People of Moscow, China in Transition, and The Europeans in 1959, and regarded their layout and form as a clue for communicating the everyday life of South Africa*20. Cartier-Bresson's The Europeans was not conceived as a country-by-country travel guide, but as a book that moved through postwar Europe and gathered differences among people, as well as a shared human presence, into a single volume*21. What mattered for Cole was not imitating a famous photographer's style, but learning how separate photographs made in different places could be connected through the flow of a book so that one society could be read. Drum addressed a primarily Black readership and, within the limits of the time, dealt with apartheid; through it Cole entered a world where Black journalists, photographers, musicians, and anti-apartheid figures crossed paths*2. After Drum he also worked as a photographer for Bantu World, and by the early 1960s he was freelancing for Drum, Rand Daily Mail, The World, Sunday Express, and other publications*1.

Behind this work was not the search for misery from the outside, but an urgent need to show the world the restrictions he encountered every day as a Black South African. The Fowler Museum states that Cole was deeply committed to making known what it meant to live as a Black person under apartheid*2. The chapter texts of House of Bondage also register the experience of being forced into daily contact with laws and bureaucracy, and the feeling that anger, even when outwardly restrained, was one of the motives for photographing*4. People classified at the time as "African" or "Black" faced restrictions on residence in cities, commuting, reporting, and night movement through passes and police checks; Cole changed his surname from Kole to Cole and was reclassified as "Coloured," which gave him greater freedom of movement and a better chance of obtaining a passport than he would have had under Black classification*7. This did not mean changing his origins; it was closer to using the racial classification system itself as a condition of access, enabling him to approach white areas, urban spaces, mines, and places under police surveillance. The Fowler Museum explains that, in places where discovery by the police was dangerous, Cole concealed his camera in a lunch bag to enter prisons and mines, and also used telephoto lenses to photograph from a distance*2. In 1966 Cole left South Africa with his photographs, and in 1967 he published House of Bondage in New York*5. The book was declared an "undesirable" publication in the South African Government Gazette on May 10, 1968, and its circulation in the country was banned; scholar Sean O'Toole treats the suppression not as an automatic reaction, but as a process involving international attention, censorship procedures, and the political climate of the time*7. Because mines, pass laws, education, housing, transport, whites-only facilities, and removal policies were connected in one volume and circulated to readers abroad, the book became a concentrated body of evidence that the South African state sought to contain.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Reading House of Bondage through Chapters and Text

The core of House of Bondage is not the compression of apartheid into one symbolic image, but the way the book moves through different sites of life and lets readers see the same power reappearing in altered forms. O'Toole describes the 1967 first edition as a book of 183 photographs arranged in fourteen chapters, including images of mines, crowded commuter trains, harsh labor, credit systems, family relations, impoverished schools, police harassment, and intimidating signs*7. KYOTOGRAPHIE 2026 also describes the book as a work conceived as "one continuous story," noting that Cole's own texts, written in exile, supplied background for the photographs and intensified their political meaning*18. Cole's text here does not mean only brief captions beside the images. It means the prose around the chapters, where he explains in his own words how living conditions and legal systems operate. The extended texts published by The Photographers' Gallery move from the separation of whites and Blacks, and a life in which being Black is treated almost as punishment, to restrictions that reach from park benches and drinking fountains to bureaucracy, imprisonment, and political exile*4. Because of that prose, readers do not see the photographs only as witnessed scenes. They are led through a chain of experiences: bodies inspected in mines, passes demanded by police, workers transported by train from distant townships, inferior schooling imposed on children, and people separated at hospitals, benches, and service counters. MoMA's gallery text similarly explains that the book showed world readers violence embedded in everyday life and addressed economic oppression, land dispossession, family separation, and the erosion of Black education*6.

Mines, Passes, Commuting, Signs

The chapter structure becomes clearer when the subjects are looked at one by one. "The Mines" deals with the medical examination, fingerprinting, contracts, low wages, illness, accidents, and replacement of men sent to the mines, so that workers appear less as individuals freely choosing labor than as interchangeable labor power supporting the gold economy*4. "Police & Passes" shows how Black men over sixteen could be required at any time to show a pass, and how missing or faulty papers could lead to fines or imprisonment; pass laws therefore worked not merely as identification but as a mechanism that unsettled the very right to be in the city*4. "Nightmare Rides" shows Black people forced to live far from white residential and commercial areas while being transported daily into the city as labor needed by the white economy; the commuter train becomes the point where segregation policy and labor policy meet*4. "For Whites Only" turns the signs on toilets, drinking fountains, telephones, station waiting rooms, post-office counters, parks, and benches into a repeated visual environment of separation rather than an abstract legal text*4. Through this order, readers do not simply encounter a series of terrible scenes; they follow a procedure that puts people to work in mines, transports them into cities, narrows their future through schooling, separates them in public space, and controls their movement through police and documents. Moderna Museet's pages for Police and Passes, Heirs of Poverty, and For Whites Only allow these subjects — police, poverty, and signs — to be seen as separate themes that nevertheless operate as outlets of the same system of rule*10.

The View from Inside and the Distance of the Book

The closeness of Cole's photographs comes not only from psychological proximity to his subjects, but from the conditions of his own life. He left school under the impact of the Bantu Education Act, his family was forcibly removed in 1960, and in order to photograph he had to deceive the Race Classification Board and alter the conditions of his movement*1. Magnum's archival essay places House of Bondage not as work by a reporter arriving from outside, but as testimony emerging from Cole's own lived world*9. Gunilla Knape's assessment also argues that, while much social documentary had photographed poverty and labor from an external viewpoint, Cole was exceptional because he represented his own South Africa, his own world, from within*19. That viewpoint appears not only in the subjects of the photographs, but in the structure of the book. Mines, police, transport, education, domestic labor, hospitals, resettlement camps, and whites-only signs appear as chapters, so that the reader's sequence of reading includes where Black bodies are inspected, where they are transported, where they are made to work, and where they are excluded. Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation likewise explains that Cole comprehensively documented miners, domestic workers in white households, transport, health, children, youth, police actions, and dispossession*12. In this sense Cole can be read as a photographer who retained the on-site force of photojournalism while moving social documentary into the structure of a photobook. MoMA classifies his work with terms such as Documentary photography, Photobook, Photography, and Photojournalism, and that grouping shows how his practice crosses reportage, book form, documentation, and institutional critique*3.

What Black Ingenuity Changes

Black Ingenuity is essential because it prevents Cole's work from being confined to a record of pain. According to The Photographers' Gallery's extended texts, Cole intended to include this chapter in House of Bondage, gathered contact sheets for it just as he did for other chapters, and selected photographs for possible inclusion, although it did not appear in the first edition*4. The Photography Legacy Project describes the chapter as looking at the possibility of Black cultural production under apartheid while also mourning the way that space was being suffocated*26. Goodman Gallery's exhibition material explains Black Ingenuity as an homage to the history of Dorkay House, and as a response to the views and limits imposed on Black artists and their work*25. Dorkay House was a base for the African Music and Drama Association and the Union of Southern African Artists, where music, theater, dance, photography, and sport came together; Cole saw there a cultural force that was not only being managed or suppressed. Sean O'Toole notes that Cole photographed the Malombo Jazz Men rehearsing and performing, and that the 2022 version of Black Ingenuity includes those photographs along with images of boxers, painters, and other musicians*23. Matthew Blackman of the A4 Arts Foundation writes that in 1960s South Africa, urban creative life centered on jazz was intensifying, and photographers from Zonk and Drum were part of that movement*24. Black Ingenuity, then, is not simply a bright chapter appended to a dark book. It adjusts the reading of House of Bondage as a whole. Mines, passes, commuting, education, hospitals, and signs show a system that narrows Black life; this chapter shows that music, performance, sport, painting, gesture, and gatherings did not disappear under that system. Cole was not looking only at the scenes in which apartheid wounded people. He also placed within the book's larger plan the strength of people who, while being harmed, still made culture in the city, moved their bodies, performed, played, gathered, and kept forms of collective life alive.

America after Exile

After leaving South Africa, Cole's attention did not move away from the question of how life is divided by race. Autograph presents the photographs he made in New York from 1967 to 1972 in the context of Harlem and Manhattan, the civil rights movement, Black Pride, and Black Power, and introduces them as part of approximately 40,000 images made during exile*13. Aperture's The True America is presented as the first substantial publication of his photographs of Black life in the United States from the late 1960s and early 1970s, including not only New York street scenes but also Black communities in urban and rural settings*14. These American photographs do not need to be treated as the same structure as apartheid in South Africa. Still, Cole's eye persists in the way he looks at another land of promised freedom and finds, in cities, streets, families, and political movements, other forms of exclusion and solidarity. Works visible in Autograph's exhibition preview, such as Black Panthers in the Park. Harlem, New York, 1968 and Harlem, New York, c. 1970, can be read as evidence that Cole, after exile, was looking not only at the anonymity of the street but also at Black community, awakening, gathering, and isolation*13.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Outside South Africa, House of Bondage circulated as a photobook that visually exposed apartheid, but inside South Africa the ban made it difficult to read for many years. O'Toole notes that the book was cut off from public circulation within South Africa for twenty-two years, and that even after the ban was lifted in 1990 its availability remained conditional and largely restricted to university libraries; it was therefore a book about the country that remained difficult for many readers inside that country to see*7.
Even so, the book had a slow, enduring effect on photographers who encountered it in limited settings. O'Toole recounts that Omar Badsha first saw House of Bondage in David Goldblatt's home, and that Badsha described its impact on young photographers who were able to see it as very large*7. Lindokuhle Sobekwa encountered the book at seventeen and was especially drawn to the crowded commuter-train photographs, where he saw the power to tell many stories within a single image or frame, along with deep concern for the subjects*7. Its influence, then, was less a matter of imitating compositions or techniques than of showing how apartheid could be made readable not as a series of isolated events, but through the ordering of photographs and the persistence of a gaze.
At the same time, a form that selects photographs under a strong theme, sequences them, and asks them to be read with text carries the risk of arranging images too neatly for an argument. Darren Newbury discusses Cole's book in relation to Edward Steichen's The Family of Man, recognizing a shared concern with selection and sequencing, while also arguing that House of Bondage does not present a universal human experience; it treats education, health care, transport, policing, and other subjects separately in order to show historically specific injustices imposed on Black South Africans*22. In other words, Cole's photobook does not gather images toward the claim that "all humans suffer alike." It identifies who is made to suffer, by which institutions, and in which places, through its chapters and prose.
O'Toole also writes that the full-bleed layouts, dramatic contrasts, and emphatic relation between images and text may now look like an older photobook design, but such a criticism misses the fact that the book was a publication forcefully addressed both to the South African government and to readers abroad*23. The book became difficult for the South African government to tolerate not because individual photographs were exaggerated, but because photographs, foreword, chapter prose, and explanatory texts worked together to make the workings of white rule legible to readers outside the country. Before publication, Cole is said to have understood that issuing the book would end his possibility of living as a photographer in South Africa, and the book was in fact declared "undesirable" in the May 1968 Government Gazette*7. According to O'Toole, the censors objected not only to individual photographs, but to the way criticism of apartheid and white rule ran through the foreword, chapter texts, and comments on the photographs*7.
Seen with that risk in mind, the importance of House of Bondage is not that it quietly arranged photographs as neutral records. Rather, in a situation where seeing, moving, and circulating printed matter were themselves regulated by the state, the act of photographing, writing, sequencing, and publishing abroad became political. That is why the book makes apartheid readable not as a collection of "terrible incidents," but as a system governing life, vision, and circulation. O'Toole argues that the book broke with representational patterns in which Black subjects had been made into props for white photographers' primitivist, pictorialist, or ethnographic imaginations*7.
The Fowler Museum values Cole's photographs not only for the shock of their content but also for their formal beauty and narrative power*2. Formal beauty here does not mean beautifying suffering. Hutchinson's biography notes that Cole persisted until a photograph was sharp enough, properly exposed, and expressive, and that Struan Robertson identified his ability to observe without being seen as one of his important qualities*20. In dangerous and chaotic scenes involving police, mines, commuter trains, and whites-only signs, bodies, gazes, crowd density, written words, and spatial relations remain readable within the frame. Cole's photographs do not merely confront viewers with dreadful content; through exposure, distance, timing, and framing, they allow viewers to follow the structure of the scene.
Cole's reassessment advanced in 2010 through the Hasselblad Foundation exhibition and Steidl's Ernest Cole: The Photographer, which shifted attention from the story of censorship and exile toward a reconstruction of his work as an artist through exhibition and book form*15. In 2024 The Photographers' Gallery exhibited all fifteen chapters, including the unpublished Black Ingenuity, strengthening the movement to reread the structure of the photobook itself*8. Around the same period, Autograph focused on the New York work, showing a way to understand Cole not only through his South African period but also through his American photographs after exile*13. Goodman Gallery's Cape Town exhibition, organized with Magnum Gallery and the Ernest Cole Family Trust, positions Cole's method for rereading from South African and African perspectives*16. The Ernest Cole Archive presented by the Photography Legacy Project on Google Arts & Culture also makes digitized materials available for education and research, offering another South African route into Cole's legacy*11.
The discovery of approximately 60,000 negatives in a Swedish bank vault in 2017 unsettled the tendency to close Cole's reputation around a single masterpiece*17. The Cannes Film Festival describes Raoul Peck's film Ernest Cole, Lost and Found as a work about exile, anger, the silence of Western society, and the 2017 discovery of the negatives*17. If a comparison is made within photography history, Gunilla Knape's references are to a lineage of social documentation such as Lewis Hine, Jacob Riis, and FSA photography. But the comparison is not meant to absorb Cole into the same pattern. Knape emphasizes that much of that work involved a viewpoint arriving from outside, whereas Cole represented his South Africa, his own world, from within*19. Cole's position in photography history therefore lies not only in the content of his anti-apartheid indictment, but in the photobook method by which photographs, prose, chapters, and publication were combined to make a social system readable as an order of experience.

erwin-wurm.html.title: Erwin Wurm | Conceptual Art, 1990s-2000s | Photo Coordinates
erwin-wurm.html.meta_description: Erwin Wurm is a sculptor whose One Minute Sculptures use everyday objects and brief instructions to turn the artist or viewers into temporary sculptures for several seconds or about a minute. Because these forms quickly disappear, photography and video fix the poses and carry them into exhibitions, books, and reenactments. His work extends histories of body performance and photography while making the camera part of the sculptural procedure itself.

erwin-wurm.html.lead_html: Erwin Wurm is a sculptor whose One Minute Sculptures use everyday objects and brief instructions to turn the artist or viewers into temporary sculptures for several seconds or roughly a minute. Because the form immediately disappears, photographs and videos fix the pose and carry it into exhibitions, books, and later reenactments. Building on the relationship between body performance and photography developed in the 1960s and 1970s, Wurm shifts the emphasis from photographs that document an action after the fact toward sculptures that are conceived through the presence of the camera.
erwin-wurm.html.thesis_html: In the 1960s and 1970s, Bruce Nauman, Hannah Wilke, Ana Mendieta, Gilbert & George, and others used the body as material for sculpture or performance and preserved those actions through photography. MoMA has described a broader development in which the camera moved beyond merely storing an event and became a reason for poses and actions to be performed in the first place. Wurm's One Minute Sculptures turns that relationship into a repeatable sequence: instruction → everyday object → body → brief duration → photograph. Because the pose disappears almost immediately, the photograph serves as evidence of what happened, but it also determines which moment is recognized as the sculpture and can function as a model when someone else follows the same instruction. Traditional sculpture was built around the persistence of the object. Wurm temporarily joins object, body, time, and camera, then makes the outcome comparable, distributable, and reenactable through photography. The photograph is therefore part of the production process through which the brief sculpture survives as a work, not an accessory documenting a completed sculpture.

sections.title: Background and Era
sections.body_html:
According to the artist's official biography, Wurm was born in Austria in 1954, trained in Vienna, and developed a career centered on sculpture. From the outset, he has resisted defining sculpture solely as a finished solid object, treating clothing, the body, time, and action as sculptural material.*23

Wurm trained as a sculptor and since the 1980s has broken the question “what is sculpture?” into problems of weight, volume, time, and action as well as form. Towada Art Center describes him as an artist who examines the human body as something continually reshaped by clothing, furniture, language, and social ideology, addressing time, mass, surface, and representation through that body.*7

When Wurm began One Minute Sculptures in the 1990s, Conceptual art and performance had already made instructions and temporary actions recorded in photographs or video into established artistic methods. Wurm brought this history back to the problem of sculpture, calling short poses that anyone could perform “sculptures” and thereby questioning the requirement that sculptural works endure materially.*10

For Wurm, then, the question of “why photography?” is better understood as a consequence of breaking sculpture down from durable object into time and action than as the starting point of a photographer. If a short pose counts as sculpture, the sculpture disappears almost immediately. Photography entered as a means of addressing that contradiction, but it also introduced a separate formal decision: which moment should be fixed and recognized as the work.*2

Museum der Moderne Salzburg presents photography, video, drawing, books, and large-scale sculpture as parts of one practice, centered on Wurm's effort to make everyday life appear from an altered angle.*1

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Turning Instructions and Time into Sculpture

In One Minute Sculptures, ordinary objects such as pedestals, chairs, sweaters, fruit, and pens are paired with short written or drawn instructions, and participants hold awkward poses for a brief period. The artist's official site explains that “one minute” is not a strict sixty-second duration, but a phrase indicating a short span of time.*4

At Middelheim Museum, instructions ask viewers to take the posture of a dog, hold their breath while thinking about Spinoza, or wear trousers over their heads. No permanent object remains as the completed form; the work exists only while a participant's body is carrying out the instruction.*9

Ephemeral Sculpture and Photography

Wurm has recalled that when he began One Minute Sculptures in 1997, he wanted to make snapshots because the works were temporary and would “cease to exist.” Once the action was fixed as a photograph, however, he realized that composition, the selection of a moment, and the history of photography had themselves become problems within the work, and for a period he stepped back from photography.*2 Photography was therefore not an unquestioned recording device from the start; the attempt to preserve an ephemeral sculpture made him confront a medium that demanded judgments distinct from sculpture.

In an interview with Musée Magazine, Wurm likewise describes photography as inseparable from the early development of One Minute Sculptures.*21 Once a brief pose is fixed photographically, choices of pose, frontal description, and serial order emerge, requiring a visual structure different from the sculpture's fleeting event.

Photography was therefore never neutral documentation. The decision of which instant to isolate and how frontally to fix the body's instability standardizes an event lasting only seconds into a single image that can be repeated in museums and books.*3

Museum der Moderne Salzburg similarly explains that recording brief performances through photography and video blurs the boundary between subject and object and adds social and temporal dimensions to sculpture.*1

Humor and Bodily Norms

Sticking pens into nostrils, twisting the body into a sweater, or balancing awkwardly on furniture may be funny, but the body appears less as free self-expression than as material temporarily deformed by objects and instructions. UniCredit's collection text places the humor alongside criticism of capitalism and social pressure.*11

Works such as Fat Car and Fat House transfer the idea of excess into swollen cars and houses, turning the way status and consumption define the self into a problem of how objects themselves “gain weight.” Tel Aviv Museum situates Wurm's work since the 1990s within an expansion of traditional sculpture through everyday objects and the body.*8

Lehmann Maupin connects Wurm's deformed bodies and enlarged cars and houses to questions of status, consumption, possession, and social norms. Everyday objects matter for more than their familiarity or comic potential: they allow the same commodities and possessions to which bodies adapt every day to become direct sculptural pressures.*16

The Role of Frontal Photography

Photographs of One Minute Sculptures often avoid adding complicated camera effects to already strange actions, maintaining a frontal view that makes the relation between body and object easy to read. On the artist's official archive page for Photographic Sculptures, C-prints of similar scale appear in sequence, allowing actions with pens, clothing, furniture, and other objects to be compared under a consistent visual standard.*5

This dry descriptive style prevents the joke from remaining a one-off event and brings differences among pose, object, and instruction into comparison. Because the camera does not dramatize the scene excessively, viewers can see where the body depends on an object for support, where it bends unnaturally, and what discomfort is required to obey the instruction.*19

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Early One Minute Sculptures

The artist's official archive preserves numerous 1997 One Minute Sculpture works as C-prints, followed by projects such as Outdoor Sculptures from 1998.*5 In this sequence, one bodily action corresponds to one photograph, and the difference between the pose's duration of only seconds and the time fixed by photography becomes part of the work's structure.

An instruction drawing from 1998 in the Lenbachhaus collection shows that the work system included drawn indications of how to position the body as well as photographs.*20

At the Städel Museum's 2014 exhibition, viewers carried out instructions in the gallery while photographs and videos of earlier actions were shown alongside the resulting live sculptures. The work's structure therefore extends beyond a single performance: instructions make repeated enactment possible.*12

Photography, Video, and Books as Part of the Process

An exhibition at Ludwig Museum quotes Wurm's assertion that “photography, video, and books are all sculpture.”*10

That statement indicates that Wurm treats media less as categories of finished objects than as means for producing, fixing, and sharing sculptural situations. A photograph is not merely a two-dimensional record of a three-dimensional object. It extracts a brief duration as a form, enables comparison among different bodies responding to the same instruction, and transports the work through exhibitions and publications.*10

When the Viewer Supplies the Body

In One Minute Sculptures, the body that completes the work need not be Wurm's own. At exhibitions at the Städel and the Taipei Fine Arts Museum, visitors produced new relations between body and object each time they carried out the instructions.*13

This participation prevents any photograph from becoming the single original form. Earlier photographs function as examples, evidence, and invitations to future performance, so photography is not the endpoint of the sculpture; it becomes a circuit connecting one enactment to the next.*14

sections.title: Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Comparing Nauman, Wilke, and Mendieta

The relation between photography and performance predates One Minute Sculptures by decades. MoMA's Staging Action describes how, from the 1960s onward, artists increasingly performed actions for the camera from the outset, producing autonomous photographic works from actions conceived for the camera; the photograph no longer served only as an after-the-fact record.*24 The exhibition also included the Vienna Actionists. Their photographs documented forceful bodily actions concerned with ritual and physical limits; Wurm replaces that intensity with everyday objects, concise instructions, and poses that anyone can perform. The comparison does not establish direct influence. It shows that an earlier generation, including artists working in Austria, had already made the question of how photography turns bodily action into an artwork a central problem.

MoMA's The Original Copy placed One Minute Sculptures within a longer history of photography mediating between sculpture and the body. Gilbert & George photographed themselves as “living sculptures” in 1969, while Eleanor Antin, VALIE EXPORT, Ana Mendieta, Dennis Oppenheim, Hannah Wilke, and others used bodily poses and photographs at the intersection of performance and sculpture in the 1960s and 1970s.*22

In Bruce Nauman's Eleven Color Photographs, wordplay and the artist's own body disrupt conventions of language and classical sculptural posing, fixing a one-time bodily action in a photograph. Wurm likewise turns the everyday body into sculpture, but shifts the center of gravity from an action performed by the artist to brief instructions that can be carried out by viewers.*22 Because the performer is not fixed, the photograph does more than prove that the artist acted; it also allows viewers to compare how the same instruction appears in different bodies.

In Hannah Wilke's S.O.S.—Starification Object Series, small gum sculptures were attached to her body as she performed poses drawn from advertising and fashion photography, preserving the temporary action as photographs. MoMA explains that Wilke used photography to extend an ephemeral event and called these images “performalist self-portraits.”*25 Wurm also fixes disappearing bodily actions through photography, but unlike Wilke's performance of a gendered self-image, his structure does not require the artist's body and can pass an instruction to other participants for reenactment.

These comparisons make clear why One Minute Sculptures cannot be reduced to photographs of funny poses. Earlier performance photography had already addressed bodily singularity, gender, and traces of temporary action. Wurm used instructions and everyday objects to turn sculpture into a brief program that anyone can run again. The photograph preserves one past execution while showing later participants how another body might take the pose.*22

Body, Consumption, and Social Norms

In an interview with Thaddaeus Ropac, Wurm explains his use of everyday objects and bodies to address social norms and anxieties.*15

Towada Art Center makes the continual reshaping of the human body by clothing, furniture, language, and social norms central to its presentation of the work.*7 When a body is forced into tight clothing or fitted awkwardly to furniture in One Minute Sculptures, the action is more than comic deformation. It condenses into an exaggerated pose the everyday process by which bodies adapt to commodities, manners, possessions, and commands.

Photography as a Basis for Reenactment

As AnOther's presentation of early One Minute Sculptures as a photography exhibition indicates, the works have circulated within photographic as well as sculptural contexts.*19

ALBERTINA MODERN's 2024 retrospective brought together roughly four decades of work, from early pieces through One Minute Sculptures, the Fat works, and recent sculpture. The exhibition confirms that the movement among photography, performance, and sculpture was not a temporary phase but a long-term structure of Wurm's work.*18

MoMA's artist page records collection holdings and exhibition histories that include photographic works, showing that Wurm's photographs have been treated as works within museum collections, not merely as explanatory documents attached to his sculptures.*6

Wurm did not invent the photographic documentation of performance. Earlier generations had already closely linked bodily actions and photography. In One Minute Sculptures, he instead made “who uses which object and assumes which pose” repeatable as an instruction, on the assumption that each action would disappear, then fixed each execution in a photograph.*22 Photography thus became a practical condition for comparison, circulation, and reenactment; it did more than explain an action that had already happened.

Yorkshire Sculpture Park's large-scale exhibition likewise placed photography, video, participatory works, and monumental sculptures together, presenting Wurm as an artist who continually questions the definition of sculpture through bodies and everyday objects. The work is better understood as one procedure moving among media than as separate bodies of photography and sculpture.*17

eugene-atget.html.lead_html: Eugène Atget photographed the streets, shopfronts, gardens, and urban margins of Old Paris for nearly three decades, producing what he marketed to painters and architects as “documents for artists.” Organized by subject, these photographs served as records of a changing city. After his death, they were assessed within the histories of Surrealism, documentary photography, and street photography.
eugene-atget.html.thesis_html: Atget photographed streets, courtyards, shops, gardens, and architectural details by subject, treating each photograph as an individual commodity and as part of an urban archive that could be searched and compared. In a 1920 letter, he described his work as an artistic and documentary collection and asked that it be preserved.This body of photographs, linking utility, classification, and preservation, formed the basis for his later reception among photographers and museums.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html: After working as an actor, Atget began photographing around 1888. By 1890, he was producing reference photographs of plants, landscapes, and objects for painters. In 1897, he began systematically photographing Paris, expanding his subjects to streets, churches, private residences, courtyards, stairways, shops, street vendors, interiors, and suburban gardens.*8 His stated purposes survive in signs, letters, ledgers, and sales records. By about 1891, the sign “Documents pour artistes” identified his business as the sale of reference photographs to painters, architects, and artisans.*23 According to The Metropolitan Museum of Art, more than 8,000 negatives were organized under categories such as “Parisian Interiors,” “Vehicles in Paris,” and “Petits métiers” (small trades).*1 The handwritten ledger Répertoire, held by MoMA, preserves evidence of how Atget managed subjects and negative numbers.*22 Before Atget, Charles Marville photographed the same city as the official photographer of Paris from 1862 onward, documenting streets threatened by redevelopment and the new infrastructure that replaced them under a municipal commission.*10 Atget’s work began as a private commercial enterprise and developed, through sustained photography, classification, and sales to public institutions, into a collection of Old Paris.

sections.title: The Core of His Work
sections.body_html:
Classification and Repetition: Organizing Documents into Urban Series

Classification by subject and the repeated photographing of similar motifs formed the basis of Atget’s method. In the album Documents pour l’histoire du Vieux Paris at the J. Paul Getty Museum, individual photographs are assembled as a body of documents “for the history of Old Paris.”*18 Paris Musées places his inventory-like sequences of door knockers and horse-drawn vehicles alongside photographs attentive to mist, light, and reflection, presenting both as parts of the same body of work.*4 Repeated photographs of courtyards, stairways, and shopfronts allow viewers to compare differences in entrance widths, paving, walls, displays, and the direction of light from place to place. This structure of classification and repetition underlies The Met’s description of Atget’s photographs as a visual compendium of the architecture, landscapes, and artifacts of French culture.*1

From “Documents for Artists” to a “Collection of Old Paris”

The surviving materials reveal two aims: the sale of reference photographs and the preservation of a collection. His “documents for artists” sign, photographs of plants, landscapes, and architectural details, and subject-based albums show that he supplied images as reusable visual references.*3 In a letter sent to arts administrator Paul Léon on November 12, 1920, Atget explained that for more than twenty years, “through my own work and personal initiative,” he had gathered artistic documents on urban architecture from the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries. Of the completed artistic and documentary collection, he wrote, “I can say that I possess all of Old Paris.”*23 In the same letter, he expressed concern that the negative collection might pass into the hands of someone who did not understand its value and be lost, and he sought its preservation by a public institution.*21 After selling part of his negatives on the art and architecture of Old Paris to the French government in 1920, he continued to photograph. Conservation research describes this later phase as a period in which he worked for his own pleasure, apart from commercial constraints.*23 Atget’s practical aims and the later interpretations of his work in terms of emptiness, dream, and modernity belong to different historical moments.

Changing Light and Time of Day

ICP identifies diffuse early-morning light and a broad field of view as characteristic features of Atget’s photographs.*2 The J. Paul Getty Museum also describes Atget walking through Paris at dawn to photograph streets, shopfronts, architectural ornament, stairways, and street trades.*5 Conservation research on MoMA’s holdings notes that Atget also worked in bright daylight when clear detail was required for reference purposes, while in his later years he increasingly chose early-morning and evening light.*23 Although many photographs show sparsely populated streets, Atget also photographed street vendors, laborers, sex workers, and spectators. When people appear, they are recorded in a way that keeps their occupation, location, surrounding architecture, and street surface legible. Working with an 18 × 24 cm glass plate and a tripod required a deliberate framing process that could register architecture and urban detail at once. MoMA describes his contact-printing process, in which the glass negative and sensitized paper were pressed together and exposed to sunlight.*6

Streets, Courtyards, and Stairways: The Continuity of Urban Space

In the early St. Étienne du Mont, rue de la Montagne Sainte Geneviève, the sloping road, building facades, and street leading toward the church are recorded as a single space. The National Gallery of Art identifies it as an albumen print made in 1898.*16 The 1912 photograph 22 rue Quincampoix, cour directs the eye through a narrow entrance toward the rear of the courtyard, holding walls, doorways, paving stones, and domestic objects within the same frame.*13 Frontal views of buildings coexist with photographs that use the depth of alleys and stairways. The city appears both as an inventory of structures and as a sequence of spaces traversed on foot. SFMOMA’s collection list likewise ranges across churches, streets, canals, shops, bridges, and châteaux, confirming that Atget’s subjects extended from monumental architecture to everyday labor and the urban periphery.*12

Shop-Window Reflections and Surrealist Reception

The 1925 photograph Magasin, Avenue des Gobelins shows mannequins and merchandise behind the window overlaid with reflections of the buildings, trees, and sky across the street. The NGA object page also notes the street scene reflected in the glass.*15 Reflection brings interior and street onto a single plane, recording commercial display and cityscape at once. Atget made these photographs as documents, while Man Ray and the Surrealists approached them from a different position. According to The Met, the photographs published at Man Ray’s suggestion in La Révolution surréaliste in 1926—deserted streets and shopfronts with mannequins among them—were received as images of Paris as the “capital of dreams,” where memory and desire intersect.*24 The 1912 photograph Pendant l’éclipse was among the published works and shows a crowd from behind as they look up at a solar eclipse.*14

Gardens, Mist, and Water: Light in the Late Work

Atget’s subjects extended beyond streets to the gardens of Saint-Cloud, Sceaux, Versailles, and the Luxembourg Gardens. In works including the Getty Museum’s Parc de Saint-Cloud, statues, stairs, water, and trees describe both the structure of the historic garden and the conditions of light.*19 MoMA presents the photographs made after World War I, especially the group produced in the Parc de Sceaux in the spring of 1925, as an important body of late work.*3 In the garden photographs, the spatial relations among architecture and sculpture remain clear, while mist, backlighting, reflections on water, and overlapping branches also remain visible. Paris Musées treats Atget’s inventory-like documentation and his responsiveness to mist, light, and reflection as two aspects of the same work.*4

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Materials
sections.body_html:
St. Étienne du Mont, rue de la Montagne Sainte Geneviève

St. Étienne du Mont, rue de la Montagne Sainte Geneviève (1898) does not isolate the church as a monument. It records the site as part of a street space that includes the hill and adjacent houses. The NGA record also lists the inventory number on the reverse, confirming that the print formed part of a classified body of documents.*16

22 rue Quincampoix, cour

22 rue Quincampoix, cour (1912) brings a narrow passage leading into the courtyard, and the layered doorways, walls, and paving beyond it, into a single frame. MoMA holds the work as an albumen print from the Abbott-Levy Collection; the object page provides the image, date, medium, and provenance.*13

Magasin, Avenue des Gobelins

Magasin, Avenue des Gobelins (1925) records mannequins, merchandise, price tags, and reflections from the street within a single image. The NGA object page can be enlarged to examine the display inside the shop and the reflected buildings, trees, and sky.*15 The series of shop-window photographs later became a central focus of the Surrealists’ reception of Atget.*24

18 × 24 cm Glass Plates and Contact Prints

Atget used 18 × 24 cm glass plates and a large-format view camera, producing contact prints by placing the negative directly against the photographic paper. Conservation research shows that he used several types of paper, including albumen paper and gelatin printing-out paper, followed by washing, fixing, and toning.*23 MoMA states that Atget made at least 8,500 photographs between 1898 and 1927.*13 The National Gallery of Art’s artist page makes fifty-eight works available online, allowing comparison of dates, media, and images.*11

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Man Ray and Surrealism

In the 1920s, the Surrealists encountered Atget’s photographs of Old Paris through Man Ray, who worked nearby. In 1926, several works, including Pendant l’éclipse, appeared without the photographer’s name in La Révolution surréaliste.*14 What drew their attention were deserted streets, shopfronts with mannequins, and reflections that overlaid the street and its merchandise. The Met explains that these photographs were received as images of Paris as the “capital of dreams,” an urban labyrinth where memory and desire intersect.*24 Man Ray’s selection and publication of the photographs helped move works that had circulated as reference documents into a Surrealist context.

Walker Evans and the American Vernacular

Walker Evans and Atget are connected through their frontal records of shopfronts, signs, hand lettering, and ordinary objects. The Met links Evans’s interest in commercial and hand-painted signs, seen in Votive Candles, New York City, to the influence of Atget’s shop-window photographs as they were valued by the Surrealists.*25 The museum further explains that Evans formed a new photographic language from the American vernacular through a comprehensive record of ordinary urban things. Atget’s shopfronts are identified as one of his early points of reference.

Henri Cartier-Bresson and Early Paris

Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson notes that the young Henri Cartier-Bresson attempted to emulate Atget in his early work.*8 In another text, the Fondation describes how, after an early phase shaped by Atget and the Surrealists, Cartier-Bresson turned from the 1930s onward to the ways people moved through and occupied the streets of Paris.*26 Their connection is grounded in Cartier-Bresson’s documented use of Atget as an early reference, as well as their shared subject of Paris.

Berenice Abbott and Institutional Preservation

Berenice Abbott met Atget through Man Ray and photographed his portrait in 1927. After Atget’s death, she and Julien Levy acquired the remaining prints and negatives, and for more than forty years she promoted the work through exhibitions, publications, and writing.*7 The Met’s Boutique, Marché aux Halles, Paris is cataloged as a print made by Abbott around 1929 from a 1925 negative, providing one example of the work’s posthumous preservation and reprinting.*17 In 1968, MoMA acquired 1,415 glass negatives and about 8,000 vintage prints, assuming responsibility for their preservation, classification, exhibition, and study.*9 MoMA currently publishes records for 2,996 works.*20 Atget’s reputation today took shape through several stages: the functional urban collection he created, the Surrealists’ selection of particular images, Abbott’s preservation and publication, and the collecting and research undertaken by museums.
