sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
From Marijampolė to Paris

Izis was born in 1911 in Marijampolė, in present-day Lithuania. The BnF authority record traces his study of photography in the 1920s, his move to Paris in 1930, and his early studio work.*1 A Lithuanian Jewish cultural heritage institution records that he learned the craft in a local photographer’s workshop, moved through different places photographing towns, festivals, and people, and eventually settled in Paris.*2 He had initially hoped to become a painter, but retouching and darkroom work undertaken to make a living turned photography into his profession. The Vilna Gaon Museum of Jewish History likewise describes his portrait studio in 1930s Paris and the rupture that war imposed on both life and work.*3 His later Paris photographs therefore do not record the city of his childhood. They repeatedly select and reshape a city acquired through migration, from the position of someone who became a resident while remaining a newcomer.

Occupation and the Resistance

During the Nazi occupation, Izis, who was Jewish, left Paris and fled to the Limousin. Lithuania’s State Commission for Cultural Heritage records that after being arrested in 1944, he was rescued by the Resistance, joined the movement himself, and photographed his fellow fighters.*4 The Musée de la Résistance in Limoges holds photographs of members of the Resistance made by Izis in 1944, preserving material evidence of this wartime work.*5 A MoMA text from the period identified the photographing of Resistance fighters as a turning point: Izis felt that the methods he had learned in a commercial portrait studio could not simply be applied to them and needed another way of working.*6 No statement by Izis has been located that directly attributes his later “poetic” photography to wartime experience. What is clear is that photographing the Resistance marked a move away from controlled backgrounds and lighting toward taking in people together with the environment in which he encountered them.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Paris Match and Everyday Life

From 1949, Izis worked for Paris Match for about twenty years, inside the professional system of mass-circulation news photography.*1 Founded with Life and Vu as reference points, Paris Match used large photographic spreads to bring narrative reportage to a broad French readership in the 1950s. An Izis feature on Chagall ran to roughly twenty pages, an unusually expansive assignment for a photographer within the magazine.*8 In a 1975 interview, however, Izis described the photograph first of all as a “document” and cautioned against imposing too much of the photographer’s personality.*20 The fog, waiting figures, playing children, and circuses that recur in his self-directed work were unlikely to lead a breaking-news story. The two editorial environments divided his output: the magazine explained events; the photobook assembled time in which little happened. BnF research on Paris Match identifies Izis as one of the magazine’s relatively few staff photographers and documents the professional setting in which commissions and self-directed photobooks proceeded in parallel.*8

The Institutions of Humanist Photography

“Humanist photography” was not a unified style or movement with a common postwar manifesto.*7 The BnF situates it within a longer tradition of street photography and describes a post-Liberation professional culture of reporters-illustrateurs photographing children, work, lovers, leisure, and street life for agencies such as Rapho, magazines, advertising, tourism publishing, and photobooks.*7 After war and occupation, such photographs signaled the resumption of daily life, but the same motifs were repeated in tourism and publishing as an image of the French way of life, often carrying nostalgia and optimism.*23 Continuous exhibition venues for self-directed photography were scarce, so print was a major route through which photographers could gather their work under their own names.*10 Izis worked at the center of that publishing industry as a Paris Match staff photographer, while his books selected fog, play, waiting, and circus scenes outside the hierarchy of news. His “dream Paris” therefore took shape inside the publishing systems through which postwar France reconstructed everyday life photographically, as well as through individual lyricism. The BnF exhibition La photographie humaniste 1945–1968 treated the field as an industry spanning agencies, magazines, advertising, tourism publishing, and books, with individual styles embedded in that system.*10 Its catalogue places Izis beside Doisneau, Ronis, Boubat, and Brassaï within that shared institutional environment while distinguishing their respective publication and reportage histories.*11 The BnF bibliography gathers the catalogues and research literature through which this postwar history of humanist photography has been studied.*13

Doisneau, Ronis, and Brassaï

Robert Doisneau, Willy Ronis, Brassaï, and Izis are often grouped retrospectively as “poets of Paris,” but their routes into the city were different. From the 1930s, Brassaï photographed nighttime Paris, brothels, cafés, and graffiti, establishing an earlier model in which a foreign-born photographer made the city’s darker spaces a modern subject.*7 Ronis sustained a left-wing social concern across working-class districts, strikes, and domestic life. Doisneau, whose early work included factories and the suburbs, developed chance encounters and humor on the street across advertising and magazine assignments as well. Izis was more deeply embedded in news production as a Paris Match staff photographer, while shifting the center of gravity in his private books toward Prévert’s poetry, fog, play, and the circus. What these photographers shared was less an abstractly “human” subject than the postwar print culture through which magazine commissions and self-directed books overlapped. Within it, Izis is distinguished by the clear separation—and continual movement—between the news event of the illustrated weekly and the dreamlike sequence of the photobook.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Paris des rêves

Published in 1950, Paris des rêves became Izis’s defining photobook, organizing fragments of the city into the flow of a single volume. The BnF bibliography records it as a major publication of 1950, while the authority record notes that Izis later selected layouts for his books himself.*1 In a 1975 interview, he said that a photograph is first a “document,” yet that a good photograph can produce something beyond documentation.*20 In Paris des rêves, that surplus does not depend on special effects. It comes from the selection and sequencing of streets, figures, fog, play, statues, and night, and from their intersections with words. The photobook becomes a medium for creating associations among fragments of reality and constructing a temporal experience of the city distinct from the news weekly. The BnF record for Boulevard Saint-Michel shows the same photograph later repositioned in Paris des poètes, demonstrating how an image could be reused under a different publishing logic.*14 Bibliographic records have continued to treat Paris des rêves, including later editions, as a central publication in Izis’s work.*12

Working with Prévert

Izis repeatedly brought photographs into relation with writers’ texts, notably in collaborations with Jacques Prévert such as Grand bal du printemps. The BnF bibliography lists the book among his major publications of 1951.*13 Through Paris Match he also photographed artists including Chagall, while circuses and street performers became recurring subjects. The Centre Pompidou’s holdings include street entertainers, urban scenes, and portraits.*15 Research at the University of Michigan analyzes Grand bal du printemps and Charmes de Londres through the interaction of urban poetry and photography, arguing that image and text jointly construct the experience of a city; neither medium merely illustrates the other.*21 Textimage scholarship similarly notes the close interplay of text and image in Grand bal du printemps and the further addition of Chagall’s painting in Le Cirque d’Izis.*22 In these books, literature and photography function as parallel editing elements, creating an order of associations across the page. The CCFr record of correspondence between Jean Cocteau and Izis points to a broader network in postwar French literature and art beyond Prévert and Chagall.*16

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
MoMA’s Five French Photographers

In 1951, MoMA introduced Brassaï, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Robert Doisneau, Willy Ronis, and Izis in Five French Photographers.*6 The five were not a coherent group defined by common nationality or a shared movement; they represented different generations based in Paris and working through magazines, agencies, and photobooks. Brassaï brought the prewar night city, Cartier-Bresson international reportage through Magnum, Doisneau and Ronis street and social life, and Izis the combination of Paris Match with authorial photobooks. MoMA’s presentation of them to American audiences as a single “French” photography is itself evidence of how postwar French photography circulated internationally under the signs of Paris, human figures, and everyday life. The continued presence of Izis’s Premier Mai, Paris in MoMA’s collection also shows that his international reception extended beyond the photobook.*17

Reassessment

Izis was widely known in the 1950s through photobooks and Paris Match, though later popular recognition did not crystallize around him to the same degree as around Doisneau or Cartier-Bresson. A 2010 retrospective at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris gathered roughly 270 photographs and documents, bringing the Resistance, Paris Match, Prévert, Chagall, Israel, and the circus back into a single career history.*18 The BnF’s 2006 exhibition La photographie humaniste 1945–1968 likewise placed him centrally alongside Boubat, Brassaï, Doisneau, and Ronis, broadening the frame from the solitary photographer of “dream Paris” to a reporter-illustrator active within postwar publishing culture.*11 Recent retrospectives and scholarship connect exile and the Resistance, Paris Match reportage, self-directed photobooks, and collaborations with writers, locating Izis within the wider question of how postwar French publishing shaped images of everyday life. A 2007 retrospective at the Maison de la Photographie Robert Doisneau centered on the Paris Match archive of 1949–69 and examined the continuity between reportage and photobook images of the “non-event” within one career.*9 In Lithuania, recent retrospective presentations have also addressed the gap between his reputation in France and in his birthplace, renewing attention to his biography as an émigré.*19

twitter.description: Through J. H. Engström’s Trying to Dance, From Back Home, and Tout Va Bien, this page examines photobook editing across color and black and white, blur, and different photographic formats, and the relation among autobiography, memory, and place.

j-h-engstrom.html.lead_html: J. H. Engström moves between naked friends, rooms, windows, streets, Paris, and his native Värmland, using both large-format cameras and handheld snapshots, color and black and white. In Trying to Dance, From Back Home, and Tout Va Bien, shifts between proximity and distance, stillness and movement, and the different speeds of city and countryside establish the rhythm of the page. In his photobooks, fragments made at separate moments are later brought together, allowing the meaning of experience to change from page to page.
j-h-engstrom.html.thesis_html: Engström uses photography to preserve what he encounters each day together with his physical and emotional response to it, then reworks those fragments into another temporal order through the photobook. The slow encounter of a large-format portrait, the speed of moving through a city with a handheld camera, color, black and white, aerial views, and unstable exposures can all appear in the same book, allowing Paris and Värmland, present experience and memory, to interrupt one another. He has emphasized choosing methods according to what he wants to express and why. Since Trying to Dance, the photobook has become the central form through which these different tempos and emotions are experienced in sequence.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Paris and Värmland — Photographing Between Two Speeds

Engström was born in Värmland, Sweden, moved to Paris at the age of ten, and returned to Sweden at thirteen, continuing to spend his youth between the two places. Steidl’s biography records that he returned to Paris in 1991 to assist Mario Testino, worked as Anders Petersen’s assistant in Stockholm in 1993, and graduated from the Department of Photography and Film at the University of Gothenburg in 1997*23. His early movement between city and countryside, and between controlled fashion shoots and documentary situations built on proximity to the subject, helps explain the coexistence of several photographic tempos in his later work.

Engström calls his method “diaristic,” explaining that what he sees every day is true to him and therefore becomes material for photographic narratives*3. Photography entered his life as a way to retain small events at the distance and emotional pitch at which he encountered them. The possibility of returning to and re-editing old negatives also lets him repeatedly connect the present of taking a photograph with the later present of editing it.

Foam’s Close Surrounding presents his movement between Paris and Värmland as a background for work concerned with solitude and existential uncertainty*16. Sleek likewise describes From Back Home as a return to the region of his childhood, where home becomes a place whose distance must be measured again with each return*17.

Learning Proximity from Anders Petersen

His assistantships with Mario Testino in 1991 and Anders Petersen in 1993 placed two very different photographic environments side by side during his formative years*23. His relationship with Petersen continued and later developed into From Back Home, their joint project on Värmland*11. These experiences help explain how a photographer familiar with both close, responsive encounters and highly controlled image-making later treated different cameras and distances without a fixed hierarchy.

Engström extends the proximity he learned from Petersen to fragments beyond the human figure. Windows, roads, sky, rooms, plants, and images that can look like failures of light may carry the same weight as a face. In an extended interview with FK, he describes photography as a way of coming into contact with his surroundings and emphasizes the act of photographing as a way of staying close to the intensity of life*10.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Trying to Dance — Breaking Chronology and Shifting Photographic Distance

Trying to Dance includes self-portraits, lovers and friends, landscapes, still lifes, and snapshots in both color and black and white. The official Trying to Dance page presents numerous photographs as a continuous project and accompanies them with a short statement by Engström on “presence”*15. What matters is the change in temperature from one image to the next as the pages turn.

In an interview with American Suburb X, Engström distinguishes his work from an autobiography that recounts a life in sequence and instead describes his method as autobiographical*3. The photographs accumulate as traces of private responses to the surrounding world. This allows blur, grain, overexposure, Polaroids, and large-format photographs to coexist in a single book.

Moving Between Large Format, Snapshots, and Aerial Views in One Book

In a Leica interview, Engström says he places no hierarchy between intuitive and planned photography, choosing color or black and white, sharpness or blur, large-format cameras, disposable cameras, or 8mm according to what he wants to express and why*1. The differences in image quality within Trying to Dance therefore follow changes in his distance from the subject and the energy of the moment. A slow large-format portrait placed beside a rapid handheld image changes the viewer’s bodily tempo within the book.

Aperture’s workshop description similarly presents his work as grounded in proximity to lived experience and an intuitive use of photography*6. The visual inconsistency is deliberate. Avoiding a single recognizable look preserves the changing distance between photographer and subject from one encounter to the next.

Making the Photobook the Final Form — Meaning Between Pages

Engström has described the photobook as the “ultimate photographic expression,” extending photographic meaning to the quality of printing and the tactile character of paper*1. He also recalls that when he published his first book in the mid-1990s, the current photobook boom did not yet exist, and that the photobook later gained rapid visibility as an art form*1. Rhythm between pages, the relation of preceding and following images, and the time of physically turning pages provide the conditions that bring his heterogeneous photographs into a single work.

LFI notes that Engström had oriented his work toward publication since the 1990s, before the photobook boom, and connects separate photographs through an editing process it describes as “visual poetry”*13. Adjacent photographs produce associations, leaving the reader to construct what lies between them. That interval makes the book itself the form of the work.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
From Back Home — What Changes When Two Photographers Picture Home

From Back Home is a collaboration in which Engström and Anders Petersen photographed Värmland over roughly seven years beginning in 2001. The National Science and Media Museum describes their return to a region formative for both photographers as a journey of rediscovery through people and place*8. With two photographers working in the same region, “home” becomes a place where several distances and memories overlap.

LensCulture notes how the two photographers’ distinct visual languages sit side by side in the book while remaining connected through their attention to people and place*9. The collaboration turns autobiographical photography away from a single first-person account and layers two different relationships to the same place within one volume.

Sketch of Paris — Editing Paris as Twenty Years of Lived Time

Sketch of Paris re-edits photographs made between 1991 and 2012, layering streets, nudes, friends, interiors, and traces of relationships into one book. Engström explains that he did not conceive a story moving from A to B, but began from the way memories mix. He also connects his time in Paris, where he discovered that art could be a profession, to the beginning of his own work*24. In the same interview, he says that the freedom he found in exhibition formats suited the photobook as a medium. The book is structured so that twenty years of personal time can appear at once.

Akio Nagasawa Gallery likewise places his work between Paris and Sweden and identifies his many photobooks as central to his production*7. Across changing locations, he continues to bring fragments made over long periods back into contact in books, presenting the city as an accumulation of lived time.

Tout Va Bien — Keeping the Tension Between Title and Image

Tout Va Bien brings together portraits, landscapes, childbirth, bodies, animals, and dark interiors, with wide differences in both subject and technique. The Leica Oskar Barnack Award described the series through the coexistence of autobiographical elements, bodies, landscapes, birth, and animals*12. The distance between the title—“everything will be fine”—and the anxiety or rawness of the images leaves a persistent tension across the book.

The Leica Camera Blog describes a working process in which numerous dummies were produced and repeatedly edited before the book was completed*14. The apparently spontaneous book is therefore the result of a long process of sequencing. The official project page also presents the series while preserving the differences among its individual images*5.

Revoir — Re-reading Old Negatives from the Present

In Revoir, Engström returned to negatives from the period around Trying to Dance, including previously unpublished photographs, and rescanned and re-edited them. The publisher’s description emphasizes the making of new prints and sequences through his present-day judgment*18. Old negatives change in meaning over time and become material to be read again through present editing.

In 2025, the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson presented DIMMA / BRUME / MIST as a photobook tracing thirty-five years of work and invited Engström to discuss image selection, layout, and sequencing within its photobook program*2.

sections.title: Reception Within Photobook Culture
sections.body_html:
Camus and “Doubt” — Linking Private Photographs to Existential Questions

Engström has said that Camus’s The Myth of Sisyphus strongly affected him when he was young, and he repeatedly returns to the sense that the world cannot be fully understood, to images that seem both inside and outside the self, and to “doubt” as a force that drives his work*25. Family, nudity, tables, forests, wounds, and children function as fragments through which life, death, time, and belonging remain unresolved. In the same interview, Engström says that “fragility” matters more to him than roughness and values the uncertainty produced by shifts in energy, a distinction that clarifies his approach to photographs*25.

Foam reads his work through questions of human solitude and absurdity, emphasizing the room the photographs leave for the viewer’s own experience*16. Even without knowing the specific event behind a photograph, a reader can register emotional movement through distance between pages, physical proximity, and sudden gaps.

After Trying to Dance — Editing Recognized Through Photobook Culture

Trying to Dance was shortlisted for the 2005 Deutsche Börse Photography Prize, From Back Home received the photobook award at Arles, and Tout Va Bien won the Leica Oskar Barnack Award. This record shows how strongly Engström’s reception has centered on editing and publishing as well as on individual photographs*4. As photobook culture expanded after the 2000s, he continued to use the book as a primary form capable of holding differences in photographic method, jumps in time, and intervals of meaning.

If attention stays only on the mixture of color and black and white, different cameras, private snapshots, and abstract images, Engström’s work can be reduced to a style of “rough” photobook-making. As he explains in American Suburb X, photography is a language for preserving personal responses to a changing environment, and keeping those responses in different photographic forms is part of the method*3. The photobook becomes a place where fragments continue to alter one another without resolving a life into a single conclusion.

The Photobook as an Ongoing Site of Production

The 2005 Deutsche Börse Photography Prize shortlisted Trying to Dance, recognizing the mixture of portraits of friends, interiors, landscapes, color, and rough black-and-white images as part of the book’s momentum*19.

The Image Museum photobook library describes Trying to Dance as a volume in which landscapes, still lifes, self-portraits, and snapshots intersect diaristically. Its reception has repeatedly focused on the way different kinds of images create the book’s temporal experience*20.

For the 2025 publication Dimma Brume Mist, Engström returned to thirty-five years of contact sheets and negatives held in more than two hundred binders, reworking pairs such as city/country, stillness/movement, and self/other into new sequences*21.

Photo Poche similarly characterizes his long-term work through countryside and city as metaphors for tensions between introspection and impulse, security and vulnerability, self and other*22.

jack-delano.html.lead_html: As an FSA photographer Delano documented poverty in American farmland, coalfields, and railroads; after moving to Puerto Rico he was involved in the island's social transformation through photography, film, music, and cultural policy. A photographer with a unique trajectory showing how New Deal social documentary moved toward postwar regional cultural policy.
jack-delano.html.thesis_html: Working within the FSA's institutional framework to document rural America, coal mines, and Puerto Rico, he then settled permanently in Puerto Rico and through DIVEDCO embodied the transition of New Deal social-record photography into postwar regional cultural policy. His practice spanning photography, film, and music is positioned as a form of social engagement that refused to be confined to a single medium.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Jack Delano was born in 1914 in Kyiv, Ukraine, to a Jewish family, and immigrated to the United States with his family as a child. After training as a painter and musician he turned to photography, and in 1940 was hired by the Farm Security Administration's photographic unit. Library of Congress materials related to Delano's FSA work show him recording across a wide range of fields — Puerto Rico, Connecticut, Georgia, Chicago*1. His documentation of the lives of migrant farmworkers, coal miners, and rural communities stands alongside other FSA photographers' work as a visual record of Depression-era America.

In 1943, while continuing to work for the Office of War Information, Delano was sent to Puerto Rico and subsequently chose to settle there permanently. The oral history interview with Jack and Irene Delano held by the Archives of American Art is primary material conveying in his own words the background of this decision and the development of his cultural work on the island*2. In Puerto Rico he became involved in the educational film and poster production of DIVEDCO (División de Educación de la Comunidad), contributing across photography, film, music, and education to the island's cultural infrastructure*3. The Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico recognizes him as a cultural contributor to Puerto Rico*4. Died 1997.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
The FSA and social documentary photography

Delano's FSA-period work was institutional photography established under Roy Stryker's direction for the purpose of making visible the social conditions of agriculture, labor, and rural communities. The Library of Congress research guide on Puerto Rican plantation life shows that Delano's work — particularly its record of Puerto Rico's agricultural economy and rural society — is managed as part of the FSA/OWI archive and played an important role there*5. Columbia University Libraries' finding aid for the Jack and Irene Delano papers manages records from 1731–2003, including photographs, music, film, and correspondence, as a research foundation covering the full career*6.

Puerto Rico as photographic site

When Delano first photographed Puerto Rico for the FSA, the context was inseparable from the colonial framework of American rule over Puerto Rico. The Interventions journal article (Taylor & Francis) critically discusses Delano's work from the perspective of "picturing our colonial problem," pointing out that power relations are embedded within the humanitarian surface of FSA photography*7. This critical reading is important as a perspective that guards against simple canonization of Delano as a photographer "on the side of the weak." The inLibra research material is a reference for tracing the formation of mid-twentieth-century Puerto Rican visual imagery*8.

DIVEDCO: filmmaking as cultural policy

The longest sustained engagement of Delano's Puerto Rican years was with DIVEDCO (División de Educación de la Comunidad), producing educational films and posters. DIVEDCO was a regional education organization established by the Puerto Rican government to pursue social transformation through film, posters, and rural community screenings. Archivo ICP's DIVEDCO archive documents the organization's full activities and Delano's role within them*9. The Smithsonian's record of the DIVEDCO film poster Desde las Nubes can be referenced as a concrete product of Delano's production work*10. DIVEDCO work, oriented toward supporting the cultural autonomy of local communities rather than serving state propaganda, occupies a position different from FSA-era institutional constraints.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Jack Delano has been evaluated primarily for his FSA work, but recent scholarship increasingly values his long-term cultural contributions after moving to Puerto Rico. Columbia University Libraries' finding aid for records from 1731–2003 shows a life trajectory far exceeding the "FSA photographer" frame, and serves as a research reference for the full picture of activities spanning photography, music, film, and cultural policy*6. The monograph Puerto Rico mío: four decades of change, accessible through Internet Archive, is an important reference for discussions of photography and historical testimony, documenting Puerto Rico's transformation from the 1940s to the 1980s*13. As demonstrated by Museo de Arte de Puerto Rico, Delano is valued in Puerto Rican cultural memory less as an FSA photographer than as a bearer of island culture — revealing the distinctive positioning of a photographer who worked between the American mainland and an insular colonial territory*4.

jacques-henri-lartigue.html.lead_html: Jacques Henri Lartigue preserved family life, play, airplanes, automobiles, sports, and fashion in photographs, diaries, and albums from childhood onward. Fast shutters and experiments made within the family rendered jumps and moving vehicles as distortions unlike ordinary vision. Half a century after many of these images were made, the 1963 MoMA exhibition, Life magazine, and Richard Avedon’s editing established them as precedents for the modern snapshot.
jacques-henri-lartigue.html.thesis_html: Lartigue’s place in photo history lies less in participation in an art-photography movement than in the later discovery of domestic picture making by museums and publishers. A private practice that preserved fleeting pleasure and movement through diaries, albums, and photographs was recognized half a century later by museums and publishers as a major example of snapshot photography The distance between the moment of exposure and the moment of recognition is itself central to his historical significance.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
A Child’s Camera and the Belle Époque: The Family’s Technological World

Born into a wealthy family, Lartigue began photographing at about eight years old after receiving a camera from his father. The official chronology records his continuing interest in family members, pets, models, automobiles, airplanes, sports, stereoscopic photography, and experiments with movement*1. Photography began as a domestic activity alongside diaries, drawings, and inventive play, not as professional training, and accumulated according to standards different from the exhibition finish expected by contemporary art photography.

Saving Vanishing Moments in a Diary: Why Did the Child Keep Photographing?

Lartigue did not begin with a plan to become a professional photographer. In a prosperous household where his father used photographic equipment, he employed the camera from around age seven to preserve everyday surprise and pleasure before they faded, combining photographs, writing, and drawings in his diary. The official archive and a Fujifilm retrospective describe an acute awareness of memory’s fragility and the pleasure of saving nearby events as the durable core of his work*16. Photography continued as a way of keeping pace with the passage of his own time, rather than as a project to produce representative images of society.

What Did Amateur Photography Record? Leisure, Class, and Modern Life

Seaside holidays, horse racing, tennis, skiing, motor races, aviation experiments, and elegant clothing recur throughout Lartigue’s early photographs. They preserve the early twentieth century’s enthusiasm for speed and leisure, while recording modern life from a privileged family environment rather than representing French society as a whole*2. The brightness of these images depended on social conditions that determined who could possess a camera and free time.

The Class Conditions of the Belle Époque: Whose “Everyday Life” Was This?

Automobiles, airplanes, seaside holidays, horse racing, and fashionable dress register new forms of life in the early twentieth century, but regular access to them belonged to a limited social group. Lartigue’s albums are internal records of a bourgeois household able to enjoy technology, travel, and leisure; they do not describe average life across France. Materials from The Photographers’ Gallery explicitly identify family wealth and access to early equipment as conditions of the work*13. Acknowledging those conditions preserves the buoyancy of the pictures while placing the resources that sustained happiness and speed back around the frame.

Cameras and Shutters: The Technical Conditions That Made Modern Speed Visible

Lartigue’s action photographs depended on more than personal talent. Glass plates, portable cameras, and fast shutters were beginning to enter domestic life. A family culture in which he handled machines with his father and brother and tested new devices encouraged him to aim the camera at racing cars and airplanes*9. His photographs record modern technology from within domestic play and invention. Camera, automobile, and aircraft belonged to the same world, making the albums a concrete account of early twentieth-century amateur culture.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Stopping Speed: How Lartigue Photographed Automobiles and Airplanes

Lartigue photographed racing automobiles, jumping bodies, and airplanes at the unstable peak of movement. In 《Grand Prix of the Automobile Club of France》, the car body and wheels warp while spectators stream diagonally across the frame*3. The distortion resulted from a focal-plane shutter exposing a rapidly moving subject in sequence. The combination of shutter scan, panning, and vehicle speed communicates mechanical velocity through deformation across the image rather than through precise contour.

Distorted Speed: Play and Equipment, Not Futurist Theory

The slanting elongation of the car and wheels in 《Le Grand Prix de l’A.C.F.》 resulted from the interaction of high speed and the scanning action of a focal-plane shutter*9. No evidence shows Lartigue presenting a Futurist theory of machine civilization. He repeatedly photographed flight, jumping, falling, and racing, testing as family play the camera’s ability to produce forms of movement different from ordinary vision. Formal novelty grew from repeated games and the properties of contemporary equipment.

Bodies in Midair: Preserving Success and Failure as a Sequence

Photographs of cousins jumping from stairs, women suspended in the air, and athletes chasing balls select the instant when the body leaves the ground. Lartigue did not seek a single successful exposure; he photographed the same games repeatedly and placed successful and failed attempts together in albums*1. Images of speed and the body emerged through this cycle of family performance, exposure, and shared results.

Avenue du Bois de Boulogne: A Private Street Photography of Fashion

In 《Avenue du Bois de Boulogne》, clothing, hats, and posture are caught quickly as women move through the street, making urban fashion an object of observation. Lartigue described these women in his diary as “beautiful people,” turning the street into a private collection of attractions*4. The gaze resembles later fashion and street photography, but at the time personal fascination and memory preceded any magazine commission.

Photography and the Diary: An Apparatus of Image, Word, and Memory

Lartigue combined photographs with diaries, handwritten accounts, weather records, and drawings, arranging them in a vast series of albums. Because descriptions of events and feelings remain around the images, photography functions as an index for replaying life rather than as an autonomous artwork*1. When later exhibitions and books extracted photographs from this setting, continuous family time was converted into independent images attributed to a named author.

The Myth of the Innocent Genius: Separating the Time of Making from the Time of Discovery

Lartigue is often introduced as a genius who saw modernity through the eyes of a boy. His photographic reputation, however, was formed half a century after many exposures, when images were reselected, enlarged, exhibited, and published in magazines. The official archive treats his career as a double chronology in which the time of production overlaps with the time of discovery*5. Including the people who selected particular pictures prevents childhood vision from being carried directly into present-day evaluation as a myth.

Stereo Photography and Continuity: Play Beyond the Single Flat Image

The official chronology records Lartigue’s experiments with stereoscopic photography, sequential exposures, and spirit photographs*1. Multiple frames of similar scenes remain in the albums, indicating how family members compared attempts to reproduce depth and motion. Concentrating only on the later selection of single images diminishes the play and repetition through which equipment was tested. His treatment of speed developed within that process of trial and error.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The 1963 MoMA Exhibition: How Was “Lartigue the Photographer” Produced?

In 1963, MoMA mounted a solo exhibition of Lartigue’s photographs under John Szarkowski. The show concentrated mainly on early images of movement and leisure, and Life featured the work that same year, turning a man long publicly active as a painter into an internationally recognized photographer*6. The museum extracted images of speed, abrupt framing, and chance from a private archive and presented a newly defined author.

Richard Avedon and Diary of a Century: Reediting the Family Album

Richard Avedon was deeply drawn to Lartigue’s photographs and diaries and participated in the editing of Diary of a Century in 1970. The official archive presents their relationship as an instance in which the maker and a later selector jointly shaped the image of an oeuvre*5. Page sequence, cropping, reproduction size, and the placement of text reorganized domestic records into an autobiographical narrative spanning the twentieth century.

The Donation to the French State: Turning Private Records into a Public Archive

In 1979, Lartigue donated his negatives, albums, and diaries to the French state. The Donation Jacques Henri Lartigue now oversees preservation, research, exhibitions, and rights management, maintaining private records of life as a public archive*1. This institutionalization allows relationships among different prints, albums, and texts to be studied, and makes the “discovery” of the 1960s available for reconsideration as a historical act of editing.

A Long Career as a Painter: The Late Arrival of the Title “Photographer”

Lartigue pursued painting as his public profession throughout his life and also worked in color photography, film, and travel photography. When later history narrows its attention to the speed photographs of his youth, his adult painting, color work, and film largely disappear. The official chronology records photography, painting, and cinema continuing in parallel before 1963*1. The canonical works produced after rediscovery represent one part of a life spent moving among several media.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
A Precursor of the Snapshot? Avoiding the Projection of Later Forms onto the Past

Lartigue’s tilted frames, cropped bodies, and accidental movements share formal traits with later snapshot photography. At the time, he was preserving his own and his family’s experience in albums. The 1963 MoMA exhibition selected from that private production the speed and abruptness later viewers recognized as modern*6. Lartigue entered photo history as a case in which images made for another purpose converged with a later conception of photography.

Who Historicizes Private Photography? The Question After Lartigue

Lartigue’s reception shows the conditions under which amateur photographs, family albums, and diaries enter the museum. When representative images are removed from the sequence shared by a family, the relations among the people photographed, the writing, and the temporality of the pages change. Materials from The Photographers’ Gallery connect the work to Belle Époque life, technology, and the class conditions of the family*13. His historical importance includes both the attraction of private photographs and the process through which museums and editors remade their meaning.

A Critique of Photographs of Happiness: Where Are War and Social Conflict?

Although Lartigue lived through two world wars, his best-known photographs center on family play and leisure, with war and poverty seldom at the front of the image. Describing him as a photographer of “the twentieth century itself” carries this imbalance of vision. His albums show what one class and one household chose to see and what it left unphotographed. Images of happiness are selections of the experience he wished to preserve, and the same album retains both their appeal and their limits as historical evidence.

MoMA and Avedon: The “Modernity” Selected from a Private Album

The 1963 MoMA exhibition concentrated on dynamic images from childhood through the 1920s, producing a particular Lartigue from several decades of work. Avedon’s subsequent editing of Diary of a Century arranged photographs, diaries, and handwriting as a twentieth-century autobiography and consolidated an international reputation*17. The value of the work was formed jointly by its original domestic use and by later exhibitions and editing. The speed, cropping, and chance selected by museum and editor became established as Lartigue’s representative style.

james-casebere.html.lead_html: James Casebere builds models of prisons, schools, tunnels, suburban houses, and historic buildings from paper, cardboard, and plaster, then lights and photographs them. He selects walls, windows, corridors, and stairways from architectural sources, films, and memory, constructing only what the camera can see. The model lets him control light, viewpoint, and depth in ways unavailable on location, revealing how spaces produce surveillance, isolation, ownership, and security. His method is examined through the Pictures Generation, his interest in Gaston Bachelard, Martin Heidegger, and modern architecture, and his differences from Thomas Demand.
james-casebere.html.thesis_html: Constructed photography in the 1970s often used performed figures and preexisting images to question narratives produced by film and advertising. Casebere removed addresses and people from models of prisons and houses, then controlled light, circulation, and scale. He thereby photographed architecture as a system that organizes human behavior, emotion, and social relations. The model was necessary because it allowed him to isolate that system.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
As a child, Casebere studied the blueprints his father brought home from his work on school buildings and drew imaginary structures of his own. In a later interview, he recalled wanting to become an architect and learning to imagine space from plans*15. At the Minneapolis College of Art and Design, he studied with Siah Armajani, whose work addressed public space and politics. At the California Institute of the Arts, he entered John Baldessari’s cross-disciplinary environment of photography, language, and found imagery*16*12*10.

In the conceptual art of the 1970s, many earthworks and performances disappeared quickly, leaving photography as the only form through which the work survived. Casebere reversed that relationship. He built temporary models so that only the photograph would remain, then dismantled them after shooting. The work came to encompass the process by which a three-dimensional construction became a single image through light and perspective*14.

A model offers freedoms unavailable when photographing an existing site. Casebere can alter the height of a wall, the width of a window, or the length of a corridor; combine elements from different buildings; and construct only the single direction seen by the camera. During the shoot he can move the lights, add water, and adjust the slope of the floor. These controls allow him to remove information that explains a building’s use and intensify the pressure, isolation, or anticipation a space produces in the body. His decision to leave seams visible reflects the influence of Constructivism and Jean-Luc Godard: the image invites immersion while also revealing how it was made*1. The model was necessary because it let him rebuild walls, windows, and circulation routes that are fixed in an actual site, then compare their effects within the same photographic frame.

The Pictures Generation refers to a group of artists working in the United States from the late 1970s through the 1980s who reconsidered authorship and the influence of mass culture through images borrowed from film, advertising, magazines, and art history, as well as photographs that performed familiar visual types. Cindy Sherman, Richard Prince, and Sherrie Levine examined how recognizable figures and product images shape ideas about desire, gender, and success*17. Casebere directed the same question toward interior settings. Corridors, cells, and suburban houses repeated across film and advertising provide visual cues through which viewers recognize “a school,” “a prison,” or “a safe home.” A photograph of an existing building ties those cues to a particular address and current use. By removing site-specific information in a model and retaining only walls, windows, lighting, and circulation, he could examine the shared images through which society understands space.

sections.title: How the Method Developed
sections.body_html:
Why Build Models?

Architectural models are usually made to verify a building’s overall structure or its appearance after construction. Casebere’s models are built for a single camera view and include only the necessary portions of walls, floors, windows, and stairs. Rooms and roofs outside the frame are omitted, while seams in the paper or plaster, slight distortions, and ambiguities of scale remain. He selects the minimum elements required to recognize a space, leaving room for the viewer’s memory to complete it*1.

Seen through the camera, paper walls acquire the mass of concrete, and a corridor only a few feet long can resemble a vast facility surrounding the body. Casebere adjusts wall heights, window positions, and angles of light to test whether the same space suggests security, isolation, or surveillance. Because the model lets him reconstruct before exposure what remains fixed in an actual building, it becomes an experimental device for comparing the conditions through which architecture affects feeling. By dismantling it after the shoot and retaining only the photograph as the finished work, he also makes the transformation of construction and light into a plausible space part of the image*7.

Prisons and Surveillance

In Casebere’s prisons, cells, watchtowers, and underground passages from the 1980s onward, doors, windows, and repeated corridors dominate the frame with no people present. Open sight lines carry the guard’s gaze, while narrow apertures restrict movement and contact with the outside. Casebere studied the prison as an institution of punishment, reform, and isolation that took shape during the Enlightenment *2. A review in Frieze likewise discusses his models of prisons, schools, and hospitals as works that make architectural authority visible*8.

This work coincided with a period of rapidly expanding incarceration in the United States. The number of people held in state and federal prisons reached approximately 330,000 in 1980 and continued to rise*18. The empty cells do not directly depict how incarceration falls unevenly across race and class. They instead expose the design of a system whose structures can be reproduced indefinitely. The abstraction created by removing people also risks diminishing the specific experiences of those confined within them, and that limitation remains central to the critical reception of the work.

Domestic Memory and Modern Architecture

Through Siah Armajani’s classes, Casebere read Edward T. Hall, Gaston Bachelard, and Martin Heidegger*14. Bachelard treated attics, cellars, corners, and drawers as concrete structures that direct childhood memory and imagination. The darkness of a cellar, the brightness of an attic, the confinement of a corner, and the opening or closing of a door give domestic experience its distinctions between high and low, inside and outside, safety and fear. Heidegger described dwelling as the activity through which people establish relations with places, things, and communities. Hall studied how interpersonal distance and the placement of walls alter behavior. From these ideas, Casebere understood architecture as both a repository for memory and an apparatus that shapes emotion and action.

Casebere extended these ideas beyond the house to prisons, schools, hospitals, and public buildings. If a home can cultivate memory and security, a cell repeats isolation, a school corridor directs movement and orderly lines, and a hospital passage treats the body as an object of administration. In models stripped of furniture and people, the viewer’s own memories enter the space, then meet the institutional demands encoded in doors, windows, and walls. Architectural historian Anthony Vidler’s research on institutional buildings also became an important point of reference for the prison series*14. Modern architecture’s history of designing for light, circulation, hygiene, and efficiency led to his interest in how the same techniques classify education, treatment, correction, and habitation. Casebere approached domestic memory and institutional discipline through the same walls, windows, and corridors. Repeated cellars and passageways, sparse furniture, and emphatic doors and windows draw the viewer’s own domestic memories into the image while making them aware of the movement, stillness, or obedience the space demands from a body.

Suburban Housing and Ownership

In “Subdivision with Spotlight,” identical houses receive theatrical illumination in darkness, emphasizing the uniformity of a sales model. Windows, lawns, and roads suggest both “a safe home” and housing as an asset, while the lives of residents remain imagined*6. In “Landscape with Houses,” his interest in housing, credit, and debt after the financial crisis is joined to an artificial development composed like a Dutch landscape painting*19. Prisons and suburban houses serve very different purposes, yet both use parcels, sight lines, and routes of movement to prescribe a desired form of life.

Light, Color, and Water

In the early black-and-white works, stark contrasts create a tension associated with surveillance photography and film noir. From the 1990s onward, blue water, yellow light, and green or peach walls introduced anxiety, cleanliness, seduction, and relief alongside the stated uses of the spaces*7. In models filled with water, floors reflect like mirrors and architectural boundaries become unstable. Flooded prisons, cellars, and houses evoke suppressed histories and the climate crisis eroding present-day security from within*3.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Spiral Staircase

“Spiral Staircase” shows only a spiral stair and a curving wall, without naming the place or depicting a person. The National Gallery of Art records it as a 2003 chromogenic print *5.The lucid geometry of the stair coexists with the uncertainty of an image that reveals neither entrance nor exit. The staircase suggests ascent or escape, yet both ends fall outside the frame, preventing the viewer from assigning it a definite use. The institutions Casebere addresses are first felt through this anticipation of movement, before they are identified through explanatory text.

Monticello

In works based on historic buildings, the generic quality of the model acquires a proper name. “Monticello” refers to Thomas Jefferson’s estate as a site where Enlightenment thought, republican government, and slavery coexisted. Its ordered symmetry carries both a national self-image and the history of exploited labor. Sean Kelly’s artist materials describe Casebere’s use of historic architecture as a vessel for political memory as an alternative to the heroic portrait*4.

Differences from Demand: Source Images

Casebere and Thomas Demand both construct models, exhibit photographs as the final works, and do not preserve the models after shooting. Demand rebuilds specific rooms, corridors, and gardens found in press or documentary images at full scale in paper and cardboard. By removing lettering, stains, and incidental detail, the model resembles a news image the viewer may remember while withholding the information that would identify the event.The Met describes his process of converting an existing news image into a full-scale paper model and destroying the model after it is photographed *20.

Casebere seldom uses a single press photograph as a blueprint. For prisons, schools, and suburban houses, he combines architectural sources, films, and personal memories to make spaces that correspond to no particular address. Demand’s photographs raise the question of which event an image refers to; Casebere’s ask why a given wall or corridor feels like a prison, school, or home.

Differences from Demand: The Models

Demand’s paper models remove traces of use and lettering from their source images, hollowing out the memory of an event preserved by the media. Casebere adjusts light, depth, water, and eye level to give bodily force to spaces that have never existed. Demand’s work depends on the gap between a source image and the photograph of its model; Casebere’s depends on the gap between a small construction and a space that feels monumental. Together, they show how model photography can address both the provenance of media images and the effects architecture exerts on behavior*11.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Constructed Photography and Architectural Critique

In the late 1970s, artists associated with the Pictures Generation quoted and reenacted figures and familiar images circulating through film, advertising, and magazines in order to examine the visual conventions through which society understands reality*17. Casebere directed the same inquiry toward architecture. Instead of photographing an existing building, he made models suggestive of prisons, schools, and houses. The model allowed him to set aside address, occupants, and event, and compare walls, windows, corridors, light, and circulation. Constructed photography could therefore examine spaces that organize bodily movement and feeling before a narrative begins, alongside staged scenes in which figures perform a story. Casebere’s significance within photographic history lies in using constructed photography to show architecture as a social mechanism that produces surveillance, isolation, ownership, and protection. Architecture becomes an active subject: a set of forms that directs behavior before any narrative unfolds*11.

Beauty and the Limits of Abstraction

Balanced compositions, deep shadows, and still surfaces of water give visual appeal even to prisons and post-disaster spaces. In “Credit, Faith & Trust,” the authority of financial, religious, and civic architecture is conveyed through sublime light and expansive interiors*9. That beauty communicates institutional force at the level of bodily sensation, while pushing the people subjected to it beyond the frame. The moment viewers feel drawn into an appealing space, they may also recognize that it organizes surveillance, isolation, credit, and ownership. This structure gives the work both its critical force and its limits.

Why Only the Photograph Remains

The model is dismantled after the shoot, leaving the photograph as the only finished form of a space that never existed. Through lighting and the lens, paper, plaster, paint, and water come to resemble stone, concrete, groundwater, and monumental architecture. Viewers begin by reading the photograph as a real building, then return to the model through a seam or an unnatural light. This movement makes clear that photography records spaces while also producing the shared visual ideas through which a place appears “prison-like” or “domestic”*13.

james-welling.html.lead_html: James Welling (born 1951, United States) moved from painting, dance, and video into photography. Through close-ups, photograms, filters, and digital compositing, he has transformed aluminum foil, gelatin, photographic paper, colored light, architecture, and the body into markedly different kinds of images. From works in which wrinkles, reflections, color, pressure, and depth register before the subject is identified to the layered color of Glass House and Choreograph, each series tests how a distinct technique can make photography act on bodily perception and feeling.
james-welling.html.thesis_html: As Pictures Generation artists used staging and rephotography to expose how images are constructed, Welling examined how ordinary materials and photographic processes could produce images charged with expansiveness, unease, and tactility. Working with aluminum foil, gelatin, photographic paper, and colored light, he brought a critique of pictorial construction together with the sensory effects of color, surface, and scale within the same photograph.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
From Painting, Dance, and Video to Photography

James Welling was born in Connecticut in 1951. He became interested in Color Field painting and Abstract Expressionism while still in high school and studied at Carnegie Mellon University with Gandy Brodie, a second-generation Abstract Expressionist. In 1969, a class visit took him to Mark Rothko’s studio, where he discussed Rothko’s predominantly black paintings with the artist.*21 When John Cage and Merce Cunningham were in residence at Carnegie Mellon, Welling repeatedly attended their rehearsals and performances. He later described that week as “life-changing.” He studied modern dance at the University of Pittsburgh, then encountered video and Conceptual art under John Baldessari at the California Institute of the Arts.*2 His early interest in fields of color remained visible in later works made with colored light.*21 His engagement with the body, time, and chance through dance and through Cage and Cunningham later informed his photograms, serial works, and Choreograph.*2

Video provided Welling’s entry into photography. His early tapes treated equipment-specific effects—noise from rough edits and abrupt shifts in white balance—as brief demonstrations. Stills photographed from a monitor on Tri-X film became his first gelatin silver prints. Welling has said that operating a large video camera and tripod led to his use of a 4 × 5 view camera in 1976 and, later, to scanners and digital cameras.*3 Photography allowed him to bring his experience of painting, dance, and video into a single body of work while retaining the idiosyncrasies of equipment, darkroom reactions, and printing misregistration as parts of the image.

Frampton and Moholy-Nagy

Welling approached modern photography partly through the films and criticism of structural filmmaker Hollis Frampton. Frampton’s Artforum essays on Edward Weston and Paul Strand led him toward Strand. After seeing Strand’s 1972 retrospective at LACMA, Welling encountered the pairing of religious sculpture and portraiture in Mexican Portfolio as something strikingly contemporary.*2 Welling has invoked Frampton’s “knight’s tour” as a metaphor for his own movement through different photographic possibilities from one series to the next.*2 László Moholy-Nagy’s photograms and elevated viewpoints offered two related models: recording objects and light directly on photographic paper, and using the camera to construct a space unavailable to ordinary vision.*12 Critics have connected New Abstractions to both Moholy-Nagy’s urban photographs and his photograms. In Welling’s work, camera-made images, cameraless processes, and negative reversal form a related set of methods for remaking perception.*23

The Pictures Generation and Expressiveness

In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Pictures Generation artists examined how established forms drawn from photography, film, and advertising produce models of identity and confer value on authorship.*17 Alexander Bigman draws attention to Welling’s description of his early works as “images about the act of feeling,” placing them alongside Cindy Sherman, Sherrie Levine, and David Salle in a broader reconsideration of what it meant to be expressive.*15 Sherman worked through performed personae, while Levine rephotographed canonical images. Welling used lighting, close-up views, exposure, and dark printing to turn aluminum foil, phyllo dough, and gelatin into images of black expanses and forceful ruptures. His concern lay in the image’s continuing effect on the body and emotions even after the material had been identified.*18

Welling later described his relation to photographic history as a form of “ventriloquism.” He transferred the rules that sustain established photographic forms to new subjects. In the railroad photographs, converging tracks produce speed and distance. In the architectural works, frontal views, raking light, and reflection layer interior and exterior through glass. In the dance photographs, arrested gestures intersect as RGB color layers. To “ventriloquize through different photographic grammars,” in Welling’s formulation, meant making viewpoint, perspective, exposure, reflection, arrested movement, and methods of output operate again through different technologies and subjects.*3

sections.title: Central Questions
sections.body_html:
Delaying Recognition of the Subject

Welling’s early photographs depict specific objects while extending the time required to identify them. In Aluminum Foil, wrinkles and reflections suggest the depth of a star field or rocky terrain. The phyllo dough in Untitled can resemble a landscape or stage, while the black masses in Gelatin Photographs evoke organisms or matter in a state of collapse.*1*5*6 The object never disappears from the image. Before it is understood, scale, space, and title generate other readings.

Welling has connected his “more abstract method” to the body, skin, and touch.*21 In Torsos, the density and folds of mesh, the passage of light, and contact with photographic paper bring pressure and weight forward more strongly than perspectival space.*18 Here, abstraction begins with a concrete object but allows surface, color, pressure, and depth to register before the subject can be described. The time a viewer needs to assemble meaning becomes part of the work.

Building Chance into the Process

For New Abstractions, Welling dropped strips of Bristol board onto film in darkness, fixing their positions, overlaps, and shadows as photograms.*10 Welling established a sequence involving the shape and fall of the paper, exposure, development, selection, and reprinting, while leaving room for unforeseen arrangements. In a conversation reflecting on Cage and Cunningham, he described continuing to make decisions while accepting unexpected results between total indeterminacy and complete control.*2 Chance entered the process as information: the material’s response could be observed and used to revise the next decision.

Treating Color as a Relation Within the Image

In Flowers, the contours of the plants remain legible while colors selected through filters and exposure replace their local color.*30 For Glass House, Welling photographed Philip Johnson’s transparent architecture through colored materials, Mylar, diffraction gratings, and lens flare placed before the camera.*7 The building’s straight lines remain intact as garden, interior, reflection, and colored material before the lens accumulate on a single plane, making interior and exterior—and the local colors of objects—difficult to separate at a glance. Welling has described the choice of viewpoint, the bodily movement of filters, changing light, and subsequent printing as a two-stage “performance.”*2 Color shifts from describing the subject to regulating relations among contour, transparency, reflection, and depth.

Recasting Analog Operations in Digital Form

Welling treats analog and digital photography as a continuous history of manipulating positive and negative, misregistration, color separation, grain, and support. Some works shown in the 2024 exhibition Thought Objects refer to the Waterhouse effect in silver-based development. He created positive and negative versions of a digital image as “two virtual sheets of film,” offset them slightly, and combined them through equidensity processing. The resulting images, with sharpening and misregistration accentuated, were printed at large scale in UV-cured ink on aluminum composite panels.*3 Digital images also involve channel processing, resolution interpolation, ink, support, and output dimensions. These choices determine contour, granularity, colored edging, and viewing distance. Welling reformulated judgments developed through analog photography as operations specific to digital production.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Aluminum Foil and Gelatin Photographs

For Aluminum Foil (1980–81), Welling folded sheets of foil borrowed from the restaurant where he worked, sometimes painted them black, and photographed them with a 4 × 5 camera. Dark contact prints the same size as the negatives maintain a one-to-one scale between object and image while turning wrinkles into spaces resembling star fields or rocky terrain.*1*4 For Gelatin Photographs (1984), Welling cooked gelatin—the substance that binds the light-sensitive layer of gelatin silver paper—as food, mixed it with black ink, and placed it on seamless paper used for product photography. The material that makes the photograph and the object depicted in it become the same substance, turning photographic self-reference into the physical structure of the work.*6

Degradés and New Abstractions

In Degradés, Welling exposed chromogenic paper to colored light, fixing fields of gradually shifting color. The Whitney Museum has described the work as evocative of Color Field painting.*18 The color fields arise from the reaction of light and photographic paper. In New Abstractions, the positions, overlaps, and shadows of paper strips dropped in darkness are fixed as photograms.*10 In both series, forms that resemble pictorial compositions are records of exposure, occlusion, contact, and time.

Diary / Landscape, Railroads, and Architecture

In Diary of Elizabeth and James Dixon / Connecticut Landscapes, photographs of Welling’s great-grandmother’s diary and other historical handwriting appear in the same sequence as contemporary views of family land.*11 By placing actual sites, family documents, and the present moment of photography in relation, the sequence rereads the past across different records and times instead of fixing it in a single image. In the later Railroad Photographs and photographs of H. H. Richardson’s architecture, Welling uses the converging perspective of railroad photography and the frontal views, raking light, and repetition associated with architectural photography, adding speed, distance, and rhythm to the description of place. After testing how materials transform an image, he turned to the ways established documentary grammars direct the perception and memory of a site.*3

Wyeth—Photographing Places Already Known Through Painting

Andrew Wyeth was a formative influence from the time Welling began painting in watercolor as a child. Beginning in 2010, he visited the landscapes, buildings, and interiors in Pennsylvania and Maine where Wyeth had worked, producing the color series Wyeth.*27 Exhibition materials describe how Welling absorbed Wyeth’s restrained palette, contrasts of surface, and effects of light while using postproduction to approach the painter’s nonnaturalistic compositions.*29 Welling has also noted Wyeth’s phrase “abstract flash” for a form that appears momentarily at the edge of vision.*28 By photographing places already known through paintings, Welling brings the actual site, Wyeth’s pictorial world, and his own memory and color processing into a single photograph.

Flowers and Glass House

For Flowers, Welling registered flowers as photograms on black-and-white film, then printed the negatives onto chromogenic paper through color filters.*30 In Glass House, he placed colored and diffractive materials before the lens while photographing transparent modern architecture.*9 The Japanese exhibition Notes on Color presented both series through their control of light, shadow, and time.*7 Across both series, filters shift from tools of color correction to instruments for exposing and photographing color itself.

Choreograph—Layering Three Photographs in RGB

In Choreograph, Welling assigns three black-and-white photographs—of dance, architecture, and landscape—to red, green, and blue channels and combines them in a single inkjet print. Bodily movement, architectural space, plants, and terrain become color layers that alter one another’s contours and depth, joining three sites of exposure within one perceptual space.*13 The title joins choreograph, “to draw in space,” with photograph, “to draw with light,” returning Welling’s early experience of dance to photographic color channels and bodily perception.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Changing Styles as a Method

Across successive series, Welling has moved among close-up photography, landscape, architectural photography, photograms, three-color separation, and digital compositing. Following Frampton’s model of the “knight’s tour,” he has described an approach that passes through different points in photographic history instead of perfecting a single style.*2 The Hammer Museum retrospective likewise framed his work across realism and transparency, abstraction and depiction, optics and description, and the material and chemical properties of photography.*22 Changes in style became a way to compare what each technique makes visible, what it delays, and what kinds of time and bodily perception it produces.

A conversation organized by ICA Philadelphia presented Welling as an artist working at the intersection of photography and painting, in a lineage extending from Gustave Le Gray and Edward Steichen. It located this connection in his attention to concrete sensory experience and in the different painterly possibilities offered by contact printing, digital layering, inkjet printing, and other technologies.*24 The color fields of Degradés, the transparent layers of Glass House, and the RGB composites of Choreograph create forms of color and layering specific to photography through light, photographic paper, filters, and digital processing.

Following Materiality Through the Output Process

In the early works, gelatin, emulsion, chemicals, paper, and physical contact determine the image surface. The Getty Museum’s 2015 exhibition Light, Paper, Process placed Welling within a history of material investigation extending from twentieth-century experimental photography, emphasizing his study of photographic paper’s sensitivity to light and its chemical processing.*20 In the digital works, on-screen processing, ink, support, and output dimensions form one continuous production sequence. A MoMA discussion likewise addressed what constitutes a photograph after film and photographic paper, and how an inkjet printer might be understood as a photographic technology.*8 Welling’s concern lies less in nostalgia for materials than in the decisions photographers make with each material and the ways their traces persist through digital processing.*3 Recent works that print the same source image through silver-based processes, inkjet, and handmade emulsions—altering even the perceived age and gender of a face—make this idea concrete.*16

Chris Wiley discussed the work of Walead Beshty, Liz Deschenes, Mariah Robertson, and Eileen Quinlan—artists concerned with supports, chemicals, lensless methods, and digital surfaces—within a lineage running from Talbot, Moholy-Nagy, and Man Ray through Welling.*25 The 2008 Whitney Biennial also brought Welling and Beshty together in a public seminar as artists whose work takes photography’s own representational field as a subject and builds abstract compositions from ordinary objects.*26 Together, these sources trace a historical sequence in which photographic supports and production technologies became subjects in their own right. They place Welling between the Pictures Generation’s examination of constructed images and a later generation’s attention to support, exposure, chemical processing, and digital surfaces.

Feeling and Reception in Constructed Images

Bigman interprets Welling’s photographs of the early 1980s as a reconsideration of expressiveness at a moment when faith in modernist self-expression had weakened.*15 In Aluminum Foil, Drapes, and Gelatin Photographs, images that initially resemble vast spaces or damaged matter return to ordinary objects once their materials are known. This shift recasts feeling as an effect of material preparation, lighting, close-up photography, exposure, title, and the darkness of the print. The emotional force appears as something produced through the photograph’s construction. Viewers can recognize that an image has been deliberately constructed and still experience its sensory force.

The 2012 exhibition Mind on Fire presented Welling’s early close-ups, photograms, and color-field works alongside materials from the period in which they were made.*19 The 2014 ICP Infinity Award recognized Welling for producing both depictive and abstract images and for bringing an experimental sensibility to photography.*14 These exhibitions and the award presented his early material experiments, architectural and landscape records, cameraless works, color, and digital output as a continuous inquiry into how different techniques produce perception and feeling.

janaina-tschape.html.lead_html: Janaina Tschäpe is an artist who has photographed herself and other women wearing fabric, balloon-like organs, and plant-like forms in the sea, forests, gardens, and cities. Focusing on 100 Little Deaths, Melantropics, and Blood, Sea, this page examines how photography, moving image, and performance produce images of metamorphosis in which the human body approaches animal, plant, water, and landscape.
janaina-tschape.html.thesis_html: Staged photography has often used costumes and sets to construct a figure as another role or character within a narrative. Tschäpe moved away from intensifying a figure’s “role” and toward temporarily deforming the outline of the human body itself. Dissatisfaction with painting and practical limits on studio production pushed her toward cameras and performance. She attached fabric, latex, water-filled and balloon-like forms to bodies and photographed states that existed only briefly in seas and forests. Where staged photography often fixed an enacted persona in the image, Tschäpe made photography a medium for preserving a body in the middle of change as it approaches animal, plant, or terrain.
