sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Hamburg to New York—Dissatisfaction with Painting and the Turn to the Camera

Tschäpe was born in Munich in 1973 and grew up in Brazil. She studied at the Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg from 1992 to 1997 and received an MFA from the School of Visual Arts in New York in 1998*16. Her official biography records a career spanning photography, moving image, performance, sculpture, drawing, and painting*2. Sarasota Art Museum’s retrospective likewise presents her early photography and video through later painting as a sustained inquiry into metamorphosis and landscape*1. In a 2024 interview, Tschäpe recalled a German art-school environment strongly shaped by male artists and conceptual art. At a moment when she was frustrated with painting and preparing to study in New York, she could not afford a studio and began making performances with a room and a camera instead*26. In a 2026 interview, she similarly explains that her initial interest lay less in photography or film as media in themselves than in using the camera to record intimate, temporary performances so they could later be shown*27. Early inflatable latex sculptures already treated the human body as sculpture; Sandra Firmin’s 2005 exhibition essay traces that concern into performance and photography*24. Firmin distinguishes moving image, which retains motion and duration, from photography, which preserves performance as a suspended possibility and prompts viewers to imagine an environment continuing beyond the frame*24. Tschäpe’s own description of seeking a state “between” human beings and nature further clarifies why these bodily transformations were never simply experiments in costume*3. A camera initially chosen under practical constraint became a way to preserve a body that existed only for the duration of the performance.

Body and Landscape in the 1990s—Body Art, Romanticism, and Staged Photography

Tschäpe’s early work emerged at a time when self-portraiture, performance for the camera, and staged photography had become major ways of thinking about gender and the body. The National Museum of Women in the Arts exhibition Live Dangerously placed artists from Ana Mendieta in the 1970s through Tschäpe within a photographic history that reconsidered relations between women’s bodies and nature*6. This does not establish direct influence from Mendieta, but it provides an institutional framework for comparing earlier body art that placed women in landscapes with Tschäpe’s staged, invented creatures. Firmin also argues that although Tschäpe grew up in Brazil, she responded strongly to nineteenth-century German Romanticism, especially Caspar David Friedrich’s landscapes and imagery of death*24. Germano Celant records that 100 Little Deaths began in 1996 and grew out of a repeated action in which Tschäpe treated her own body as part of the landscape while traveling*22. Vitoria Daniela Bousso distinguishes photography as a “piece of time” that prompts viewers to imagine what comes before and after from moving image as a medium of duration and sound, clarifying the logic behind Tschäpe’s use of multiple media*25. In a later BOMB conversation, water and changing nature remain central elements across media, confirming that the relation between body and landscape in her early photographs was not a temporary stylistic phase*23.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Moving the Body from “Person” Toward Part of the Environment

The National Museum of Women in the Arts describes Tschäpe’s work through water, dreams, women’s bodies, and metamorphosis, and holds He Drowned in Her Eyes as She Called Him to Follow, in which a mermaid-like figure appears by the sea*4. The figure is not the central subject of a portrait meant to communicate character or biography. Lying face down, covered in fabric, or extending tentacle-like forms, the body approaches a shape that cannot be securely classified as a single species. Photography’s clarity intensifies that uncertainty by preserving the sense that this strange body really stood before the camera.

100 Little Deaths—The Repeated Fallen Body

100 Little Deaths, made between 1996 and 2002, repeatedly shows Tschäpe lying face down on the ground in different locations. NMWA situates the series within her exploration of landscape, transformation, and death*5. In Live Dangerously, the museum presented all one hundred images together, emphasizing the structure of a repeated bodily pose against changing travel landscapes*6. Because the body remains prone as the setting changes, the commemorative claim of the tourist photograph—“I was here”—recedes. The figure can seem absorbed by the site or expelled into it as a foreign object. In the artist’s account quoted by NMWA, the series grew from a feeling of leaving a part of herself in each place she traveled through; the fallen posture is repeated to register how location alters the self rather than to produce a conventional souvenir photograph*5.

Melantropics—Photographing an Invented Botany

The Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis presented Melantropics as a body of work combining natural environments with artificial costumes and props, mythology and folklore, and invented botanical naming*7. As the title’s fusion of “melancholy” and “tropics” suggests, the work does not simply celebrate tropical abundance. Plant-like figures, fabricated organs, and humid landscapes make the boundary between natural and artificial unstable. Costume functions less as a special effect that conceals the body than as a joint through which the body can adopt the same formal vocabulary as its environment.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Blood, Sea—Water Dissolves the Body’s Boundaries

Blood, Sea was filmed and photographed at locations including Weeki Wachee Springs in Florida, with women in sculptural costumes floating underwater. USF Contemporary Art Museum describes the work as high-definition moving imagery in which sculptural costume and nature move between dream and reality*8. The museum’s media materials also document a multi-screen installation and related works in which still and moving images form a single environment*9. Underwater, weakened gravity keeps fabric, hair, and bodies in motion, making the outline of the human figure difficult to stabilize even in a still image.

Chimera—Several Forms of Existence Converge in One Body

The Irish Museum of Modern Art exhibition Chimera used the hybrid creature as an idea extending across photography, moving image, and painting: several identities or biological features merge into a single being*10. IMMA’s Sultry Moon likewise records a submerged, magical scene in which figure, moon, and landscape depart from realistic scale*11. Such photographs do not narrate transformation step by step. They fix one intermediate state as a convincing surface, leaving the unresolved condition of being impossible to classify more persistent than the question of what the figure has transformed into.

Photography as Series—Turning a Single Transformation into a Repeatable Vocabulary

The official presentation of 100 Little Deaths makes the series structure explicit through the recurrence of the same bodily form across many locations*12. Official documentation of Blood, Sea similarly shows moving and still images emerging from the same bodily vocabulary*13. In TBA21 Academy’s Aquatica, Tschäpe describes a method that crosses geological and biological nature with imagination, developing fabricated costumes and invented species through photography, moving image, and drawing*14. The shoot is therefore not documentation of a finished sculpture. It is the production itself: a one-time joining of body, costume, and place.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Photography Was Never Merely a Preliminary Stage for Painting

Centre Pompidou records and holds works including Blood, Sea and Dreamstructure, placing Tschäpe’s photography and moving image within museum collections as autonomous parts of her work*15. Sean Kelly’s artist profile likewise traces her exploration of organic forms and landscapes across photography, moving image, and sculpture, without reducing the work to painting*16. Even as her later paintings receive wider attention, the early photographs and performances are more than experiments preceding a return to painting. They are the place where her method of dislodging the body from a fixed, self-contained subject first became concrete.

Reading Women’s Bodies and Nature—Institutional Framing and the Artist’s Own Account

Tschäpe has been exhibited within feminist and post-Mendieta histories of artists placing women’s bodies in nature. The National Museum of Women in the Arts exhibition Live Dangerously placed Mendieta and Tschäpe within a history of women repositioning their own bodies in the landscape*6. Tschäpe herself, however, has said that the use of her body in early works was intended to express her subjectivity as an artist, not specifically female agency*28. The two accounts are best kept distinct as reception history and self-definition. A photographic and institutional history clearly exists around the female body in nature, while Tschäpe’s works themselves direct attention beyond gender alone toward states in which the body changes into water, plant, animal, and memory.

Reception in Japan and Tschäpe’s Place in 2000s Staged Photography

Nichido Contemporary Art records several exhibitions in Japan beginning with Lacrimacorpus in Tokyo in 2005, showing that Tschäpe has been presented there continuously since the period of her photography and moving-image work*17. Galerie Max Hetzler likewise documents her international exhibitions and collections, situating the work’s movement across media within contemporary art*18. A 2002 review in Der Tagesspiegel treated the repetition of 100 Little Deaths and the questions of body, transformation, and identity in works using performers as contemporary concerns*19. Xippas’s presentation of Melantropics emphasizes the retreat of the conventional human figure toward beings that combine plant, animal, and artificial elements*20. Inclusion in Photo Art further indicates that this work was recognized as part of photography’s expansion in the 2000s*21.

Photographic Significance—From “Who Is Photographed?” to “How Far Can a Body Change?”

Tschäpe’s photographs connect with histories of self-portraiture and the representation of women while weakening the portrait’s conventional emphasis on face and personality. Through performances made for the camera, she treats the body as material on the same pictorial plane as fabric, water, plants, and ground, temporarily transforming it into another kind of organism. At a moment when staged photography often moved toward cinematic narrative and psychological drama, Tschäpe used staging to destabilize the category of the human body itself. Because photography stops transformation, an organism that never existed can appear to have existed before the lens. The medium’s stillness therefore becomes a device for thinking through metamorphosis.

twitter.title: Jean-Luc Moulène | Documents, Strike Objects, and Photography | Photo Coordinates
twitter.description: Jean-Luc Moulène's Documents, Objets de grève, Produits de Palestine, and Opus connect photography, labor, commodities, circulation, and object production.

jean-luc-moulene.html.lead_html: In Documents, Jean-Luc Moulène photographed cities, commodities, political signs, and objects made by workers. In Objets de grève and Produits de Palestine, he connected the visual codes of product photography to the problem of circulation. He later made objects himself in Opus, treating photography and sculpture as one working system. His work transformed photography from neutral record into an operation that produces an object's value, use, movement, and public appearance.
jean-luc-moulene.html.thesis_html: Moulène treated documentary photography as a productive act: finding an object, photographing and printing it, then circulating the image through union journals, museums, and product catalogues. Photography was immediate and portable, capable of recording an object's state while sending its image into another social circuit when the object itself could not move. In Objets de grève, he photographed items made by workers who redirected a company's equipment and skills, using the precision of advertising photography. In Produits de Palestine, he moved commodities excluded from markets beyond borders as images. In the later Opus, he intervened in the formation of objects through design, mathematics, industrial technique, and the resistance of materials. His consistent question is who makes an object, who owns it, and through which circuits its meaning and status change. The movement between photography and sculpture was necessary for turning transformations from object to image, and from image or plan back into object, into the work itself.

sections.title: Documents and the Background to Choosing Photography
sections.body_html:
Why Photography? Recording Objects and Sending Them into Other Circuits

After receiving a degree in art and literature from the Sorbonne in 1976, Moulène worked in performance, teaching, and corporate communications. In the 1980s he produced product presentations for the defense company Thomson-Sintra. Within an organization of engineers and factory workers, he learned how manufactured goods are explained, classified, kept confidential, and presented to society*26. Centre Pompidou's artist materials relate his movement across photography, printed matter, and objects to an interest in technical culture and social production*4. When Moulène recalled in the Centre Pompidou's 2016 exhibition that he had occupied the point where industrial communication met the bodily experiments of 1970s art, he identified two experiences that continued to shape his work*1. His approach of first establishing a problem and then choosing materials and techniques for that problem is also evident in the museum's video material*8。

. Photography became his first major means because, as he has said, it was “everywhere”: a tool for recording out of curiosity and for understanding social life and the ways people respond to objects*23. Dia's catalogue notes that photography and drawing were portable and compact, which made them his most frequently used media throughout the 1990s*26. A photograph does more than record an object in place. It can be reproduced and move into newspapers, union journals, posters, catalogues, and museums, reaching a range distinct from the original object. Sculpture alone could not send small objects made during a factory occupation, or products cut off from markets, into public space at the same speed and scale. For Moulène, photography was an operation that altered an object's social status and route of circulation, more than a passive image of reality. This portability and reproducibility became the basis for treating photographs, printed matter, exhibitions, and sculpture as one protocol.

Disjonctions: Turning Everyday Objects into Open-Ended Documents

Documents, begun in the late 1980s, includes a body of photographs known as Disjonctions: images of cities, streets, signs, bodies, commodities, and landscapes. The frames often have a frontal clarity, but offer no explanation of an event or continuous narrative. Crousel describes them as indeterminate topographic references found within the real world*3. Even when a title specifies place, season, or date, the reason an object was photographed remains unsettled. Centre Pompidou's 04 07 1996 (os) is a large Cibachrome presenting bones and leaves as a color still life*7. The bones might appear as natural-history specimens, criminal evidence, or sculpture, but the photograph assigns them to no single institution. The term “document” names a form that temporarily makes an object visible and submits it to public reading, rather than declaring photographic objectivity.

sections.title: Methods for Photographing Commodities, Labor, and Politics
sections.body_html:
Objets de grève: Reclaiming Equipment, Skill, and Circulation

Objets de grève is a series for which Moulène located and photographed goods made by French workers in factories occupied during strikes, using production equipment, materials, and skills. Hats, cigarettes, perfume, clothing, cookware, tickets, and banknotes departed from the products ordered by company management; workers made them in small quantities to raise strike funds and gather public solidarity. Paolo Magagnoli's research confirms that the objects were intended to support workers financially and attract public backing, and that many disappeared through use*24. Each object records a temporary redirection of machinery owned by the company and knowledge held by the workers. The strike appears as a dispute over the right to produce, not simply a suspension of production. Centre Pompidou's Vingt-quatre objets de grève presents individual items like equivalent catalogue illustrations while tying each one to a factory and struggle*6. Moulène did more than preserve the objects in a museum. By photographing them and sending the images into union journals and exhibitions, he recirculated an action inside the factory as an image outside it. MACBA's Trente-neuf objets de grève treats photographs and printed matter as one work because circulation itself belongs to the document*9。

Repurposing the Codes of Advertising Photography

The strike objects are photographed with the ordered backgrounds and clear presentation of form and color associated with product photography. Moulène did not homogenize their surfaces through studio lighting; he used a large-format camera and natural light to preserve scratches, distortions, and material differences. Centre Pompidou's commentary notes that, as workers redirected corporate resources, the artist borrowed advertising codes while emphasizing the specificity of each object through natural light and large-format photography*5. Conventional product photography removes histories and labor that might interfere with purchase. Here, orderly presentation brings the object's exceptional production history to the foreground. The tension of the work arises from the mismatch between photography's neutral appearance and the political background of strike, occupation, and solidarity.

Produits de Palestine: Moving Photographs When Objects Cannot Move

For Produits de Palestine (2002–04), Moulène collected food, cigarettes, medicines, clothing, and household goods made in Palestine, photographing them frontally in a manner close to product imagery. Bidoun reports that the photographs—from olive oil to underwear—concretely show the breadth of life and production that persists under occupation*14. Carlier | Gebauer likewise places the series at the center of Documents' inquiry into production, display, and circulation*20. The photographs do not free markets as substitutes for commodities, but they fill a visual absence in which “Palestinian products” can be treated as though they do not exist, placing concrete objects with names, packaging, colors, and uses before viewers. The movement of the image does more than symbolize political content. By bringing packaging, trademarks, and places of manufacture into international viewing spaces, it uses photography's actual circulation to bypass, provisionally, the systems through which occupation and sanctions determine what may exist as a commodity. ICP's copy of the photobook 48 Palestinian Products shows that this detour persisted beyond a temporary exhibition as a publication available in libraries*10。

Foregrounding the Act of “Presentation” Over the Artist's Name

The full title of Objets de grève includes the phrase “presented by Jean-Luc Moulène.” It identifies his role as an intermediary who finds, photographs, distributes, and exhibits objects, instead of claiming ownership as their maker. Centre Pompidou explains that the work includes the circulation of photographs through exhibitions, distributable booklets, and newspaper inserts, and that the word “presented” signals the artist's withdrawal*5. This withdrawal does not remove responsibility. It strengthens the editorial authority exercised through selecting what appears, setting its sequence, and choosing the medium through which it circulates. The photographer's work therefore extends from the instant of exposure to the image's entire social route.

sections.title: Treating Photography and Objects as One System
sections.body_html:
Documents: Placing Heterogeneous Objects on Photography's Common Surface

Documents includes city views, nudes, animals, plants, industrial products, and political signs alongside strike objects and Palestinian products. Refusing to unify subject matter makes visible photography's power to give heterogeneous things a shared surface, scale, and viewing distance. Kunstverein Hannover described a trajectory from early, prototype-like product photographs to series that retrospectively document temporal and social situations, treating the function of photography as the central question*15. As a Frieze review notes, Moulène's photographs are designed as images that change scale and use in response to support and exhibition environment, and that can be reused, enlarged, and repositioned*13. The four-volume Documents 1999–2016 rearranged images across individual series and presented the photographs as a mutable archive*11. Galerie Chantal Crousel's Documents 2016 likewise presented photography as a continuous investigation of the social state in which objects appear, rather than classifying the images under one subject*12. The meaning of one photograph changes not only through the depicted object's attributes but through the document placed beside it and the printed matter or institution it enters. At this stage Moulène was examining the way already existing things change status by becoming images.

Opus: Thinking of Object Production as a “Protocol”

From the late 1990s onward, Moulène increasingly made sculptural objects of his own alongside photography. Documents searches for existing things and transforms them through photography and circulation; Opus intervenes in design, material, and manufacturing technique before an object exists. Dia's exhibition presented Opus and photography together as “object and image,” making their relation of transformation the subject*2. Body (2011) gives this connection a concrete form. Moulène established a shape through ideas of topology and branching, then worked with Renault automotive engineers to form twelve strip-like components into a hollow object resembling a vehicle body yet lacking a practical function*26. Diagrams, calculations, and three-dimensional models become matter through an industrial process. Kunsthal Extra City points to his inseparable treatment of medium, authorship, delegation, and collaboration with materials across photography and sculpture*18. Because materials resist plans and engineers or craftspeople alter forms through their decisions, the completed object is not a faithful realization of a shape held in the artist's mind. Documents and Opus are linked by a protocol for examining where transformations occur among images, objects, labor, and technology, not by a shared appearance.

A “Retrospective of Protocols,” Not a Conventional Retrospective

For his 2016 solo exhibition at Centre Pompidou, Moulène conceived a “retrospective of protocols” in which he made roughly thirty new works instead of arranging established works chronologically*1. Rules involving materials, mathematics, sets, intersections, and cuts unfolded across the gallery, designed so that one work would become a tool for reading another. In describing an ideal exhibition, the artist speaks of using one work to read others, then moving to the next in a repeated process*1. Kunsthal Extra City's ENDWARDS likewise presented photographs and objects as concurrent operations crossing time, material, delegation, and collaboration*18. The “retrospective of protocols” was therefore more than an abstract declaration of method. It was an exhibition form that compared the redirected equipment of Objets de grève, the detoured circulation of Produits de Palestine, and the industrial forming of Body as problems applied to different objects.

sections.title: Reception, Criticism, and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Preserving Workers' Creativity and the Ambivalence of Artistic Appropriation

Seen in a museum, the items of Objets de grève become clear still-life photographs attributed to Moulène. This transformation preserves workers' skill and struggle, yet it also risks allowing an artist to appropriate others' labor and endow it with new commodity value. Magagnoli analyzes the series as an ambivalent archive that can be read both as a celebration of working-class creativity and as its unjust appropriation, preserving labor history while also enabling forgetting and reification*24. An ArtReview exhibition review likewise values the way Moulène's objects retain contradictions of production and display instead of fixing political meaning as a clear message*17. This criticism is not external to the work. It concerns why Moulène identifies himself as a “presenter” and differentiates the positions of author, producer, owner, and exhibition institution. The clean appearance of advertising photography is not a neutrality that erases politics. It returns to viewers the question of whether workers' objects are commodities, artworks, or historical documents, exposing how image-making necessarily produces a new valuation.

Making Photographing, Printing, and Circulation One Document

Bernd and Hilla Becher's industrial photography and Conceptual Art opened photography from the expressive single image toward systems of record, typology, and information. Moulène added the production of the recorded object, its transformation into a commodity, its political restriction, and its entrance into another circuit as an image to the work itself. Dia describes his career as “one continuous performance” of collecting the surrounding world, rearranging it, and placing it in another frame*25. An exhibition at the Secession presented photographs and fabricated objects as one spatial operation, establishing an early reception that did not divide his work by medium*16. Beirut Art Center similarly introduced this continuity internationally through an installation crossing photographs, objects, and production materials*19. Centre Pompidou's exhibition catalogue assembles new protocols, conversations, and production material and remains a major source for examining the connection from photography to Opus*21. Publications and records held by the Bibliothèque Kandinsky provide a basis for studying the work across photobooks, printed matter, sculpture, and dialogue*22. Alain Badiou's Matter and Form, which analyzes five objects individually, indicates the development of a philosophical reception centered on matter, form, and operation*27. Moulène demonstrated that a document need not be evidence produced after a completed reality. The acts of finding, photographing, printing, and moving an object—and of manufacturing a new object from a diagram or model—can themselves become documents that act on real structures of production and ownership.

jean-luc-mylayne.html.lead_html: Jean-Luc Mylayne (b. 1946) is a French photographer whose long-standing fascination with birds has developed into an inquiry into the conditions under which common species and humans can share the same space. In 1976, he and his wife and collaborator Mylène gave up their settled life to devote themselves fully to the work, choosing to spend weeks or months in places where rural environments and human habitation meet. Using large-format cameras and custom-made multifocal lenses, he brings birds, grass, buildings, and sky into a single image without subordinating them to one plane of focus, allowing the eye to move among different distances as it does in the world. Titles that record the period of production, together with color prints that are generally unique, build into the work the time required for the distance between photographer and bird to shift before a photograph can be made.
jean-luc-mylayne.html.thesis_html: Wildlife photography developed methods that place the photographer at a distance, using telephoto lenses and camouflage to record avian behavior from afar. Mylayne repeatedly returns to the same site and waits until birds recognize both photographer and equipment and come close again. His multifocal lenses keep the bird within its surroundings, directing the eye toward grass, buildings, and sky as well. The work therefore makes the time spent sharing a place with the bird and the viewer’s movement through the image part of what constitutes the photograph.

sections.title: Background and Points of Departure
sections.body_html:
From Philosophy to Photography — Joining Work and Life in 1976

Jean-Luc Mylayne was born in Marquise, northern France, in 1946 and studied philosophy. Although deeply interested in painting and poetry, he chose photography as the center of his work at an early stage*23. Material from the Museo Reina Sofía describes Mylayne as treating photography as a medium of “truth,” grounding his inquiry in the camera’s ability to record what exists in the world*23. In 1976, he and his wife and collaborator Mylène gave up their house, car, and other possessions, reorganizing their lives around photography*1. Sprüth Magers connects this change in their way of living to the method that followed*2. From then on, the couple stayed for extended periods in places inhabited by birds, preparing composition, light, and focus over time while preserving the fact that an actual bird had to enter the frame.

The Attraction of Bluebirds — How Birds Became the Subject

The Lannan Foundation describes Mylayne’s work as bringing together two passions: art and ornithology*27. Speaking about North American bluebirds, Mylayne has said that from the age of ten he imagined one day going to the United States to see them*1. FRAC Auvergne likewise notes his strong childhood interest in birds and the encyclopedic knowledge he developed outside the discipline of science*30. He was especially drawn to the blue of the three North American species—the Mountain, Western, and Eastern Bluebirds—and his later work in the United States developed into a long-term project in “blue,” linking the color of the birds to the blue of the sky*1. Over years of photographing birds, this sustained attachment opened onto questions of time, distance, otherness, and control within photography.

Familiar Birds as Individuals

Mylayne’s interest in birds centers on individual relationships more than on collecting rare species or identifying species. He has described his aim as understanding how humans are situated within the life of a bird, instead of producing a likeness of the bird itself*1. John James Audubon (1785–1851), the naturalist and artist, is best known for the monumental The Birds of America (1827–38), which depicted the birds of North America*28. At the Nevada Museum of Art, Mylayne characterized Audubon as an ornithologist and portraitist of birds who enabled viewers to recognize species through color and habitat; he located his own concern in the conditions under which humans might live in harmony with nature*22. The Museo Reina Sofía exhibition booklet similarly places the exchange between human and animal, and the recognition of birds as beings both comparable to and different from humans, at the center of the work*23. Birds move on their own, keep their distance, and recognize the photographer; their behavior therefore participates in whether the image can come into being.

Mylayne repeatedly works with small birds that also appear near human habitation—sparrows, thrushes, wrens, starlings, and bluebirds among them. Josef Helfenstein notes that he mainly chooses ordinary small songbirds and does not pursue large birds of prey*24. The Museo Reina Sofía describes his sites as farmland, gardens, and suburban areas where human influence remains visible, avoiding isolated, uninhabited nature*23. Helfenstein also argues that the tendency of small birds to avoid human proximity and move quickly intensifies the tension with photography’s stillness*24. Their proximity to human life, combined with their continuing freedom to leave, gives rise to the waiting and mutual regard that shape Mylayne’s method.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Waiting and “Mutual Regard” — Adapting to the Bird’s Time

In Mylayne’s photographs, the time of making the work is difficult to separate from the time of everyday life. Twin Palms Publishers notes that the couple repeatedly returned to the same places in France and the American West, sometimes spending several months on a single work*15. The Lannan Foundation describes long stays at shooting sites, where Mylayne first locates a setting and then studies the birds’ habits and recurring behavior*1. Kestner Gesellschaft likewise emphasizes that composition is prepared through changes in season, weather, and light*10. The final exposure may be brief, but extended residence and observation are built into the making of the image.

Mylayne developed his fascination with birds into a method in which the human side adapts to the animal’s time. Sprüth Magers explains that he prepares the site, composition, and light, then spends weeks or months—and at times close to a year—until the bird grows accustomed to the people and equipment*20. He selects the site, determines the frame, studies the bird’s behavior, and repeatedly installs the equipment. Waiting is an active process of preparing a situation in which the photographer and camera become part of the bird’s everyday environment.

Sprüth Magers describes Mylayne as a self-taught photographer who studied philosophy and situates his work within an inquiry into time and the relation between humans and nature*2. The Museo Reina Sofía identifies several forms of time in his photographs: the long period of preparation, the instant recorded by the shutter, the cyclical return of migratory birds, and the historical time in which human and nonhuman life have shared a place*3. By waiting for a bird, learning the cycle in which an individual returns, and revisiting a site until the distance of alarm changes, Mylayne makes time both a subject and a physical requirement of the photograph.

According to the Lannan Foundation, Mylayne avoids the telephoto lenses and camouflage common in wildlife photography. He leaves a heavy large-format camera in place and waits for birds to become accustomed to both human and equipment*1. He makes his presence known and returns until it becomes part of the bird’s daily surroundings. The instant of exposure arrives at the end of a relationship formed over weeks or months.

The Arts Club of Chicago calls this relationship “mutual regard.” Mylayne distinguishes individual birds before photographing them, while the birds in turn recognize the photographer and his equipment. The Arts Club explains that he sets up a view camera and lighting equipment in the same place each day and makes the photograph when a bird enters the position he has anticipated*7. The Museo Reina Sofía notes that it can take weeks for a bird to become accustomed to his presence and to the sound of the shutter*23. The photographer designs the composition; the bird’s approach and willingness to remain complete the photograph.

Within this reciprocity, the bird remains wild and free to leave. Helfenstein describes the bird as an “untamable other,” resisting absorption into the human world and withholding any easy promise of coexistence or communication*24. Huis Marseille explains that trust must develop, while feeding and taming are excluded from the method*6. A photograph becomes possible when an individual that remains free to depart temporarily stays within the composition.

Custom Lenses and the Tableau — Moving the Eye Through Multiple Planes of Focus

A photograph fixes a single exposure, while human vision continually shifts focus in the world—from bird to tree, from foreground to distance. Mylayne designs and makes his own lenses to place several planes of focus within one image and translate this moving vision into photographic form. Material from macLYON explains that the lenses create multiple focal points, keeping the viewer’s gaze in motion and bringing the image closer to the functioning of the eye*29. Sprüth Magers likewise describes combinations of hand-ground custom lenses that distribute sharpness and blur across several layers, producing a layered image in which light appears almost sculpted*20.

The Berlin Art Week text for Reflection explains that multiple focus creates abrupt transitions between sharp and blurred areas, loosening the control of a single focal point and one-point perspective and moving the viewer’s eye through different spatial layers*19. Mylayne’s custom optics allow several distances to register at different degrees of clarity at once, making the act of looking itself unfold over time.

Mylayne calls his images tableaux. Before a bird arrives, he prepares the site, composition, light, color, and the anticipated position of the bird as an “actor.” macLYON compares this process to the way a painter builds an image in stages, selecting its content and structure, the placement of figures, and the distribution of color*29. FRAC Auvergne likewise discusses the friction between prolonged waiting and instantaneous exposure through the idea of the tableau, describing an image constructed in a manner closer to painting*30.

FRAC Auvergne connects Mylayne’s multifocal lenses to art-historical debates around optical devices and the construction of paintings by Holbein, Caravaggio, Ingres, and Vermeer*30. The same text compares his shifts between sharpness and blur to the eye moving from one plane to another, to localized blur and halos in Vermeer, and to disjunctions suggestive of Cézanne’s multiple viewpoints*30. The connection to painting therefore lies in a method of construction: information seen from different positions can coexist within one image without being subordinated to a single fixed viewpoint.

This decentering through the lens corresponds to Mylayne’s frequent use of the square format. Curator Ralph Rugoff argues that where the vertical “portrait” and horizontal “landscape” imply directional orientation, the square does not tell the viewer where to look and creates an even, decentered pictorial field*29. The square leaves the direction of the image open, while multifocal optics prevent attention from settling on a single center. Bird, grass, building, and sky can therefore coexist at different distances and degrees of sharpness. Sprüth Magers’s description of Mylayne’s visual space as nonhierarchical, with birds rarely placed at the center of the image, follows the same logic*20.

Helfenstein interprets Mylayne’s avoidance of telephoto capture and his adaptation of the camera to the bird’s unpredictable behavior as a shift in the role of the photographic apparatus*24. Sprüth Magers explains that multiple focus and nonhierarchical composition keep the bird connected to its surroundings and send the viewer’s eye moving through the image*20. Waiting and multifocal optics thus operate in parallel: both organize the terms of relation and perception without placing the bird under unilateral control.

Production Time Written into the Titles

The works are generally titled with a sequence number and the months and year of production, foregrounding duration over species name or location. Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles explains that the titles withhold place while indicating the time required to reach the bird as an other*5. In the 2026 Reflection exhibition, titles that omit place and species while retaining the months of production were again identified as central to the temporality of the work*19. The eye moves through several distances within the image, while the title extends production across weeks or months; together, these structures stretch the photograph’s brief exposure through both space and time.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Unique Photographs and Collaboration with Mylène

Mylayne has consistently worked with analog color photography, prints that are generally unique, and extended periods of production. Huis Marseille identifies this combination—analog photography, unique prints, decades of concentration on the same subject, and long periods spent on individual works—as fundamental to his work*6. The time required for a particular composition to become possible is specific to each photograph, and that singularity is echoed by the unique-print format.

Alongside Jean-Luc’s waiting, collaboration with his wife Mylène is equally integral to the work. Huis Marseille explains that Mylène is deeply involved in production and exhibition design, and that the couple adopted Mylène’s given name as their shared surname, inscribing that bond into the authorial name itself*6. The Arts Club of Chicago likewise conceived Mutual Regard as a collaboration involving Jean-Luc and Mylène, two art institutions, birds, gardens, and architecture*7. Huis Marseille also notes that the arrangement of works was redesigned for each venue on the exhibition tour*6. From the artist’s name to shared life at the shooting sites and the design of exhibitions, the work is presented as an ongoing collaboration between the couple.

From the Early Works to No. B4 — The Tableau and Titles as Records of Time

FRAC Auvergne presents N°4, Juin–Août 1979 as a “foundational work” in which Mylayne understood how a tableau could be constructed*30. A bird appears within the opening of a barn; the colors of its plumage connect with the barn, roof, and wall, while the curve of its tail corresponds to the shapes of a distant roof and trees*30. The same text compares the partly blurred roof and white wall to Nicolas de Staël and the relation of curves to verticals and horizontals to the pictorial construction of Piet Mondrian*30. From early in Mylayne’s career, waiting for the instant when the bird entered the frame was joined to a tableau method in which color, line, shape, and depth had already been organized.

N°68, Janvier Février Mars 1987 shows that by 1987 Mylayne had established the use of a number and months of production in the title*12. According to Berlin Art Week, his titles record only the number in the production sequence and the months and year of making, omitting location and bird species*19. The number marks the order of production; the months register the time required for an image to come into being. Repetition of the same broad subject—birds—is thus divided into durations specific to individual works.

The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston holds No. B4, Novembre–Décembre 2000, Janvier 2001, whose title preserves a production period extending across three months*11. The title alone makes visible the gap between a momentary exposure and a process lasting several months. It places the instant recorded by the shutter and the extended preparation that made that instant possible within the same record.

North American Bluebirds — From a Childhood Fascination to a Project in Blue

From 1999 onward, with support from the Lannan Foundation, Mylayne spent extended periods in New Mexico and Texas and realized the project with the three North American bluebird species he had imagined since childhood*1. He conceived these stays as a long-term project in “blue,” linking the blue of the birds’ plumage to the color of the sky*1. Huis Marseille notes the chromatic character of the works made over successive winters in Texas: intense blue skies, ocher earth, and small songbirds*6. In discussing N°498–499, Janvier Février Mars 2007, Berlin Art Week describes a diptych in which two birds and a broad landscape are organized through abrupt shifts between blur and sharpness, producing space without a single point of focus*19. Because the landscape is not ordered by one-point perspective, the viewer’s gaze moves among several spatial layers*19. A childhood fascination with bluebirds thus develops into work that joins the color of the bird, the color of the sky, spatial depth, and moving focus within a single image.

Print Scale and Exhibition Space

Mylayne’s prints are unique, and some exceed the scale of the human body. The Huis Marseille exhibition page shows works ranging from the 33 × 33 cm N°25 to the 228 × 183 cm N°524*6. The Museo Reina Sofía explains that the size of each print is determined individually in relation to the physical scale of viewer and bird, maintaining an intimate distance by avoiding enlargement of the bird beyond life size*23. Scale adjusts the distance between bird and viewer without turning the bird into a monumental protagonist.

For Mutual Regard in 2015, gallery rooms facing the gardens of the Arts Club of Chicago and the Art Institute of Chicago were linked with Lurie Garden and a pavilion in Millennium Park, creating movement between nature within the photographs and nature at the exhibition site*7. Fondation Vincent van Gogh Arles organized the 2018–19 exhibition The Autumn of Paradise into nine chapters, bringing together thirty-nine works made between 1979 and 2008 through relations among time, place, and light*21. Huis Marseille notes that the exhibition design was adjusted for each venue on the tour*6. Architecture, windows, and gardens at the place of viewing, as well as the original shooting sites, can therefore reorganize the relations among the photographs.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Between Nature Photography and Contemporary Art — A Contemporary Review from 1995

The difficulty of placing Mylayne’s work was already evident in its reception during the 1990s. Reviewing his 1995 solo exhibition at ARC, Musée d’Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, Le Monde critic Michel Guerrin noted that, at first glance, the work could invite familiar objections to contemporary photography at the time: pastoral animal imagery, large-format color, and an excess of theory*31. Guerrin nevertheless identified Mylayne’s particularity in bringing the worlds of bird and human into the same frame and manipulating format, scale, color, focus, blur, empty space, movement, and time*31. The simultaneous presence of familiar birds and a rigorously constructed investigation of perception, time, and pictorial organization has continued to make the work difficult to contain within either nature photography or contemporary art alone.

Wildlife Photography and Natural History — From Capture and Classification to Relationship

Mylayne photographs birds outdoors, but works under a different set of terms from the long-distance capture developed in wildlife photography. The Lannan Foundation distinguishes him from a conventional wildlife photographer by noting his avoidance of telephoto lenses and camouflage: he sets up a heavy 8 × 10-inch camera with custom lenses and waits for birds to become accustomed to the presence of photographer and equipment*1. The photograph is made with the bird aware of the human presence, and Mylayne chooses ordinary small birds found near inhabited environments*8. Value lies in gradually establishing a situation in which a bird can remain near the photographer. The photograph shifts from a record of wildlife captured at a distance to a record of a situation in which a wild animal and a human could occupy the same place.

The comparison with Audubon clarifies how an image of a bird can produce different kinds of knowledge. In Mylayne’s account, as reported by the Nevada Museum of Art, Audubon functions as an ornithologist and portraitist who showed color and habitat so that viewers could recognize birds*22. At Krannert Art Museum, related programming compared Audubon’s bird illustrations with Mylayne’s photographs, and Andy Warhol’s portraits with Mylayne’s birds*13. Mylayne removes species and place from the center of the title and leaves an individual bird as one that appeared during a specific period of production. The number functions less as a taxonomic code than as an order that records time spent establishing a relation.

Jochen Lempert draws on his background as a biologist to photograph plants, animals, and natural phenomena in black and white, using sequences of images to unsettle divisions such as natural/artificial, classification, and time*14. Mylayne also works with common species, but concentrates meaning in a singular encounter rendered as a unique large-format color photograph. In Lempert, the space between photographs destabilizes categories; in Mylayne, photographer, bird, site, waiting, and shifts of focus form relations within a single image.

Tableau Photography — The Boundary Between Construction and Control

As Mylayne’s method took shape in the late 1970s, contemporary art was increasingly presenting photography as an autonomous single-picture construction comparable to painting or film. Photography historian and curator Matthew Witkovsky places Mylayne within a French lineage of the peintre-photographe—the painter-photographer—and connects him to the development of “near documentary” by Jeff Wall and Jean-Marc Bustamante, in which a photograph retains the appearance of reality while being carefully composed*9. Mylayne’s extended preparation likewise combines observation of birds with the construction of site, light, color, and focus into a tableau. The bird that completes the image remains independent of the photographer’s direction, leaving an autonomous event inside a precisely arranged composition.

Wall prepares figures, locations, lighting, and actions, reconstructing scenes through a process close to film production*25. Bustamante’s Tableaux turn uneventful places at the boundary of city and nature into large color photographs, giving everyday sites the autonomy of a tableau*26. Mylayne also prepares site, light, color, camera position, and focus with great precision, while Huis Marseille notes that he neither feeds nor tames the birds and photographs only after trust has developed*6. Wall can repeat a human action, and Bustamante can work with a stable site; in Mylayne, a wild bird supplies the final element of the composition. A meticulously designed tableau and an uncontrollable event remain present in the same photograph.

Repetition, Construction, and Singularity — The Bechers and Authenticity

The Museo Reina Sofía retrospective catalogue examines the relation between Mylayne and Bernd and Hilla Becher, whose repeated photographs of industrial structures such as water towers and blast furnaces under consistent conditions produced photographic “typologies”*4. Both establish rigorous shooting conditions, return to the same subject over long periods, and organize works through numbering and seriality. The Bechers repeatedly photographed structures of the same type under comparable conditions, creating typologies in which differences among objects could be compared. Mylayne’s repetition leads instead toward an irreproducible encounter in which a bird enters the composition once. Repeating the same conditions increases comparability in the Bechers’ work; in Mylayne’s, it emphasizes the singularity of an event. Repetition becomes a duration that allows an unforeseen arrival to occur.

The Museo Reina Sofía catalogue also examines Mylayne through the problem of “constructed authenticity,” considering his distance from documentary photography*4. Background, color, light, and focal positions are carefully planned, while the photographer cannot control when the bird will arrive, how close it will come, or which way it will ultimately face*3. Authenticity emerges at the point where parameters set by the photographer coincide once with the bird’s autonomous behavior. Recording and construction operate together within the same image.

Ecological Readings and Recent Reassessment

Mylayne’s work has also been received through concerns with ecological fragility and coexistence between humans and nature. Sprüth Magers’s 2023 exhibition Mirror centered on the vulnerability of a shared ecosystem and the brevity of life on earth*20. The e-flux announcement for The Autumn of Paradise likewise framed the work through time and perception as they emerge through birds and their environments*16. These ecological meanings connect to a method in which the photographer adjusts his own time, distance, equipment, and position of viewing before attempting to alter the other. Coexistence appears as an action required for the photograph to come into being, not simply as a symbol within the image.

Sprüth Magers’s Reflection, presented within Berlin Art Week 2026, returned to Mylayne’s long-running work through temporality, perception, and community. The Berlin Art Week text, focusing on photographs made in Marfa, emphasizes how multiple focus disrupts a single focal point and one-point perspective, moving the viewer’s gaze through different spatial layers*19. It links this optical movement to the work’s painterly character*19. Along with titles that record months of production while withholding place and bird species, the exhibition reads the waiting, multifocal optics, tableau construction, and recording of time that have marked Mylayne’s work since the late 1970s as parts of one sustained approach.

Recording the Formation of a Relationship

MoMA’s collection records show that Mylayne’s work has been received within major collections of modern and contemporary photography*17. Exhibition and collection records at France’s Centre national des arts plastiques (Cnap) likewise show his continuing place within the institutions of contemporary art and photography*18. Helfenstein argues that Mylayne transforms the camera from an instrument of domination or capture into a device for slow observation that adapts to the bird’s unpredictable behavior*24. Extended waiting, an encounter with a wild bird, and perception structured through multiple focus become interdependent elements of a single photograph.

jean-pierre-khazem.html.lead_html: Jean-Pierre Khazem photographs models wearing highly crafted masks in still images, video, and live performance. Through Pause, Mona Lisa Live, and First Ladies, this page considers the techniques of advertising and fashion photography, the tension between a moving body and a fixed face, and the documentary appearance that photography lends to fiction.
jean-pierre-khazem.html.thesis_html: Khazem fixes the expressions of models with elaborate masks and breaks apart the process through which photography authenticates a person by resemblance, hairstyle, clothing, lighting, and a familiar story. In Mona Lisa Live, a face known through mass reproduction is attached to a living body; in First Ladies, public images of women are reconstructed through another person’s body and the conventions of official portraiture. The body breathes and shifts its balance inside the mask, gaining duration in live performance, while photography fixes scenes that never occurred as though they belonged to an established past. Khazem brings fashion production, prosthetic makeup, performance, and still photography into one process. Identity in portraiture no longer belongs to the face alone; it appears as an image produced through social role and media repetition.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
From Fashion Photography to the Construction of the Face

Khazem was born in Paris in 1968 and worked across fashion magazines, advertising, moving-image production, and contemporary art. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the pose of the model, lighting, prosthetic makeup, and image retouching allowed the human figure to be precisely designed, and artificial bodies circulated widely in both advertising and contemporary art. The Guardian introduced his work through the relation among fashion, image, and identity.*1 Using techniques learned in commercial photography, Khazem shifted attention from the assumption that the face naturally expresses an interior self toward the visual conventions through which a person is recognized.

A Masked Face and a Live Body

Khazem has said that he chose the Mona Lisa because reproduction on posters and postcards had made it an omnipresent face, mysterious yet almost anonymous.*2 An elaborate mask restricts the model’s expression and field of vision, leaving posture, stride, and breath to sustain the scene. Färgfabriken explained that these conditions turn the shoot into a performance and alter the model’s relation to her body, the outside world, and the audience.*3 The mask produces immediate recognition of a famous face while maintaining its mismatch with a moving body, adding time before the photograph to the work.

In Pause, five nude figures wearing the same mask move through a space containing mirrored surfaces; in Mona Lisa Live, a model remains on a pedestal. Sperone Westwater describes a production in which photography, video, and performance overlap.*4 A live audience witnesses breathing and duration, while a later viewer receives that time as one photograph of a past event. Khazem requires photography because it can give a constructed action the appearance of something that has already happened.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
How a Fixed Expression Intensifies Bodily Performance

In a conventional portrait, changes in eyes and mouth provide cues to emotion. Khazem’s masks fix those features, making the tilt of a shoulder, the position of an arm, the length of a step, and the movement of the chest through breathing more conspicuous. Eyestorm explains that the mask reduces the model’s awareness of the camera and encourages a full-bodied response to the assigned situation.*5 The habit of reading psychology from a face is dispersed across the body’s center of gravity, the material of the mask, and the duration of performance.

Separating “Likeness” across Face, Body, and Setting

In First Ladies, the modeled face, hairstyle, clothing, upright posture, official-portrait lighting, and title of the series call up the memory of a public figure. Christie’s records show the series circulating as large C-prints, fixing political icons as autonomous photographs apart from the live role.*6 Identity appears when several visual conventions align; facial resemblance alone is insufficient.

A nearly seamless mask, even lighting, and large print make the fabrication appear real. The immobile expression, the position of the eyes, and the boundary between artificial skin and neck retain signs of construction. Viewers test which details support recognition and how much discrepancy they will accept before the figure ceases to be the person named. Photographic detail does not immediately settle truth or falsehood; it reveals how plausibility is built. *5

Prosthetic makeup, sculpting, casting, and skin coloring are involved in making the masks, and photographic lighting brings the artificial skin closer to the appearance of a living face. Materials from CNAP and Eyestorm treat the mask as a sculptural component of the work, beyond its role as a prop.*7 Its hardness and seams become visible nearby, while from an appropriate distance it reads as a celebrity face. This change with distance reverses the expectation that photographic resolution necessarily uncovers truth: additional detail can also increase the persuasiveness of the artificial object. *5

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Pause: A Still Face and a Moving Body

Made in 2002, Pause combines figures, reflections, masks, video, and photography within an architectural environment of mirrored surfaces. Färgfabriken presented the installation as a space altered by the viewer’s position and reflection.*3 The “pause” of the title connects the instant of photography with the duration for which a live body holds a pose. The figure occupies an intermediate state, never fully becoming a still image and never returning to unmarked movement; the work makes the freezing of time in portraiture physically perceptible.

Mona Lisa Live and the Embodiment of a Famous Painting

Mona Lisa Live (2003) is a performance in which a nude model wearing an elaborate Mona Lisa mask stands on a pedestal in a field of light. Sperone Westwater records its first presentation at Deitch Projects and later appearances at the Prague Biennale and the Rubell Family Collection.*4 When the face of one of the world’s most reproduced paintings moves onto a living body, the mystique of the masterpiece and the appeal of spectacle appear together. The poses of painting, sculpture, fashion presentation, and photography overlap in one scene. *8

First Ladies: Reconstructing Official Portraiture on Another Body

First Ladies attaches the face, dress, etiquette, and media visibility through which the wives of U.S. presidents have been made into public roles to the bodies of other women. The series was shown in New York in 2005 and later circulated through the market and collections. The position of the “First Lady”—close to political power yet without a distinct elected office—becomes visible through borrowed portraiture and substitution. *6

Khazem continued to stage masks, characters, and bodies in fashion media, including collaborations with Misi Park. AnOther describes the image known as fashion’s “white rabbit” as a work in which charm and unease coexist.*9 He does not separate commercial and artistic fields; both construct figures through lighting, clothing, face, and story. Because he uses the seductive surface of fashion rather than refusing it, the work remains between critique and participation.

At Mona Lisa Live, an audience shares the time in which the model breathes and maintains her posture. In the photograph, that duration contracts into one uncanny portrait. Sperone Westwater treats the performance history and photographic works as one production history because the two modes of viewing transform one another.*4 Live, the fixed mask and bodily fatigue become visible; in the still image, surface and composition gain force. The work resides in the conversion of a time-bound body into a fixed image.

The model’s eyes can be seen through openings in the carefully made mask, while the facial muscles remain still. The discrepancy creates an uncanniness associated with dolls or corpses, although the body continues to breathe and hold its pose. Eyestorm identifies this disturbance of facial reading and human psychology as a feature of the work.*5 A surface that does not respond exposes how viewers infer personhood from minute movements of the face.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Bringing Staged Photography and Performance into One Production Process

Since the 1970s, photographs of performance have often been exhibited as records of actions, while staged photography in the 1980s and 1990s constructed scenes for the camera. Khazem transforms an unstable action sustained before an audience into a highly finished photograph. The uncertainty of the live event and the decisiveness of the photograph enter one production process. The exhibition history of photographs from Pause at a Paris photography institution also records this movement between forms.*3

The Tension among Images of Women, Nudity, and Fashion

In images of nude women wearing masks, the face is read as a celebrity or fixed expression while the body breathes, shifts posture, and remains exposed before an audience. This gap destabilizes the subject, yet it can also repeat the display of the female body as an object of viewing. Criticism in The Guardian and Paris Art has addressed the coexistence of seduction, artificiality, and objectification.*1 A mask may critique a social role without automatically making the presentation of the nude body critical. *10

The power of authentication in Khazem’s photographs changes according to whose face the viewer sees, which historical image comes to mind, and whether they witnessed the live work or only encounter the still photograph. Fashion projects and collaborations preserved on the official site also connect the mask to immediate recognition in advertising.*11 The discrepancy between mask and body exposes the way photography uses context and familiarity to create the appearance of an event that has already occurred.

Separate from their legally defined authority, First Ladies have circulated as photographic images representing nation, family, decorum, and the style of an era. First Ladies turns the face into an exchangeable mask, exposing the dependence of public recognition on media repetition as much as on an individual’s actions. The series simultaneously reenacts an institution that attaches women to their husbands’ political histories, leaving a tension between critique and reproduction. Sperone Westwater likewise emphasizes the automatic chain of associations from a face to a president and to American history.*12

Khazem’s photographs and performances appeared at Perrotin, a Paris photography institution, the Prague Biennale, and the Rubell Collection, establishing Mona Lisa Live as a work moving among live event, documentary photograph, and museum display, rather than as a one-time spectacle.*13*14*18 Gallery archives and lists of works show masked portraiture recurring beyond Mona Lisa and First Ladies in fashion, nude figures, and cinematic scenes.*16*17*15

The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston collection record for Mona Lisa: Problematics of Identity Theory I & II confirms that the joining of a famous face to another body entered collections as an autonomous photographic work as well as a performance record. Smithsonian exhibition materials explain that the First Lady has visually represented an administration and nation despite being distinct from a statutory public office, clarifying the background to Khazem’s treatment of face, dress, and posture as interchangeable forms.*19*20

jens-ullrich.html.lead_html: Jens Ullrich cuts press photographs, sports images, and photographs of historical sculpture from newspapers and magazines and joins them to other images. From Masken, Flieger, and Plakate to the free-reproduction project Bilder ohne Geld, his work examines how photographic meaning begins at the moment of exposure and continues to change through cutting, displacement, context, ownership, and copying.
jens-ullrich.html.thesis_html: Photomontage had used newspaper photographs to construct political arguments since the early twentieth century, while appropriation in the 1970s and 1980s borrowed existing images to question authorship and originality. Ullrich uses the shared operations of cutting and borrowing to ask what remains after an image loses its original context. Flieger collides press photography with the history of state sculpture, while Bilder ohne Geld opens reproduction itself to the viewer. If appropriation often asked “whose image is this?,” Ullrich extends the question to who uses, owns, and redistributes an image.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Born in Tanzania in 1968, Trained in Düsseldorf—Biography and the 1990s Artistic Environment

Ullrich was born in Tukuyu, Tanzania, in 1968, studied at the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, and has been based in Berlin since 2008. ZKM’s current profile records his year and place of birth and describes his method of combining fragments from found images into new motifs*1. Goethe-Institut Villa Kamogawa gives the same biographical information and notes that from 1999 to 2006 he ran the exhibition space Alexanderstraße in Düsseldorf with friends*2. Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek’s authority record also confirms his 1968 birth in Tukuyu, which rules out older references that identified him as born in Germany in 1972*3. In Düsseldorf during this period, photography, painting, sculpture, and installation were often treated beyond medium-specific purity, and post-conceptual artists used existing cultural images and exhibition systems as material. Ullrich likewise turned away from searching for new subjects and toward reusing images that already circulated with established meanings in newspapers and magazines.

Press Photography and Appropriation—When the “Original Context” Falls Away

Press photographs of news, politics, and sports became a major source for Ullrich in the 2000s. In the ongoing Masken series, begun in 2004, he digitally combines black-and-white newspaper photographs taken in various African countries with images of African masks; the European Month of Photography Berlin describes a group of roughly forty such collages*23. In the 2006 Willkommende Gemeinschaft / Plakate, the concrete demands written on protest placards were already replaced with abstract ornament. Bergische Kunstpreis materials record that Ullrich had collected press photographs of political demonstrations for years and replaced the protesters’ critical messages with abstract, decorative images*22. Schirn Kunsthalle later presented this work in an exhibition on political representation, describing how slogans found in newspaper photographs were removed and replaced with abstract Letraset forms before the images were remade as posters*21. Appropriation here is not simply the borrowing of existing art. By detaching words, faces, or body parts from photographs originally made to communicate information, Ullrich tests how readily political meaning can become another image.

After Photomontage and Appropriation—From Heartfield to the Pictures Generation

The method of cutting printed images and reconnecting them to new meanings has a long history. MoMA presents John Heartfield’s photomontages as works that combined fragments from newspapers and magazines to attack Nazi propaganda politically*24. The Met describes the Pictures Generation of the 1970s and 1980s as a period in which the rephotography and reuse of magazines, advertisements, and artworks made appropriation a central photographic method for unsettling authorship and originality*25. No source reviewed here establishes direct influence from these artists on Ullrich, but his work emerged after both methods had already been historicized. His difference lies in making fragmentation itself a test of how much political or historical meaning disappears when an image is detached from its source—and what still remains afterward.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Flieger—Joining the Instant of Photography to the Permanence of Sculpture

In Flieger, Ullrich combines contemporary sports press photographs—soccer players, gymnasts, runners suspended in midair—with heads and body fragments cut from classicizing sculpture of the Nazi period. In an interview with Sport in Art, he explains his attraction to airborne athletes as moments the naked eye can barely perceive but the camera can freeze, while noting that once sculptural fragments are cut from their original setting, their ideological origins become harder to identify*5. VAN HORN’s exhibition text for Flieger likewise records the method of cutting and joining sports images from newspapers and magazines with state sculpture produced between 1933 and 1945*4. The photographic medium is crucial to the comparison. Sports journalism freezes the body as a decisive instant of victory; sculpture monumentalizes an ideal body in stone or bronze. Two opposing temporalities are attached within a single image. Because Ullrich works with photographs that have already circulated in the press rather than staging new athletes himself, the media system that produces contemporary heroic bodies remains present as part of the material. The ideal body fixed by the state and the ideal body produced moment by moment by the press can then be seen through similar poses and radically different histories.

Removing Language from Protest Photography—Tate Modern’s Media Burn

In Tate Modern’s 2006–07 exhibition Media Burn, Ullrich showed altered press photographs of demonstrations in which writing on placards had been turned into meaningless signs. Tate’s announcement preserved by e-flux frames the exhibition around the boundaries among art, politics, protest, and media and notes Ullrich’s hollowing out of slogans within documentary photographs*6. A contemporary Guardian review also discusses this operation and offers a critical assessment of its political effect*7. The crowd’s bodies and expressions remain visible while the words identifying their demands disappear, exposing the gap between a generic “image of protest” and specific political content.

Collage Does More Than Mix Histories—It Breaks the Authority of Images

Ullrich’s 2008 Kollekte, made with Jan Albers at Museum Morsbroich, was cataloged as an intervention that combined works from the museum collection with the artists’ own production and altered meaning through display*8. The museum’s institutional history likewise records Ullrich as an artist who intervened directly in the collection*9. A contemporary KUNSTFORUM review describes how Baroque sculpture and modern painting were joined to other objects and arrangements to produce new associations*10. The same attitude appears in Flieger: instead of preserving existing photographs intact, Ullrich cuts them and places them in contact with other images so that classifications and values that once appeared natural become unstable.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Refugees In A State Apartment—Placing the Press Image’s “Waiting Body” Inside a Historic Residence

For Refugees In A State Apartment (2015), Ullrich composited people photographed around the refugee reception center in Berlin-Moabit into black-and-white photographs of a historic industrialist’s residence in Bremen that was then for sale. ZKM explains how the “nowhere” condition of waiting immediately after arrival and the temporary placement of bodies inside opulent interiors create simultaneous impressions of intimacy and rootlessness*11. CONTACT Photography Festival presented the series in Toronto in 2016 within the European refugee crisis and questions of reception and visibility*12. In the artist’s account published by ArtRabbit, the house’s overlapping meanings as refuge, living space, and cultural property become part of the project’s metaphor*13.

Bilder ohne Geld—Returning Reproducibility to the Economy of the Work

In the 2021 book Bilder ohne Geld, Ullrich made roughly three hundred earlier photomontages available as templates for scanning, allowing anyone who borrowed the book from a public library to enlarge, print, and hang them independently. Museum Abteiberg describes the project as removing artworks from ordinary systems of purchase, price, and ownership and turning the book into an analog image source*14. In the artist’s statement cited by the museum, Ullrich argues that although photographs and images are technically reproducible, framing, conservation, transport, insurance, and limited editions create scarcity and restrict that freedom*14. WDR likewise reported on the photobook as a collection of works and printing instructions that made Ullrich’s large photomontages reproducible by anyone*15. Kunststiftung NRW records its support for a publication that distances itself from art-market systems of edition size, image rights, and sale price*16. An artist who cut other people’s photographs in Flieger now gives others permission to cut out, enlarge, and rehang his own images. The logic of appropriation reverses direction: from an artist’s freedom to use other people’s images to a viewer’s freedom to use the artist’s images.

From “Viewing a Work” to Taking It Home and Reproducing It

A K21 discussion of Bilder ohne Geld presented the release of twenty years of photomontages as a commons, considering both collage’s political force and its resistance to the art market*17. In a taz interview, Ullrich speaks of the difficulty of seeing an image in a gallery without also seeing the price and capital that surround it*18. The technical reproducibility of photography thus becomes a concrete design question about who can access a work, not simply a general theory of mechanically reproduced art.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
After Appropriation, Making the “Source” of a Photograph Part of the Work

Contemporary Art Library records show Ullrich’s work recurring in solo exhibitions, collaborations, and installation settings*19. His collages do not primarily erase sources in order to make seamless fantasies. They force image systems with different origins—sports journalism, state sculpture, demonstration photography, real-estate photography—into the same pictorial field. Meaning depends on what the photograph depicts, what it was made for, and where it circulated. If the source disappeared completely, the collage could end as an exercise in strange bodily form. By preserving the difference between institutions such as the sports press and state sculpture, Ullrich makes the viewer parse several histories within a single image.

Photographic Significance—From Photographer to Editor, Distributor, and User

Ullrich was included in Photo Art: Photography in the 21st Century, a survey of twenty-first-century photography that situates him among practices expanding beyond a photography centered on taking pictures*20. In Flieger he cuts photographs; in Refugees he transfers bodies into another space; in Bilder ohne Geld he asks viewers to reproduce the work themselves. Seen together, the three projects make clear that photographers alone do not determine an image’s meaning. Ullrich makes the life of a photograph—through editors, display institutions, owners, and copyists—part of the work. His practice examines how photographs continue to acquire new meanings through politics, memory, and markets after they enter public circulation; appropriation becomes more than simply “using someone else’s image.”
