sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Joel Meyerowitz studied painting and graphic design and was working as an art director at an advertising agency when he saw Robert Frank at work in 1962 and turned to photography. Watching Frank move his body in response to his subjects made the street appear to Meyerowitz as a “text” he had previously been unable to read*17. He then encountered The Americans, Henri Cartier-Bresson’s The Decisive Moment, and Walker Evans’s American Photographs, deepening his interest in the language of photobooks, where multiple images shape a way of seeing the world*17. His initial question was how much of conscious, lived experience could be transferred into a photograph by entering the street with a camera.

From the beginning, Meyerowitz worked in both black and white and color. He found in 35mm color a descriptive capacity that preserved distinctions among clothing, light, shadow, and signage. In a 2012 interview, he recalled believing in the force of color from 1962 onward while continuing to work amid resistance within the photographic establishment*21. During the 1970s, he began using an 8×10 camera to turn the fleeting image of a slide projection into a print that could be held and viewed over time*18. He carried the responsiveness learned through 35mm into the large-format camera, allowing a broad field of detail and the full state of light to enter a single image. At Cape Cod, he said, sustained attention to a limited set of elements—sandbar, water, sky, old houses—taught him how to see the place*18. With Aftermath in 2001, his purpose was to preserve the recovery effort as a public record for New York City*13.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Early Color — Color as Information

Meyerowitz chose color as a descriptive means of preserving differences within reality. A red coat, yellow sunlight, and blue shadow each establish spatial distance and a particular quality of light—information that black-and-white photography converts into nearby shades of gray*18. Color relates clothing, cars, walls, advertisements, and reflections at the edges of the frame. As information increases, meaning spreads in several directions. Meyerowitz used that density to retain the complexity of simultaneous events on the street.

Field Photography and the Decisive Moment

Meyerowitz’s early work was strongly shaped by Cartier-Bresson’s decisive moment. He gradually sought to open the photograph to the whole of unstructured experience*19. A figure in the foreground, a distant sign, a car, a reflection, and an empty interval can carry comparable weight, dispersing events across the frame. His term “field photography” emerged from this problem. The low sensitivity of early color film also redirected his attention from freezing rapid gestures toward observing presence and absence, recurring colors, and the density of a place*19.

From 35mm to 8×10

Meyerowitz introduced the 8×10 camera to extend the attention developed on the street into longer observation and larger prints. He wanted to give the smooth description and chromatic depth he found in 35mm color a stable form that could hang on a wall and sustain extended viewing*18. The camera could hold clouds, tides, windows, interior lamps, and distant views at the same resolution, while its weight slowed the photographer’s movement. Meyerowitz recalled carrying the 8×10 on errands and walks, preserving a street photographer’s readiness for chance scenes*18. The change in format brought quick response and sustained observation into the same body of work.

Cape Light — Light in an Ordinary Place

Cape Cod offered Meyerowitz a spare landscape of sandbars, low houses, roads, water, and sky. Before he had any plan to become a landscape photographer, he repeatedly attended to the limited elements before him*18. The color temperature of light, humidity, moving clouds, and differences between indoor and outdoor illumination transformed the place from hour to hour. Aperture identifies Cape Light as a major work that broadened the reception of color photography*10. The large-format camera became an instrument for renewing attention to a place through prolonged observation.

Bay/Sky — Repeating the Horizon

In Bay/Sky, Meyerowitz repeatedly photographed the horizon dividing bay and sky. “Bay/Sky, Provincetown, Massachusetts” is a 1977 chromogenic print reproduced on The Met’s collection page*7. Cloud cover, the water’s surface, color temperature, and the height of the horizon change, producing temporal differences specific to the same place. The artist’s official website also presents the series as an independent body of work*9. Repetition makes it possible to compare how light and atmosphere remake the appearance of a place each time.

Aftermath — The Time of Recovery

After September 11, 2001, Meyerowitz was stopped from photographing at the World Trade Center site. He argued that the recovery work needed to be preserved as an archive for New York City and secured continuing access to the site*13. His photographs follow nine months of debris removal, the cutting of structural elements, workers at rest, nighttime illumination, and seasonal change. He explained that he wanted to convey even the sensation of being there to people who could not enter the site*20. Large-format color retained the details of steel, dust, fire, work clothes, and artificial light, translating personal perception into a form of public memory.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Early Color 1962–63 and 35mm Street Photography

The official website’s “Early Color 1962–63” shows that Meyerowitz used color as an everyday photographic medium from the beginning of his career*2. In the street work that followed, color, figures, advertising, traffic, and reflections overlap within single frames, recording the city as a field of relationships. The lightness of the 35mm camera allowed him to redirect his gaze while walking and approach moments in which multiple elements briefly came together.

Cape Light, 1978

Cape Light is a photobook that turns seaside illumination into an extended period of observation through an 8×10 camera and color film. Howard Greenberg Gallery describes it as a classic of color photography and notes the book’s broad readership*1. In works such as “Cape Cod, Massachusetts,” different kinds of light touching buildings, sky, and ground become the central subject*8. Across the pages, morning, midday, evening, and the hours around storms shift, while color articulates time.

Aftermath: World Trade Center Archive

Aftermath records the recovery of the World Trade Center site in large-format color. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum describes long-term access to the site and 400 color photographs as the basic structure of the project*12. Monumental structures, minute tasks, illumination by day and night, and seasonal change enter the same archive. The descriptive capacity of the large-format camera preserves the extended time following the event.

The Time Constructed by Photobooks

Meyerowitz transferred the distinct temporalities of each photographic format into the structure of his books. In Cape Light, pages moving among morning, midday, evening, and the hours around storms sustain changes in light. In Bay/Sky, the repeated horizon invites comparison among minute chromatic differences. Aftermath accumulates nine months of work, giving duration to the time after the event. Given his early interest in the internal language of photobooks, editing became a means of determining the pace at which an instant, a place, and a memory would be read*17.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
A Pioneer of Color Photography

Meyerowitz is recognized as one of the photographers who helped establish color photography within the field of art. In a 2012 interview with Transatlantica, he described believing in the force of color from 1962 and continuing to work amid the resistance of the period*21. William Eggleston, Stephen Shore, Helen Levitt, and Saul Leiter expanded color photography from different places and through different channels of presentation. Meyerowitz’s particular contribution lay in treating rapid 35mm color work on the street and large-format color observation at the shore as part of the same problem, demonstrating that color could describe perception unfolding at different speeds.

Winogrand, Eggleston, Shore, and Meyerowitz

Garry Winogrand and Meyerowitz used 35mm cameras on New York streets to photograph unpredictable arrangements and gestures. Meyerowitz added relations among colors and later moved into large-format work. Eggleston gave everyday objects and interiors in the American South the density of saturated color and the force of the single image. Shore used road trips and large-format color to describe intersections, meals, and motels. Cape Light remains within one place and joins color to the temporal changes of light and atmosphere. Across their work, color photography opened onto distinct questions of the city, everyday objects, travel, and the duration of place.

A Photography of Attention — Instant, Place, Memory

The early street photographs, Cape Light, and Aftermath share an attention distributed between center and periphery. On the street, figures, advertisements, reflections, and empty intervals produce a temporary field. At Cape Cod, light and atmosphere alter a place. At Ground Zero, workers, machines, structures, and seasons build an extended duration. Meyerowitz described the motive for street photography as feeling the moment of being alive and conscious, then leaving a record of that consciousness*17. Color widened the range of information available from the world and became a means of sustaining attention.

joel-sternfeld.html.lead_html: Joel Sternfeld began with color as a way to register season and atmosphere, then expanded from 35mm street photography to cross-country work with an 8×10-inch view camera. American Prospects uses color and distance to hold beauty and devastation together across suburbs and roads; On This Site joins present-day landscapes to written accounts of past events. This page traces how Sternfeld developed color photography into a way of reading American society, memory, and transformations of the land.
joel-sternfeld.html.thesis_html: Sternfeld combined the interaction of colors, the distance afforded by an 8×10 view camera, the sequencing of the photobook, and his own writing to treat the American landscape as a social record in which nature and development, ordinary life and accident, present and memory overlap. American Prospects presents beauty and devastation across a sustained series, while On This Site incorporated the gap between the present visible in the photograph and the past conveyed by text into the structure of documentary.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html: In the late 1960s, about a month after he began taking photographs, Sternfeld decided that color was necessary to convey changes of season and atmosphere. He reached this conclusion after photographing the same landscape in color and black and white, printing both versions, and comparing them. The experiment opened a larger question: what were the aesthetic principles of color photography, and where did its greatest strength lie?*11 In the mid-1970s, while following the seasons at Nags Head, North Carolina, Sternfeld faced a serious health scare and the accidental death of his brother Gabriel. After returning to New York, he experienced a moment on the Rockaway shoreline when the colors of apartment blocks, sand, and an overcast sky formed a coherent order. He later recalled that the resulting photograph directed the course of his subsequent work.*11 Color harmony consequently became a way to perceive a disordered reality as a whole, instead of a rule for selecting beautiful subjects. His early First Pictures used a 35mm camera to photograph figures and gestures on the street. A Guggenheim Fellowship in 1978 then enabled extended journeys through suburbs, farmland, industrial zones, and roads beyond the city.*1 Sternfeld described his task as a search for beauty and harmony within an increasingly standardized and technological nation, guided by a childhood memory of an “ordered, rural America.”*2 The move from 35mm to an 8×10-inch view camera gave him a method for observing nature, architecture, human activity, and the traces of consumption as relations across an entire landscape.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Color Photography: Season and Atmosphere

Color was central to the construction of meaning in Sternfeld’s photographs. He studied the color theories of Josef Albers, Paul Klee, and Johannes Itten and photographed the way adjacent hues alter one another’s brightness and temperature within a landscape. Yet these theories of painting did not provide a universal system that could simply be transferred to photography.*11 Sternfeld instead pursued photographs whose meaning arose through the operation of color. Autumn orange signals season; the colors of road signs and building materials indicate development and consumption; collisions between natural and manufactured colors register changes in the land. Drawing as well on social historian Lewis Mumford’s idea that each era possesses a characteristic color system, Sternfeld identified low-saturation pastel tones of similar density as the colors of the technological America emerging in the late 1970s and early 1980s.*11 Color carried atmosphere and social history at once, linking personal perception to changes across the nation.

From 35mm to 8×10

In the early 1970s, Sternfeld learned to react quickly to the street with a 35mm camera. Street photography had already developed a sophisticated vocabulary of speed, grain, blur, and tilted framing for the modern city, and he began pursuing questions that extended beyond the urban instant.*2 With an 8×10-inch view camera, he set up a tripod, inspected every part of the frame, and waited for the movement of people and cars to enter the space. During the journeys funded by his Guggenheim Fellowship, he often limited himself to about two negatives a day and used a journal in his car at night to imagine scenes for the next day.*11 This slow procedure turned a house fire and a farm stand, a road and a collapsed elephant, or flood damage and a housing development into what has been described as a “narrative tableau,” encompassing both the central event and the surrounding uses of land.*2 Clues dispersed across the broad frame invite viewers to infer multiple timelines and causes, making their own judgment part of the work.

American Prospects: Beauty and Devastation

American Prospects moves across places where housing, agriculture, industry, and leisure have altered the land, drawing on “prospects” as both a future outlook and a physical view of America. Sternfeld researched each region’s industries, seasons, geology, vegetation, and literature, then photographed the many roles through which people manage, preserve, decorate, control, and damage the land.*2 Derelict factories, suburban development, and the remains of disasters appear alongside the unmistakable beauty of light, climate, and the horizon. The text for the 2003 edition describes the book’s America as a nation filled with gleaming new construction while its human spirit remains deeply uneasy.*2 The precision of large-format color prevents social problems from being reduced to accusatory symbols. It sustains the contradiction of people loving the land as they use it, and ordering it as they harm it. The “harmony” Sternfeld sought gave perceptible order to fractures in reality while keeping those fractures present in the image.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
McLean, Virginia: Can a Photograph Explain Cause?

In McLean, Virginia, December 4, 1978, a firefighter in the foreground selects a pumpkin at a farm stand while smoke and flames rise from a house in the distance.*3 Sternfeld remained apart from the fire, arranging the stand, firefighter, road, and house along the depth of the frame. The orange of the pumpkins, protective clothing, and flames connects the scene visually, while the photograph offers no explanation for the firefighter’s actions. Anne Tucker has discussed the image as a representative example of Sternfeld’s distance from an event and his retention of a broad setting and abundant information.*2 Viewers may infer dereliction of duty, a break, or a training exercise from the visible arrangement. Because the photograph withholds the information needed to settle those stories, its irony also addresses the viewer’s habit of converting visual placement into causality.

After a Flash Flood and Exhausted Renegade Elephant

After a Flash Flood, Rancho Mirage, California records cars pushed through mud, broken ground, and houses on a slope as terrain remade by a flood.*4 In Exhausted Renegade Elephant, Woodland, Washington, June 1979, a collapsed elephant appears at the convergence of a sheriff’s car, onlookers, road markings, and power lines.*5 Kelly Brougher noted how the elephant is absorbed into the landscape, whose road, buildings, and rough vegetation appear equally exhausted.*2 Sternfeld often chose the moment when an extraordinary event had begun to enter the ordinary appearance of a place. His equal attention to the residual signs of an event and its surroundings later developed in On This Site into a structure for reading past violence through a quiet present.

On This Site: Memory, Place, and Text

The 1996 series On This Site: Landscape in Memoriam photographs locations across the United States associated with murder, political violence, racism, and accidents as present-day landscapes in which few traces of the events remain. The official description explains its pairing of crime-scene sites with short texts that restore lost histories to places that appear peaceful.*6 Images of houses, roads, parking lots, and vacant land describe the present surface precisely, while the writing identifies the events and the people involved. The gap in time reveals how quickly a place can recover an innocent appearance and how fragile the institutions that preserve memory can be. Sternfeld has repeatedly questioned the habit of treating the photographic grain as fact itself and has stressed that a photograph cannot convey a subject’s entire history.*7 He assigned different functions to image and text and made the distance between them a form of memory.

Stranger Passing: Distance in Environmental Portraiture

Stranger Passing is a series of environmental portraits made between 1985 and 2000, photographing people Sternfeld encountered across the United States together with roads, parking lots, commercial sites, and residential districts. SFMOMA’s 2001 exhibition connected individual portraits to late-twentieth-century American culture through approximately sixty-five large-format color photographs.*8 The distance between camera and person remains broadly consistent: the subjects pause and return the lens’s gaze. Clothing, occupation, possessions, and setting offer signs of social position without reducing a life to a single type. Douglas R. Nickel has discussed the tension between a procedure that recalls August Sander’s social classification and the individuality that escapes it.*13 In A Young Man Gathering Shopping Carts, Huntington, New York, labor and commercial space function as signs that describe the young man, while his expression and stance leave room beyond that account.*9 Sternfeld’s environmental portraits make the classificatory impulse of looking part of the frame and show what remains outside its reach.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
New Color and New Topographics

Sternfeld brought together the contingency of street photography, the restrained distance of New Topographics, and the color structures of New Color. Kevin Moore, quoted in the artist’s official biography, has described his work as an integration of street photography’s humor and social insight, observation of the man-altered landscape, and the formal concerns of late-1970s color photography.*12 William Eggleston made everyday color an autonomous photographic subject, and Stephen Shore described the visual order of roads and buildings. Sternfeld connected color to time accumulated in the land. The hues of seasons, building materials, advertisements, cars, and vegetation carry layers of development, consumption, disaster, and memory at once. By sustaining beauty and political unease within the same landscapes, his work extended color photography from a means of reproducing the world’s vividness into a critical method for reading social change over time.

Photobooks and Writing: From Image to Sequence

Sternfeld constructs time beyond a single frame through the sequence of the photobook and through writing. In American Prospects, photographs from different regions and seasons make suburban development, disasters, labor, leisure, and remnants of wilderness legible as recurring signs across the United States. Steidl’s revised edition added portraits and clarified the book’s continuity with Stranger Passing, revealing the long development through which Sternfeld treated landscape and portraiture as aspects of the same relation between people and place.*10 In On This Site, the temporal gap between the present conveyed by the image and the past conveyed by writing becomes the work’s central device. The official biography explains that his later photobooks expand their narrative possibilities through the artist’s own texts and form an interconnected body of series that respond to one another.*12 Through the sequence, readers move among histories beyond the frame, structures repeated in other places, and the limits of what photographs can know.

Sweet Earth and Oxbow Archive

While photographing On This Site, Sternfeld also began visiting idealistic communities alongside sites of violence. He rejected an early plan to balance violence and utopia within one volume, concentrated On This Site on the memory of violence, and continued photographing communities as a separate series. Against a period in which large-scale urbanization and market principles gained momentum after the collapse of the Soviet system, Sweet Earth records religious communities, communes, ecovillages, and other models for organizing life collectively through photographs and text.*14 For Oxbow Archive, begun in 2006, Sternfeld returned to the Massachusetts fields Thomas Cole painted in the 1830s and walked them almost daily for a year and a half. He had also photographed the land in 1978; the later series follows it through the seasons as a place now marked by an interstate highway and the effects of climate change.*15 These works move Sternfeld’s landscapes from observing contradictions in American society toward political and environmental questions about how people live, use land, and choose a future. Color and season became the forms needed to show how those choices enter the time of nature.

john-riddy.html.lead_html: John Riddy is a British photographer whose work includes London streets and architecture, Palermo, the Norfolk coast, and series devoted solely to the sky. In Low Relief, Palermo, Horizon, and Sky, he selects a different method for each place, from night photography and shifts from color to black and white to repeated photographs from a single viewpoint. His work is rooted in a background in painting, the use of large-format cameras, and a sustained commitment to series and publications.
john-riddy.html.thesis_html: In the Bechers’ typologies and New Topographics, consistent photographic rules and restrained compositions provided a basis for comparing multiple buildings and landscapes. Riddy’s photographs can look close to that tradition, yet he does not force every place into one system. During roughly three years of work on Palermo he shifted from color to black and white; for Horizon he photographed from the same point for two years; in Sky he removed architecture from the frame altogether.For each place, he reconsiders color, viewpoint, and duration according to what he wants to see there. He has continued to vary the photographic conditions from site to site instead of fixing an ostensibly objective style for urban photography.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From Painting to Photography — Choosing an Existing Place Instead of Starting from a Blank Surface

Riddy began taking and printing photographs as a teenager and studied painting at Chelsea School of Art. He has recalled that after graduation he never felt comfortable beginning with a blank canvas; working from objects and places that already existed suited him better*24 He later photographed works in the studios of sculptors including Anthony Caro and has described the routine use of a large-format camera in that work as a practical education for his own photography*1 Frith Street Gallery likewise traces his move from painting into photography and his long-term engagement with architecture and place*22Riddy’s move toward photography cannot be explained by an interest in place alone. The camera allowed him to begin with an existing building or street, choose a viewpoint and frame, and still admit details he had not made—light, dirt, signs, passing objects—rather than inventing an image from a blank surface.

Urban Photography in the 1990s — Choosing Description over Event

During the 1990s, Riddy began photographing buildings and streets in sustained series. The Government Art Collection describes his work through a continuing interest in architecture, cities, and place*2 London (Marylebone Road) retains the name of the street photographed as its title*3 London (Garrick Street) similarly treats a specific street as an individual work*4 Riddy has since described this work in terms of “description” rather than “storytelling”: instead of imposing a narrative on the city, the photograph records what he selected and where he placed the camera on site*24 Muizenberg, also in the Government Art Collection, is another early work that retains the specific name of a place outside London*5.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Working in Series — Deciding What to Keep through Comparison

In an Artdoc interview, Riddy explained that the “decisive moment” is not his point of departure and that his decisions are made over time*24 In the Sky series, including Sky 14 (Camberwell), he preserves the sky as a sequence of numbered works instead of condensing variations in cloud cover and color into one dramatic instant*6 In the same interview he described the print as both a window onto a place and a physical surface structured by color, tone, and composition*24 Michael Fried likewise discusses Riddy’s work through the differences in composition and light that become clearer when several prints are compared rather than viewed in isolation*23The series keeps a single decision at the moment of exposure from becoming the definitive answer. Riddy makes several images from the same place or subject, compares their differences after printing, and then decides which photographs to retain. Allowing judgment to continue after the exposure is consistent with his preference for describing a place without deciding its story in advance.

Le Gray, Hokusai, and Ruskin — Different Historical References for Different Series

Riddy draws on different historical works for different series. A 1994 exhibition situated his photographs in relation to nineteenth-century French photography and twentieth-century American photography; later projects took John Ruskin’s autobiography, Hokusai’s woodblock prints, and Gustave Le Gray’s photographs as specific points of departure*7 Riddy has said that he did not know the Düsseldorf School when he began. In architectural photography he was looking at Werner Mantz and Ezra Stoller, and only later became aware of similarities with the Bechers, Thomas Struth, and Andreas Gursky*24These historical references are not decorative devices meant to make the photographs appear classical. As with Le Gray in Palermo, they provide a way to examine how an earlier photographer framed a particular place and then photograph the same city under different conditions in the present. A 1996 Frith Street Gallery exhibition brought together sites with markedly different light and interiors—a roadside café in the Pyrenees, a psychiatric hospital in Tunisia, and disused port architecture in Valencia. Valencia (Port) contains a closed port building, an aging mural, a Benetton advertisement, and Republican graffiti within the same frame*8.

Ideal World — Viewing Modernist Ideals through Weathered Buildings

Ideal World looks at the rational ideals of modern architecture through buildings as they appear after use, including stains and weathering. The 2000 exhibition text centers on the utopian ambitions of modernist architecture, including Le Corbusier, and on the subsequent effects of weathering and time*9 Recent Places likewise photographs individual buildings together with the environments in which they now stand*10By retaining stains, repairs, vegetation, and changes in the surroundings that newly completed architectural photography often excludes, Riddy makes the design ideal and the building after use available for comparison within the same photograph.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Sky and Low Relief — Comparing the Sky and London at Night

Sky repeats the sky as a subject, while Low Relief photographs London buildings at night or under low light. Frith Street’s Skies exhibition presented slight differences in weather and illumination as numbered photographs, turning the sky from background into an object of comparison*11 Low Relief was presented as a series in which London architecture emerges as a flattened field under low illumination, emphasizing details of facades and the distribution of artificial light over the recognizability of landmarks*12The descriptive capacity of the large-format camera is used in Sky to compare changes in cloud cover and color, and in Low Relief to compare windows, wall surfaces, and artificial light from image to image.

Palermo — Returning to the Same City for Three Years with Le Gray as a Reference

For Palermo, Riddy did not settle on an image of the city during a single trip; he returned over roughly three years. Exhibition materials cite Gustave Le Gray’s 1860 photographs of Palermo as a point of reference and describe the project as a contemporary reconsideration of the historic city’s architecture, sea, and light*13 Adrian Searle, writing in The Guardian, argued that the extraordinary level of detail makes daily changes in rubbish, graffiti, cars, and lights visible on the same street, leaving the question of “why this day?” unresolved*25 Riddy has explained that he switched to black and white because he felt color was too strong and prevented other qualities of the place from coming through*24 Half-light similarly uses the transition between light and darkness, separating photographic description from the requirement that a place be shown brightly and clearly*14In Palermo, duration is produced through three years of repeated visits and editing, not through long exposure.

Horizon — Two Years from One Viewpoint, Nine Final Photographs

Horizon was made over two years from a single fixed viewpoint at Blakeney Point in Norfolk and edited down to nine photographs*15 Riddy has said that although he had visited the area for more than thirty years, beginning in the early 1990s, Horizon was the first time he photographed it as a body of work*1The composition remains nearly constant: salt marsh in the foreground, a shingle ridge, the Watch House, and sky. Seasons, clouds, and light change. The procedure itself—returning to the same camera position for two years and selecting only nine final images—distinguishes Horizon from a landscape series made in a single visit.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Books and Exhibitions — Giving a Series an Order of Reading

Riddy organizes his work into series by city or subject and has presented them in books as well as exhibitions. Frith Street Gallery’s John Riddy: Photographs brings several urban and landscape series together in one volume*17 Steidl’s Photographs also gathers work made over an extended period, allowing architectural, sky, and landscape series to be compared within one publication*18 Lawrence Markey’s biography likewise shows that exhibitions since the 1990s have repeatedly been organized around named series*19 The gallery’s publication history lists Rome (1999), 8 SKIES (2004), Views from Shin-Fuji (2010), and Palermo (2013), showing that individual cities and series have also been given separate books*20 A 2015 Frieze review discusses an exhibition that paired Riddy’s photographs of South Africa’s Cape Peninsula with drawings by James Castle, comparing specific forms in the images such as rough vegetation and fences*21.

Similar to the Becher School in Appearance, but without a Fixed Photographic Rule

Riddy’s frontal viewpoints, large-format cameras, and sparsely populated urban scenes can resemble the Bechers, the Düsseldorf School, and New Topographics. He has said that his own starting points were architectural photographers such as Werner Mantz and Ezra Stoller, along with painting and sculpture, and that he arrived at “a similar place by a different route” from the Becher school*24 Nor does he apply one photographic rule across every series in the manner of the Bechers’ typologies. In Palermo he moved from color to black and white because blue skies and ocher tones overwhelmed other elements; in Horizon he repeated one viewpoint; in Sky he removed architecture itself from the frame*24 De Pont Museum’s collection page likewise lists six works from Palermo, five from New York (Black Star), and London (Rail Sidings Road 1 and 2) under the same artist, confirming his long-standing use of separate series for different cities*26.In the 2026 Winter Landscape, Riddy moves away from his earlier tendency to avoid people in urban scenes, at times working with a handheld camera and bringing individuals, crowds, and everyday activity back into the frame*16.Because his equipment and treatment of the human figure change within his own work, his career cannot be reduced to a single style of quiet, large-format urban photography.

john-vachon.html.lead_html: John Vachon began as a file clerk for the FSA photographic unit and grew into a photographer under Roy Stryker's direction. Rather than symbolic images, he recorded the ordinary textures of small towns, roads, grain elevators, and working people — evidence that the FSA archive was built as much from accumulated dailiness as from decisive moments. After the war he worked for Look magazine and covered postwar Poland.
john-vachon.html.thesis_html: Growing from an FSA file clerk into a photographer under Roy Stryker's guidance, he demonstrated an alternative possibility within FSA's visual record by accumulating the everyday temperature of regional cities, roads, and grain elevators rather than dramatic symbols. That unassuming accumulation embodied how documentary is sustained not only by masterworks but by the layering of the ordinary, and he went on to cover postwar photojournalism for Look magazine.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: John Vachon was born in Saint Paul, Minnesota, in 1914 and joined the FSA photographic unit in Washington, D.C., in 1936 as a file clerk*1. Through Roy Stryker's guidance and daily contact with the work of Walker Evans and others, he taught himself photography and became an official FSA photographer from 1938, recording the Midwest, the Plains, and rural America*2. After the war he worked as a staff photographer for Look magazine*3. In 1947 he photographed postwar Poland for UNRRA, a dimension of his career distinct from FSA domestic documentation*4. He gave an oral history interview at the Smithsonian's Archives of American Art in 1964, leaving a first-person account of the FSA years*5. He died in 1975.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
From file clerk to photographer

Vachon's entry into the FSA as a messenger and file clerk, followed by Stryker's encouragement to photograph, makes his career a case study in how the FSA photographic unit functioned as a training institution as well as an employer. MoMA holds his work and provides an artist page for career reference*6. The Library of Congress resource "Selecting Photographs for the FSA/OWI Print File" includes a Vachon case study showing the institutional selection process*7.

The ordinary register — small observations accumulated

Vachon's photographs are characterized less by dramatic symbol than by the ordinary materials of small-town America: street corners, road signs, grain elevators, storefronts, and unnamed working people. The MoMA Bitter Years catalogue PDF provides a critical context for FSA photography in which Vachon's position can be located*8. The Museum of the City of New York's project Digitizing the Work of John Vachon in the LOOK Magazine Collection documents the transition from FSA to magazine photography*3. The MNopedia entry from the Minnesota Historical Society situates his career within its regional context*9.

Poland and the postwar scope

The series of photographs archived by the JDC Archives under "Post-World War II Poland" documents postwar European reconstruction and displaced persons — a context distinct from FSA domestic social recording*4. The Photogrammar / Yale University FSA database allows spatial and geographic mapping of Vachon's FSA-period photographs*10.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Vachon does not figure as prominently in FSA historiography as Walker Evans or Dorothea Lange, but his relative obscurity reflects something essential about the FSA archive: that it was built from the accumulation of ordinary photographs as much as from decisive images. The John Vachon Papers at the Library of Congress hold primary material across the FSA, OWI, and Look periods*11. ICP's constituent page documents his career from FSA through Look and the Photo League*12.

jose-antonio-hernandez-diez.html.lead_html: José Antonio Hernández-Díez is a Venezuelan artist who encased a taxidermied “saint dog” in a display case, connected a cow’s heart to Sacred Heart imagery and medical equipment, and turned pigskin skateboards and sneaker logos into artworks. In San Guinefort, Sagrado corazón activo, La Hermandad, and Thinkers, religion, science, youth culture, and consumer goods borrow one another’s powers of persuasion. Trained in film and video, he uses photography and sculpture as well to stage the moment when familiar objects acquire authority or become objects of desire.
jose-antonio-hernandez-diez.html.thesis_html: The saint dog in San Guinefort, the cow’s heart in Sagrado corazón activo, and the sneakers in Thinkers place religion, medicine, and branding within the same field of belief-making. His early videos loop events; San Guinefort asks viewers to touch the saint dog; Thinkers uses the clarity of advertising photography to make philosophers’ names immediately legible. Hernández-Díez assigns video, objects, and photography different tasks according to how religion, consumption, youth culture, and technology produce authority.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Caracas in the 1980s — From Cinematic Time to Looped Video and Objects

Hernández-Díez studied at the Centro de Formación Cinematográfica in Caracas and began working through film and video. MACBA presents him as part of a Venezuelan generation that emerged in the 1980s, opening its retrospective with early experimental videos and works built around screens and display cases*2. New Museum likewise describes him as trained in film and video and as one of the artists who produced early video work in Venezuela*1. María Elena Ramos’s 1991 essay, digitized by ICAA, traces his movement from an interest in film to video and then video installation*6. In works from the late 1980s, brief recorded actions loop so that an event from the past repeatedly returns as a present occurrence on the monitor. e-flux describes these electronic images as early experiments in which video takes on magical, possessive qualities*11. In a 1991 review, Luis Ángel Duque identifies the 1988 Los sueños no duran más de cinco minutos as Hernández-Díez’s entry into the public art scene and discusses him as part of the period’s “neo-conceptual” generation*4. The attention to time and repetition developed through film continues in later works built around a beating heart, operating machinery, footage of a dog eating, and objects altered by viewers’ actions.

International Exhibitions in the 1990s — Caracas Street Culture and Global Contemporary Art

Hernández-Díez’s international activity expanded during the 1990s, as debates over contemporary art as a “global language” intensified and Euro-American institutional dominance came under scrutiny. SITE Santa Fe places the emergence of a new Venezuelan generation, including Hernández-Díez, alongside the economic and social crisis of the late 1980s and describes work that engaged both local culture and international postmodernism*7. MACBA situates his participation in Aperto ’93 at the Venice Biennale, Cocido y crudo at the Museo Reina Sofía in 1994, and the first Gwangju Biennale in 1995 within this period*3. Reina Sofía’s exhibition record shows that Cocido y crudo brought artists from different cultural regions into the same exhibition*18. That international circuit continued with the 1999 Carnegie International, where Carnegie Museum of Art lists Hernández-Díez among the participating artists*17. New Museum emphasizes the way he connected international languages of Pop and Minimalism to the streets, religious imagery, and consumer goods of Caracas, reading the work outside the color and exoticism often expected of “Latin American art”*1. Ivo Mesquita’s discussion of the MACBA collection similarly cites San Guinefort and Vehículos perfectos as examples of youth culture and street pop entering international institutions*21.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
San Guinefort — Building a Relic as a Preservation Device

The 1991 San Guinefort translates the medieval French legend of a dog venerated as a protector of children into a display apparatus made from taxidermy, Plexiglas, metal, a tank, and rubber gloves. Christie’s record confirms both the 1991 date and the material construction of a taxidermied dog enclosed in an industrial preservation case*8. An exhibition essay from the period, digitized by ICAA, analyzes the legend and the technical structure in parallel, showing the importance of an early work that places religious imagery and machinery on the same plane*4. In New Museum’s 2003 survey, viewers could insert their arms into the gloves fixed to the case and touch the “saint dog” inside*1. Faith becomes an experience produced through preservation technology, museological display, and the viewer’s bodily action.

Sagrado corazón activo — Constructing the Sacred Heart with a Cow’s Heart and Medical Equipment

In Sagrado corazón activo, also from 1991, Catholic Sacred Heart imagery is assembled from a cow’s heart, a transparent cross, tubing, and medical equipment. MACBA’s exhibition material notes that Hernández-Díez referred to the works from this period as a “new Christian iconography”*2. A contemporary article preserved by ICAA records the artist discussing his interests in film, photography, video, and religious imagery together as he sought to produce new iconographic forms*5. An essay by Latitudes published by MACBA closely analyzes the structure in which a heart connected to life-support equipment and devotion to the Sacred Heart place corporeal “real presence” and devotional “presence” in the same work*20. Technology and religion establish presence through different procedures. A beating heart reads as life; an image of the Sacred Heart reads as sacred. The work places those two forms of visual persuasion side by side.

La Hermandad and Arroz con Mango — Skateboards, Pigskin, and Baseball Bats

The 1994 La Hermandad combines skateboards made from pigskin with video, bringing street culture, food, and the animal body into the same work. Revista Estilo records an installation of three televisions, pigskin skateboards, and metal-and-rubber wheels, with video showing three phases at once: frying the skateboard, riding it in the street, and a dog eating it*16. Arte Al Día discusses the footage of the pigskin skateboard being eaten by a dog as a central example of the artist’s “conceptual dissonance,” which unsettles ordinary recognition*13. In the 1997 Arroz con Mango, each strike of a baseball bat against the apparatus changes the audio, so the viewer’s action advances the work. New Museum describes this participatory structure as an experience in which the play, competition, force, and violence contained in sport continually change register*1. The objects shift from relics to skateboards and sports equipment. In each case, a familiar thing is made to behave according to unfamiliar rules, destabilizing its usual meaning.

Thinkers — Reading Hume, Kant, and Marx in Sneaker Logos

In Thinkers, sneakers are stacked so that letters drawn from brand logos spell the surnames of Western thinkers including Hume, Kant, Jung, and Marx. New Museum presents the series as a point of overlap between two forms of self-formation: the “thinking subject” and the “buying subject,” joined through advertising signs and philosophers’ names*1. Reviewing the 2003 exhibition, The Brooklyn Rail discusses Hume and Marx, praising the direct use of youth culture and globally recognizable consumer signs while also noting the risk that some works collapse into a single-line idea*10. Photography turns the stacked shoes into a single legible word with the clarity of an advertising image. Once “HUME” resolves, the authority of the brand logo and that of the philosopher depend on the same act of reading a visual sign. Galería Freijo provides images of several works from Thinkers*15.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Monitors Repeat the Past — When Video Becomes Necessary

In Hernández-Díez’s early videos, the temporal structure of repeated events and the monitor as an object matter as much as the recorded content. The Latitudes essay published by MACBA analyzes the late-1980s loops through the image of domestic television as a “ghost machine” that repeatedly summons the recorded past into the present*20. e-flux likewise describes the screens and display-case works of this period as treating electronic images as magical and possessive phenomena*11. In La Hermandad, three videos hold separate stages of the pigskin skateboard’s transformation at the same time: frying, street use, and being eaten by a dog*16. Video preserves the object’s transformation as duration. It is assigned to events that unfold through time—life, memory, consumption, destruction—while the preservation case in San Guinefort and the life-support apparatus in Sagrado corazón activo perform different kinds of work.

Petare 2009 — A Still Photograph Lets Viewers Read Urban Density at Their Own Pace

Petare 2009 is a case in which photography turns directly toward the city. Arte Al Día presents the work as a large-scale photographic installation about Petare, the vast barrio in Caracas, and records an exhibition structure that paired the image with writing by H. G. Wells*14. In the wall-sized still image, the accumulation of housing enters the field of view at once: viewers can step back to see the whole slope or move closer to follow individual buildings. Here, viewing time belongs to the viewer. The photograph holds the city on one surface while allowing its interior to be reread in any order. Wizard Gallery summarizes an artistic trajectory that began with film training and moved among photography, video, and sculpture*19. Within the same body of work, repeated events call for video, tactile situations call for an apparatus, and an expansive city is held by a still photograph that can be scanned at the viewer’s own pace.

sections.title: Reception: Religion, Youth Culture, and Globalization
sections.body_html:
The Speed of Humor and the “One-Liner” Critique

Hernández-Díez designs devices that can be grasped quickly: philosophers’ names spelled with sneakers, an apparatus struck by a baseball bat, hands inserted into a case to touch a saint dog. That immediacy draws the viewer into the work. BOMB argues that his reversals of everyday objects, medical equipment, and religious motifs use humor in ways that make viewers complicit in the work’s absurdity*9. In its review of the 2003 survey, The Brooklyn Rail values the dense conjunction of faith and technology in San Guinefort while warning that works such as Thinkers can approach the logic of a “one-liner”*10. A later retrospective review in ArtNexus argues that when the early works are shown again after a quarter century, the obsolescence of what once counted as current technology produces a new layer of meaning*12. As the machines age, they become objects that require preservation and reactivation, much like religious relics.

What Photography, Video, and Installation Each Do — Thinkers Is Read, La Hermandad Holds Time, San Guinefort Requires Touch

MACBA’s retrospective brought early experimental video, screens, display cases, photography, sculpture, and drawing into a single chronological account of the artist’s work*2. San Guinefort requires a display case and the viewer’s body because the viewer inserts an arm through a rubber glove to touch the saint dog*1. Sagrado corazón activo places the cow’s heart and tubing physically in the gallery so that religious imagery and the material presence of life-support technology are experienced together*20. La Hermandad uses video to hold three stages in the pigskin skateboard’s transformation simultaneously*16. In Thinkers, color photography gives the stacked shoes the clarity of an advertisement so that “HUME” or “MARX” can be read at once*1. Petare 2009 leaves an immense quantity of urban detail still, allowing viewers to vary their distance and viewing time*14. Across these works, acts of reading, touching, waiting, and approaching are tied to specific choices of medium.

jules-spinatsch.html.lead_html: Jules Spinatsch is a Swiss photographer who uses automatic and semiautomatic cameras and vast image sequences to photograph security around the World Economic Forum, the Vienna Opera Ball, and Alpine landscapes maintained with artificial snow. Through Temporary Discomfort, Vienna MMIX, and Snow Management, he shifts documentary attention away from the “decisive moment” and toward the systems that determine who makes something visible, by what rules, and for what purpose.
jules-spinatsch.html.thesis_html: Photojournalism has traditionally moved toward the center of an event and condensed a meaningful instant into a single frame. Spinatsch instead predetermines camera position, shooting interval, and scanning sequence, then delegates the act of exposure to the machine. He relocates the photographer’s decisions from the moment of pressing the shutter to the “protocol that produces the photographs,” extending documentary from the event itself to the systems through which visibility is produced and managed. By using technologies closely related to surveillance cameras while reversing the visual priorities created by security, tourism, media, and elite social events, his work offers an important way to think about machine vision after the 2000s.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Documentary Training to the Conditions Around the Event

Spinatsch was born in Davos in 1964, a town now widely associated with the World Economic Forum. In the 1990s he studied documentary photography at the International Center of Photography in New York and worked in photojournalism before turning, around 2000, toward long-term conceptual projects. Engadin Art Talks outlines his activity as a photographer, editor, and lecturer and his movement from documentary training toward research-based work*1. Lars Müller Publishers similarly describes his shift from 1990s press photography toward long-term projects spanning politics, tourism, and surveillance*8.

This transition did not mean that Spinatsch stopped photographing political events. The mechanism by which news photography selects a “center of the event”—leaders, demonstrators, speeches, clashes—became the subject itself. In a video interview, Collection Pictet explains that, while the media concentrates on actors, Spinatsch observes the general visual conditions occupied by political, economic, and social power*2. Photography shifted from a tool for obtaining one representative image of an event to a method for investigating the apparatuses and operations that make the event visible.

Temporary Discomfort: Summit Space Produced by Security Infrastructure

Temporary Discomfort is a long-term project following cities transformed by venues, fences, checkpoints, surveillance, temporary structures, and security around the World Economic Forum in Davos and G8-related meetings. Lars Müller Publishers describes the book as five chapters of photographs and documents spanning Davos, Genoa, New York, Évian, and Geneva, tracing the temporary pressure political gatherings place on public space*7. Publication material from the Centre de la photographie Genève records that the 2004 book was produced with the institution’s collaboration*19.

1854 / British Journal of Photography discusses the series as a response to the photojournalistic consensus that getting closer to the “center of the action” brings the photographer closer to truth*12. By turning away from leaders’ handshakes toward fences, cameras, roads, and backstage infrastructure that keep them secure and separated, Spinatsch makes what normally forms the background of the news into the subject. The series asks both who becomes visible and what systems are built to show some people while screening off others.

The Gulf War and Sophie Ristelhueber: Why Spinatsch Moved Away from Photojournalism

Spinatsch himself cites the 1990–91 Gulf War and Sophie Ristelhueber’s photobook Fait as catalysts for seeking another visual method beyond photojournalism. CNN’s night-vision footage and postwar press images of “victory,” he recalls, strongly controlled the image of the war, while Ristelhueber’s photographs of tracks in the desert and remnants of weapons offered another way of seeing*21. This experience makes the later surveillance panoramas more than technical experiments. Spinatsch works with the contradiction that even exhaustive recording can miss what matters, examining photographic evidence from the side of the system that produces it.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Surveillance Panorama: Delegating the Shutter to the Machine

In 2003, Spinatsch began in Davos the method later called the Surveillance Panorama Projects, using a computer-controlled network camera. His documentation for Vienna MMIX explains how the camera is programmed to scan a space in fixed directions and numbers of exposures, after which the artist no longer chooses the instant of the shutter*17. Collection Pictet likewise describes this semiautomation as distinct from conventional photography, in which the artist decides from moment to moment “what to see”*2.

Authorship appears in advance through decisions about camera placement, shooting interval, scanning range, and later arrangement. As a result, ceilings, equipment, empty seats, backs, and accidental gestures—the details a news camera pursuing important figures would discard—accumulate under the same rules. Spinatsch’s own documentation explains that the method works against the fast, spectacular production of mass-media imagery by preserving large quantities of overlooked detail*17.

Vienna MMIX: Folding Eight Hours into a Single Space

For Vienna MMIX, two programmed cameras scanned the 2009 Vienna Opera Ball over the course of a night. Collection Pictet records 17,352 images taken at three-second intervals from 8:32 p.m. to 5:17 a.m., later presented as a roughly 35-meter, 360-degree panorama*3. The University of Chicago Press bibliography describes the photobook as a two-volume structure: the first contains more than 10,000 images as a chronological sequence, while the second selects just over seventy*10.

From a distance, the installation appears to be a continuous interior panorama, yet adjacent fragments were photographed at different times. David Campany discusses the work as an intersection of multiple systems of seeing involving surveillance, power, spectacle, time, and space*11. Frieze similarly notes that two computer-controlled cameras produced a mosaic of roughly ten thousand images over eight hours, with unattended recording making even private moments among the participants visible*13. The panorama connects different moments within one spatial field and makes them appear like a complete view of a single instant. Its apparent comprehensiveness exposes surveillance imagery as an accumulation of fragmented time.

Turning Surveillance Apparatus into a Means of Production

Spinatsch does not simply photograph surveillance cameras from the outside; he incorporates an analogous form of automated scanning into his own production. Collection Pictet notes that, in Vienna MMIX, fragments recorded without the subjects’ knowledge make the ubiquity of security apparatuses and the contraction of privacy difficult to ignore*3. Le Mois de la Photo Montréal similarly describes the work as an eight-hour scan of the ball with a telephoto camera close to surveillance technology*18.

From Panorama to Panopticon: The More That Is Photographed, the Further the Whole Recedes

The Centre de la photographie Genève, which first exhibited Temporary Discomfort – Chapter IV PULVER GUT in 2003, describes the later semiautomatic photography as a “double-edged” method. The enormous images accumulate enough information for handwritten notes to remain legible, while the same technology can readily become an apparatus for total spatial surveillance; the institution observes that there is only “one step” from panorama to panopticon*26. Spinatsch does not assume that delegating vision to a machine will produce an objective total view. His own texts make a central point of the fact that even thousands or tens of thousands of images made under the same rules do not guarantee complete comprehension*24. Automated photography undermines the surveillance system’s claim to “see everything” through an excess of fragments.

The critical force of this method does not depend on opposing bad surveillance images to good art photography. The same automation becomes surveillance in a police or institutional setting, scenic transmission in tourism, and panorama in art. As Camera Austria’s comparison of Vienna MMIX with stage photography and model books suggests, the work has been received across photographic genres as an image that edits time through rules*14.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Snow Management: The Alpine Landscape as Managed Production

Snow Management began in 2001 and follows ski resorts remade at night through artificial snow, grooming machines, heavy equipment, and lighting. The Prix Pictet series page brings together several works from 2004–08*4. Collection Pictet reads the nocturnal landscapes, occupied only by snow cannons and grooming machines, as the final stage in “producing” nature to meet the demands of the tourism industry*5.

Snow Management treats landscape as a process of management and production. Tourist photography consumes the white mountain as a symbol of nature, while that whiteness is maintained by machinery, electricity, water, and labor. As with the security infrastructure of Temporary Discomfort, operations normally hidden behind the finished appearance of a place move to the center of the image.

Welcome to Photostudio Titlis and Davos Is a Verb: Tracing the Production of Tourist Images

Spinatsch works not only with photographs he makes himself but also with images produced daily by the tourism industry. Welcome to Photostudio Titlis examines the system of souvenir photography in a mountaintop studio; Collection Pictet presents the work in relation to a tourist site’s self-image and the standardized form of the souvenir portrait*6. In Davos Is a Verb, he examines his hometown as a place defined not just by winter scenery but by corporations, brands, conferences, and services. Lars Müller Publishers describes the publication as a combination of photographs, documents, and texts built around the idea that the city’s name itself becomes a kind of “verb” for political and economic activity*9.

Across these works runs an interest in the institutions that produce images behind the surface of a place. Souvenir photographs desired by tourists, images of leaders sought by the media, and surveillance images required by institutions serve different purposes, yet each makes certain subjects visible while pushing others into the background. Spinatsch turns attention to this process of selection and includes within the work the social purpose for which an image is made.

Photobooks and Monumental Installations: Making Quantity Itself Legible

Spinatsch’s method becomes difficult to see when the work is reduced to a representative single image. The Vienna MMIX book prints images numbering in the tens of thousands as a chronological sequence, while the exhibition version unfolds as a monumental band around the walls*10. Photography Now’s exhibition and publication record likewise documents his movement between photobooks and large-scale installations*15. The official website organizes the work since Temporary Discomfort and the Surveillance Panorama Projects by project, reinforcing the fact that the operative unit is the system as a whole rather than the isolated photograph*16.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
From the “Decisive Moment” to the “Photographic Protocol”

Spinatsch’s place in photographic history cannot be reduced to the subject of surveillance society. As 1854 notes, his method is a specific response to a photojournalistic tradition that approaches the event and entrusts truth to one forceful image*12. In the panoramas, the camera moves every three seconds without judging importance. Meaning emerges afterward, when the accumulated fragments are read, arranged, and compared.

With digital photography, images became not only pictures made individually by people but data continuously generated by machines used in surveillance, transportation, tourism, and research. Spinatsch incorporated the operation of those imaging systems into artistic form early in that transition, recasting documentary authorship and evidence as problems of the photographic system itself.

Reception as Post-Documentary Photography

Temporary Discomfort received the Prix du Livre at the Rencontres d’Arles in 2005, and works including Vienna MMIX have continued to be exhibited internationally in photography and contemporary-art contexts. Material from Le Mois de la Photo Montréal summarizes the BMW Photography Prize at Paris Photo, the Arles award, and exhibitions at MoMA, Tate Modern, SFMOMA, and other institutions*18. Collection Pictet also holds several series and presents his work as contemporary photography spanning politics, tourism, and surveillance*20.

The significance of the work does not rest on a claim that machine-made images are objective. Automated images also carry the politics of installation, programming, purpose, and selection. Spinatsch makes those conditions visible and places the photographer inside the same system. In an era of mass automated image production, the structure of his work insists on asking which apparatus made an image, according to whose rules, and what span of time it rendered visible.

Panoramic Vision and the Contradictions of Surveillance

Media scholar Alexander Streitberger discusses Spinatsch’s Surveillance Panorama in Quaderni as a case linking the history of nineteenth-century panoramas to digital surveillance. Early photographic panoramas also stitched together images made at different moments and presented them as a simultaneous total view; in Temporary Discomfort and Panopticon, those seams expand to the scale of thousands of images*27.

Streitberger emphasizes that, while systems such as Google Street View suppress distortions and color shifts at their joins to create a smooth space, Spinatsch intentionally retains blur, distortion, color differences, and temporal discontinuities*27. The article places this work alongside Mario Santamaría, Michiel van Bakel, and Hito Steyerl as forms of “counter-surveillance panorama.” Their position is defined by destabilizing, from within, the continuous total view promised by surveillance systems through the multiplicity of fragments and seams that make the image.

Cartier-Bresson and Muybridge: The Decisive Moment Versus Scanning

Using 10,008 images from the Vienna Opera Ball as an example, Spinatsch’s project documentation explains that mechanically recording everything with equal weight still fails to produce a total understanding. As a conceptual alternative to Cartier-Bresson’s “decisive moment,” it describes a camera that moves through fixed horizontal and vertical steps over an extended period*24. Existing Vienna MMIX documentation also connects the method to Eadweard Muybridge’s sequential photography, since both divide time into smaller units and later assemble them into a visual field instead of privileging a single instant*17. In the Davos work, a remotely controlled camera made more than 2,176 images over three hours, showing the construction of the security zone rather than the main event*22. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art likewise describes the method as a reversal of the same surveillance technology used by security authorities*23. Where Muybridge made motion analyzable through sequential images, Spinatsch turns the opposite paradox into a work: the more information accumulates, the more the complete picture recedes.

The 2026 Retrospective: Thirty-Five Years of Chance and Control

The Kunstmuseum Graubünden retrospective that opened on August 22, 2026, frames thirty-five years of work as an inquiry moving from directly observed documentary photography toward semiautomatic imaging. It identifies chance and control, power, authorship, and the instability of the photographic image as central concerns*25. The surveillance panorama is thus being reconsidered not as a short-lived digital technique but as an ongoing method for asking who sees and who can be said to have made an image.

The issues highlighted by the 2026 retrospective were already present in the work’s early reception in 2003. After exhibiting the first Surveillance Panorama that year, the Centre de la photographie Genève organized a 2018–19 retrospective of semiautomatic photography and noted that, despite a change in equipment from webcams to SLR cameras, the same principle remained: the artist determines the duration and scanning range, while individual moments are delegated to the machine*26. Once the novelty of the technology has faded, the enduring questions concern how far a photographer can transfer judgment into prior rules and who will read the large quantities of images those rules generate—and how.

justine-kurland.html.lead_html: In Girl Pictures, Justine Kurland photographed provisional communities of girls in American forests, suburbs, and roadside spaces. This page follows her use of the large-format camera, her discussions with participants, the histories of road photography and the frontier myth, her travels as a mother, and the later works This Train and SCUMB Manifesto to trace a changing engagement with mobility, freedom, and care.
justine-kurland.html.thesis_html: In Girl Pictures, the free subject crossing the American landscape shifts from the solitary male traveler to groups of girls who make places for one another. They braid hair, sleep, swim, keep watch, and occupy the foreground and depth of the image with several bodies at once. Kurland discussed actions and arrangements with participants she met on the road, using the preparation required by a large-format camera as time for collaborative production. Road photography, pastoral landscape, and stories of runaway girls overlap in the same frame, holding freedom beside danger and fantasy beside differences of age and authority. Later works made during travels with her son add care, waiting, and the history of infrastructure to mobility. In SCUMB Manifesto, she physically re-edited photobooks from a male-dominated canon. Across the placement of sitters and the ownership of photographic history, her work asks who creates freedom and who records it.
