sections.title: Background and Historical Moment
sections.body_html:
Shiga first began making photographs with an autofocus compact camera she had used at a high school sports festival. With the remaining film, she moved a desk and cup little by little and photographed them. When she saw the developed prints, she felt uneasy that a scene she had carefully constructed had returned as something like “proof of reality”*1. What she received from this experience was less a belief in photography’s correctness than a sense that a made scene, once printed, could stand apart from the photographer’s intention and appear like evidence of reality. SFMOMA explains that Shiga had studied classical ballet from childhood and began photographing with her parents’ compact camera around the time changes in her teenage body made that path difficult to continue*2. Photography emerged as a way to transfer sensations that had become difficult to express through the body into the camera, light, and photographic paper. In an ART iT interview, Shiga says that in drawing the hand is too close to the image, while in photography the arranged subject can finally be handed over through the shutter*1. This provides a starting point for understanding her later staging, strong flash, the gap between body and image, and the reality that enters the photograph.

Shiga’s move to London was also shaped by a desire to think about photography within a broader field of art. In an interview with Ashley Rawlings, she says that she felt constrained by the way photography was discussed in Japanese photography schools, and that while visiting museums and galleries in London she learned of a school where photography could be studied within a wider art context*3. Her official website records that she completed Fine Art New Media at Chelsea College of Art and Design, London Institute, in 2004*4. SFMOMA explains that during her London years Shiga photographed people close to her—friends, roommates, and neighbors—as unsettling scenes that also evoke nineteenth-century spirit photography*2. Although she photographed people close to her, Shiga did not move toward explaining their faces or personalities. Through light, pose, rephotography, dark interiors, and the relation with the photographer, these people appear as actual individuals and at the same time as other kinds of beings.

After Lilly and CANARY in the mid-2000s, Shiga received the 33rd Kimura Ihei Photography Award and, in 2009, the ICP Infinity Award for Young Photographer*5. In 2008, she moved to Kitakama, a coastal village near Sendai, and became a local photographer, asked to photograph residents, sports days, festivals, meetings, and other community events. SFMOMA explains that in Kitakama she photographed residents and local events while attempting to build an unofficial archive through photographs and oral accounts*2. In the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami, her home and studio were swept away, and many Kitakama residents died. In an essay published by Aperture, Mariko Takeuchi notes that after the disaster Shiga took part in washing, drying, and returning photographs found in the debris to their owners*6. Rasen Kaigan is often seen as a post-disaster work, but its making began in Kitakama before the earthquake and tsunami. The disaster made clear within Shiga’s work that photography can be an artwork, a local record, a memorial portrait, damaged paper, and an object returned to someone’s hands.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Images Returning on Photographic Paper

Shiga’s understanding of photography begins with the sensation of holding an image that has appeared on photographic paper. In her words, as introduced by SFMOMA, it was a shock that an image she had imagined could be reproduced as a material sheet of photographic paper and held in her hand; that experience led her to photography as a form of self-expression in place of dance*2. The key point is that a sensation held within the body appears, once photographed, as an object outside the body. The image separated from the artist’s body returns bearing the subject’s gestures, the fall of light, and the humidity or atmosphere of a place. The dark interiors, strong light, unnatural poses, and rephotography in Lilly and CANARY become ways of repeatedly working with this “image outside the body.”

Reality Entering the Constructed Image

Shiga’s photographs emerge between an image imagined before shooting and the reactions that occur during the act of photographing. In Rawlings’s interview, Shiga describes the image and setup she brings in advance as conditions that allow unexpected moments to arise*3. The photographer makes a scene. The subject responds. Light enters, the body moves, and after development the image returns. In that process, a reality that departs from the plan enters the image the artist had imagined. Shiga’s interest turns toward the sensation that a made scene can appear on the print with the face of evidence while also becoming another reality, rather than toward deciding whether photography captures truth.

The staging, lighting, participation of subjects, and color filters described by SFMOMA are operations that make the world appear fantastic while also moving traces of reality into another image*2.In Shiga’s photographs, skin, shadow, the direction of the eyes, and the stiffness of the body remain strongly present within staged scenes.Strong flash flattens the figure while emphasizing skin, shadow, the direction of the eyes, and the rigidity of the body. Darkness conceals the scene while intensifying the presence of the person who was there. The constructed image and the traces of reality that remain within it give Shiga’s photographs their instability and force.

Photography as Being Photographed

For Shiga, photography turns from an act in which the photographer controls the subject into an experience that unsettles the photographer herself. In her interview with Ashley Rawlings, she describes photographing as the reverse of “shooting”—as an experience of “being shot”—and explains that the time of her own existence is revived within the photograph*3. The Brooklyn Rail review of Blind Date treats this idea concretely as a problem of photographing people. It describes the elongated pages of couples riding motorcycles in Thailand as a panorama of passing faces and focuses on the women who look back at the lens from the passenger seat*8. That gaze does not leave the viewer in the safe position of an observer. The viewer is placed as if standing beside a motorcycle passing by and suddenly receiving the gaze of a stranger. The Brooklyn Rail also reads the power relations around objectification through Shiga’s connection of “eyes” with desire and curse*8. Here, objectification means treating another person as a one-sided object of the photographer’s or viewer’s gaze, erasing that person’s own gaze and response. In Blind Date, the subjects look back into the lens, and the viewer receives that gaze, making the act of looking at the photograph unstable. The figures in Blind Date also lead toward the figures in Rasen Kaigan. Kitakama residents stand before the camera within local records, memorial portraits, event photographs, oral accounts, and memories of the land. In Shiga’s photographs, photographing a person means seeing that person while alsobeing looked back at by that person and seeing the time of the land and of the dead at the same time.

Photography as Medium, the Body as Medium

SFMOMA introduces Shiga’s idea of the camera as something like a “portal,” away from metaphors such as weapon, tool, or witness. It also describes her work as grounded in place-based fieldwork, human experience, staging, lighting, the participation of subjects, and color filters*2. Within this “portal,” the appearance of the outside world and fear or unease felt in the body pass through the subject, light, and memories of the land to become one image. The artscape International review of CANARY refers to Bataille’s thinking on sacrifice and reads Shiga’s phrase “being photographed” as a moment in which the photographer offers herself to the image*7. In Bataille, sacrifice can be understood as an experience that removes the body from the everyday order in which things are managed for use, bringing it into contact with death, excess, and fear. In Shiga’s photographs, this idea helps frame the work as an experience in which the photographer herself is exposed to light, bodies, and the presence of death, instead of simply mastering a subject. In a Tokyo Art Beat interview related to Bipolar, Shiga speaks of photography as an act that creates a space-time outside past, present, and future through an image that appears on paper*31. Photography is a device that records the external world, and it is also a medium that gives fear felt in the body, unease, and imagination toward the dead a form that can be sensed through light, paper, and exhibition space.

People Carry Land and Time

In Shiga’s photographs of people, the orientation of the body, hidden faces, strong light, dark interiors, and exchanges with the photographer determine how a person appears more than face, expression, or personality. Tate Photography calls her works “intimate portraits” and describes them as photographs that bring together mystical landscapes and interiors, personal experience, and larger myths*9. The intimacy Tate describes includes psychological closeness between artist and subject, as well as the sense that the body, place, light, myth, and memory are joined within the same image. The figures in Lilly and CANARY appear in dark rooms, fire, floating postures, hidden faces, and strong light, as if their bodies have been moved into another reality. In Rasen Kaigan, those bodies become tied to the land of Kitakama, oral accounts, memories of cultivation, and imagination toward the dead. Marco Bohr, writing in TIME, places CANARY alongside the folkloric night landscapes and portraits of Masatoshi Naitō’s Tono Monogatari and describes it as work concerned with the fragility of the body and psychological landscapes*10.In Shiga’s images of people, what comes forward is less who is photographed than what atmosphere the body takes on through light and staging. The time of land and myth accumulates there.

In Kitakama, Photography Becomes Local Work

In Kitakama, Shiga made artworks while also serving as a local photographer, photographing residents, sports days, festivals, meetings, weddings, funerals, and other community occasions, and continuing to collect oral accounts*2. In this place, photography was used at the same time as the artist’s work, a record of community events, family photography, memorial portraits, and material for oral history. Aveek Sen’s essay for ART iT connects Shiga’s life in Kitakama and her gradual assumption of the role of local photographer to questions of memory and photography after the disaster*11. What Shiga made here includes works made from the landscape of Kitakama and also a situation in which photographs were requested, used locally, chosen for the dead, connected to oral accounts, and needed in residents’ lives.

This work can appear too calm if it is read only through its relation with the community. In ART iT’s “Critical Fieldwork 34,” Minoru Shimizu criticizes readings of Rasen Kaigan that rely on the language of collaboration and mediation while pushing the artist’s decisions into the background*12. When cooperation with residents or local record-keeping is emphasized too strongly, Shiga’s decisions—what photographs to choose, at what scale to show them, in what order to install them, and whose voices to include—become less visible. That is the core of the criticism. The point is severe, but it shows that Shiga’s photographs have been received as work that carries the authority of record, collaboration, staging, and exhibition at once. In portrait of cultivation, a person, tree roots, a body, and memories of cultivation overlap within a single image. The fact that SFMOMA, MoMA, Getty, and others hold this work or related works from the series shows that this image of a person has been seen within contemporary photography*13.

After the Tsunami, Photographs Themselves Become Relics

After the 2011 tsunami, Shiga took part in washing, drying, and returning photographs found in the debris to their owners*6. This work is inseparable from her understanding of photography. In the Rawlings interview, Shiga speaks of the photograph less as a representation of “murdered time” than as a place where time and life are revived*3. The photographs washed after the tsunami translated that idea into the physical act of cleaning dirty paper by hand, drying it, and returning it. In those soiled photographs remained families, the dead, lost homes, and time that could not return. Getty News introduces Shiga after the disaster as an artist involved with Kitakama’s community archive and conveys how photographs take on roles within memory and loss*14. Photographs Shiga made, photographs entrusted to her by residents, photographs soiled by the tsunami, and photographs installed in the exhibition space were different kinds of photographs, but in Kitakama they belonged to the same life. What becomes visible here is the range of roles photography can take: preserving the past, supporting events and families, becoming memorial portraits, being damaged by disaster, being washed, and returning once more to someone’s hands.

Making Time for Looking in the Exhibition Space

Shiga’s work does not sit easily within the photobook or the single print. CANARY was also presented as a slide projection with sound, and artscape International points out that still photographs are connected within the time of edited projection*7. The Rasen Kaigan exhibition at Sendai Mediatheque was structured as an exhibition that included photographs, texts, oral accounts gathered in the community, and large-scale prints*15. Tokyo Photographic Art Museum also introduced Human Spring as an exhibition of new work that included photographs made with participants and the experience of the exhibition space*16. The time of looking at Shiga’s photographs shifts from checking images one by one to walking through a dark space, changing the direction of one’s body, and encountering photographs, texts, and the traces of voices.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Lilly and CANARY

In Lilly and CANARY, Shiga’s understanding of photography appears with particular directness. SFMOMA describes Lilly as an attempt to reconstruct the atmosphere of adolescence, and CANARY as a complex engagement with society and the outside world*2. Art Platform Japan records CANARY as a 61-part work from 2007*17. In CANARY, the people are real human beings, yet through blown-out flash, dark backgrounds, fire, floating postures, and hidden faces, they become bodies within dream and fear. Priska Pasquer’s introduction to the FOAM exhibition describes CANARY as a work that combines local myths, stories of ordinary people, personal memories, and emotions, and writes that Shiga imagines an image before meeting people or places and, in the process, seems to enter a state beyond her own body*18. In this series, Shiga creates a state in which bodies pass through light and darkness and take on another time; the images are more than a sequence of strange scenes.

International criticism has placed CANARY within staged photography, spirit photography, myth, and the temporal expression of slide projection. Marco Bohr, writing in TIME, reads CANARY as an attempt to choreograph emotionally and psychologically charged inner landscapes through photography rather than as a record of recognizable physical reality, and writes that it recalls the folkloric night landscapes and portraits of Masatoshi Naitō’s Tono Monogatari*10. The artscape International review of CANARY connects the work to Bataille, spirit photography, and mythic realms, and, in relation to the slide-sequence form, refers to Nan Goldin’s The Ballad of Sexual Dependency and Robert Smithson’s Hotel Palenque*7. Goldin showed friends, lovers, sexuality, and dependency through slides accompanied by music, allowing private photographs to be experienced as a flow of time. Smithson’s Hotel Palenque presents slides of buildings and ruins encountered during travel together with narration, serving as a precedent in which still photographs become a lecture, a story, and an experience of time. The connection with Shiga lies less in subject matter than in the form of projecting and editing still photographs to create a duration for viewing. CANARY intensifies the presence of the body and of death through the strangeness of its images and through the time in which photographs appear one by one, disappear, and move to the next image.

Blind Date

Blind Date is a series of couples riding motorcycles in Thailand and is an important work for thinking about Shiga’s photographs of people. The Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art introduces the exhibition as an installation dealing with photographs of lovers taken in Bangkok, loss, death, capital, light, and darkness*19. The Brooklyn Rail review writes that the horizontal pages create a panorama of faces passing by on motorcycles and notes that the viewer is placed near the couples themselves*8. In many photographs, men drive while women look toward the lens from the passenger seat. The review argues that this gaze shifts the relation between the image and the viewer, turning the act of looking at the photograph into the experience of being placed before the eyes of an unknown person*8. It further notes that the women are not flattened into familiar roles such as sadness, sexuality, loss, or muse, but appear as figures who examine the viewer in return*8. In this series, strong colors and fantastic props are restrained. Even so, faces that approach and recede at speed, gazes from the passenger seat, and negotiations between photographer and subject show how Shiga thinks about “photographing people.” Here, a person appears as a momentary encounter with the viewer, not as a fixed portrait.

Rasen Kaigan

Rasen Kaigan is Shiga’s central body of work, bringing together life in Kitakama, oral accounts, her work as a local photographer, and the rescue of photographs after the disaster. The official page of Sendai Mediatheque records that the exhibition was based on her activities in Kitakama and was a large-scale presentation that included photographs and texts*15. In an SFMOMA video, Shiga explains that when she found a subject that attracted her, she felt she first needed to live around it and share life before photographing, and that this is why she moved to Kitakama*20. In the same video, she recalls being asked for a photograph for a funeral while photographing festivals and meetings as a local photographer, and describes how this led her to approach the invisible spirit and history of Kitakama*20. The people who appear in this series are Kitakama residents, partners in oral accounts, and figures close to those who requested memorial portraits. People, land, and the time of the dead overlap within the same image.

Rasen Kaigan has the character of a local archive and, at the same time, that of a strongly staged body of photographs and exhibition. Minoru Shimizu’s ART iT “Critical Fieldwork 33” reads the exhibition as a “stage set” in which remembering and mourning alternate, and places Shiga outside the categories of straight photographer or pictorial photographer, calling her a “director of images” who uses photographs like actors*32. This evaluation includes criticism, but it shows that Shiga’s work has been read not just as a record of Kitakama, but as the work of an artist who arranges photographs, exhibition space, walking bodies, and the time of memory. The photobook Rasen Kaigan album and the text volume Rasen Kaigan notebook offer an entry point into oral accounts, memories of the land, and residents’ words that photographs alone may not convey*22.

Regarding Portrait of Cultivation, Shiga says that she did not stop at listening to accounts of cultivation; she actually dug up pine roots and photographed a person holding them*20. In that image, the person does not simply stand as an explainer of the land; the figure becomes an image that bears the excavated roots, the weight of the body, and memories of cultivation. MoMA holds portrait of cultivation and rasen kaigan 31, while SFMOMA and Tokyo Photographic Art Museum hold Rasen Kaigan 46*21. Kitakama was the stage for the work and also a place where the process by which photographs are needed within a community, damaged, preserved, and moved into exhibition became concrete. What Shiga treats is the landscape and residents of Kitakama, and also the movement by which photography is used in daily life, lost, and returned bearing another meaning.

After Human Spring

After Human Spring, Shiga’s attention moves from Kitakama toward Miyagi’s landscapes, bodies, death, living beings, and social change. Amanda Maddox of Aperture discusses Human Spring as work following Rasen Kaigan and Blind Date, linking natural disasters, the body, and questions of seeing*23. SFMOMA also explains that her recent projects consider the landscape of Miyagi through changes in Japanese society during the Heisei era and cycles of life and death*2. Artizon Museum’s Hyōchaku placed Chikako Yamashiro and Lieko Shiga together as artists concerned with the land, memory, disaster, movement, and regeneration of Okinawa and Tohoku*24. In a Tokyo Art Beat interview related to Bipolar, Shiga speaks of photography as an act that creates a distinctive space-time through images that appear on paper*31. Here, too, Shiga’s interest reaches beyond records that explain events, toward how the body comes into contact with changes in the land and how photography gives that contact another space-time.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photo History
sections.body_html:
The Body, Self-Image, and Women Photographers

Since the 2000s, Shiga has been introduced internationally alongside Rinko Kawauchi, Yuki Onodera, Chino Otsuka, Tomoko Sawada, Miyako Ishiuchi, and others. Getty’s The Younger Generation presents Kawauchi, Onodera, Otsuka, Sawada, and Shiga as diverse practices after the era often referred to as “girl photography”*25. This grouping points to changes in the body, self-image, and relations of seeing and being seen in photography, more than to a category of young women artists. Alongside Sawada’s self-portraits, Otsuka’s self-image and memory, Onodera’s constructed images, and Kawauchi’s sense of light and the everyday, Shiga draws the subject’s body into light, staging, and memories of place.

I’m So Happy You Are Here, organized by Aperture and Rencontres d’Arles, also includes Shiga within a broad lineage of Japanese women photographers*26. Seeing Shiga here matters because her work changes relations among portrait, body, self-image, and subject, rather than simply adding her to a list of representative women photographers. The returning gaze in Blind Date, the floating bodies in CANARY, and the figure holding roots in Rasen Kaigan extend portraiture from the communication of face or personality into images where body, land, and the time of the dead overlap.

Between Record and Staging

Shiga’s place in photographic history lies where documentary record and staged photography overlap. Photography has the ability to leave, as traces of light, people and things that were before the camera. In photographic history, this quality has been discussed as record or indexicality. Shiga, however, entered photography by making scenes before shooting, as in her movement of a cup on a desk. In the desk-and-cup episode from the 2009 ART iT interview, a deliberately made scene returned, once printed, as something like “proof of reality”*1. Here, photography’s ability to leave traces of what was there and the photographer’s staging of a scene exist in the same image. Shiga has worked with the moment when an image gains an unexpected sense of reality at that overlap.

Minoru Shimizu’s ART iT “Critical Fieldwork 34,” written as a critique of responses to Rasen Kaigan, refers to Takuma Nakahira, Walter Benjamin, daguerreotype portraits, landscape photography, Eugène Atget, and spirit photography*12. Mediation here refers to the way a photographic trace gains meaning through the photographer’s choices, the relation with the subject, printing, exhibition, and the viewer’s interpretation. The discussion around Nakahira includes both a suspicion toward treating photography as a simple copy of the world and a commitment to the trace left by photography’s contact with the world. Benjamin, daguerreotype portraits, landscape photography, and Atget are invoked to think about the uncanniness that clings to early photography: faces and places that remain after time has passed, and empty streets that appear as traces. Spirit photography points to the desire, long attached to the history of photography, that even invisible things might be captured. Shimizu’s essay is critical in tone, but it shows that Shiga’s photographs have drawn discussion around record, mediation, the invisible, and photography’s early uncanniness.

After 3.11, What Can Photography Do?

In photography after 3.11, the question was how to record the earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident, as well as how photography might participate in loss, recovery, and the transmission of memory. MFA Boston’s In the Wake presented responses to the disaster by seventeen photographers, including Naoya Hatakeyama, Nobuyoshi Araki, Takashi Arai, Rinko Kawauchi, Takashi Homma, Tomoko Yoneda, and Lieko Shiga*27. A review in Musée Magazine explains that the exhibition was structured around documentary approaches to the disaster, experimental uses of photographic technology, and the development of new visual narratives around Tohoku*33. In this field, photography became an image that conveyed damage, a means of thinking about invisible radiation and loss, and an act of recovering lost family photographs.

Shiga’s position within this field is somewhat distinct. She had lived in Kitakama before the disaster, photographing residents and events and being asked to make photographs for funerals. The washing of photographs after the tsunami occurred within a life in which she was already involved as a local photographer, rather than as work documenting the disaster from outside. Musée Magazine notes that Shiga’s project was placed near Naoya Hatakeyama’s work on his hometown of Rikuzentakata, and that Shiga was introduced, alongside Munemasa Takahashi’s Lost & Found, as an artist involved in recovering lost family photographs and returning them to their owners*33. Sendai Mediatheque organized a dialogue between Shiga and Hatakeyama titled Anya Kōro—What Can Photography Do?*28. Artizon Museum’s Hyōchaku placed Chikako Yamashiro and Shiga together as artists concerned with Okinawa and Tohoku, land, memory, disaster, movement, and regeneration*24. Seen in these groupings, Shiga’s work in Kitakama appears as a practice concerned with the process by which photography supports community memory, becomes damaged, is washed, and returns to someone’s hands.

Why Shiga Matters in Contemporary Japanese Photography

Shiga’s reception rests on more than the novelty of strong color or strange staging. TCAA evaluates her work as an inquiry into the equivalence between photography as a medium and the human psyche, and as a perspective that crosses between the nature of photography and the human body*29. This “equivalence” can be understood as the way movements of the mind take form in the same place as photographic materials, rather than as explanations placed behind the work. Anxiety appears as darkness or strong flash; imagination toward the dead appears as memorial portraits or damaged paper; unease toward a place appears as unnatural posture or as the viewer’s body moving through the exhibition space. In Shiga’s photographs, what is inside the mind does not arrive afterward as verbal explanation; it appears as the intensity of light, the damage to paper, the stiffness of bodies, and the movement of the viewer.

In an exhibition on Japanese photography from the postwar period to the present, SFMOMA traced a trajectory in which Shōmei Tōmatsu and Daidō Moriyama addressed Americanization and urban change, Nobuyoshi Araki and Eikoh Hosoe developed more personal and performative forms of photography, and photography turned toward contemporary culture, including the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident. Within that account, SFMOMA identifies Miyako Ishiuchi, Rinko Kawauchi, and Lieko Shiga as significant women artists in contemporary Japanese photography*2. Tate Photography introduces Shiga’s photographs as works that bring together intimate portraits, mystical landscapes, personal experience, and myth*9. In a context that includes A Portrait of Cultivation, Anselm Franke of HKW discusses media as something through which bodies, environments, communities, and invisible transmissions pass*30. Taken together, these sources position Shiga as an artist who gives concrete form, within images and exhibition spaces, to record, staging, body, portrait, disaster, and community.

louis-faurer.html.lead_html: Louis Faurer photographed passersby, street vendors, people with disabilities, and isolated figures amid neon, shopwindows, reflections, blur, and double images around Times Square and Fourteenth Street in the 1940s and 1950s. While continuing fashion assignments for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, and other magazines, his private street photographs used darkness, glass, and layered light to resist a clean, orderly description of the city. This page examines the tension between commercial and personal work, his relationship with Robert Frank, and his reassessment from the 1980s onward.
louis-faurer.html.thesis_html: In New York in the 1930s and 1940s, the Photo League connected street photography to social documentary on labor, poverty, and urban life. After the war, amid McCarthyism and the conformist pressures of consumer society, street photography increasingly moved from the presentation of social types toward subjective images of the city that carried the photographer’s own anxiety and perception.*21 Working outside the Photo League, Faurer placed beggars, street vendors, people with disabilities, and isolated figures in Times Square and along Fourteenth Street amid neon, advertising lettering, reflections, double exposures, and darkroom intervention, allowing the bright urban image promised by postwar prosperity and the individuals isolated within it to occupy the same frame. William Klein’s 1954 work transformed urban collision through wide-angle lenses, grain, and tilted compositions into a more aggressive visual language.*23 Robert Frank’s The Americans expanded alienation, class, race, and political ritual into a photobook sequence at the scale of the nation.*21 Faurer had been returning to the narrower territory of New York at night since the late 1940s, placing his work between reform-minded documentary and the Beat-inflected, subjective street photography of the 1950s. Where Diane Arbus later moved toward portraits that isolate the figure from the urban environment, Faurer’s subjects remain caught within the pressures of advertising, glass, and darkness.*20

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Times Square

Faurer was born in Philadelphia in 1916. After studying commercial art, he began working professionally in photography in the late 1930s. The Philadelphia Museum of Art retrospective spans 1937–83 and places particular emphasis on his New York work of 1947–51.*1 In a 1979 text, Faurer recalled photographing almost every day, following the twilight light to Times Square, then developing and printing at night in Robert Frank’s darkroom until the routine became a “way of life.”*18 New York at night grew from this repeated daily rhythm; the visual language followed the routine. He also wrote that commercial assignments for magazines such as Harper’s Bazaar supported him and made his private photography possible.*18 Magazine work and nighttime street photography were parallel circuits within the same New York life. Getty’s authority record gives the basic biography: an American photographer born in Philadelphia in 1916 and deceased in 2001.*3

Times Square and Fourteenth Street

Faurer repeatedly photographed Times Square, Fourteenth Street, movie theaters, buses, and ferries—places dense with people, advertising text, and artificial light. The Philadelphia Museum of Art catalogue describes theater lines, ushers, B-movie signs, and passersby as part of a melancholic, psychologically charged image of the city.*4 The National Gallery of Art’s The Streets of New York places Faurer with Roy DeCarava, Ted Croner, and others in the history of New York photography between Walker Evans’s American Photographs and Robert Frank’s The Americans.*5 Neon in Faurer’s work carries more than the visual excitement of the metropolis. Lettering overlaps bodies, glass reflects another space, and faces emerge from shadow, bringing the prosperity promised by advertising into the same field as individual isolation. He keeps the street’s information overload intact and turns density itself into psychological pressure. In Staten Island Ferry (1946), reflections in the ferry window overlap with the distant city and fragments of seated figures; the Jewish Museum describes the image in terms of people separated from one another within the metropolis.*2 Reflection and doubling structure the division between person and city and become part of the photograph’s psychological organization.*2

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Figures at the Margins

Faurer’s repeated attention to beggars, street vendors, people with disabilities, and visibly isolated figures was rooted in a form of self-projection; he was not collecting social “types.” The Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson retrospective notes that he avoided excessively violent situations that might humiliate his subjects, consciously projected himself into the people he photographed, and often found himself in them.*19 The Met likewise emphasizes his recurring attention to people at the social margins during the apparent prosperity of postwar America.*6 His proximity seeks continuity with the anxiety and solitude of anonymous others instead of organizing poverty or disability as representative social cases. In some photographs the photographer’s own reflection enters the picture, disturbing a clean division between observer and observed.*19 Smithsonian Magazine has similarly described his recurring interest in Times Square light and marginalized figures as a way of setting the psychology of a still person against the movement of the surrounding city.*7

Reflections, Double Exposures, and Darkroom Intervention

Faurer described his motivation as an urgent desire to record life as he “sees” and “feels” it.*20 Low light, reflections, blur, double exposure, and darkroom intervention recur as ways of keeping visible facts and the sensations produced in the moment within the same image, instead of classifying the street with documentary clarity. In New York, N.Y. (1946), The Met identifies the white form at lower left as a darkroom addition that heightens psychological tension.*8 The Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson also notes Faurer’s active use of blur, superimposed negatives, and grain produced by nighttime illumination.*19 These procedures leave interruptions, overlaps, and delays of seeing on the photographic surface. His subjectivity lies less in dramatizing the people he photographs than in allowing unstable perception to remain visible.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Frank, Klein, and Arbus

Faurer and Robert Frank were close in late-1940s New York and shared a darkroom. Faurer’s 1947 portrait Robert Frank is held by the National Portrait Gallery.*10 Their work nevertheless develops different forms of subjective street photography. Faurer repeatedly returned to Times Square and Fourteenth Street, layering people with advertising, glass, and nighttime light to probe the psychology of a single city. Frank edited his 1955–57 travels across the United States into The Americans, connecting race, class, political ritual, and consumer culture at a national scale.*24 From 1954 onward, William Klein used wide-angle lenses, close range, grain, tilted framing, and page layout to turn New York’s collisions into an aggressive visual field.*23 Diane Arbus later isolated figures from the city and concentrated on frontal encounter and bodily specificity. Faurer’s people remain embedded in neon, advertising, reflections, and darkness; the urban environment itself becomes part of their psychological situation. The Met’s reference to his influence on Frank, Friedlander, and Arbus is tied to this simultaneous subjectivization of city and person.*8 San Gennaro Festival, New York City (1950), now at MFAH, came from Robert Frank’s collection, leaving a material trace of their exchange in the photograph’s provenance.*11

From the Photo League to Psychological Street Photography

In the 1930s and 1940s, the Photo League linked labor, housing, and poverty to collective study and social reform, using street photography to make social problems visible.*21 Faurer was not a member. Although he also photographed people at the margins of the city, he did not organize them as examples of class or poverty. Advertising text, window reflections, shadow, and blur overlap the figure, while his own loneliness and unease enter the construction of the image. The Milwaukee Art Museum exhibition Street Seen: The Psychological Gesture in American Photography, 1940–1959 brought Lisette Model, Faurer, Ted Croner, Saul Leiter, Klein, and Frank together as part of a shift from social record toward psychological and subjective street photography.*22 Within that transition, Faurer was treating the street as a site of unstable perception before the major photobook culture of the 1950s was fully established.

Fashion Magazines and Private Photography

Faurer worked in fashion for Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, Flair, Seventeen, and other magazines over many years. MFAH describes a career in which the precision applied to a model’s line and expression in magazine work coexisted with psychologically unstable figures in his private street photographs.*12 Postwar American magazines, under art directors such as Alexey Brodovitch, modernized the relation among photography, typography, and page layout and provided a livelihood for photographers including Faurer and Frank.*13 In Faurer’s case, the clear presentation of the figure demanded by commercial photography contrasts with the reflection, darkness, and cropping of the private work. Both depend on his ability to organize artificial urban light and bodily posture quickly; according to use, that skill divides between the body presented as a commodity and the body isolated within the city.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
The 1981 Exhibition and 2002 Retrospective

Faurer was not as widely known early in his career as he is today. The exhibition history for NGA’s Champion shows the 1981 University of Maryland exhibition Photographs from Philadelphia and New York, 1937–1973 as an important moment of reassessment.*14 A major retrospective organized by the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston in 2002 traveled to the Addison Gallery, the Art Institute of Chicago, and other venues before reaching the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 2003.*1 ICP’s library holds the accompanying 2002 monograph; research by Anne Wilkes Tucker and others became a standard source for later study.*15 Faurer’s reputation was thus built in stages through solo exhibitions, retrospectives, catalogue scholarship, and entry into public collections from the 1980s onward. MoMA currently makes thirteen works available online, sustaining his place within a museum history of postwar American photography.*9 The Smithsonian American Art Museum’s Fifth Avenue, New York, New York is another example of his New York street work entering major public collections.*17

A Junction in Postwar New York Photography

Faurer occupies a junction among several histories of postwar New York photography. The Photo League’s reformist documentary, the sophistication of magazine culture, the subjective turn associated with Klein and Frank in the 1950s, and the experiments of Friedlander and Arbus in the 1960s each reorganized the relation between city and person in different ways. From the late 1940s, Faurer repeatedly photographed the nighttime territory of Times Square within that transition, placing socially marginal figures and the artificial environment of advertising and neon in the same image. The Jewish Museum’s New York: Capital of Photography brought Hine, DeCarava, Model, Faurer, Klein, and Arbus together to describe New York photography as multiple lineages in which social criticism, immigrant culture, magazines, and authorial subjectivity intersected.*16 Faurer’s early position within this history connects the reform-oriented documentary of the 1930s with the increasingly psychological and personal urban photography of the 1950s and 1960s.

louis-vaire.html.lead_html: The site entry "louis-vaire" corresponds to the photographer documented as Louis Vert (1865–1924). He recorded Parisian street trades between approximately 1900 and 1906; his works are held at the Musée Carnavalet. Alongside Atget and Géniaux, he represents a key figure in the documentary photography of Parisian street life at the turn of the twentieth century.
louis-vaire.html.thesis_html: As an amateur associated with the Société Française de Photographie, Vaire recorded the street workers of Paris between 1900 and 1906, treating individuals and their specific movements rather than social types. His inclusion alongside Atget and Geniaux in ICP exhibitions opened a way of reconstructing 1900s Paris street photography as a practice with multiple contributors, rather than a history organized around Atget alone.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Louis Vert (1865–1924) is the photographer documented by the Musée d'Orsay and the ICP under this site's entry name "louis-vaire," which reflects a variant spelling. He worked as an amateur photographer connected with the SFP (Société Française de Photographie) and produced an intensive series of photographs of Parisian street trades between approximately 1900 and 1906. The majority of his works are held at the Musée Carnavalet.*1

His documented activity is the subject of Alain Fourquier's monograph Louis Vert (1865–1924): photographe de l'animation de la rue à Paris — the primary scholarly reference for understanding his work systematically.*2

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Recording the "petits métiers" of Paris — a visual catalogue of disappearing trades

The subjects of Louis Vert's photographs are the street tradespeople (petits métiers) who made their living in Paris around 1900: tinkers (étameurs), bill posters (afficheurs), porters (portefaix), café au lait sellers (marchandes de café), ragpickers (chiffonniers), boatmen (bateliers), basket weavers (vanniers), and chestnut sellers (marchands de marrons). Many of these occupations disappeared rapidly after the 1910s under industrialization and modernization.*3

The Paris Musées collection makes several of Vert's works available online. The close-range framing used for each worker suggests an approach oriented toward recording individual movements and expressions rather than classifying occupational or ethnic types. The period around the 1900 Paris World's Fair was one of rapid urban transformation; Vert's photographs constitute a visual inventory of traditional Parisian street life at the moment of its disappearance.*4

Positioned alongside Atget and Géniaux — three visions, methodological differences

The ICP's exhibition "Géniaux, Atget, Vert: Petits métiers et types parisiens" placed Louis Vert in the same context as Eugène Atget and Paul Géniaux.*6

Where Atget recorded the form of the city — architecture, shop windows, streets — Vert and Géniaux focused on people and occupations. Vert's photographs, without Géniaux's movement between Brittany and Paris, concentrated entirely on the Parisian street, making him in some respects the more focused recorder of Parisian working life. The Histoire par l'image collection includes a flower seller photograph by Vert and contextualizes it within the visual evidence for Belle Époque Paris.*19

SFP and the amateur photography movement — institutional context

Louis Vert worked as an amateur photographer connected with the SFP. In late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century France, the amateur photography movement was extensive, with amateurs active across documentary, travel, and scientific photography. Vert's Paris street work is one example of practice that emerged within this broader amateur culture. The SFP's educational document La République des amateurs provides context for this movement.*8

Museum Barberini research materials situate this period's Parisian street photography within the emergence of "a new art," providing a framework for understanding what it meant to document the city's street trades as Vert did. The Galerie Roger-Viollet database holds an itinerant photographer image by Vert (c. 1900), situating his work within an international photographic archive.*21

Key works and the Carnavalet collection — institutional preservation

The Musée Carnavalet holds multiple works by Vert, including Étameur, Balayeuse place de l'Hôtel de Ville, Afficheur, Portefaix, Marchande de café, Bateliers, Vannier, and Chiffonnier.*3

These works function simultaneously as factual records of occupations that existed and as images of individuals within the movements of daily work — positioned between documentation and poetry. The Squal Photographie archive includes a flower seller photograph (1900–1906), and the Paris Musées database records a loueur de bateaux (boat rental) photograph among the Carnavalet holdings.*15

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Louis Vert has not been incorporated into the main narrative of photographic history to the extent that Atget has, but the publication of Alain Fourquier's monograph established a systematic basis for understanding his work as a distinct and significant body of photography.*2

The Musée d'Orsay's documentation of Vert and the ICP's exhibition placing him alongside Atget and Géniaux have confirmed his position within the context of Parisian street photography around 1900. His inclusion in the Musée Carnavalet's collection indicates institutional recognition of his photographs as part of Paris's urban cultural memory.*1

Recent photographic history research has increasingly attempted to reconstruct early twentieth-century Paris not through the image of a single solitary genius like Atget but through the depth of record created by multiple practitioners including Vert and Géniaux. The BnF's Atget-related exhibition materials also provide context for comparing this generation of street recorders. Wikimedia Commons holds a category of Vert photographs from the Musée Carnavalet, increasing public accessibility to his archive.*20

luc-delahaye.html.lead_html: Luc Delahaye began as a photojournalist covering Lebanon, Afghanistan, Rwanda, Chechnya, and Bosnia. Since 2001, he has made History, a series that presents wars, trials, and international conferences through distant panoramas and large-scale prints. Questioning how dramatic news events predetermine an image’s meaning, he chose compositions that retain peripheral information and a museum setting that supports extended viewing. Comparisons with Jeff Wall and Andreas Gursky clarify how direct encounters with historical sites, digital construction, and the tableau form overlap and diverge in his work.
luc-delahaye.html.thesis_html: War reporting tends to select a single image that communicates an event immediately, leaving peripheral figures, buildings, sky, waiting, and silence outside the printed page. Delahaye retained his position as a reporter on the scene while adopting distant views, panoramas, and large-scale prints. He preserved photojournalism’s physical contact with reality while creating a form in which an event could be examined at length in the museum without being reduced to a conclusion or symbol.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
From the 1980s onward, Delahaye covered war and politics for agencies, Newsweek, and Magnum Photos, working in Lebanon, Afghanistan, Rwanda, Bosnia, Chechnya, and elsewhere. Galerie Nathalie Obadia’s biography traces his move, after years of reporting, toward History around 2001, with museums becoming the primary setting for the work*4. The shift began with his doubt that the complexity of an experience on location could be compressed by a newspaper or magazine headline, reproduction size, and brief caption into a single central event. A conversation at the Getty also confirms that the bodily judgments formed in the field carried into the large-scale works*1*5.

News reporting demands images that convey the apparent center of an event quickly: an explosion, an injured person, victory or defeat, a political leader. Delahaye later observed that a subject as forceful as war can make a photograph seem sufficient on the basis of importance alone, weakening the photographer’s decisions and the image’s internal complexity. In a conversation with Michael Fried, he describes the need to move away from images dependent on strong news subjects and to make photographs that encounter “the resistance of the world”*2.

Portraits/1, L’Autre, and Winterreise prepared this problem before History. Through an automatic passport-photo booth, unannounced street photography, and a journey across Russia, Delahaye reduced the photographer’s heroic intervention and tested how fully a person before the camera could enter an image. SFMOMA’s artist materials place these works across journalism, portraiture, and social observation as a line leading toward the later large-scale photographs*14.

Around 2001, Delahaye adopted a panoramic camera and large-scale printing. The horizontal frame could hold a central figure together with surrounding soldiers or residents, buildings, sky, and debris. In prints several meters wide, viewers first stand back to see the whole, move close to read details, and then return to the overall arrangement. The Getty presents Recent History as a group of large color photographs that reconsider the relations among art, information, and history*3. Delahaye needed a frame that restored contradictory peripheral information to the central scene selected by the news and kept an event open beyond a single understanding.

sections.title: Distance and Large-Scale Prints
sections.body_html:
Distance and Peripheral Information

Delahaye often positions the camera at a distance on the battlefield. That distance has been criticized as a cold refusal of empathy with suffering. It also prevents one wounded figure or symbolic gesture from standing in for the entire event, as frequently happens in press photography. The National Science and Media Museum explains that reading the image’s details over time is essential to the experience of the large-scale works*10. Viewers see the whole from afar, move closer to identify figures and wreckage, then step back to reconsider their arrangement.

Large-Scale Prints and Viewing Time

Newspaper and magazine photographs are consumed quickly alongside headlines, short captions, and adjacent articles. Delahaye exhibits photographs several meters wide, using a scale that cannot be taken in at once to slow the reception of information.The Getty exhibition page explains that the works address events also found in news imagery while demanding attention to detail, spatial relations, and sustained looking *3.The large print gives the image greater authority, while also providing the physical capacity to retain peripheral information that articles tend to omit.

History Painting and an Unresolved Present

Western history painting arranged wars, coronations, revolutions, and national events on a monumental scale, presenting narratives for collective memory. Delahaye draws on horizontal composition, groups of figures, and perspective, while multiplying the image’s centers and reducing dramatic gestures that lead toward a resolution. Frieze discusses History as a body of work in which journalistic fact and the compositional finish of painting destabilize one another*11. A date and location in the title identify the event, while the figures and objects within the frame preserve a complicated present before its historical interpretation has settled.

Direct Photography and Digital Construction

Many early works in History were made in a single exposure at one site. Their importance lay in holding figures, debris, buildings, and sky that coexisted at the same moment within a single duration. Later works use multiple exposures, digital compositing, and staging to combine fragments from different times or places in one image.*8. This change expanded the subject from what occurred simultaneously at a site to how a historical event is later constructed as an image. Even in composited works, fragments of people and architecture are based on direct observation and photography. Delahaye edits relations among times while retaining photography’s contact with the world. A Jeu de Paume retrospective likewise presents the move from direct photography to constructed images as a continuous development.*9*12

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Medium
sections.body_html:
Taliban

Taliban presents the body of a Taliban fighter lying in a road within a horizontal frame that includes the surrounding ground and distant view. The High Museum holds the work as part of History, photographed in Afghanistan in 2001*6. The body lies near the center, yet the composition prevents attention from concentrating solely on facial expression; it includes the expanse of ground, clothing, nearby objects, and distant figures. The distance that makes the body small carries a risk of anonymity, while also slowing a gaze that might consume the dead person’s face as an emotional news symbol.

Jenin Refugee Camp No. 1

In the work depicting the destruction of the Jenin refugee camp, rubble, roads, buildings, and figures are dispersed across a panorama. The High Museum’s collection text notes that the composition avoids condensing the scale of destruction into one symbol and instead asks viewers to move through the image*7. From a high viewpoint, the terrain appears as a whole; closer inspection reveals traces of life within the debris. The movement between an abstract overview and particular destruction makes it difficult to remain with the image’s beauty as landscape alone.

Conferences, Trials, and the Interiors of Power

Alongside battlefields, Delahaye photographed OPEC meetings, the United Nations, trials, and state ceremonies. Prix Pictet notes how table arrangements, interpreters’ booths, security, and waiting bodies reveal the institutional power that supports scenes of military force*13. In conference rooms, those who determine policy and distribute resources are organized spatially. Bringing battlefields and meetings into the same series connects sites of decision with the places where their consequences appear.

Comparison with Gursky: Distance and Detail

Delahaye and Gursky share distant, elevated viewpoints, wall-filling prints, and compositions that disclose numerous details at close range. The Met explains that Gursky enlarged photographs to wall scale in the 1990s, treating industry, electronic systems, and urban interiors as expansive wholes*20. Both artists make photographs that require viewers to move and cannot be exhausted at a glance. The temporal status of their details, however, differs.

Comparison with Gursky: Systems and Events

Gursky’s Times Square, New York seamlessly reconstructs multiple photographs on a computer, turning architecture, advertising, and crowds into a single visual system. MoMA describes it as an invented image derived from photographs but extensively reconfigured*19. Figures can be read as repeated units within markets, labor, consumption, and tourism. Delahaye also uses groups and elevated views, but his dead, soldiers, and negotiators remain tied to specific dates and locations; the pattern never absorbs them completely.

The distinction appears in the historical role assigned to detail. Gursky orders multiple moments and viewpoints, presenting individuals as repeated units within markets, labor, and consumption. Even when Delahaye uses compositing in later works, fragments of people and objects remain connected to particular events, dates, and sites. Gursky’s large images intensify the regularity of global systems; Delahaye’s retain the uneven times and judgments that persist within a single event.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beauty and Violence

Delahaye’s photographs possess controlled composition, color, and print quality and are designed for sustained museum viewing. Their beauty can prolong attention to war, but it has also drawn criticism for turning bodies and rubble into expensive tableaux. A review in The Guardian addresses both the discomfort and the force involved in transforming actual conflicts into monumental, painterly works*18. A review in Blind likewise observes that the photographs confront fragments of reality while producing attraction and unease at once*15. Delahaye leaves this contradiction within the sequence of looking. Viewers are drawn toward an ordered whole and encounter death or destruction when they move closer.

Between Journalism and Art

Building on his experience as a reporter, Delahaye made works whose scale and viewing time no longer fit the immediate use of a news article. He continued to witness particular events and retain the accidents and resistance encountered on location. In a conversation with Conscientious Extended, he describes how, even after leaving journalism’s immediate function, the photographer’s position in the world and conduct within it remain conditions of making the work*16. Working between journalism and contemporary art, he combines factual information with autonomous pictorial construction and creates time for prolonged examination of an event.

Looking at an Event Over Time

War reporting in newspapers and magazines selected a single image to stand for an event under the constraints of limited space and speed. By the 1990s, large-scale photography in contemporary art had become an established tableau form for extended viewing of constructed scenes and social systems such as markets, labor, and crowds. Delahaye retained the reporter’s physical presence at an event while adopting the scale and viewing time of that second tradition*3*20. On a small printed page, one dead person or explosion easily becomes the symbol of the event. A distant panorama can retain surrounding figures, buildings, sky, debris, and periods of waiting within the same frame. The large print prevents this information from being consumed as a single overview; viewers stand back, move close to read details, and revise their judgments.Delahaye combined physical contact with the site and the sustained viewing of the large-scale tableau, creating a form in which historical events remain open to examination. This connection defines his significance for both photojournalism and contemporary art *17.

lucas-blalock.html.lead_html: Lucas Blalock photographs ordinary objects on 4×5-inch film, scans the negatives, and then deliberately makes Photoshop erasures, cloning, masks, and drawing conspicuous. His subject is not a game of detecting whether an image has been digitally altered*1. Commercial retouching removes evidence of its labor to create a natural-looking image, while a return to analog photography can also leave the contemporary image-processing environment outside the frame*4. Blalock keeps optical description and manual software operations in the same image. Through odd forms and humor, he makes photography legible as the product of continuous work across camera, scanner, editing software, and output*7.
lucas-blalock.html.thesis_html: Digital retouching in advertising and magazines has treated the removal of cloning, erasure, and masking from the finished image as a mark of quality. Blalock photographs everyday objects in fine detail on 4×5-inch film, then deliberately leaves repetitions, shifted contours, and incomplete erasures in the scans.He turned the general observation that photographs are manipulated into a question viewers can follow with their eyes: which tool acted on which part of the image, and what kind of gesture did it leave behind. Darkroom techniques alone could not directly address the software operations that support contemporary commercial images, while seamless retouching would conceal those operations again. Blalock therefore needed both large-format photography and conspicuous digital editing.

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Blalock was born in Asheville, North Carolina, in 1978. He studied at Bard College and later earned an MFA from UCLA. He first learned to use a large-format camera in a required course, but continued with it because the format made him consider his distance from the subject and the details at the edges of the frame with unusual precision. Even when photographing familiar objects, he emphasizes constructing his relation to them as a single “picture”*18.

The immediate route to his current method began during a period in the American South when he lacked access to a conventional darkroom and started scanning film to examine it on a screen. Photoshop initially served as a substitute for the darkroom*6. Around 2009, he read Bertolt Brecht’s writings on theater and recognized that their insistence on exposing backstage labor could be applied to image editing, as he has explained*7.

By the 2000s, digital manipulation had become routine, yet discussions of it often divided into two positions. Advertising and publishing demanded seamless retouching, while in art photography a return to film and the darkroom was sometimes presented as a distance from digital culture. Blalock chose neither position. He placed optical precision and software operations in the same frame*11. MoMA’s Ocean of Images and Aperture’s writing on contemporary photography presented his work within a situation in which analog and digital processes intersect and the meaning of a photograph changes with its printing and its appearance online*13.

This history shows that his photographs did not emerge from a simple endorsement or rejection of digital technology*2. Large-format film carries the precise descriptive capacity accumulated in photographic history; scanning and Photoshop belong to the present workplace of image production*5. Keeping both processes visible in one image allows him to examine photographic history and the current editing environment together*19.

sections.title: Core Ideas and Methods
sections.body_html:
Why Make the Editing Visible?

In advertising, product photography, and fashion photography, a finished image is expected to conceal the work used to alter skin, objects, and backgrounds*3. Viewers can easily receive a retouched image as the natural appearance recorded by a camera*4. Blalock leaves repeated cloning, incomplete erasures, and shifted contours in place, making it possible to recognize not only that the image was edited but also the motions performed with a mouse and software tools*13.

Brechtian theater exposes staging and performance mechanisms so that audiences do not absorb the narrative as a natural reality. Blalock applied this principle to editing that refuses to hide its seams*5. The large-format negative, the scan, and the software repetitions remain legible as distinct layers. Viewers can therefore locate photographic persuasion across the post-production process instead of assigning it solely to the moment of exposure*7.

Why Keep Using Large-Format Film?

An image generated entirely in software has a weaker relation to an object that stood before a camera. Blalock photographs shoes, fruit, fabric, erasers, animals, and other physical things, accumulating details of light, surface, and depth on a large-format negative*1. Editing intervenes in that record instead of replacing it wholesale*2. Film provides a basis for comparing the optically recorded object with the parts transformed on screen*17.

Large-format photography also slows the work down. Setting up a tripod, checking the plane of focus and the frame edges, and making one exposure at a time differs from the speed of smartphone and online imagery. Because he later alters the image dramatically in Photoshop, this care at the moment of exposure does not protect the purity of the final photograph*2. It creates a specific object and space substantial enough to withstand editing and supplies a basis for seeing what the software changed*18.

The Role of Awkwardness and Humor

His photographs include multiplied strawberries, bent shoes, and strangely flattened animals*1. Humor prevents the question of manipulation from becoming a didactic diagram of retouching techniques*16. The software’s promise of total control appears beside the repetitions and errors produced when a person handles a tool, allowing manipulation to be understood as a visible form*20.

As the exhibition title Low Comedy suggests, everyday objects are not destroyed beyond recognition; they are made only slightly wrong. Viewers identify a shoe or a piece of fruit immediately, then notice the unnatural form*1. This humor produces familiarity and unease between the seamless commercial image and the instructional diagram that displays nothing but a procedure*20.

Within Post-Internet Photography

MoMA’s Ocean of Images situated Blalock within a moment when photography moved between print and web and acquired different meanings with each venue*11. MoMA’s artist page brings together works in the collection and his exhibition history*8. The museum’s collection writing also addresses the way analog capture and digital editing form a single production process*12. Walker Art Center’s Ordinary Pictures placed his still lifes in a history of industrial image production that includes stock photography, product photography, and the repetition of existing images*21. The exhibition glossary clarified this relation to appropriation since the 1960s*22. Unlike artists who quote found images, Blalock photographs his own source images in the manner of commercial product photography and retains, as part of his composition, the software labor usually hidden as outsourced or post-production work.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Right Shoe and Shoe: Disrupting the Finish of Product Photography

In Right Shoe and Shoe, Blalock photographed a subject familiar from product photography with a large-format camera, then repeated its forms and altered its contours*9. MoMA’s collection and exhibition history presents the works as examples in which digital editing becomes central to composition instead of remaining an aftereffect*10. A technology normally used to make a commodity attractive instead makes the object unstable*11.

Strawberries: The Clone Tool and Fruit That Does Not Rot

In the strawberry works, perishable fruit multiplies through cloning and retains the same form indefinitely. The reproducibility of a digital image without physical decay is compared with the time of fresh food within a single frame*11. Because the traces of the operation remain visible, viewers can follow how an enduring commodity image is made*13.

Donkeys Crossing the Desert: Billboard and Smartphone

Donkeys Crossing the Desert (2019) combined three donkeys in different states of manipulation and was presented on an outdoor billboard near the Whitney Museum*14. A smartphone-based AR component shifted the image into another state, joining the large street photograph and the handheld screen within one viewing experience*15. The work required both billboard and mobile device to address an everyday photographic environment no longer contained by print*16.

Shooting, Scanning, Editing, and Output

In Blalock’s work, post-shooting procedures do not disappear as auxiliary labor*3. Scanning the large-format negative, erasing and cloning on screen, print scale, and exhibition location successively alter the image’s appearance and meaning*4. He presents the photograph as an object produced continuously by camera, scanner, software, and printer, not as the result of an isolated instant of exposure*6.

Dodging, burning, and retouching existed in the darkroom, but digital tools allow an operation to be undone, the same area to be duplicated, and another version to be produced immediately. Blalock does not use that convenience solely to achieve a natural-looking finish; he leaves hesitation, repetition, and revision in the image*6. Authorship therefore appears in the time spent continuing to work on the image after exposure as well as in the decisive moment*7.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beyond the Category of the “Manipulated Photograph”

Evaluating these works only by the skill of their manipulation misses the central question. The issue is not whether editing occurred, but who performs retouching in contemporary image production and why that labor disappears from the finished image*1. Blalock retains cloning and erasure as authorial gestures, bringing together roles often separated among photographer, retoucher, and software*7. Instead of making an abstract claim that photography lacks objectivity, he renders the division of labor and the tools themselves as repeated forms and displaced contours*19.

Using Photographic History in the Present Tense

The large-format camera, still life, and studio setup belong to older photographic traditions; Photoshop, augmented reality, web publication, and reposting belong to the current production environment*2. He does not cast the former as a pure tradition to preserve and the latter as an external force that corrupts photography*11. By using both, he makes visible the way photographic history continues by absorbing new tools*13.

The large-format camera is therefore not an instrument of nostalgia. The more clearly it records detail, the more legible the digital seams added to the frame become. Blalock does not fuse old and new technologies seamlessly; he lets viewers compare what each process recorded and what it transformed*3. The final image shows within one frame that contemporary photography is produced through several devices and periods of labor, not by a camera alone*19.

Criticality and Visual Pleasure

The traces of editing make an argument, but they also produce visual pleasure through odd forms, color, and repetition. Multiplied fruit and bent shoes first attract the viewer as photographs, not as diagrams explaining a retouching process*3. Once the unnatural operation becomes apparent, viewers move between familiarity with the image and awareness of the technology that produced that familiarity*13. Blalock’s contribution to photographic history is a frame in which the optical detail of a large-format negative and the gesture of software editing can be read at the same time, not a seamless merger of old and new techniques*17.

luisa-lambri.html.lead_html: Luisa Lambri photographs the interiors of buildings by Schindler, Neutra, Barragán, Breuer, SANAA, and others from positions and moments that differ only slightly. Through Locations, Autoritratto, and Breuer Revisited, this page follows the relation between art history and feminism, her understanding of architecture as autobiography, and the way variations in light and bodily position become photographic sequences.
luisa-lambri.html.thesis_html: Lambri adds the photographer’s duration of stay and bodily position to the image of architectural authorship conventionally condensed into an all-encompassing view of modern buildings. She moves the camera by a few centimeters within the same house or museum, producing closely related photographs through changes in the height of an opening, exterior vegetation, reflection, and color temperature. The building and its architectural history remain identifiable, while each sequence records differences experienced by one body; the images therefore retain both the appearance of abstract color fields and the specificity of place. Her work established a form through which the imagined user of modernist space, the architect’s design intention, and the experience of resident and photographer can be compared frame by frame. Architectural photography gains an additional question: who experienced the building, from where, and at what moment?
