sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Photographer to Investigative Artist: Documentary After the 1990s

Poloni was born in Amsterdam in 1962 and has worked across photography, moving image, and installation. His 2010 exhibition at Kunsthalle Bern presented his work as historical research combining photography and film, emphasizing his treatment of facts as an “open historical arrangement” rather than a closed narrative*2. His exhibition history records activity across Switzerland, Germany, France, and Italy from the late 1990s onward; in the 2000s, Passengers, Displacement Island, and The Majorana Experiment became central projects*11.

In Europe during this period, border control, migration across the Mediterranean, globalization, and surveillance technologies unsettled the assumption that showing the scene would make an event legible. Poloni’s work has been described as research into precisely this difficulty of seeing, tracing subjects who fall outside systems of social control*1. Prix Elysée likewise presents him across the roles of photographer, filmmaker, and artist, and selected him for support toward a photobook and new work*7.

The Mediterranean and the Island: Where Movement and Information Intersect

For Poloni, the Mediterranean is not simply a landscape backdrop. An announcement for The Analogue Island describes the project as indexing the Mediterranean’s “plots and problems” through film, photography, and installation, addressing social invisibility and the relations among power, subjectivity, and ideology*14. The Analogue Island Bureau, which he later founded, was conceived as an ongoing archive that collects and rewrites anthropological narratives and geopolitical scripts around the Mediterranean*16.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Displacement Island: Lampedusa as a 69-Image “Non-Cartographic Atlas”

Displacement Island (2006) treats Lampedusa, Italy’s southernmost island, as an ensemble of 69 images. A Brill study analyzes the work as a “non-cartographic atlas” that connects heterogeneous visual materials in constellations instead of fixing geography, history, and politics into a classificatory grid*12. Campagne Première’s project page documents both the images and the installation structure, in which 69 pigment prints are arranged in several clusters*9.

Lampedusa brings together different forms of movement: tourists and migrants or refugees attempting to reach Europe. An exhibition at Württembergischer Kunstverein presented the island’s landscape as a place where political borders overlap with tourist imagery*8. Es Baluard also included Displacement Island in a 2015 exhibition on the Mediterranean, situating the work within questions of maritime politics and movement*19.

Photography becomes material for comparing who makes images of the same place and for what purpose. By placing his own photographs alongside tourist imagery, press photographs, and other existing visual material, Poloni shows how an image’s meaning depends on circulation and editorial arrangement as well as on the photographer’s intention.

The Majorana Experiment: Exhibiting Uncertain Evidence Without Solving a Disappearance

The Majorana Experiment combines photographs, film, lightboxes, stereoscopic devices, and historical documents around the Italian physicist Ettore Majorana, who disappeared in 1938. Campagne Première describes it as an “open narrative dispositif,” underscoring a structure in which multiple media do not converge on a single answer*10. The Kunsthalle Bern exhibition likewise presented the disappearance without closing it into the solution of a mystery, bringing the history of science, war, nuclear physics, and movement across the Mediterranean into contact*5.

In Majorana Eigenstates, an actor plays Majorana while the parallax of two cameras splits the same figure between two locations*18. The reenactment does not fill gaps in the record as fact; it makes visible how much what is missing from historical sources depends on performance and conjecture. roots§routes discusses The Majorana Experiment and The Analogue Island as a continuous investigation of invisibility as a political, geographical, and narrative condition*17.

Why the Migrants Themselves Are Absent: Absence as Ethics and Method

The near absence of people in Displacement Island was not the result of an inability to approach the subject. In an interview with SCHIRN, Poloni says that his concern was with questions of representation rather than journalism, and that early in his work on Lampedusa he decided not to show the migrants themselves*21. Instead, he mixes traces such as clothing and cigarette packs found on the beach with tourist postcards, travel catalogs, and news images, leaving viewers unable to determine which photographs are his and which are appropriated. Flattening authorship and refusing to concentrate the ethical burden in one forceful evidentiary image are structural decisions in the work.

In a 2021 interview in Image & Narrative, Poloni is even more explicit. Because photography has difficulty conveying the full intricacy of human beings and suffering, he explains, Displacement Island began from the decision “not to represent migrants,” using metaphor and metonymy to generate a different mental image*22. In the same conversation, he refers to Deleuze and Guattari’s “striated space” and Latour’s actor-network theory, describing the Mediterranean as a fluid space crossed by human and nonhuman flows—tourists, migrants, soldiers, commodities, aircraft, and more*22. His refusal to condense the subject into the face of a single victim was also a method for presenting the Mediterranean as a field where numerous actors and institutions intersect.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
“Narrative Montage”: Photography, Moving Image, and Documents on Equal Terms

Photography does not monopolize the wall in Poloni’s installations. At the Centre culturel suisse, Codename: Osvaldo combined photographs, moving images, documents, and research to construct a series of case studies around the less widely known history of guerrilla struggle in Bolivia and Monika Ertl*3. A Paris Art review likewise describes an exhibition in which photographs and texts supplement fragments of political history while viewers construct their own route through the material*4.

Why Arrange Multiple Images as a “Constellation”?

Poloni avoids a structure in which one photograph stands for the subject as a whole. Speaking about Displacement Island, he explains that individual images are intentionally treated as “flat,” without self-contained artistic depth, so that relations emerge only when they are brought together*21. He also makes the distinction between his own photographs and appropriated images invisible to the viewer, flattening authorship and deliberately reducing each image’s power to represent the subject on its own*21. Each image is kept from becoming self-sufficient so that no single photograph can stand for migration, tourism, the military, or the island itself. Meaning develops in the intervals between adjacent images. In both books and installations, fragments are arranged as constellations whose relations viewers must trace.

Combining moving images, photographs, documents, and exhibition space allows the same fact to be examined through different temporalities and kinds of evidence. Film brings duration; photography brings arrest; documents carry sources; exhibition space creates sequence. Istituto Svizzero describes the Analogue Island Bureau’s output as spanning film, photography, installation, and text, connecting individual works to an ongoing body of Mediterranean research*13.

Making Photography’s Limits Part of the Work to Address What Cannot Be Seen

SUPSI’s presentation of A Theory of Waves connects the sea, waves, scientific measurement, and apparatuses of social control, asking through photography and research how “invisible subjects” emerge from such systems*1. LOOP Barcelona likewise presents Poloni as an artist who uses moving image and photography to address history, movement, and political memory*6. Institutions that produce invisibility, gaps in sources, and limits on viewpoint all become material for the work.

Photography Now’s exhibition record includes Displacement Island at the Centre de la photographie Genève, The Majorana Experiment at Kunsthalle Bern, and Persian Gulf Incubator at FOTOHOF, showing the work’s reception across both specialist photography institutions and contemporary-art venues*15. Photography functions as a primary medium for examining the conditions under which political information becomes an image.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
From Witness Photography to an Arrangement of Research

Poloni does not reject photography’s evidentiary force; he develops a method in which evidence does not conclude within a single image. Brill calls Displacement Island a “constellation” because knowledge is produced by relations among heterogeneous images*12. The Majorana Experiment at Kunsthalle Bern likewise leaves uncertainty in place rather than integrating its materials into one conclusion*2.

This method departs from a classical documentary model in which the photographer possesses the decisive moment, making research, sourcing, editing, and exhibition part of authorship. The critical record preserved in Campagne Première’s press archive shows that Majorana and Analogue Island have been discussed across contemporary art, moving-image culture, and visual studies as well as photography*20.

The Ethics of Political Images: Absent Subjects and Gaps in the Archive

Histories of migration, disappearance, guerrilla struggle, and nuclear science risk reducing lived experience to a single explanation when they become artworks. Poloni’s case-study format leaves gaps, contradictions, and different temporalities in the material. Stella Maris describes the Analogue Island Bureau as an “index,” emphasizing a structure to which multiple narratives continue to be added*16.

The Ethics and Limits of Displacement Island: A Reassessment Through Surveillance Studies

Surveillance scholar Torin Monahan discusses Displacement Island in Crisis Vision (2022), viewing the decision to keep refugees’ bodies outside the frame as a way of avoiding renewed exposure of vulnerable people to surveillance and objectification. In his reading, fragments such as life jackets, detention facilities, military zones, and tourists are separated by blank space, prompting viewers to infer connections among the institutions and places that regulate movement rather than concentrate on one image of individual suffering*27.

The same study identifies blind spots produced by that choice. Monahan argues that death, loss, and destruction are scarcely represented, and that the history linking Italian colonialism in North and East Africa to contemporary migration is difficult to read from the work itself*27. Poloni’s use of absence supports an ethics of caution, but withholding images can also thin out the historical background. Displacement Island offers no solution; it returns to the viewer the documentary choice of what to make visible and what to leave outside the frame.

A 2026 “Borderscape” Study: Fragments and Absence Reconsidered as Method

Two decades after it was made, Displacement Island continues to appear in research on the representation of migration. A 2026 article in the Journal of Intercultural Studies discusses European borders as dynamic “borderscapes” where language, material traces, and human actions intersect, examining Poloni’s work in detail as an earlier example that overlays Lampedusa’s geography, history, politics, aesthetics, and signs*26. The article focuses on his refusal to show migrants or border guards directly, and on the way traces such as clothing, cigarette packs, military vessels, and barbed wire are mixed into a heterogeneous image field*26. The 2006 decision not to photograph people also became a way to read the border as an accumulation of institutions that produce what can and cannot be seen, instead of representing it through a single dramatic event.

Poloni does not seek to represent political reality with a stronger single image. He exhibits what images show, what they miss, and how they become knowledge when combined with other sources. His method parallels a broader shift after the 1990s in which photography came to function as a site for testing information as well as a medium for making individual pictures.

In Relation to Allan Sekula: Reading the Sea as a Chain of Institutions

The comparison with Allan Sekula has a direct basis in scholarship. The peer-reviewed volume “Disassembled” Images: Allan Sekula and Contemporary Art, published by Leuven University Press, considers Sekula’s legacy through ecological disaster in maritime space, geopolitics, solidarity, and critical realism; its section “Maritime Failures and Imaginaries” includes Poloni’s The Land Seen by the Sea*23. A Burlington Contemporary review likewise groups recent maritime investigations by Poloni, Trevor Paglen, and Véréna Paravel/Lucien Castaing-Taylor under the politics of recording, discussing them as questions that continue after Sekula*24.

The shared point is an understanding of the sea as an institutional space linking labor, logistics, borders, the military, tourism, and movement, rather than a scenic backdrop. Poloni, however, deliberately erases distinctions of authorship between his own photographs and appropriated images, generating narrative through combinations of traces from which human figures are absent. As he explains, he deliberately keeps each image “flat,” allowing meaning to emerge only through combination*21, Poloni thus moves beyond Sekula’s photo-text critical documentary toward constellations in which even the question of who made an image remains unstable.

“Unfinished Ruins” and a Connection to Robert Smithson

Poloni’s points of comparison are not confined to documentary photography. In discussing the unfinished Sicilian dam in The Analogous Dam, the Centre d’Art Contemporain Genève connects the work to Robert Smithson’s idea of public projects that never reach completion becoming “ruins in reverse” within the landscape*25. Photography is used to read the distorted temporality produced by politics, funding, organized crime, and stalled development. Here the Mediterranean appears as a space where suspended institutions and unfinished plans leave traces on the ground.

marey.html.lead_html: A physiologist who used chronophotography — multiple exposures on a single plate — to analyze motion as scientific data. While Muybridge spread time across sequential frames, Marey condensed it onto a single image, transforming bodies, labor, and flight into measurable, analyzable form.
marey.html.thesis_html: By layering multiple exposures onto a single plate, Marey developed chronophotography — a method that condensed motion into an analytical diagram within a single image — and transformed the movements of bodies, birds in flight, and fluids into measurable visual forms. Where Muybridge unfolded time into a sequence of independent frames, Marey chose the contrasting approach of folding time into space, providing a visual precedent that modernist painters would later draw on when rendering movement as divided planes. His insistence on photography as an instrument of physiological measurement rather than aesthetic expression connects to the formation of a modern scientific gaze toward the body, and his work continues to be discussed across both the history of photography and the history of science.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Étienne-Jules Marey was born in Beaune, France, in 1830 and trained in medicine and physiology in Paris. He held a professorship in physiology at the Collège de France, where he spent years measuring and recording bodily functions including blood circulation, respiration, and muscle contraction.*1 He adopted photography as a research tool from the 1880s onward, developing the technique he called "chronophotography," which exposed multiple images onto a single photographic plate.*2 This method allowed him to render bird flight, human running and jumping, and airflow as visual analytical diagrams.*3 In 1882 he completed his chronophotographic gun, achieving twelve frames per second. He died in Paris in 1904.*4

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Chronophotographic method

The core of Marey's method lay in superimposing multiple exposures on a single plate, condensing the passage of time into one analytically structured image. The Metropolitan Museum's Bird in Flight is widely cited as a canonical example: the wings of a bird appear as overlapping figures, making every phase of the movement visible simultaneously within a single photograph.*5 The Met's notes on Chronophotograph explicitly state that "unlike Muybridge's motion studies, Marey used multiple exposures on a single plate," framing the methodological difference between the two as a key contrast in photographic history.*6 For Marey, photography was not a means of aesthetic expression but a measuring instrument for quantifying patterns of movement invisible to the naked eye. The Linda Hall Library characterizes his place in the history of science as "the intersection of physiological motion measurement and photography in the second half of the nineteenth century."*7 What chronophotography visualized was not the "instant" of time but the "structure" of time.

Body, labor, and science

Marey's investigations extended beyond bird flight and acrobatics to encompass the working body. His collaborative research with Fremont on bodily movement and energy expenditure carried implications for the efficiency principles underlying modern industrial production.*8 A publication issued by Université Paris Cité Éditions, subtitled "Chronophotography: Science and Art," situates Marey's work at the intersection of science and art while connecting it to a broad range of questions including sport, labor, and comparative physiology.*9 Educational materials from the Cinémathèque française present his chronophotography as a precursor to cinema and motion analysis, and the interpretation that he laid the groundwork for optical devices capable of producing continuous imagery is also valid from the standpoint of film history.*10 The Camera Museum's permanent exhibition similarly frames Marey's technique as one of the innovations that prepared the way for the century of film.*11

Contrast with Muybridge

The comparison with Eadweard Muybridge sharpens Marey's distinctiveness. Where Muybridge divided time using multiple cameras and presented the results as a sequence of independent still images, Marey folded time into a single frame.*12 This difference is not merely a matter of visual method; it reflects different answers to the question of what photography should do. Marey's single-plate images presented movement as an abstract diagram — time converted into spatial form.*13 This model became a visual point of reference for later Modernist painting and Futurism when they represented motion as divided planes, connecting Marey not only to the prehistory of cinema but to twentieth-century visual culture more broadly. ACMI holds and exhibits Marey's chronophotographic prints in the context of screen culture, demonstrating the continuity between motion photography and moving-image culture.*14

Critical reception

Marey's reception has been built up through institutional holdings and exhibitions at institutions that evaluate his work from both photographic and film-historical perspectives, including MoMA, the Musée d'Orsay, and SFMOMA.*15 The Musée d'Orsay exhibition "Movements of Air: Marey, Photographer of Fluids" was a significant attempt to reposition chronophotography within the context of visual art.*16 Chronophotographic films held by the Science Museum Group are preserved as material evidence of the prehistory of cinema and are consulted as sources for the history of technology.*17 Critically, Marey's photographs were not made with aesthetic expression in mind, but the perspective that treats the body as measurable motion data laid the foundations for later body science, sports measurement, and image analysis, while also raising questions about the modern gaze that processes the body as information.*18 Scholarly studies published by OpenEdition and CNRS Éditions discuss Marey's practice in relation to the formation of modern concepts of the body rather than confining him to the history of technology, demonstrating the continuing critical interest in his work.*19 The National Gallery of Canada's Study in Motion by Chronophotography shows that Marey's photographs have been received as works of a caliber that belongs in fine-art museum collections.*20

margaret-bourke-white.html.lead_html: Margaret Bourke-White photographed American industry, Soviet modernization, the founding of LIFE magazine, and the front lines of World War II, visualizing the machinery and power of modernity in sweeping compositions. Her photograph ran on the first cover of LIFE (1936); she was the first woman officially accredited as a war photographer in the Second World War. MoMA and ICP hold major collections of her work.
margaret-bourke-white.html.thesis_html: Documenting industrial facilities, machinery, and dams with bold compositions and strong artificial lighting, she contributed to the institutionalization of photojournalism as a dominant medium by appearing on the cover of LIFE's inaugural issue. As the first woman officially accredited to cover combat in World War II, she made the machines, power structures, and wars of modernity visible through monumental framing.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Margaret Bourke-White was born in New York City in 1904. Her father was a printing engineer, and an environment of industrial interest shaped her later turn toward industrial photography. She took up photography seriously at Cornell University and gained recognition in the late 1920s by photographing industrial facilities in Cleveland. From 1929 she contributed to Henry Luce's Fortune magazine, establishing a style of precise large-format documentation of steel mills, factories, and machinery under strong artificial light*1. In 1930 she traveled to the Soviet Union and became one of the first foreign photographers to document socialist industrialization. In 1936 she photographed Fort Peck Dam for the cover of the inaugural issue of LIFE magazine, beginning a long working relationship with the publication*2. During the Second World War she was the first woman to receive official accreditation as a war photographer — an official US Army designation — and covered North Africa, Italy, and Germany. In 1945 she photographed the liberation of Buchenwald concentration camp while accompanying General Patton's advance, transmitting the reality of the camps to Western readers*3. She also covered the Korean War and is known for her portrait of Mahatma Gandhi. ICP's constituent page serves as an international record of her works, publications, and career*4. She died in 1971 after years with Parkinson's disease.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Industrial photography and machine aesthetics

Bourke-White's industrial photographs used bold angles and strong artificial lighting to render blast furnaces, cranes, dams, and machinery as aesthetic objects — positioning the machine as a subject of visual contemplation. This approach aligned with the American culture of technological celebration in the 1920s and connects to the visual language of "industrial sublime" shared by Precisionist painters such as Charles Sheeler. Her use of the Graflex large-format camera, strong contrast, and meticulous composition can be situated within the context of making industrial capital visible, while also read as an attempt to elevate modern machinery to the status of fine art subjects. MoMA holds her work and artist page in its collection*5. The Saint Louis Art Museum constituent page provides a baseline for artist information and holdings*6. The MoMA Memorable Life Photographs catalogue PDF provides a supplementary resource for situating her within photojournalism history*7. The MDPI peer-reviewed article "The Hands of Fortune: Margaret Bourke-White's Magazine Photographs" provides scholarly analysis of her magazine work, labor imagery, and photo-essays*8.

LIFE and the institutionalization of the photo-essay

The founding of LIFE in 1936 transformed the status of photography in American magazine journalism, and Bourke-White became its symbolic figure. LIFE established the photo-essay form with photographs as primary carrier rather than text, and her large-scale, dramatic compositions were the best fit for this format. LIFE's official photography archive continues to make her work accessible*2. Princeton University Art Museum's LIFE didactics installation PDF details the institutional and visual character of LIFE magazine, providing context for understanding how Bourke-White's photo-essays functioned within its editorial framework*9. The Columbia University Libraries finding aid PDF documents the location of her photographs, negatives, correspondence, and publications as a primary source index*10.

Soviet coverage and "recording modernity"

Her Soviet assignments in the 1930s — documenting factories, dams, and collectivized agriculture — raised questions about the visual representation of the relationship between machine and state from an early date. This work positions her as a visual chronicler of global twentieth-century modernization rather than simply a photographer of industrial America. The International Photography Hall of Fame recognizes her as an inductee and its archive allows confirmation of her historical standing*11.

War photography and the ethics of witness

In her Second World War and Korean War coverage, Bourke-White leveraged hard-won access to dangerous zones as a vehicle for visual witness. Her photographs of the liberation of Buchenwald became among the most powerful instances of photography as testimony to a Western readership*3. Her combination of access to elevated or hazardous vantage points, strong lighting and composition, and LIFE covers can be read as a tension between visual spectacle and photographic witness. Her struggle to obtain official accreditation as a woman war photographer is inseparable from the fact that 1940s media institutions routinely excluded women from the front.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: Bourke-White is frequently framed as a pioneering woman photographer, but narratives of individual exception can obscure the position of her work within a visual culture shaped by industrial capital, the state, and magazine media. Exhibition materials from Reggio Emilia, Italy, indicate the reach of her European reception*12. LIFE's official archive and ICP together provide the institutional foundation for international research*4. A Musée Magazine / Monroe Gallery feature documents her contemporary gallery reception*13. The J. Paul Getty Museum artist page provides the official entry point for its holdings*14.

marine-hugonnier.html.lead_html: Marine Hugonnier works across film, photography, and collage with military views in Afghanistan, a road in Brazil, newspaper photographs, and Monet’s garden. Through Ariana, Travelling Amazonia, Art for Modern Architecture, and Meadow Report, this page examines how permission to film, camera position, technologies of movement, and editing determine what can be seen.
marine-hugonnier.html.thesis_html: Hugonnier makes filming permission, mobility technologies, editing, printing, and failure—elements often concealed behind a finished image—into the primary events of her work. In Ariana, negotiations over access to a military vantage point determine the film. Travelling Amazonia uses a dolly built from the same materials as a road constructed under dictatorship, while Art for Modern Architecture covers newspaper photographs with colored paper. Each work specifies the institutions and technologies that make a viewpoint possible. Before offering a finished explanation of a subject, the work follows where a camera can enter, with whom the filmmaker must negotiate, how the apparatus moves, and which images can be distributed as the public present. Hugonnier makes the distribution of the right to see and the right to edit legible through failed shoots, roads, printed pages, and routes through exhibitions.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.body_html:
From Anthropology to Films and Photographs That Expose the Observer

Hugonnier studied anthropology and developed an interest in ethnography, maps, and the relation between observer and subject. She has said that she did not pass through the conventional production routines of film school. Her works developed through access negotiations, walking, waiting, and failures encountered during travel.*1 Still photography allows her to examine how newspapers and maps edit reality into a single image; film records the time required for a filmmaker to enter a place, request access, and move through it. Her choice of medium centers on how the observer’s cultural and political position shapes the frame. Explanatory records of another culture are not her aim. *2

In 1990, Hugonnier worked on the exhibition Passages de l’image, encountering an institutional setting in which photography, film, and video intersected.*1 After the Cold War, twenty-four-hour news, international military interventions, tourism, and air travel reinforced the sense that distant places could be viewed immediately. Hugonnier takes that expectation as a starting point and builds into the work the practical questions of where a camera can enter, whose permission is required, and which position will be presented as an overview.

Turning Plans That Collapse on Location into the Film’s Argument

Hugonnier constructs films from questions and events that arise while moving through a place. The location changes the structure as production proceeds. She has described her works as fragile films produced by experience.*1 The crew cannot reach the desired height in Ariana; the dolly shot in Travelling Amazonia continues into the night; a balloon accident interrupts the plan for The Last Tour. Film duration and the production process allow these failures of control to remain visible and become routes into military vision, road building, and tourism, instead of being erased in the edit.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Ariana: Reading the Military History of the Panorama through a Failed Shoot

The crew of Ariana seeks a high position overlooking Afghanistan’s Panjshir Valley, but local people refuse permission to film. The failed plan and the access negotiations become the subject of the finished work. Hugonnier explains that the panorama is both a movement of the cinematic camera and a military position from which terrain can be surveyed.*1 The commanding view is therefore connected to the question of who has the right to look down from above, instead of being treated as a neutral aesthetic achievement. *3 *4

Travelling Amazonia: Camera Movement and Road Building as Related Technologies

The Trans-Amazonian Highway, advanced by Brazil’s military dictatorship in the 1970s, cut a straight line through the forest as a state project of surveying and development. Hugonnier worked with local people to build tracks and a dolly from materials used in road construction.*1 The camera glides smoothly along the rails while the state road extends beneath it. Cinematic lateral movement and the line of development overlap in the same image, bringing the technology that makes space easy to survey close to the infrastructure that turns space into a resource to be conquered. *4

Art for Modern Architecture: Newspaper Editing and Collective Memory

For this series, Hugonnier removes the photographic area from front pages reporting events such as the assassination of John F. Kennedy and the fall of the Berlin Wall, covering the space with sheets of paper that recall standard printing colors. Even after the image disappears, headlines, dates, and layout allow viewers to reconstruct the event. In a conversation with The White Review, she describes the work as adding another layer to the newspaper’s “present” and removing the image from the continuity of time.*1 The absent press photograph measures how deeply particular images have been inscribed in collective memory. *5

In anthropology and news production, access to a subject is often treated as evidence of successful research. Hugonnier leaves refusals and limits of access in the work, making the question of who can photograph whom, and from which position, part of the film. A Jeu de Paume conversation identifies the mechanisms through which colonialism, capitalism, and patriarchy shape images, together with the distance between observer and subject, as central concerns.*6 Consent and power appear as concrete conditions of production on the way to a finished image.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
The Last Tour and the Tourist Gaze

The Last Tour addresses the desire to visit a site closed after disaster and the difficulty of making the invisible available to a camera. Guggenheim Bilbao presents the works in Field Reports across moving images, environment, and colonial and patriarchal bias.*7 Tourism can appear to sell a right to see, but disaster, residents, and state control restrict the available viewpoint. Hugonnier leaves invisibility in place instead of filling it as a lack, preserving the structure that determines who receives permission to look.

Apicula Enigma: Watching the Film Crew More Than the Bees

Apicula Enigma begins like a nature film about bees, then redirects attention toward the crew’s procedures, waiting, expectations, and failures. Mudam describes the mixture of reality and fiction as producing discrepancies in the situation of production, instead of an objective account of the subject.*8 By showing personnel and equipment normally concealed in documentary imagery, the film breaks with the fantasy that nature presents itself automatically before the camera. *9

Choosing Film, Photography, Newspapers, and Books for Different Projects

Hugonnier uses film when duration and the process of securing access need to remain visible, newspaper collage when the editing of news is at issue, and books when the order of documents must be constructed. An interview in The White Review describes her method of temporarily taking up positions such as soldier, pilgrim, and journalist in order to see the world from different locations.*1 The medium changes what can be seen and whose position organizes it.

The color fields in Art for Modern Architecture are cut to the dimensions of the photographic area and physically inserted into pages that retain headline, text, and date. The procedure makes visible the editorial authority that selects images, places them, and determines the importance of events. Hugonnier explains the series as a way of removing the photograph from the daily “present” produced by newspapers and creating another temporal layer.*1 The title refers to Le Corbusier’s use of magazine and newspaper photographs in thinking about modern architecture. Architectural standardization, printing standards, and the reuse of press photographs converge on one page; the colored paper exposes the blank as something designed through editing, as much as the image itself.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Tracing the Right to See and the Right to Edit through Filming Apparatuses

The history of road building, military terrain, a newspaper date, and a refusal of filming remain concrete elements within the work. They keep the question of “the gaze” tied to specific events and institutions. Guggenheim Bilbao identifies the links among conventions of representation, ideology, desire, and colonial and patriarchal bias as central to Hugonnier’s work.*7 In Ariana, access to the high ground; in Travelling Amazonia, the people who build the road and dolly; and in Art for Modern Architecture, the editor who selects and places newspaper photographs determine what can be offered as a total view.

Post-documentary practices can treat the photographer’s position, editing, funding, technologies of movement, and limits on access as objects of analysis equal to the completed image. Hugonnier leaves failed plans unresolved, and her films specify the infrastructures on which a camera depends. Jeu de Paume describes film here as a political act that reconstructs the apparatuses used to capture and re-present the world while searching for new regimes of images.*10

Meadow Report and the Viewpoint Reorganized by Exhibition Space

A film unfolds according to a fixed duration; in an exhibition, viewers move among several films, photographs, and newspaper works; in a book, they can return to earlier pages. Hugonnier chooses a medium for each project in order to change the time of viewing and the method of comparison. At Guggenheim Bilbao and Mudam, films, photographs, and newspaper works organized by different viewpoints shared a space, and comparison emerged through the visitor’s movement.*8 A Jeu de Paume exhibition guide likewise integrated films, newspaper works, photographs, and documents into one route.*11

Access to high ground in Ariana, the road and dolly in Travelling Amazonia, newspaper editing in Art for Modern Architecture, and the human-centered viewpoint in Meadow Report each operate as a specific apparatus that organizes vision. In The White Review, Hugonnier records how cultural frameworks change the meaning of the same landscape from project to project.*1 The broad phrase “politics of vision” can therefore be understood by returning to who selects a position, what enters the frame, and through which medium the image is distributed.

Guggenheim Bilbao’s exhibition materials and conversations with the artist organize Field Reports around apparatuses—filming permission, maps, roads, newspapers, and military viewpoints—that determine who can see what across several regions.*12*14*15 Materials from Annet Gelink, e-flux, and Ingleby Gallery show that her project-specific movement among film, photography, collage, and newspapers has continued through gallery exhibitions and publishing as well as film festivals and museums.*16*17*18*13

A conversation in BOMB and Vdrome’s presentation of The Secretary of the Invisible describe a method that returns invisible labor, unheard voices, and events that were never filmed to the present through editing and narration, instead of simply quoting existing footage.*19*20

marnix-goossens.html.lead_html: Marnix Goossens photographs planted landscapes in Almere, palm-tree wallpaper, faux wood grain, windowsills, dikes, and revetments with the precision of a technical camera. Across Regarding Nature, Deep Light, Yonder, and Het wassende water, he examines how Dutch nature is shaped through urban planning, interior decoration, water management, and the desire for distant places before it is experienced as a view.
marnix-goossens.html.thesis_html: Goossens placed wallpaper at the center of landscape photography and extended the same line of inquiry to dikes. Regarding Nature records young trees and gardens planted in the reclaimed city of Almere; Yonder turns to interiors decorated with printed palms and forests; Het wassende water photographs dikes and revetments that regulate water levels. Across these series, nature appears through concrete acts: planting, printing, pasting, and holding back water. Yonder joined interior photography to landscape, while Het wassende water brought hydraulic infrastructure into the same field. Planned land, domestic walls, and structures that protect the country emerge as three sites where nature is made in the Netherlands.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Art Education and the Decision to Photograph Existing Places

Born in Leeuwarden in 1967, Goossens studied at the Utrecht School of the Arts, De Ateliers in Arnhem, and the Rijksakademie in Amsterdam, completing his residency in 2000*21. The AkzoNobel Art Foundation describes his work as moving among nature, portraiture, and still life while tracing the marks that human habits and desires leave on objects and environments*18. The Rijksmuseum records his photobooks and commissioned projects in its collection database*4, while UMC Utrecht notes how easily overlooked details acquire an unexpected presence within his images*14.

Across these bodies of work, Goossens repeatedly points his camera toward interiors, plantings, household objects, and dikes already in use. A 2003 documentary shows him carefully photographing a single willow in the landscape and describes his images as realistic with a slight Surrealist inflection*22. Photographing an existing place preserves more than the wallpaper pattern: it also records a resident’s choice of product, the age and repair of a building, and the path of incoming light. No single author controls the arrangements in these pictures. The decisions of residents, designers, maintenance workers, and organizations responsible for planting or flood defense remain embedded in the details of the site.

Dutch Photography and Artificial Landscapes Since the 1990s

In the Netherlands, reclamation, dikes, roads, housing developments, and planting continually shape the contours of the country. Since the 1990s, photographers have increasingly approached land as an environment where planning, agriculture, tourism, recreation, and water management overlap. The exhibition catalogue Nature as Artifice identified this tendency as a new Dutch landscape*16. Research from Leiden University likewise traces the simultaneous emergence of elevated views of development sites, repeated signs of maintenance, and close attention to everyday decoration*11.

In 2000, Goossens received a commission in Almere, a city built on reclaimed land, and photographed young trees, lawns, gardens, and ornamental plants. He chose the height and distance of everyday viewing instead of an overview of the urban plan. Leaves, support stakes, spacing between trees, and the surface of the soil make the logic of planning tangible. Large-scale land design and the routines of tending a garden meet within the same color photograph.

sections.title: Core Ideas
sections.body_html:
Yonder—The “Elsewhere” Placed Indoors

Yonder focuses on tropical wallpaper, posters, tiles, plastic wood grain, and window light inside deteriorating rooms. Foam calls these motifs “surrogate nature” and describes them as traces of longing for another place within confined interiors*1. The title refers to an elsewhere beyond the present location. Nature appears as a secondary image that someone bought, installed, looked at, and eventually abandoned. Longing and disappointment, consolation and inexpensive decoration, occupy the same surface.

Why Yonder Uses Existing Interiors

Photography is essential to Yonder because it can retain both the mountains or forests printed on wallpaper and the condition of the room that contains them. Foam notes how floral tiles and adhesive coverings convey a desire for faraway places*1. By photographing real interiors, Goossens records the selected motif, the room’s confinement, the wallpaper seams and peeling edges, and reflected light at once. The desire for nature appears within an environment assembled by residents through products and architecture.

A technical camera requires deliberate preparation. Its slowness allows Goossens to reconsider the entire wall and hold both image and support in focus. A crop of the tropical scene alone would turn the motif into decoration. Including the room reveals how the distant place was purchased as a commodity and how long it has remained in use. The camera’s resolution gives equal precision to printed nature and to the domestic setting that carries it.

Regarding Nature—Looking at Nature in the New City of Almere

Regarding Nature examines plantings, development sites, gardens, and interior decoration in Almere. A study of Dutch photography from Leiden University argues that the city’s engineered character supports a larger question: which landscapes are accepted as nature?*11 The catalogue Nature as Artifice observes that Goossens photographed cultivated nature—pink flowers and lawns, for example—with light humor and surprise instead of reducing it to a diagram of criticism*16. Nature in the planned city appears as an unfinished environment that residents grow, decorate, and invest with meaning. A Rijksmuseum bibliographic record confirms that the publication was produced around the nature of Almere*5.

Windows, Reflections, and Light—The Thresholds of Deep Light

In Deep Light, windows, glass, and reflected illumination recur as thresholds between interior and exterior. The Van Abbemuseum library record places the project within the circulation of artist books and exhibition publications*12. Huis Marseille describes Goossens as moving between intimate interiors and public exteriors, presenting a personally inflected way of seeing nature*2. A window opens onto a landscape, yet reflection overlays the room of the viewer, making every outward gaze pass through the present domestic environment.

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Catch and the Perceptual Delay of Still Life

In Catch, 2012, familiar objects and light form a still life whose meaning does not settle immediately. Foam presents the photograph as an example of Goossens’s attention to detail and compositional control*6. His still lifes delay recognition. Color, texture, and illumination take precedence over the known use or scale of an object, returning household things to a briefly unnamed visual state.

Editing Yonder as a Photobook

Yonder edits seven years of photographs through recurring wallpaper, windows, artificial materials, and light. Roma Publications describes these substitutes for nature as signs of a desire for freedom, independence, and the natural world, and records the book as a 132-page publication with a text by Maria Barnas*17. Each turn of the page enters a different room, while tropical and woodland scenes remain trapped on paper or plastic surfaces. The sequence gives repeated form to the desire for elsewhere and links separate interiors into a psychological geography.

“Rising Waters”—Hydraulic Tension in Quiet Images

For a Rijksmuseum commission, Goossens photographed dikes, dunes, revetments, waves, and life along the water. The museum publication Het wassende water edits dikes, dunes, and waves into a series on Dutch water management*19. Quiet color photographs of flood defenses, flat terrain, and everyday use keep the country’s dependence on repeated design and maintenance present beneath the surface. Wallpaper and hydraulic structures operate at different scales, yet both maintain a desired environment through artificial means. Huis Marseille likewise brought together the engineered Dutch landscape and the threat of rising water within a single exhibition context*3.

Cowboy Couple, Cloud, and Silver—From Images of Nature to Manufactured Things

The Stedelijk Museum’s Cowboy Couple shows how borrowed roles and images enter everyday interiors*7. In Cloud, an atmospheric phenomenon is replaced by an object or printed image, turning nature into a portable surface*8. Silver, which entered the Stedelijk context through the Sanders Collection, is recorded as a work that brings material reflection into contact with the photographic surface*13. Together, these works show that Goossens’s inquiry extends beyond plants and landscape to the distinctions photography draws between ready-made images and physical things.

sections.title: Criticism and Reception
sections.body_html:
Nature as Artifice and Contemporary Photographs of Engineered Landscapes

Leiden University research traces the rise, since the 1980s, of Dutch landscape photography concerned with land shaped and managed by people, culminating in the nineteen projects assembled in the 2008 exhibition Nature as Artifice*11. The same study places Regarding Nature alongside Hans van der Meer’s views behind amateur soccer fields, Bas Princen’s construction sites and leisure landscapes, Erwin Driessens and Maria Verstappen’s yearlong study of a single park, and Gert Jan Kocken’s photographs of overmanaged land*11. Goossens brought the engineered landscape close to the level of decoration: repeated saplings, flat arrangements of flowers, and wallpaper seams. Aperture’s touring-exhibition material presented this tendency as a new Dutch landscape in which nature, architecture, planning, and images overlap*10.

Separating Existing Arrangements from Photographic Decisions

Huis Marseille describes Goossens as an artist who draws out the strangeness embedded in everyday life through viewpoint and framing*2. Existing interiors and household objects allow decorative choices, cleanliness, repairs, and combinations of products to register as forms of daily staging. A Wall Street Journal review of the 2011 exhibition Still/Life singled out Melon, a watermelon placed on a chair, as an example of unease produced through arrangement and color*20. An international still-life exhibition in 2018 likewise presented him as a photographer who reconsiders the reality of ordinary things*15. His careful compositions keep existing arrangements and photographic decisions distinct enough to be compared.

Almere, Interiors, and Dikes as Three Artificial Environments

Regarding Nature shows young trees and gardens in Almere as landscapes planted in anticipation of future greenery. In Yonder, distant landscapes purchased by residents remain on interior walls. In Het wassende water, dikes and revetments protect land below sea level as part of everyday life. The Stedelijk Museum’s exhibition of contemporary Dutch photography presented Goossens through both the national photography collection and the culture of the photobook*9.

Viewed together, the three series reveal different agents and scales within the broad category of artificial nature. In Almere, urban planning meets residents’ gardening; indoors, product industries meet personal choice; along the dikes, public administration meets civil engineering. Goossens moves close to support stakes, wallpaper seams, and the joints of revetments. His chosen distance presents institutions through places that have been built, used, and maintained.

martin-polak-lukas-jasansky.html.lead_html: Lukáš Jasanský and Martin Polák are a Czech artist duo who photograph Prague streets, architecture, villages, monuments, churches, and everyday objects in restrained series. In Pragensia, Abstraction, Ignatius, Churches, Churches, and other projects, they deliberately use the visual conventions that make a photograph appear to be an “objective record,” exposing the judgments of value, institutions, and historical assumptions embedded in those conventions.
martin-polak-lukas-jasansky.html.thesis_html: Late-1980s Czech art photography still carried a strong tradition of personal symbolism and subjectivity. Jasanský and Polák adopted a restrained language of frontal views, repetition, black-and-white prints, and typological series to ask what kinds of visual conventions allow genres such as documentary, abstraction, landscape, and heritage photography to exist as recognizable categories. By applying the visual rules of established genres to familiar subjects, they joined the recording of everyday life to a critique of photographic categories, taking a path distinct from subjective expression.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
Prague in the Late 1980s: Moving Away from Subjective Art Photography

Jasanský was born in Prague in 1965 and Polák in 1966, and the two began working together in the mid-1980s. Their series list already includes Old & Arranged, Pragensia, and Television in 1986–88, with the joint authorship functioning as the basic unit of the work*3. In its reconsideration of Czech photography, the Museum of Contemporary Photography describes the post-Velvet Revolution moment as one in which photography’s role itself was reexamined, and presents the duo as artists who distanced themselves from the pronounced subjectivity then prevalent in Czech art photography*1.

Their earliest works, Old & Arranged and New Arranged, have been discussed in relation to photographic education, the Slovak New Wave, and staged photography. In a 2012 interview, Polák identifies the visual artist František Skála, rather than a direct photographic reference, as the strongest influence on him at the time*25. The frontal, undramatic description of Pragensia was later called “Becher-like,” but the duo did not know the Bechers when the work was made. They have recalled that they independently “discovered” the act of photographing ordinary things with no obvious element designed to please a viewer*25. What they sought through photography was a way to test what remained when familiar reality was stripped of the conventional appeal of art photography.

They repeatedly photograph streets, buildings, villages, and everyday objects from a measured distance, suppressing dramatic moments and overt authorial emotion. Artlist describes the work as post-conceptual photography that restrains “artistic” effects while testing the conventions of the medium*2. VVP AVU’s archival record of series since the late 1980s likewise documents their deliberate adoption of established genre names in projects such as Report – Humanistic Photography, Abstraction, Nature, and Ignatius*11.

Making Collaboration a Question of Authorship

Their photographs do not make the question of who pressed the shutter central to viewing. In its 2013 exhibition, the Moravian Gallery treated “collaboration” itself, alongside individual series, as a concern running through their method*6. The exhibition catalog likewise organizes the work around three axes: photographic genres, exhibition, and collaboration*13. Their shared authorship, which does not center the signature on an individual point of view, corresponds to the restraint of the images and weakens the habit of reading a photograph as a confession of its maker’s inner life.

Why the Series Matters: Avoiding the Isolated Single Image

For the duo, a series is not simply a style for arranging impassive photographs in a uniform format. They explain that a “field” or “phenomenon” has to be investigated step by step and that making an isolated, self-contained photograph is difficult for them to imagine*25. They also describe the deliberate clouding of meaning—so that a work can be “misread”—as a basic pillar of their production, avoiding the consolidation of the work into one correct interpretation*25. Together, these statements clarify why the series is necessary. A single photograph can easily become a strong symbolic image of its subject; a series accumulates differences, exceptions, repetitions, and boredom among similar pictures, forcing viewers to notice the photographic genres and social categories through which they are reading the images.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Abstraction: How a Photograph of Something Real Comes to Look “Abstract”

Abstraction (1994–96) presents stains on floors, walls, light, and fragments of objects—things that physically exist—as sharp black-and-white photographs. Galerie Rudolfinum situates the series within the ways Czech photography from 1990 to 2010 transformed the medium itself*8. MoCP explains that, by photographing clearly representational subjects while imitating the visual language of abstract photography, the work exposes the codes through which “abstraction” is recognized*1.

Abstraction depends on photography’s tendency to be received as a record of something that “was there.” Instead of transforming the subject into an abstract painting, the duo photographs real surfaces directly and creates the moment at which the resulting image is classified as abstraction. Because photography’s documentary character collides with the conventions of an art genre, the work returns viewers to the rules of classification they use without thinking. An ARTMargins review likewise places the duo in an exhibition that approached contemporary Czech photography through its institutions and conventions more than through the question of what was depicted*19.

Ignatius and Landscapes: Using Heritage and Landscape Photography from Within

Ignatius – Photography of Historical Sights (1996–2002) and Landscapes – County Photography (1998–2000) borrow the visual vocabulary used to “properly” record heritage sites and regional landscapes. VVP AVU material shows that institutional genre names such as “historical-sights photography” and “county photography” are built into the series titles themselves*11. PhotoRevue describes their work as repeatedly probing photographic canons—architecture, heritage, reportage, abstraction, and landscape—through restraint and humor*16.

Uniform, frontal photography does not erase judgments of value; it shows how those judgments arise from photographic form. A commonplace building can look like “heritage” worthy of preservation when photographed with the conventions of a historical-site record, while a familiar landscape distance can attach regional meaning to suburbs or vacant ground. By keeping the mismatch between subject and form slight, the duo quietly unsettles the authority viewers expect from a genre label.

Making the Relation Between Shooting Site and Exhibition Site Part of the Work

At NoD Gallery in 2025, the duo spoke during installation about how meaning can arise from the combination of where a photograph was made and where it is exhibited*7. An exhibition at Galerie Závodný connected the material traces of analog photography to placement in the gallery, treating photographs as responsive to spatial conditions instead of isolated wall images*9. PLATO Ostrava likewise explains how their use and disruption of established photographic genres extends into the structure of the exhibition itself*10.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
From Pragensia to Brussels Sprouts: Reading the Signs of Cities and Institutions

Pragensia (1986–90) is an important early work that approaches tourist Prague as a sequence of fragments accumulated in the street. The dates of the series and its later cataloging are documented by both SVIT and VVP AVU*3. In the later Brussels Sprouts (2007), their attention shifts toward the visual forms through which design, exhibition, and institutions represent a nation or culture. MoCP compares the work with Louise Lawler’s institutional critique and notes the irony embedded in codes of national representation*1.

From the earliest work onward, the duo repeatedly reproduces established social modes of “showing” things with a slightly excessive fidelity. A Masaryk University bibliographic record for Colour Photography (2010) indicates that the color still-life series again addressed collaboration and the boundary between photography and art*15. In Colour Photography, color itself becomes another means of testing the rules of a photographic genre.

Na bílém papíře: Everyday Objects and Life in 1989

In Na bílém papíře (literally, “on white paper”) (1989), passports, banknotes, clothing, food, and other objects are photographed against a white background. Their combinations evoke travel, work, identity, consumption, and other aspects of life at the time. Pavel Vančát discusses the fourteen color photographs as an early work that uses still-life conventions to make unexpected connections among fragments of everyday Czechoslovak life, placing it before the mismatched matter-of-factness between objects and photographic representation developed later in Vtipy and Abstraction*26.

According to the artists, the white paper served as a “sterile” background that removed objects from their surroundings, while adjacent objects—such as a passport and coffee—were given relations that evoke situations from everyday life*25. From the beginning, they reduced contextual background and created conditions in which meaning emerged from relations within a sequence. The later method of examining how photographic genres themselves guide interpretation in Abstraction and Churches, Churches is already visible here.

Churches, Churches: Typology and Social Traces

Churches, Churches (2012) is a series of contemporary churches in Poland photographed in succession. Culture.pl’s image gallery presents a substantial group of the coolly repetitive architectural images*20. Galeria Arsenał describes their method as spanning documentary and conceptual photography, combining the appearance of a trustworthy record with an ironic distance from the subject*21.

Seeing church architecture repeatedly through the same method makes it possible to compare the forms through which religion, regional architecture, and public space persisted in post-socialist society. GHMP’s J/P/K exhibition likewise identifies repetition, series, and archives as basic tools of the duo, describing their engagement with relics, history, and time in the post-socialist sphere through a distance shaped by nostalgia and irony*4.

Photobooks and Catalogs: Media for Reading Sequences Rather Than Single Images

Their work is more readily understood through series and publications than through a single representative photograph. A 2013 monograph from JRP|Ringier / tranzit.cz brings together long-term series in one volume, and D.A.P. lists it as a major monograph on the photographic duo*18. The Moravian Gallery catalog published the same year appeared as a 106-page exhibition publication; library records specify that it covers photographs from 1986 to 2013*14. The 2019 GHMP catalog for J/P/K was also published in Czech and English, reflecting a reception in which the series move back and forth between exhibition and print*12.

10 000: Deliberately Making “Photographic Photographs” the Old-Fashioned Way

10 000 (1987–2010) is a series governed by an almost excessive rule: photographing the counter of an open-reel tape recorder from 0 to 9999. When the work was completed, the duo said that it would make no sense to use an efficient contemporary output; it had to be realized through a “completely old-fashioned photographic route” using old photographic paper and glossy processing*25. More than the numbers themselves, the labor and material procedure of repeatedly producing small glossy photographs became the core of the work. The historical object called “a photograph” is itself made a subject. A concept that could have existed as a list or database is deliberately bound back to the time, paper, and processing of analog photography, showing how consistently the duo has addressed the conventions and materials that produce the appearance of “photographicness” as well as photographic content.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Beyond Deadpan as Mere Impassivity

Their images are restrained enough to be described as deadpan, but they do not pursue an affectless objectivism. The Moravian Gallery argues that, from the beginning of their careers, they have fundamentally reconsidered how photography is used and redefined its premises with each new body of work*6. A 2010 exhibition review similarly identifies their thorough engagement with banality and their gently mischievous treatment of established photographic canons as characteristic of the work*16.

The humor emerges from a structure in which stricter adherence to the grammar of “proper documentary photography” makes the mismatch between subject and institution more conspicuous. An Art+Antiques interview shows the duo treating decisions about works, collaboration, and exhibitions as practical conversations rather than expressions of a fixed myth of authorship*17. Cool description itself becomes a critical method.

Within Czech Photographic History: Using Photography to Examine Its Own Genres

In Czech art after 1989, the transformation of social institutions coincided with a reexamination of what photography could prove and what it presented as art. MoCP’s 50% Grey traced this change across several generations and treated Jasanský/Polák as major artists directly engaging the conventions of the medium*1. GHMP’s 2019 exhibition summarized repetition, seriality, and the archive as basic means of expression for a remarkably stable collaboration lasting more than three decades*5.

One of their important contributions to photographic history is the refusal to oppose documentary and conceptual photography. At the moment when a record looks most “ordinary,” they read the institutions and tastes that make that ordinariness legible. Without depicting major events, their work repeatedly asks how streets, churches, villages, walls, and everyday objects become “history,” “heritage,” “abstraction,” or “landscape” through photographic arrangement. Their photographs examine, from within photographic culture, what gets selected as a record worth preserving rather than illustrating post-socialist memory directly.

Shared Authorship, Copying, and Repetition: Another Line of Czech Postmodernism

Art historian Karel Císař reconsiders the duo around 1989 beyond a strictly Czech photographic context, relating the seriality, shared authorship, and direct appropriation of Kresby and Na bílém papíře to Rosalind Krauss’s discussions of copies, reproduction, and the repeatability of signs*27. He does not present this as a claim of direct influence. Instead, he frames the work as a “local response” to poststructuralist postmodernism emerging in Czech art at the time and connects it to debates about photography’s “expanded field” and the “anti-photography” of the 1970s*27.

Císař’s research also examines why the duo’s early work did not fit easily into the category of “postmodernism” as it became established in Czech art history. He cites later exhibitions and catalogs in which their work was removed from postmodern sections and placed in separate chapters*27. A history organized primarily around stylistic changes in painting and sculpture made photographic operations such as collaboration, seriality, and copying harder to see. The restraint of these images also carries late-1980s questions about photographic authorship, originals, and the series as an institution.

In Relation to Bernd and Hilla Becher: Different Uses of Typology

Bernd and Hilla Becher The resemblance lies in central perspective, the absence of figures, and cool description that avoids dramatic skies or theatrical effects. Yet the origins and purposes of the two methods differ. Jasanský and Polák explicitly state that they did not know the Bechers when they used in Pragensia a form later read as Becher-like*25. Critic Josef Chuchma acknowledges the similarity while stressing the difference: the Bechers typologized monumental industrial structures under standardized conditions, whereas Jasanský/Polák direct an equally cool surface toward Czech small towns, suburbs, and vacant lots, producing irony through the gap between the seeming insignificance of the subject and the rigor of the photographic form*23. The visual restraint may be similar, but typology serves different functions. The Bechers’ typologies create comparability; in Jasanský/Polák, even photography’s judgment about what is worth comparing becomes unstable.

SVIT exhibition material credits the duo with applying conceptual procedures to ordinary, inconspicuous situations since the late 1980s and with reconsidering photography’s position within contemporary Czech art*22. A substantial 2012 publication similarly identifies typological series, paradoxes of the photographic image, the performative character of working as a duo, and deadpan humor as long-term features*24. Where the Bechers’ method placed subjects under identical conditions to make formal differences comparable, Jasanský/Polák use the very form of classification as an apparatus for examining how land, institutions, public space, and cultural signs come to appear “ordinary” within Czech society.

Chlapi and Český člověk: Accidental Social Images over Typological Precision

Chuchma places Chlapi alongside Český člověk by Jan Malý, Jiří Poláček, and Ivan Lutterer, as well as the tradition of Irving Penn’s typological portraits, while emphasizing the differences. Český člověk gathers people under standardized conditions; Chlapi encounters men in the street in an almost reportage-like manner, using the series to show how the category “men” bundles heterogeneous people together rather than pursuing photographic perfection*23. The typology of Chlapi exposes the roughness of the category itself instead of completing an orderly system.

marville.html.lead_html: Commissioned by the city of Paris, Marville documented both the medieval streets swept away by Haussmann's urban renovation and the new Paris that replaced them. Intended as administrative records, his photographs have been reread as a major visual archive of modern urban transformation.
marville.html.thesis_html: Commissioned by the city of Paris during the Haussmann transformation, Marville systematically documented both the disappearance of the old city and the emergence of the new, demonstrating that administrative photographic practice could function as a visual archive constituting the city's self-image. The process by which a body of photographs produced as official records came to be reread by later generations as cultural testimony to memory and loss concretely illustrates the layered significance that documentary photography can carry. As the direct precedent to Atget's later personal traversal of the same Parisian streets, Marville established an early model for the planned, institutional visualization of urban transformation.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Charles Marville was born in Paris in 1813 and began his career as an illustrator and engraver before turning to photography when the medium emerged. From the 1850s he photographed Parisian urban scenes including cathedrals, city halls, and streets, and in the 1860s he was commissioned by the city authorities to document the transformation of Paris under Napoleon III.*1 The commission covered both the medieval streets of the old city that would be demolished by Haussmann's renovations and the new boulevards and public buildings that replaced them. The Metropolitan Museum's exhibition text makes this explicit, noting that Marville's photographs spanned both disappearance and emergence.*2 He worked as the official photographer of the city of Paris, systematically recording the narrow lanes, alleys, and back streets of the old city until the urban reorganization was complete. He died in Paris in 1879.*3

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Haussmann and the commission

To understand Marville's photographs, it is essential to recognize that his client was the city administration and that his work functioned as part of a state-led urban restructuring. The National Gallery of Art describes his project as "one of the earliest and most powerful explorations of large-scale urban transformation," acknowledging a significance that exceeds local documentation.*4 Haussmann's renovation was at the heart of nineteenth-century urban politics, combining sanitation, traffic management, military control, and landscape reorganization; Marville's photographs made that institutional restructuring visible as streets, buildings, squares, and the desolate peripheries being cleared.*5 The Getty Museum's artist page positions Marville as a photographer who produced his work administratively for the city of Paris, indicating that his photographs functioned as instruments of urban self-management and record-keeping.*6

Dual record of disappearance and emergence

Marville's distinctiveness lies in the fact that his work is not simply a nostalgic record of the old city. While photographing the old quarters, he simultaneously documented the construction of new boulevards and public facilities. The Paris.fr article on Haussmann and Marville frames this duality within the context of the "grands travaux de Paris," showing that his photographs functioned not only as a record of what was being lost but also as a self-image of the modern city as it was being formed.*7 In its Changing Paris piece, Aperture reads Marville's photographs alongside images of what came after, using visual comparison to demonstrate the contemporary reach of this record.*8 The Metropolitan Museum's exhibition press release notes that, viewed from today, the administrative records of the time have been transformed into "an accumulation of memories of old Paris as it disappeared."*9

Urban visual discourse

What distinguishes Marville's photographs is a quiet compositional register quite unlike journalism or sensationalism. Within the constraints of long exposure times and large-format equipment, his pictures render empty streets, the facades of buildings on the eve of demolition, and hanging mist or dust as the structure of space rather than as sentiment.*10 The Houston Museum of Fine Arts exhibition text prizes this quietness as "a method of soberly presenting urban transformation as visual fact," clearly differentiating it from the accusatory energy of documentary journalism.*11 A scholarly review in CAA Reviews repositions Marville's work at the intersection of urban history, photographic history, and administrative history, arguing that his photographs function as "an archive constituting the visual self-representation of the modern city."*12 Individual works such as the photograph of the Palais Royal held by Paris Musées are in the city's own collection, where they are preserved as both records and cultural patrimony.*13

Critical reception

Marville's reception has grown, particularly from the latter twentieth century onward, as his photographs have been reread not as mere urban documents but as a visual archive through which the formation of the modern city can be analyzed. His work being shown at the Met, NGA, and MFAH reflects an institutional evaluation that repositions it at the intersection of photographic history, museum holdings, and urban history.*14 The National Gallery of Art maintains a dedicated artist page for Marville and holds works including Cloud Study, Paris.*15 The Städel Museum's digital collection also holds Marville's work, indicating his spread into European museum collections.*16 Within photographic history, Marville has been read not only as a precursor to Eugène Atget but as a figure who shows how photography records a city being administratively and technically restructured while simultaneously participating in its memorialization.*17 Princeton University Art Museum and the Morgan Library & Museum also hold related works, attesting to continued scholarly interest.*18 The Art Institute of Chicago's Museum Studies journal has referenced and reproduced Marville's work, connecting individual street photographs to the materiality of collodion and albumen, urban naming practices, and administrative classification.*19 A Washington Post exhibition review conveyed the contemporary significance of Marville's project to a general audience as "photography standing between record and loss."*20 Photographic records of Parisian sites held by the Library of Congress confirm that his documentation has entered international archives.*21

masahisa-fukase.html.lead_html: Masahisa Fukase photographed his wife Yoko each morning from an upstairs window, staged his family in the portrait studio of his hometown, projected himself onto ravens and cats, and eventually brought his hands, feet, face, and fingerprints into the image and onto the print. His methods grew from the staging he learned in a family studio and commercial photography, the rise of I-photography in the 1970s, and the shift from magazines toward the original print. Through Yoko, Family, Ravens, Sasuke, Private Scenes, and Bukubuku, this page asks why his work required the pleasures and burdens of photographing intimate others, the compulsion to repeat lost relationships, and forms of play that ranged from crude jokes to bodily contact.
masahisa-fukase.html.thesis_html: Through the repeated photography of Yoko and Family, the sequencing of Ravens, and the self-portraits and fingerprinted prints of Private Scenes, Fukase recorded more than private life. He made visible the photographer’s instructions to another person, his authority to select and publish an image, and the body at work behind the camera. The daily rule that required Yoko to respond, the staging of relatives, the pursuit of ravens, the body lowered to a cat’s level, and fingerprints pressed onto paper all retain the photographer’s desires and actions. As I-photography became a first-person mode for narrating everyday life in the 1970s, Fukase placed collaboration with intimate subjects and the asymmetries within that collaboration in the same work. Nudity, fundoshi loincloths, enlarged views of a cat’s mouth, and tongue-touching self-portraits also kept these relationships from hardening into solemn confession. He extended I-photography from a record of private life into a form that examines how photographer and subject are joined, exhausted, separated, and still preserved as images.
