sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Painting to Photography—Addressing Representation at the Speed of His Own Time

Terrier-Hermann was born in France in 1970. He studied at the art school in Rouen and the School of the Art Institute of Chicago before making Intercontinental (1996–2000) at the Rijksakademie van Beeldende Kunsten*24. He has said that since his youth he had thought about “representation” through painting and fashion, but reached an impasse trying to make images of contemporary reality through painting and came to see photography as a more direct connection to his own time*25. In France in the 1980s and 1990s, the photographic field and contemporary-art world remained comparatively separate, while in North America large-format photographs by Jeff Wall and Andres Serrano were being shown as contemporary art; understanding that situation was one reason he went to the United States*25. Villa Medici’s biography records his subsequent work in cities including Rome, Paris, and Tokyo*3. Fondation Pernod Ricard’s exhibition history shows his continued movement between photography and moving image after 2000*4, and pointligneplan likewise places photographic series and filmmaking within one sustained body of work*5. His turn to photography allowed a question first pursued in painting—how people come to believe images—to be tested inside the contemporary image environment.

Jeff Wall, Andres Serrano, and Renaissance Painting—Constructed Reality

Terrier-Hermann explicitly names Jeff Wall and Andres Serrano as important contemporary reference points. He values Wall in particular as an artist with a broad “culture of images” extending across painting, printmaking, and cinema*25. At the same time, his compositional roots lie in Renaissance and early modern painting. He has spoken of his attraction to Caravaggio, Grünewald, Cranach, Dürer, and Georges de La Tour, especially their placement of figures, use of light and darkness, and mixtures of sacred and secular imagery*25. In his own account, a photograph is both a “fragment of reality” and a staging of that fragment through framing, light, depth of field, and off-screen space*25. Documentary and construction therefore coexist within the same image: every photograph of reality already contains selection and composition, and those choices can activate cultural codes that the work then makes visible.

The Photographic Tableau After the 1990s and the Global Circulation of Images of Place

CNAP describes Terrier-Hermann’s photographs as staged images of film and television actors that resemble production stills from nonexistent movies and are then returned to advertising display surfaces*1. Gallifet Art Center similarly connects his work with the models of power, beauty, and success produced by cinema, television, and advertising*2. In an essay published with Internationales in 2001, Hilde Van Gelder discusses his photographs and moving images as “photographic and video tableaux,” situating the work within the convergence of photography and cinematic tableau after the 1990s*22. Masha Tupitsyn reads The American Tetralogy through a culture in which gestures and desires are learned from film, photography, and advertising and then repeated in everyday life*21. Centre Pompidou likewise identifies fascination and conditioning through stereotyped images circulating in cinema, television, and advertising as shared concerns across his photography and moving image*23. The background is therefore broader than staged photography’s convergence with film: cities, tourist destinations, and human types were increasingly consumed across borders through prepackaged advertising and lifestyle imagery.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Intercontinental—Cinema, Advertising, and Hotels as Models of “Desirable Reality”

Beginning around 1996, Intercontinental/Internationales arranged international cities, hotels, modern architecture, and polished figures with the familiarity of cinema and advertising. For Internationale at Fundació Mies van der Rohe, the Mies van der Rohe Pavilion became a showcase for photographic works, overlaying modernist architecture with the aesthetics of commercial display*6. The series is less concerned with exposing luxury locations from a position of critique than with asking from which kinds of images viewers have learned to recognize “success,” “beauty,” and “internationalism.” Centre Pompidou’s later account similarly describes his work through fascination and conditioning and its relation to typical images from film, television, and advertising*7.

From Sacred Images to Brands and Advertising—Following Images in Which Value Is Invested

Terrier-Hermann’s interest in film and advertising develops from an earlier concern with sacred images. While in art school, he photographed images of the Virgin and other devotional objects in Eastern Europe and sold the photographs like inexpensive religious souvenirs. He recalls that the same image could thereby acquire different values as an object of devotion, a tourist keepsake, or a work by a young artist*25. From there he began to connect the way an artist’s name, a brand, or a place of purchase changes the value of an object in contemporary society with the way religious images receive value through belief*25. A 2001 contemporary review records how Intercontinental expanded from photographs into furniture, clothing, perfume, and ceramics, with the artist’s name operating almost like a production brand*26. Hotels, actors, luxury goods, and cinema are therefore connected experiments in the systems through which institutions, names, places, and familiar imagery confer value on images and objects.

Cinema as a Preexisting Script Through Which Viewers Complete the Story

FRAC Franche-Comté places cinema in Terrier-Hermann’s work as a machine that produces models and celebrities and directs desire under globalization*8. Terrier-Hermann explains his use of photographic series through the space “between” images: viewers fill those gaps and can invent the unseen movie from only a few stills*25. His first experience of California—where accumulated cinematic images made both the city and people’s gestures appear like a film set—also informs The American Tetralogy*25. Tupitsyn likewise discusses the project through the way everyday life repeats gestures and desires learned from cinema, photography, and advertising*21. “Cinematic” here refers to more than lighting or camera angle; it includes the viewer’s tendency to fill gaps between images with stories already known from visual culture.

106 beautés japonaises—Producing “Japanese Beauty” Through the Procedure of Market Research

For 106 beautés japonaises, Terrier-Hermann asked roughly one hundred people connected with Japan in Paris to name places or concepts that represented “Japanese beauty,” then used their answers to determine what he would photograph. CNAP describes the process as an aesthetic treasure hunt filtered through something like an opinion survey or market study and situates it as an update of nineteenth-century photographic travel for contemporary social and economic conditions*9. The artist’s statement published by Paris Art likewise shows a method in which national imagery is assembled through other people’s recommendations instead of through his own intuitive selection of what looks “Japanese”*10. The decisive operation therefore occurs before the photograph is taken: the work asks who gets to designate something as “beautiful.”

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Romans / Fascination—Male Images, Sacredness, and Power in Rome

Made during Terrier-Hermann’s residency at Villa Medici, Romans / Fascination centers on portraits of men in Rome. He has explained that he became conscious of how museums and the city foreground male nudity, musculature, and symbols of power, and photographed contemporary men in order to compare them with historical forms of representation*25. Actors, film professionals, clergy, and politicians spontaneously performed the way they felt they looked best before the camera, bringing into the work the fact that people associated with power or attractiveness often already know the codes of self-presentation*25. Terrier-Hermann also links Rome, Catholic sacredness, and Fascist cults of the body through a shared question: which images attract and command attention*25. CiNii Books records the publication as an exhibition catalog centered on male portraiture*11. Van Abbemuseum holds a publication related to 106 beautés japonaises*12, while the ARTBOOK record for 93 Beautés Hollandaises confirms that he extended this comparative method of people, places, and cultural types to another national setting*13.

La trilogie française—Inserting Cinematic Memory into Real Landscapes

For the 2013 public photographic commission La trilogie française, Terrier-Hermann placed film and television actors in landscapes across France, making photographs that resemble production stills and circulating them on large advertising panels and postcards. CNAP’s En situations presents the project specifically as photography intended for display in public space*14. Paris Art records how the exhibition returned photographs made in those locations to urban circulation, treating production, display, and distribution as one continuous process*15. MAC VAL clearly describes the work’s structure: actors, performance, framing, and natural light insert fiction into real French sites already remembered through cinema*16.

Books and Public Space—Circulating Photography as a Series

Les presses du réel’s artist page shows 106 beautés japonaises, The American Tetralogy, and La Trilogie française as parts of a continuous production history spanning photobooks, films, and projects*17. La trilogie française, meanwhile, appeared in the city on display surfaces measuring roughly four by three meters and as postcards. Terrier-Hermann uses existing channels—travel books, advertising displays, film screenings, public space—to make their conventions part of the work. The same photograph can consequently be read through different institutional frames as tourist information, advertising, film publicity, or art, even though the image itself has not changed.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photography History
sections.body_html:
Beyond “Staged Photography”—Fiction as an Institutional System

The publication La Trilogie française returns photographs produced through a public commission to the book, where locations, actors, and cinematic references can again be read as a sequence*18. The book version of The American Tetralogy similarly examines cinematic clichés of California and real landscapes through page sequence as well as film screening*19. Moving between photobook and film reveals a basic premise of the work: models for seeing reality already circulate socially before the camera encounters a supposedly neutral world. For Terrier-Hermann, the series is not simply a way to multiply a theme. It is a comparative unit for observing how places and figures adhere to preexisting images.

Place in Photography History—From “Photographs Like Films” to Images That Condition Viewers

Terrier-Hermann was included in Photo Art: Photography in the 21st Century, a 2007 survey of international photographic directions, placing him among artists working at a time when photography and contemporary art increasingly overlapped*20. To describe the work only as another example of cinematic staged photography after Jeff Wall would miss its central concern. Terrier-Hermann does bring cinematic composition into photography, but he also incorporates the systems through which cinema, advertising, tourism, and market research preclassify “beautiful places,” “successful people,” and “what belongs to a nation.” Photography thus becomes an instrument for testing how reality is perceived through already available fictional types.

pieter-hugo.html.lead_html: Pieter Hugo is a South African photographer based in Cape Town. Through frontal, large-scale portraits, he fixes people, places, animals, waste, and family inside forceful images, making post-apartheid memory, whiteness, marginalization, electronic waste, and the unease of representing others visible. In The Hyena and Other Men, Permanent Error, and Kin, the portrait becomes a place where the viewer's distance, judgment, and desire are also brought into question.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html:
Pieter Hugo was born in Johannesburg in 1976 and is now based in Cape Town. Stevenson describes his practice as an inquiry into "the possibilities and limits of portraiture" and into the way images shape relations between people*1. What matters in Hugo's work is not whether a photograph can explain its subject correctly. It is what happens when a person is placed frontally before the camera and the viewer begins to judge that person through clues such as skin, clothing, place, animals, waste, race, and class. Portraiture becomes not only a way of presenting a person, but also a form in which the viewer's expectations and assumptions become exposed in front of the image. On Hugo's official site, projects such as The Hyena and Other Men , Permanent Error , and Kin are not organized simply as regional records, but as groups of work around belonging, memory, inheritance, and his work in West Africa*2.

The background to Hugo's work across parts of Africa is his own position as a white South African photographer. In an interview with Saint Lucy, he says that Africa is his home, but that he is white, and that his uneasy fit within South Africa's social terrain was one of the main reasons he became a photographer*3. This unstable position leads his work away from recording "strange realities in Africa" and toward the question of where the photographer stands, and from what distance another person is seen. Hugo also describes photography as a medium that allows him to go out, encounter people and places, and respond to the environment rather than inventing a work entirely in the studio beforehand*4. At the same time, he has said that photography carries a trace of reality while the image itself is made through selection, framing, light, and distance; in this sense, he treats photography as a medium in which documentary evidence and artistic construction cannot be separated*5. His portraits therefore do more than record people. They pull the photographer's own position and the viewer's judgment into the same image.

Hugo occupies an important place in post-apartheid South African photography because his work emerges after the period of direct denunciation and photojournalistic exposure, yet remains bound to the political pressure of portraiture. The V&A's Figures and Fictions presented South African photography after the 2000s as a field in which identity, race, gender, class, and politics were being reconsidered, and it placed Hugo within that context*6. In Hugo's work, the question is not only who the subject is. When a white South African photographer photographs the African continent, his own family in South Africa, sites of electronic waste, and marginalized people, the photographer's position, the subject's self-presentation, and the expectations of an international audience enter the same frame. The frontal figure is both someone being presented and someone who holds the viewer's gaze in return.

sections.title: Expression / method
sections.body_html:
Frontal portraiture: Sander, Arbus, Ruff, and Hugo's distance from them

Hugo's frontal portraits have been discussed not through one single predecessor, but across several portrait traditions. Greta Schoeman writes that his flat, frontal portraits recall August Sander, Diane Arbus, Roger Ballen, Rineke Dijkstra, Zwelethu Mthethwa, Nontsikelelo Veleko, and Alec Soth, while his still lifes suggest William Eggleston and his impassive architectural photographs bring to mind Bernd and Hilla Becher, Walker Evans, Dan Graham, and Paul Graham*7. This list matters because it shows that Hugo's photographs do not stand only on the novelty of unusual subjects. They combine typology, frontality, large prints, the flatness of everyday detail, and the force of images seen in a museum. The Prestel volume Between the Devil and the Deep Blue Sea also describes Hugo's work as a convergence of Sander's typological portraiture and Arbus's recording of private and psychological reality*8. Even so, placing Hugo too directly in Arbus's line would blur what is specific about his work. The closeness to Arbus and Ballen lies in marginal subjects, psychological unease, and the uncertain distance between viewer and subject. In Hugo, however, that unease is crossed by his position as a white South African photographer, by post-apartheid history, by colonial othering, and by the risk that such images may be consumed in the international art market. The connection to Dijkstra, Mthethwa, Veleko, and Soth is also less about portraits revealing an inner self than about how posture, clothing, place, and scale position a person within a social space.

The character of Hugo's frontality becomes clearer when it is set beside Thomas Ruff. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation's Look at Me exhibition grouped Pieter Hugo, Thomas Ruff, Rineke Dijkstra, Seydou Keïta, Alec Soth, Thomas Struth, and others around the representation of people*9. Such a grouping shows that portraiture is not only a record of a face. Through frontality, repetition, the handling of background, print scale, and the exhibition space, a person can become linked to age, class, race, profession, urban life, or institutional identity. Schoeman also argues that Hugo's photographs confront the viewer across the boundaries between fact and fiction, art and document, record and performance, history and expectation*7. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes Ruff's Portrait series as portraits that take up Becher-like typology, minimalist repetition, and the bright world of identification photography and surveillance*10. In conversation with Gil Blank, Ruff himself explained that he wanted the pictures to look like passport photographs while withholding information such as address, religion, profession, criminal record, and even emotion*11. In Ruff, the face is large, uniform, and almost without background or story. Hair, skin, eyes, facial features, and the collar of a shirt are visible, but the person's life, place, voice, and relations withdraw from the image; what remains is an impassive surface close to an ID photograph or surveillance image. In Hugo's Mallam Mantari Lamal with Mainasara, Nigeria , by contrast, the man's body, the hyena, the chain, and the dry ground remain in the same frame, so the portrait never becomes an ID-like image of a face alone*14. In SFMOMA's Al Hasan Abukari, Agbogbloshie Market, Accra, Ghana , the frontal figure cannot be separated from the landscape of electronic waste; portrait and labor environment appear together*17. If Ruff's frontality creates a face that is visible yet unreachable, Hugo's frontality keeps place, objects, animals, labor, and history around the person, returning the viewer's basis for judgment to the image itself.

The Hyena and Other Men began when Hugo saw a cellphone photograph of men walking with a chained hyena. According to the official text, rumors around the image described the men as bank robbers, bodyguards, drug dealers, or debt collectors, but Hugo found that the people he followed were itinerant performers who used animals to gather crowds and sell traditional medicine*12. Hugo first tried to follow the group's activity as it moved through markets, but the official text explains that this method did not capture the relationship that interested him. What he wanted to see was not the street spectacle itself, but a relation in which wild animals walked through urban roads and human beings seemed both to dominate the animals and to depend on them for a living*12. The work therefore shifts from recording a moving marketplace to fixing one performer and one animal in streets or open ground. By holding person, animal, chain, ground, and surrounding city within a single frame, the photograph leaves undecided whether power belongs to the human being, the animal, poverty, or the viewer's imagination.

The series is difficult because the images are so forceful that the viewer may first see only an "extraordinary" subject. Elizabeth Biondi wrote in The New Yorker that the pictures at first appeared simply spectacular, but that a closer look brought forward the group, the animals, the environment, everyday life, and wider relations in African societies*13. In the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Mallam Mantari Lamal with Mainasara, Nigeria , the man and the hyena are not only a strange pairing; chain, posture, distance, and gaze hold dominance and dependence in the same image*14. Hugo himself wrote that after the second shoot the words "dominance," "co-dependence," and "submission" kept appearing in his notes, positioning the work as more than an exotic account of West African itinerant performers*12. The significance of the series is not that it presents hyena handlers as rare figures. It turns a scene that might otherwise pass as spectacle into a portrait, layering economic marginalization, survival, human-animal relations, and the viewer's curiosity within one image.

Permanent Error moves to Agbogbloshie in Accra, Ghana. Hugo's official text describes the site as one of West Africa's major destinations for electronic waste and explains the structure by which unsellable electronics finally arrive there*15. Prix Pictet presents the series within the theme of "Disorder" and includes several images from Agbogbloshie Market*16. The portraits here do not merely turn people in a polluted place into objects of pity. They show how the updating of digital devices, overproduction, disposal, metal recovery, migrant labor, and international inequality gather around a single body. SFMOMA's Al Hasan Abukari, Agbogbloshie Market, Accra, Ghana, from the series Permanent Error is at once a portrait and an image in which the landscape of waste and the site of labor are held together*17. Hugo writes that it is impossible to stand in such a place without taking a political position, yet the photographs are not simple protest posters. They make visible a structure in which the afterlife of technologies used elsewhere is pushed onto bodies in a distant place*15.

Kin marks a major turn in Hugo's work. Aperture presents the book as a set of images made across South Africa, with the focus moving toward family, community, and the artist himself*18. Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson also describes Kin as a personal exploration of South Africa through landscapes, portraits, and still lifes*19. This shift does not mean that Hugo retreated into a safe private world in order to avoid the risks of representing others. By bringing family, wife, children, domestic workers, land, landscape, and whiteness into the same series, he turns the gaze previously directed toward "distant others" back onto family history and social relations in South Africa. Foto Colectania presents Hugo's own description of Kin as a project that examines the gap between the ideals a society declares and the realities actually lived*20. Works on Hugo's official page such as Tamsyn Reynolds pregnant with our first child, Cape Town and Daniela Beukman, Milnerton show family intimacy and the historical asymmetries that remain in South African land and employment relations without separating one from the other*21.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html:
Hugo's photographs have been widely received through museums, photography festivals, and photobook circuits. His official biography lists the Rencontres d'Arles Discovery Award, the KLM Paul Huf Award, the Seydou Keïta Award, a Deutsche Börse Photography Prize shortlist, and a Prix Pictet shortlist*22. Fotomuseum Den Haag described its 2012 exhibition as the first museum survey to present a comprehensive view of his work from 2003 to 2011*23. Stevenson's publication list also shows how his practice has been continually structured through photobooks, from The Hyena and Other Men , Permanent Error , and Kin to 1994 , La Cucaracha , and Californian Wildflowers *24. In this sense, Hugo is not only an exhibition artist, but also an artist who reorganizes how subjects appear through the series and the photobook.

At the same time, Hugo's work is inseparable from criticism around the violence of looking and the risk of stereotyping. Artthrob's review of Kin acknowledges that his images can be received as racialized stereotype or exploitation, while also suggesting that anger and voyeuristic pleasure can be bound together*25. This criticism is important not only as a challenge to Hugo's work, but as a way to explain why the pictures are both powerful and dangerous. In an interview with AnOther , Hugo says that photographs show surfaces and that we give those surfaces meaning, sometimes correctly and sometimes wrongly*26. From this perspective, Hugo's photographs do not extract the "essence" of a subject. They expose, through the form of the frontal portrait, how quickly viewers give meaning to a photographic surface and how unstable the grounds for judgment can be.

The difference between Ernest Cole and Hugo is important for understanding the trajectory of South African photography. The Photographers' Gallery describes Cole's House of Bondage , published in 1967, as one of the twentieth century's most important photobooks, a work that revealed the brutality and injustice of apartheid to the world and vividly recorded the everyday lives of Black South Africans*27. Foam also positions Cole as an early Black freelance photographer who showed Black life under apartheid from within, documenting mines, police checkpoints, and the destruction of townships at great personal risk*28. The "system" Cole exposed was not an abstract prejudice. It was a concrete set of mechanisms — pass laws, residential segregation, mine labor, whites-only facilities, commuter trains, fences, and overcrowded, airless transport — that determined where Black bodies could go, where they were made to work, and which entrances they were forced to use. A Kronos review of Defiant Images also describes Cole's work as moving South African photography toward systematic social criticism through dark interiors, fences, and overcrowded transport*31. Cole's photographs recorded the scenes in which state violence entered bodies and urban space, making that system legible beyond South Africa.

The legal and spatial machinery revealed by Cole did not simply disappear with the end of apartheid. Ways of seeing that quickly bind a person to race, poverty, danger, marginality, Africanness, victimhood, or strangeness remain active after the formal system changes. Hugo addresses that residue not through the urgency of hidden cameras or reportage, but by placing the subject frontally and allowing the photographer's distance, the subject's self-presentation, and the judgment of an international viewer to operate at the same time. Okey Nwafor argues that while the work of Cole, Peter Magubane, and David Goldblatt often contains movement and incident produced by apartheid, Hugo's work emerges in the post-apartheid period and fixes people in a state of "quiet unease"*29. The same essay also presents the claim that Hugo's frontal method is new in the context of South African social representation because it involves facing the subject, working with the subject, and requiring the viewer to face the image as well*29. KYOTOGRAPHIE's recent focus on South Africa similarly separates three generations of voices: Cole as a record of life under apartheid, Hugo through works around life, death, and ritual, and Lebohang Khanye through memory and inheritance*30. Rather than linking Cole and Hugo in a single line of succession, it is clearer to say that Cole recorded how state systems bound bodies and cities, while Hugo examines how people remain exposed to classificatory ways of seeing after those systems have changed. In Hugo's portraits, the subject is not processed as an example of a social problem. Person, place, object, and history remain in one image, and the viewer's grounds for judgment return as part of the work's own problem.

Hugo's recent series What the Light Falls On does not simply relocate the concerns of his portraiture onto private subjects such as family and death. KYOTOGRAPHIE's exhibition text describes the series as comprising more than one hundred photographs made over the past twenty-three years, and explains it as a body of work oriented toward life, death, and the transitions between them — distinct from the clearly themed photo-essay form of his earlier projects*33. In an interview with IMA, Hugo said he felt the 2017 mid-career retrospective marked the end of one chapter; after that he began looking through his archive and searching for photographs that could stand alone*32. The birth of a daughter, the death of his father, family, aging — these are not simply events in a life, but connect to the conditions of portraiture itself: what time, what distance, and what light a person appears in. Hugo has spoken of Helmar Lerski, noting that changing only the direction of light on the same person produces entirely different aspects, and that Lerski was challenging the "truthfulness" of photography*32. Rather than extending this recent work into a general theory of photographic truth, however, the shift that matters in Hugo's practice is the expansion of what portraiture can do: from frontal portraits that position people within social categories, toward images in which the way a person appears changes with light, time, family, and loss. In his early and middle career, the viewer's impulse to assign meaning to others was returned to the image through place, animals, waste, clothing, and labor. Hugo now directs that same question not only toward external others, but toward his own father, his children, and his own aging. At the end of the same interview he says that this work belongs strongly to a particular period in his life, and that he no longer sees the world in the same way he once did*32.

rashid-johnson.html.lead_html: Rashid Johnson moved from Seeing in the Dark, portraits of unhoused men in Chicago made with an 8 × 10 camera and Van Dyke brown printing, to an invented Black social club and installations built from black soap, shea butter, books, and plants. He expanded Black portraiture beyond the demand that a face provide the answer, examining how class differences between photographer and subject, the authority of historical processes, clothing, titles, possessions, and museum institutions participate in the making of self-image.
rashid-johnson.html.thesis_html: Black portraiture served nineteenth-century racial classification, while Frederick Douglass, W. E. B. Du Bois, and others used it to construct images of dignity, citizenship, and education. In the late 1990s, Johnson invited unhoused Black men he had met in Chicago into the studio, photographed them slowly with an 8 × 10 camera, and made Van Dyke brown prints by hand. Photographer and subject shared racial identity but occupied different class positions and living conditions. That distance remains visible in closed eyes, lowered faces, and hands that interrupt the frame. Johnson chose a historical process to give portraits of named unhoused Black men the brown surface and extended making time associated with museum portraits. In the later The New Negro Escapist Social and Athletic Club, he used the same historical appearance to invent members and an institution, examining how costume, title, printing process, and collection status give photographs the credibility of records. He then distributed self-image across books, music, domestic materials, plants, and architecture, turning the question of how Black people are photographed into a spatial inquiry into which cultures individuals select and which objects and institutions help them construct a self.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
The History of Black Portraiture and Photographic Education in Chicago

In nineteenth-century America, images of Black bodies were used in the classifications of slavery and racial science. Frederick Douglass, by contrast, sat repeatedly for portraits and presented himself to the public as a thinking, acting citizen. The National Portrait Gallery notes that Douglass became the most photographed American of the nineteenth century and consciously used photography’s social power to shape his public image.*3 Black portraiture has therefore carried both the image imposed by others and the public construction of dignity by Black subjects themselves.

For the 1900 Paris Exposition, W. E. B. Du Bois and Thomas J. Calloway assembled roughly five hundred photographs for the “American Negro Exhibit,” presenting African American life and progress through education, work, family, and organizations. The Library of Congress makes available portraits and scenes of daily life originating in that exhibition.*1 Johnson’s early photographs were made within a history in which Black people had been classified by the camera and had also used photography for self-representation.

Johnson studied photography at Columbia College Chicago with Dawoud Bey, known for sustained work with communities. According to Shelley Rice, photographic education at the time treated the power relations involved in photographing people in poverty as a central issue and drew on critiques of social documentary by Martha Rosler, Allan Sekula, John Tagg, and others.*14 The danger that photographers might use other people’s lives to explain a social problem formed part of the environment in which the young Johnson worked.*16

The subjects of Seeing in the Dark were unhoused Black men Johnson met near his studio on South Michigan Avenue. Johnson was himself a Black man and shared aspects of racial experience with them, while his photographic education, studio, and access to art institutions placed him differently in class terms. Because racial proximity and class difference coexisted, reducing each person to a representative of “Blackness” or “homelessness” would have erased the relation’s complexity. Rice identifies the varying degrees of trust, resistance, and self-disclosure from one sitter to another as central to the series.*14

In 2001, the work was selected for Freestyle at the Studio Museum in Harlem. The term “post-black,” used by Thelma Golden for the exhibition, described a situation in which Black artists addressed racial history while moving beyond the demand to represent a single, stable idea of Blackness.*9 Johnson’s photographs likewise avoid defining one affirmative Black image, altering the relation among subject, photographer, process, class, and institution from picture to picture.

Seeing in the Dark: A Slow Encounter Shaped by a Historical Printing Process

Van Dyke brown printing is a nineteenth-century process in which sensitizer is brushed onto paper, a large negative is contact printed, and exposure is made with ultraviolet light or sunlight. Johnson used an 8 × 10 Deardorff camera to make close studio portraits.*14 Because preparation and exposure take time, the sitter is not captured in a passing street instant. He has time to sit, face the camera, close his eyes, or raise a hand between himself and the lens.*5

The years 1998–99 coincided with the rapid spread of digital photography and images made quickly and in volume. Johnson chose an older chemical process and made each brown-toned print individually.*14 Coating the paper and making a contact print gave the portrait a temporality different from the immediate record of news photography or identification. By directing a format associated with historical museum portraiture toward named unhoused Black men, Seeing in the Dark brought the description of poverty into the same frame as the formal bearing of a portrait intended to endure.*6

The dark tonal range has also been linked to Roy DeCarava.*14 Details of face and clothing do not appear all at once, and the viewer must spend time reading the image. In Jonathan, a large hand interrupts the approach to the face; in Eugene, the hat and lowered eyes limit access. The men are not fully opened to view as evidence explaining poverty. Each retains a particular way of responding to the camera.

sections.title: Core Approach
sections.body_html:
Staging Du Bois’s Double Consciousness as an Imaginary Social Club

The New Negro Escapist Social and Athletic Club (2008–) imagines a secret club of Black intellectuals and photographs formally dressed men in the format of membership portraits. In the National Gallery of Art’s Emmett, the figure appears twice; the chair, dark background, historically indeterminate clothing, and brown print create the look of an old archival photograph.*7

Johnson connects the series to W. E. B. Du Bois’s “double consciousness,” the condition of seeing oneself through one’s own experience while also seeing oneself through the judgments of white society. The doubled figure, historical clothing, and formal pose translate these two viewpoints into the photograph’s structure.*4 The club offers temporary distance from external racism while also establishing its own standards of education, class, and masculinity.

Contemporary friends and models perform as imaginary members, and the photographs are made as records of an organization that never existed. Title, costume, printing process, and exhibition give Black history an invented social space. At the same time, the old brown print, formal pose, and museum collection status reveal the conditions through which a photograph comes to resemble a credible historical document.

Dispersing Self-Image from the Face Across Soap, Books, Music, and Plants

As Johnson moved into sculpture and installation, he spread Black self-image beyond the face across black soap, shea butter, wax, mirrors, tiles, houseplants, books, and records. These materials connect to barbering, self-care, the home, study, music, and life across the African diaspora. MCA Chicago describes this incorporation of domestic materials into art structures as “hijacking the domestic.”*2

Writing about Wifredo Lam, Johnson considers the way African diasporic religion, Cubism, and modern art meet within a single painting. His interest in allowing different cultural references and art histories to coexist without reducing a figure to one racial sign continues in later works that gather books, records, plants, and household objects.*11

The materials carry symbolic associations and physical effects. Shea butter changes shape with temperature, black soap leaves gloss and residue on the wall, and mirrors reflect the viewer. Books and records show how knowledge and taste are selected, owned, and presented to others. Gridded shelving organizes a personal cultural history like furniture and also recalls museum systems of classification and display.*18 *10

Portrait photography encourages viewers to read race, class, education, and psychology together from a single body. Johnson’s shelves and spatial works treat books read, music heard, substances applied to the body, plants tended, room arrangements, and the viewer’s movement as elements of self-image alongside the face. Blackness appears through multiple acts of selecting, possessing, and presenting culture, rather than as a single appearance.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Jonathan’s Hands, Calvin, and Emmett: Changes in Naming and Historical Appearance

Jonathan’s Hands (1998) places the hands prominently before the face, stopping an approaching gaze. In Calvin (1999), face and clothing emerge gradually from the dark print. Personal names bring each sitter into the work as an individual before the social category of “homeless person.”*8 *15

The name Emmett (2008) evokes Emmett Till, although the model is a different contemporary person. The present-day sitter, the appearance of an old membership photograph, and the doubled image bring several periods together. In the early work, names resist anonymity; in the later series, a name connects one model to another figure or narrative in Black history.

Seen together, the three works trace a shift from making dignified portraits to examining the forms through which dignity becomes visible. Formal dress, historical printing, and learned titles present Black men as historical subjects. The same elements can also confine dignity within codes of education, class, and masculinity.*16

Shelving and Architectural Space: Extending Self-Image into Possessions and the Viewer’s Experience

MCA Chicago’s 2012 exhibition Message to Our Folks brought together fourteen years of work, from early photographs to sculpture, film, and installation.*2 Gridded shelves support books, plants, records, ceramics, incense, and monitors, recalling domestic storage, modernist architecture, and the order of museum display at once.

Choosing what to place on a shelf resembles choosing clothing and background in a portrait. After viewing an image from the front, visitors walk around the structure, see themselves in mirrors, and encounter sound and smell. In the Whitney’s New Poetry, the structure extended from the museum interior into outdoor space, connecting the act of looking with movement through a public setting.*12

At an architectural scale, viewers can follow the books, music, domestic materials, plants, furniture, and institutions through which a person shapes a self. Selection and arrangement once contained within the photographic frame become an experience of walking, reflection, scent, and sound.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Black Portraiture After Lorna Simpson and Carrie Mae Weems

Since the 1980s, Lorna Simpson has combined Black women turned away from the camera, bodies without visible faces, and text to question the habit of reading race, gender, and psychology directly from a portrait.*19 Carrie Mae Weems reused historical materials that photographed Black people as scientific types, exposing photography’s and the museum’s participation in racial classification.*20

Working after these interventions, Johnson used historical processes to make new photographs. Simpson limits information about the figure; Weems rereads an existing archive; Johnson produces fictional portraits that look like historical materials. New Negro Escapist imagines a social club absent from Black history while showing how costume, title, printing process, and museum collection create the appearance of historical truth.

The method also contains an affirmative image. Formally dressed Black men, personal names, and learned titles clearly express aspirations toward dignity and self-formation. Class selection, male-centered membership, and awareness of white social judgment accompany that image, revealing the rules that structure an ideal self.

From the Appearance of Historical Portraiture to the Objects and Institutions That Support Self-Image

In Seeing in the Dark, the slow Van Dyke brown process and its brown surface extend the encounter between photographer and sitter and present unhoused Black men as historical portraits with personal names. In New Negro Escapist, the same appearance gives documentary credibility to imaginary members and an invented institution. The historical process gives real people the temporal weight of portraits made to be preserved; it can also make a history that never existed look like a trustworthy record.

In the installations, the elements that form self-image expand from expression, clothing, and background to books, music, bodily materials, plants, furniture, and museum display structures. The portrait’s task of describing a person continues as the problem of exhibiting how an individual selects culture, arranges a life, and becomes visible within institutions.

In the early photographs, the sitter’s gesture, distance from the photographer, and the surface of the historical print build an image of one person. In the spatial work, possessions, architecture, sound, scent, and the viewer’s reflection divide that work among themselves. Johnson’s movement from photography into multiple media forms a continuous expansion: Black self-image is no longer assigned to a single face but extended to the objects and institutions through which a life is made.

Museum collections including SFMOMA hold the early photographs and later mixed-media works as parts of the same artistic development. The Guggenheim’s 2025 retrospective likewise traced Black self-image, domestic materials, anxiety, and escape across photography, sculpture, film, and painting.*17

This retrospective reception allows Johnson’s move from photography into three-dimensional work to be read as a widening of the elements that make a portrait—from the face to objects, architecture, and the viewer’s experience—rather than as a break between media.*13

renger.html.lead_html: Renger-Patzsch made the photographed object itself central, rejecting both pictorialist beautification and Bauhaus-style visual experiment in favor of precise structural description.
renger.html.thesis_html: From a position distinct from both Pictorialist beautification and Bauhaus visual experiment, Renger-Patzsch observed the structure of things themselves with precision and pulled the subject of photography back to the matter-of-fact form of the object. His approach became central to New Objectivity photography and proposed a way of describing the world objectively.

sections.title: Biography
sections.body_html: Albert Renger-Patzsch was born in 1897 in Wurzburg and learned photography early through his father*1. After serving in the First World War, he worked in the early 1920s above all on plant photography and images made for printed publications, then gradually widened his field to industrial products, machine parts, and architectural detail*2. In 1928 he published Die Welt ist schon (The World Is Beautiful), a photobook that was quickly received as a defining statement of New Objectivity photography*3. In 1929 he moved to Essen, where he maintained a studio and office at Museum Folkwang while photographing mines, steelworks, and limestone landscapes across the Ruhr over long periods*4. After losing much of his early archive in wartime bombing in 1944, he shifted his base to the Wamel / Mohnesee area, continued photographing the Ruhr industrial region and trees after the war, and died in Wamel in 1966*5.

sections.title: New Objectivity and Neues Sehen: The Photography of Things
sections.body_html:
Neither pictorialism nor the Bauhaus, but a third path

In 1920s Germany, photography was being pulled toward two dominant directions. One was the lingering pictorialist tradition, which used soft focus and artisanal print processes to align photography with the established language of fine art*1. The other was the Bauhaus and the New Vision, where steep angles, aerial views, montage, and optical experiment treated photography as a medium for reorganizing perception itself*6. Renger-Patzsch chose neither route. He rejected pictorialist embellishment and also kept his distance from the dramatic perceptual shocks associated with figures such as Laszlo Moholy-Nagy and Aleksandr Rodchenko. Instead, he committed himself to rendering the form, surface, repetition, and material texture of things with maximum technical clarity*2.

The World Is Beautiful and the parallel display of things

Die Welt ist schon, published in 1928, assembled one hundred photographs of factory chimneys, railway bridges, plant structures, ceramic reflections, cast-metal tools, and other subjects. What unifies the book is not romantic atmosphere but a single insistence that things already possess their own structural beauty, and that photography can disclose it without beautifying it further*3. Plants, industrial objects, animals, architecture, and human figures are deliberately interwoven so that natural and manufactured forms can be compared across the book as a visual table of correspondences*10. Renger-Patzsch is said to have preferred the plain title Things, while the publisher chose Die Welt ist schon for commercial reasons, which makes the point even clearer: his interest lay less in lyrical world-view than in the factual presentation of things themselves*3. His experience with botanical close-ups carried directly into industrial subjects. Close proximity, even light, deep focus, fine tonal control, and stripped-down composition let surface grain, reflection, and repeating modules become the real subject of the image*2. The procedure does not simply make objects look beautiful; it pulls their latent order into the picture plane.

New Objectivity, editing, and the myth of neutrality

This approach developed alongside August Sander's typological archive of people and Karl Blossfeldt's enlarged studies of plants, and the three are repeatedly placed at the center of New Objectivity photography*11. Where Sander organized social types and Blossfeldt treated plants as formal morphologies, Renger-Patzsch applied the same cool scrutiny to industrial objects, everyday manufactured things, architecture, and natural detail*8. Yet this supposed objectivity was never a neutral recording of the world. Distance, angle, cropping, light, and tonal control all actively shape the object's formal legibility*10. The photographs look as if things reveal themselves, but that appearance is achieved through a series of decisions that isolate structure, regularize the frame, and suppress everything that would distract from material and form*10.

Toward the Bechers and the argument for a specifically photographic method

The pattern of judgment established here would later echo through the Bechers' typological documentation of industrial architecture and, further on, through Dusseldorf School and typological photography*11. German advertising photography, product catalogues, and architectural magazines of the late 1920s and 1930s also drew on this style, and when read alongside Germaine Krull's photographs of metal structures they show how a modern vocabulary for seeing industrial things was assembled across several practices at once*7*16. Shared devices included severe low angles, close-ups of mechanical parts, frontal views of factory facades, cropped views of trusses as abstract pattern, serial repetition, and attention to matte metallic surfaces*7. These methods took shape under very different political and theoretical commitments. Rodchenko treated radical camera angles as part of a revolutionary visual language of labor and machinery*14. Moholy-Nagy developed photography at the Bauhaus as a program for re-educating perception under the name of the New Vision*15. Krull moved between photojournalism and abstraction, especially in Metal, where bridges and cranes became dynamic constructions of line and repetition*16. Renger-Patzsch, by contrast, remained more narrowly committed to the exact presentation of structure*10. What later gets inherited is therefore not a single unified method but the proof that a stance of objectivity can become a compelling photographic practice. In that sense, he is less the sole origin of later typological work than an early and durable baseline to which later photographers kept returning*11. The posthumous translation and publication of his writings in The Absolute Realist also made it easier to read his photographs together with his theoretical insistence that photography should not imitate painting but discover its own proper way of presenting the structure of things*9*10.

sections.title: Criticism and reception
sections.body_html: The decisive contemporary criticism remains Walter Benjamin's objection in A Short History of Photography. Benjamin suggested that the very attitude summarized by The World Is Beautiful risked absorbing historical contradiction into aesthetic order, turning structural beauty into a way of not seeing the social conditions around it*4. That criticism has remained central because it challenges not only Renger-Patzsch but the political limits of New Objectivity itself*11. Postwar museum reception, meanwhile, has been sustained by major holdings at Museum Folkwang, the Pinakothek der Moderne, Tate, MoMA, the National Gallery of Art, George Eastman Museum, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art*7*8*12*13. With the Getty Research Institute's archival work and the English publication of his writings, Renger-Patzsch is now read both through the history of works and through the history of ideas, as one of the key starting points for arguments about photographic objectivity in modern art*9*10.

ricarda-roggan.html.lead_html: Ricarda Roggan seeks out disused furniture, cars, machines, and empty rooms, alters the physical setting, and photographs it with a large-format analog camera. Her use of photography grew from an interest in literature and space and developed through works such as Garage, Attika, Apokryphen, and 1971. Although the objects and places are real, her images make it difficult to separate what she found from what she constructed, bringing documentation and staging into the same photograph.
ricarda-roggan.html.thesis_html: Staged photography has often approached the boundary between fiction and reality through reenacted events or constructed models. Roggan begins instead with rooms and objects that already exist and have already been used. She removes dust, moves furniture, and at times rebuilds floors or walls, yet the final result still resembles a precise documentary photograph.She does not exhibit the altered rooms or objects themselves; what remains is a single photograph. The photograph alone does not reveal where discovery ends and staging begins. By shaping reality before photographing it, Roggan made documentation and mise-en-scène part of the same pictorial problem.

sections.title: Background and Period
sections.body_html:
From Literature and Space to Photography: Building a Room for a Single Image

Ricarda Roggan was born in Dresden. From 1996 she studied photography with Timm Rautert at the Academy of Fine Arts Leipzig, receiving her diploma in 2002 and completing her Meisterschüler studies in 2004. She also studied at the Royal College of Art in London from 2003 to 2005, establishing the basis of her work in the late 1990s and early 2000s.*1

In Roggan’s account, her path to photography began with literature and space, not with a fascination for cameras. As a child she was drawn to literature and enjoyed making rooms and thinking about spaces; photography initially served as a practical tool for those interests. She gradually recognized photography’s particular ability to fix the relationship between space and objects in a single image. In a 2021 conversation, she explained that once she reached a territory language could no longer fully describe, this process of turning a dialogue with objects into an image could, for her, happen only through photography.*24 This helps explain why, in her work, “making the room” comes before taking the photograph: altering the set or space prepares it for the way it will appear on the photographic plane.

Kino, 1994–99: Photographing the Movie Screen as Another Reality

The early series Kino, made from 1994 to 1999, used high-speed 35mm film to photograph screens showing American movies in cinemas, then grouped the images into categories such as landscapes, cars, roads, disasters, and hotels. Spector Books situates the project within a pre-digital desire for the analog images produced by the movie theater.*9 Roggan has also spoken about working as a projectionist; those memories later led to APPARATE, a series centered on projection equipment.*2 Before her later photographs of furniture and abandoned interiors, Kino was already treating reality and “reality that has already become an image” as part of the same photographic question.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Seeking Objects After Use and Slowing Down Their Time

Roggan repeatedly turns to chairs, tables, beds, damaged cars, projectors, game machines, and empty rooms that have outlived their original function. She has described being drawn to objects that remain after losing their practical value.*2 In a 2021 interview, she recalled that decades of use seemed to settle into the tears, corners, and surfaces of old furniture, and that she felt a need to preserve those objects once more as images before they were discarded.*24 Old objects matter in her work because their surfaces retain the time of human use at the moment when that use is about to end. The Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation similarly describes her as a “photo-archaeologist” in search of traces, emphasizing her search for abandoned buildings and furniture and the strict procedures she uses to reduce chance.*3 The Zabludowicz Collection connects her early furniture photographs to the material culture and memory of the former East Germany.*15

8×10 Analog: Using a Slow Process to Decide Before Exposure

Roggan says she continues to use an 8×10-inch analog view camera because it lets her define a portion of reality with particular clarity and because the process is slow and labor-intensive.*2 In another conversation, she noted that seeing a smartphone snapshot too early can determine the image too quickly and weaken the process of constructing the space mentally. With a large-format camera, she instead values the time spent thinking of the space in three dimensions, waiting, and searching for an image that is not yet visible.*24 Large-format photography requires decisions about camera position, light, the placement of objects, and even small traces in the background before exposure. The essay “Von den Dingen,” published on Roggan’s website, emphasizes that she works directly on reality before the photograph is made, preparing the final image instead of substantially remaking the negative afterward.*20 For Roggan, the slowness of large-format photography provides time to observe a space in three dimensions, decide where objects and the camera should be placed, and organize physical reality into a single image before exposure.*24

Stuhl, Tisch und Bett and Schacht: Rebuilding the Room Before Photographing It

In her early furniture works, Roggan removed discarded chairs, tables, and beds from the places where she found them and repositioned them in sparse photographic settings. KW Institute for Contemporary Art notes that the objects can appear naturally placed at first glance, while the precision of the image reveals the staging; small interventions in the physical space detach them from their former meanings and uses.*4 In Schacht and Attika, the interventions extend to the entire room. A 2008 Frieze review notes that the floor in Schacht was recast, windows and doors were sealed with plasterboard, and the spaces in Attika were thoroughly cleaned, challenging a simple reading of the work as photographs of East German ruins.*8 FOTOHOF’s book Schacht/Attika/Stall likewise connects the nearly empty interiors and the detail of Roggan’s large-format photographs with memories of a disappearing East Germany.*12

Garage, Baumstücke, and RESET: Applying the Same Rules to Cars, Forests, and Machines

Roggan applies the same process beyond interiors. In Garage, wrecked cars are placed in strongly frontal settings, making their damaged bodies resemble either advertising photographs or specimens. Galerie EIGEN + ART publishes images from Garage, Baumstück, SET, RESET, and other series, showing how Roggan continues to isolate her subjects, reduce their backgrounds, and create images that invite close scrutiny of detail even as the subjects change.*6 “Von den Dingen” records that Roggan prunes branches and leaves when photographing forests and removes stickers and cleans surfaces in RESET, demonstrating that she does not preserve things exactly as she finds them.*20 Sammlung Philara’s exhibition Ex Machina brought together such obsolete machines and devices, detached from their functions and presented as a kind of typology within carefully arranged spaces.*16

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
SET / RESET: Reducing Obsolete Machines to the Photographic Plane

In SET / RESET, disused game machines and other equipment appear without the noise or users that once surrounded them, reduced to combinations of rectangles, apertures, screens, and fields of color. The book SET RESET EXITS SEDIMENTS brings together several series made around 2008–11, including work photographed in Cyprus, and sequences them around the time embedded in spaces and objects.*7 The sequencing of the book is central. It places similarly quiet, structured images in succession, allowing objects that have lost their function to enter a different visual order without explaining the provenance of each one.

Apokryphen: Separating Personal Effects from Their Owners’ Stories

Apokryphen is a series of small gelatin silver prints depicting personal effects and relics associated with figures including Bach, Beethoven, Heidegger, Schnitzler, and Bloch under closely comparable conditions. The artist’s website lists works from 2013–15 and the specific objects they depict, including shells, eyeglasses, pocket watches, and hearing aids.*11 In 2016, PIN. Freunde der Pinakothek der Moderne acquired five works from the series and described Roggan’s method of removing commemorative objects associated with well-known figures from their original display contexts and placing them in a uniform, neutral setting.*19 Spector Books published Apokryphen as a standalone volume devoted to the series.*10 By leaving fingerprints, wear, and unusual forms visible instead of illustrating the owners’ biographies, the series creates a gap between knowing whose object it was and seeing what it looks like in the photograph.

1971: Restaging Timm Rautert’s Photograph Fifty Years Later

Presented in the 2022 MdbK Leipzig exhibition, 1971 (2021) reconstructs, roughly fifty years later in a former Leipzig spinning mill, Timm Rautert’s 1971 photograph of Walter De Maria’s New York studio. MdbK surveyed Roggan’s process of finding, transforming, and restaging places and objects before photographing them on analog film, placing this series between her earlier work and new production.*5 Here, Rautert’s 1971 photograph becomes the reference for a restaging that is itself photographed again. The earlier photograph and the present-day space move back and forth within a single process of reconstruction and image-making.*5

Offerte: Advertising Scale Without a Product Name

Offerte, made in 2016, enlarges photographs of two hands holding everyday objects; in 2021 the images were shown on outdoor billboards in Bremerhaven. Kunsthalle/Kunstmuseum Bremerhaven identifies the project’s central device as using the scale of advertising while withholding prices, product names, and promotional copy.*14 When Roggan’s method of isolating small objects against nearly blank backgrounds is transferred to the scale of urban advertising, viewers instinctively look for what is being sold and receive no answer. The isolation created during photography and the choice of display medium produce the same uncertainty.

sections.title: Criticism, Reception, and Connections to Other Photography
sections.body_html:
Rautert, Demand, and Wall: Comparing Documentation and Staging

Roggan studied with Timm Rautert, who had trained under Otto Steinert and worked both in social documentary and in Bildanalytische Fotografie (“image-analytical photography”), an inquiry into the mechanisms of photography itself. Rautert taught at the Academy of Fine Arts Leipzig from 1993 to 2008. Museum Folkwang lists Roggan among his students alongside Viktoria Binschtok and Tobias Zielony.*23 The Zabludowicz Collection exhibition Recent Photography from Leipzig likewise brought together HGB graduates including Roggan, Binschtok, and Falk Haberkorn, describing their shared ground in careful objectivity, conceptual rigor, and sustained questioning of the photographic medium.*22

Martin Hochleitner discusses Roggan’s spaces in relation to staged photography and distinguishes them from the “model worlds” of artists such as Thomas Demand: in Roggan’s photographs, an existing place and a constructed state remain present at the same time.*21 The same essay refers to Jeff Wall’s “near documentary.” Roggan takes a different route, reducing traces of events in existing objects and places and arranging them into quiet images.*21 Her staging can therefore be understood as a way of testing how far a real object or place can be transformed within a photograph while remaining materially itself.

East German Ruins and the Role of Staging in the Documentary Look

Roggan’s early work has often been discussed in relation to memories of East Germany because of her birthplace and the locations she photographed. The Zabludowicz Collection reads furniture and empty rooms as carriers of social memory, while FOTOHOF places the disappearance of East Germany among the work’s important backgrounds.*15 A 2008 Frieze review cautioned that limiting the work to a romanticism of ruins overlooks Roggan’s process of rebuilding floors, sealing walls, and moving objects.*8 Reading the early work solely as a record of a vanished East Germany leaves out a crucial part of how the images are made.The Zabludowicz Collection also notes that in Leipzig, in the former East Germany, inexpensive post-industrial spaces existed alongside active art schools and galleries, providing an important environment for younger photographers*22. This does not reduce Roggan’s subjects to urban history, but it helps clarify the working environment in which HGB’s photographic education existed in close proximity to former industrial spaces. Because Roggan photographs real objects that carry historical traces only after reducing or rearranging those traces, documentation and staging remain visible in the same image.

Suspending the Time of Objects: Critical Readings of an Afterlife

In Roggan’s work, objects separated from their original locations or owners do not lose their histories completely. Writing on Apokryphen, Hubertus von Amelunxen argues that photography temporarily detaches an object from the time of its setting, allowing its history of use and its present appearance to be considered together. Drawing on Rilke, Heidegger, George Kubler, and Walter Benjamin, he reads Roggan’s objects as things in which past events seem to have stopped yet continue to appear in the present.*25 This is a critic’s interpretation, not Roggan’s own philosophical declaration, but it offers one way to understand why she repeatedly photographs real objects that have lost a function or an owner instead of new ones.In Apokryphen, knowing an owner’s name and looking at wear, shape, and material in a small photograph happen simultaneously. The series depends on the fact that an object’s provenance never fully coincides with the surface presented by the photograph.

Japanese reception has likewise emphasized this act of looking at objects again.In 2005, Roggan participated in German Contemporary Photography at the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, where her work was presented within German photography shaped by social change after reunification and the development of digital technology.*18 In an essay published by ANDO GALLERY, Futoshi Hoshino emphasizes Roggan’s active interventions over objective classification and reads the photographs as giving objects that have lost their function another “afterlife.”*17 Set against Roggan’s working process, this interpretation suggests that cleaning and repositioning create a degree of distance from an object’s former use and establish the conditions for seeing it again in a photograph.

From APPARATE to REVISION: Continuities Revealed by Retrospective Exhibitions

Since 2013, Roggan has taught photography at the State Academy of Fine Arts Stuttgart, while her subjects have expanded from interiors to machines, cinema, and reenactment.*1 A 2022 exhibition at the Leonhardi Museum brought together ATTIKA, BAUMSTÜCKE, APOKRYPHEN, the newer REVISION, and moving-image work, surveying her production since 2005.*13 Across these changing subjects, the procedure persists: Roggan seeks objects and places that have lost their use or context, intervenes in physical reality, and fixes the result in analog photographs. The work repeatedly tests whether a photograph can still look like a record after the photographer has altered something that already carries a history.
