sections.title: Background and Formation
sections.body_html:
From Earthworks to Photography

At college, Soth initially concentrated on temporary outdoor sculpture influenced by Richard Long, Hamish Fulton, and Andy Goldsworthy. He used a camera to document walking and interventions in the landscape, and later recalled that his interest gradually shifted from making objects in a studio to moving through the world and responding to what he encountered.*1 In another interview, he recalled entering Sarah Lawrence College intending to become a painter and graduating in 1992 as a photographer.*27 Photography allowed Soth to preserve the acts of moving, searching, and encountering the unexpected as part of the work itself.

Photography also became a means of making contact with other people. Soth has described himself as intensely shy since childhood. Early on he was drawn to earthworks that allowed him to avoid people, but after encountering the portraits of Diane Arbus and Peter Hujar, he made approaching strangers itself a photographic task.*1 Perfect Strangers was an early series in which he turned that difficulty into a concrete procedure by approaching and photographing people he did not know in parks. He later described the car as a “safety bubble” that protected him from the outside world, and recognized a similar quality in photography: it connects him to the world while preserving a degree of distance.*4 His description of photography as a medium that “stops time,” and of the lens as a separation that remains between photographer and subject, belongs to the same awareness of distance.*34

In an interview first published in IMA 2019 Winter and posted online in 2020, Soth also said that as a young artist he chose photography over painting partly because he felt he could reach his own “voice” comparatively quickly through the medium.*47 In the same interview, he described photographing as an excuse to go out, meet people, and experience nature and places.*47 Photography let Soth approach other people while retaining the freedom to travel alone and the separation created by the lens. Those three conditions became fundamental to his later road projects and portraiture.

Learning Through Photobooks

Soth’s understanding of photography was shaped by reading photobooks before he had regular access to exhibitions. He has explained that he learned photography before the internet in a place with few exhibitions, so books became his primary way of seeing photographs. From the beginning, he also treated the photobook as an essential form for presenting his own work.*31 In Aperture, he recalled finding a sense of “romantic loneliness” in Robert Adams’s Summer Nights when he was young, and compared photographic history to a vocabulary and the influence of individual photographers to dialects.*2 In an interview with Canon, he identifies Masahisa Fukase’s The Solitude of Ravens as an important photobook that combines elements of the road with a strong emotional register.*26 Before becoming an established photographer, Soth had already learned to think of photography as a language in which mood and meaning accumulate across multiple images in a book while each photograph retains its own specificity.

At Sarah Lawrence College, he studied with Joel Sternfeld, whom he later described as a “very influential teacher.”*27 Jeu de Paume notes that during his studies from 1989 to 1991, he developed a deeper interest in 1970s American photography and New Topographics.*55 Soth has also said that after graduation he continued trying to establish a difference from Sternfeld, eventually acknowledging that influence while developing his own method.*12 Two lessons came together in his later work: thinking through photographs by arranging them in sequence, learned from photobooks, and seeing by moving through places, learned from American photography.

sections.title: The Core of Soth’s Work
sections.body_html:
Why Narrative?

Soth has said that storytelling does not come naturally to him, yet he has repeatedly been drawn to the narrative force of film and the novel. At the same time, he regards photography as poorly equipped to narrate what happens before and after an event, or to establish causality in continuous form.*48 In a conversation with Aperture, he said that he prefers to approach narrative indirectly through photographs and photobooks.*41

In The Brooklyn Rail, Soth identified “longing”—a desire for some other state—as a recurring term across his work. He associated Sleeping by the Mississippi with movement and freedom, NIAGARA with love and romance, Broken Manual with escape, and Songbook with the desire for community and social connection.*27 These subjects have no single factual form that a photograph can simply record. MoMA’s Quentin Bajac cites Soth describing how he photographs real places without treating them as objective topography; through photographing, he constructs a place and thinks of it as something closer to a novel.*30 For Soth, narrative became a structure through which desires and losses that cannot be contained in a single photograph recur across separate people, rooms, objects, and landscapes. The sequence leaves the life of the person photographed unexplained.

Road Trips and Shooting Lists

The road functions as a working procedure for gathering otherwise unrelated fragments. Rebecca Bengal compares Robert Frank’s list of subjects in his Guggenheim application with Soth’s habit of taping shooting lists to his steering wheel, locating both within an American road-photography tradition in which departures from the planned route generate other narratives.*53 Soth’s lists mix practical subjects such as “motels” and “wedding chapels” with associative or difficult-to-realize prompts. The lists set a direction in which unexpected subjects and people might be encountered; completing every item is beside the point.*5 In an interview with IMA, Soth likewise describes this as a “half-conceptual” method: he begins with a flexible concept and keywords, then changes the plan when reality offers more than he anticipated.*47

In Aperture, Soth acknowledges the road trip as a familiar, even clichéd form, yet explains that he keeps returning to it because it functions as a process of making and because a line with a direction of travel can suggest narrative.*52 Magnum, drawing on Soth’s own analogy, describes his search as something like surfing the web in the physical world.*23 The road gives the act of photographing a temporal order: one place leads to the next, and people and places unknown to one another can later be gathered into a single photobook. For Soth, the road is both an emblematic American subject and a method for producing a succession of chance encounters.

The 8×10 Camera and the Encounter

If the road keeps him moving toward the next place, the 8×10-inch view camera stops that movement in front of a single person. Soth has said that he values the camera for the way three-dimensional space becomes a flat image on the ground glass, and for the fact that photographers such as Nicholas Nixon, Sally Mann, and Stephen Shore have produced very different pictures with the same tool.*4 In an interview with 1854 Photography, he explained that he first approaches a person without the camera, then brings out the large-format camera and continues the conversation while working under the dark cloth and making the photograph slowly.*38 The Smithsonian Institution’s National Portrait Gallery similarly notes that the time required to prepare an 8×10 camera can produce a strong relationship between photographer and sitter.*37

The 8×10 records fine detail, but it also interrupts the motion of the road and creates time spent in the same place with a stranger. The resulting frame retains clothing, walls, gardens, furniture, and possessions alongside facial expression. A study in PÓS places Sleeping by the Mississippi between the immediacy of snapshot or photojournalistic photography and a more emotionally restrained, deadpan formalism.*28 A single portrait therefore becomes a field of details that can enter into relationships with beds, rooms, objects, or other people on later pages, leaving personality open rather than fixed.

Photobook Sequencing

For Soth, the book is a working space in which relationships between images are made. In an international questionnaire on the photobook, he describes laying out large numbers of small prints, moving them around like a card game, and making dummies to test the actual movement from page to page.*31 SFMOMA notes that Frank spent a year selecting and sequencing photographs for The Americans through themes, forms, emotions, and verbal associations. In this tradition of road photography, editing is one of the processes through which travel becomes a work.*42 The National Gallery of Art likewise identifies the post-Frank photobook as a major form for conveying a photographer’s own experience of the world, beyond the idea of an objective record.*36

Soth compares photographic sequencing to a game of connecting the dots. If the points are too close, the relationship becomes obvious; if they are too far apart, coherence disappears. His aim is to create an interval that viewers can complete for themselves.*47 In The Photographic Journal, he similarly describes his work as closer to poetry than to a story with a plot, calling the photobook a “semi-narrative structure.”*48 Alfredo Brant’s peer-reviewed study of NIAGARA analyzes this process through the concepts of storyworld and worldmaking. Brant argues that the arrangement of different photographs creates possible temporal and causal relations, allowing viewers to connect fragments and construct a narrative world.*29

Discussing a new edition of Sleeping by the Mississippi, Soth has said that adding a single photograph, turning an image into a spread, or even changing the color of the endpapers can alter the feel of the entire book.*46 By placing an empty bed, a river, or another person after a portrait, Soth can let “loneliness” recur throughout the book without assigning it to one individual’s psychology. The sequence can also leave unresolved who wrote a letter, what a person is thinking, or what happens next. Editing becomes a way to create an emotional continuity across several photographs without fixing real people within a single plot.

Documentary and Narrative

Soth’s people and rooms are real, and the encounters at the time of photographing are concrete experiences. Yet the currents of loneliness or love that emerge once the pictures are sequenced do not correspond to a verified order of events. In a GQ interview about Songbook, Soth explained that he removed much of the text and news context from the earlier Dispatch material to make a more lyrical and open-ended book.*49 Fraenkel Gallery also describes Songbook as a work that removes precise explanations of events and addresses community and isolation through lyrical flow more than logical exposition.*17

Soth’s storytelling can move in the opposite direction from using text to fill what photography cannot narrate. In an interview with Phaidon, he described photography as a fragmentary medium closer to poetry than the novel. For Songbook, he said that even when a compelling true story lay behind an image, he tried to forget it and ask whether the photograph itself retained mystery and contributed to the feeling of the book as a whole.*50 The process has three distinct stages: gathering different fragments on the road, spending time on a single encounter with the 8×10, and arranging photographs in a book without overloading them with factual explanation. This allows records of real encounters and imagined connections between photographs to coexist within the same work.

sections.title: Major Works and Publishing
sections.body_html:
Sleeping by the Mississippi

Made between 1999 and 2002, Sleeping by the Mississippi began without the aim of producing a continuous topography of the Mississippi River. In the official series, people, houses, beds, cemeteries, religious signs, and riverside landscapes alternate, and many photographs do not show the river at all.*6 Soth later explained that he was interested in the dreams and imaginations of people he met along the river, and that the work was never conceived as austere documentary photography.*7 In SFMOMA’s Charles, Vasa, MN, 2002, a man holding a model airplane appears together with snow, a house, and objects in the yard; the photograph does not reduce its meaning to the sitter’s eccentricity.*8

Critic Rick Poynor argues that the photobook is inherently sequential, and that this book moves among people, unoccupied interiors, and landscapes to create a world through the tension between presence and absence.*39 Beds, chairs, photographs within photographs, and religious signs recur throughout the book. The Mississippi therefore functions as a guide that places distant fragments within the same current. Rebecca Bengal similarly writes that the subjects on Soth’s lists seldom become the work exactly as written; just as the river gives him a reason to travel alongside it, movement produces other discoveries.*53 Taken together with Soth’s comments on editing later editions, the book’s structure tests how far geographically separate people and places can be placed within a shared emotional current.*46

NIAGARA

NIAGARA (2006) combines the tourist spectacle of the falls with honeymoon motels, portraits of couples, nude figures, vacant rooms, and handwritten love letters, bringing ideals of romance and their breakdown into the same geography.*10 Soth has recalled that on his first visit, the aging motels and economic deterioration on the American side made a stronger impression than the romantic image he had associated with Niagara.*9 Writing in The New Yorker, Vince Aletti described Niagara as both a geographical place and a psychological state, and argued that the letters add an emotional layer to Soth’s restrained documentary photographs.*32

Love letters play a particular role in the book’s narrative construction. Brant notes that the letters remain unmatched to specific portrait subjects. As viewers move among people, rooms, the falls, and fragments of writing, they can provisionally construct several possible relationships.*29 The book never explains that a particular couple separated in a particular way. Letters whose authors remain unidentified sit beside different people and empty rooms, allowing love, separation, and fantasies of marriage to recur across the book instead of belonging to one biography. Editing is central for Soth because it lets the theme of romance disperse across several photographs without fixing real people inside a single storyline.

Broken Manual

Broken Manual (2010) follows monks, hermits, survivalists, underground bunkers, and cabins in the woods, tracing the desire to disappear from society. The project began in the American South through a commission from the High Museum and expanded from an interest in fugitives and monastic life toward men who had withdrawn from society.*11 The published work includes photographs alongside a manual-like format containing texts by the fictional writer Lester B. Morrison, placing an explicitly fictional voice outside the photographs.*13 Soth has described the project as holding together two things: the desire to escape and the recognition that complete withdrawal from society is impossible.*12

In The New Yorker, Aletti observed that some photographs have a coolness reminiscent of surveillance records or mug shots, while other portraits convey empathy.*33 In Sleeping by the Mississippi and NIAGARA, gaps between photographs leave room for narrative. Broken Manual deliberately intensifies that narrative apparatus by introducing a fictional narrator and text. Yet the book never becomes a practical guide to “how to escape.” The more it searches for ways to hide, the more Soth’s own desire to disappear is placed beside the actual lives of the people he photographs. In retrospect, given that Songbook removes specific true stories and I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating weakens the larger narrative structure, Broken Manual can be seen as the work in which Soth brings the machinery of narrative most visibly to the foreground, including a fictional voice.

Little Brown Mushroom

Founded in 2008, Little Brown Mushroom (LBM) extended the photobook beyond a means of distributing finished work into a place for testing forms of narrative. Soth’s official biography describes LBM as a publishing and multimedia enterprise.*24 LBM itself describes its purpose as an experiment in “visual storytelling,” and has developed publishing and educational projects with writers and designers as well as photographers.*51 Magnum’s profile likewise presents Soth’s work as spanning photobooks, independent publishing, commissions, and his work with the agency.*23

LBM experimented with combinations of photography and writing, newspapers, children’s books, and slideshows, testing forms that could carry narrative while preserving gaps in photographic meaning. In Phaidon, Soth described LBM as a place to experiment with the relationship between photography and storytelling.*50 The approach Soth describes in Aperture—selecting and discarding photographs, building dummies, and thinking through the final physical form of the book—also appears in LBM as an activity in which making, editing, and publishing remain connected.*41

Songbook

In Songbook (2015), Soth’s method of creating narrative shifts from adding information to removing specific true stories. MACK describes the book as a reediting of black-and-white photographs made between 2012 and 2014 for The LBM Dispatch and magazine assignments, detached from their original news contexts.*14 In Dispatch, Brad Zellar’s writing and Soth’s photographs conveyed specific places and events. In the photobook, Soth removed much of that background information and gave priority to the rhythm between photographs.*15 Dances, school events, bars, gatherings, and family occasions appear in the official series. Detached from a report on particular communities, they become a sequence in which gathering and isolation alternate.*16

In GQ, Soth explained that he wanted to remove words and news context and make the photographic sequence more intuitive and non-narrative.*49 In Phaidon, he cites Sherwood Anderson’s Winesburg, Ohio as an important reference and describes his attraction to the sense of a place suspended between the real and the fictional.*50 Fraenkel Gallery similarly describes the series as removing specific information and addressing the longing for American community through lyricism more than logic.*17 By removing true stories gathered during reporting, the events in individual photographs become harder to fix, while separate images acquire new relationships within the book. Songbook makes especially clear that, for Soth, creating narrative is not the same as explaining events.

I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating

I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating (2019) questions the large-scale series structures that had become one of Soth’s established methods. The official series consists of people and interiors photographed around the world, without first imposing a geographical subject such as the Mississippi or Niagara, or a category such as “fugitives.”*19 Foam describes the series as narrowing its attention to people, private rooms, windows, and possessions, returning the work to the act of looking at another person itself.*43 In an interview with The Guardian, Soth also said that bookshelves and details within a room can speak about a person, allowing a still life to function as a portrait.*44

The series centers on the power involved in photographing and editing people as material for a larger theme; the move from outdoor subjects to interiors is one consequence of that concern. In IMA, Soth described an ethical discomfort with the photographer’s control over the instant of exposure, the selection of images, and their presentation in exhibitions or books—and with the use of another person as an element within the photographer’s work.*47 In Musée Magazine, he also discussed his discomfort with portraiture becoming a professional routine and the need to think of photographing again as an exchange between people.*45 Soth stays with one person and one room for an extended period, without subsuming the sitter into a larger subject such as the Mississippi River or “fugitives.” Faces and possessions are rendered in detail, but no storyline converts those details directly into an explanation of inner life. The series reexamines Soth’s long-standing use of storytelling through the question of how far another person can be incorporated into the photographer’s own narrative.

A Pound of Pictures

A Pound of Pictures (2022) returns to driving across the United States while making photographing, collecting, and preserving pictures its subject. MACK describes the book as combining photographs made from 2018 to 2021 with vernacular photographs inserted randomly into each copy, addressing photography’s desire to preserve experience as images.*20 The official series includes darkrooms, boxes of old photographs, camera clubs, graves, people, and tourist sites, placing the making of new photographs and the keeping of existing ones along the same road.*21

Soth has explained that the project initially followed the route of Abraham Lincoln’s funeral train. The work stalled when he tried to make the photographs conform to that clear idea, and only moved toward its final form after he abandoned the plan.*4 In an Aperture conversation with Siri Hustvedt, Soth calls the book the ultimate form for his work while cautioning against dependence on a single narrative. He describes the road as a line that does not provide a story directly but can “suggest” one.*52 Associations among flowers, old photographs, graves, cars, Lincoln, and Walt Whitman never converge into one plot. Photographing, collecting, and keeping recur throughout the book, making photography’s attempt to preserve experience and memory the subject itself.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Walker Evans and Literature

Walker Evans is a key precedent for understanding Soth’s approach to storytelling. David Campany emphasizes Evans’s editorial work in Fortune and elsewhere, where text and photograph do not simply explain one another; the gap between them leaves interpretation to the reader.*40 MoMA’s Bajac likewise invokes Evans’s “documentary style” when placing Soth within a lineage of contemporary photographers who use series to give meaning to otherwise isolated photographs.*30 What Soth took from Evans includes frontal composition and the use of signs, as well as an editorial attitude: recording the details of reality while allowing meaning to emerge from the arrangement of multiple photographs and texts, without closing it within one image or caption.

While making Songbook, Soth has said that he looked to Walker Evans and James Agee’s Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, along with books combining photographs and writing by Dorothea Lange and Paul Taylor, and by Margaret Bourke-White and Erskine Caldwell.*50 What ultimately interested him most was a form in which writing did not settle the meaning of a photograph, and image and text could retain separate voices while entering the same world. That interest continued in Little Brown Mushroom, where photographers, writers, and designers collaborated on books.

Robert Frank and Road Photography

In Robert Frank’s The Americans, the road and the edit transform travel records into the photographer’s own image of America. MoMA describes Frank, a Swiss-born photographer, traveling roughly 10,000 miles and using the mobility of a small handheld camera to register tensions of race, class, religion, and consumer culture in postwar America.*35 The National Gallery of Art argues that the book showed later generations how a photobook could inscribe the photographer’s own experience of the world, expanding the form beyond the expectation of objective description.*36 SFMOMA emphasizes that a year of selection and sequencing organized themes, forms, emotions, and verbal associations.*42

Bengal directly compares Frank’s proposed list of subjects with Soth’s lists, finding continuity in the way detours on the road generate narratives other than those initially planned.*53 Soth’s strongest identification with Frank was not with grainy black-and-white style, but with the presence of the photographer in images such as those looking out from hotel windows.*12 In his Canon interview, he likewise cites Frank as an important precedent for bringing feelings of love and longing into road photography.*26 Frank used a handheld camera to catch social fractures and gestures while moving. Soth stops the car, sets up a tripod, and spends time with a stranger, then relates that encounter to other people and places on the page. In Soth’s work, the subjectivity of the traveling photographer appears in both the encounter before the exposure and the sequencing that follows it.

Shore, Sternfeld, and Large-Format Color

The line from Stephen Shore and Joel Sternfeld to Soth involves more than the shared use of large-format color. Soth studied with Sternfeld and, after college, absorbed a large-format color approach associated with Shore and Sternfeld into his own road-based work.*27 Soth has described Shore as a photographer strongly concerned with composition and form, while locating himself closer to Robert Frank in the way outward-looking photographs can be directed toward inward desires.*47 In an Artdoc interview, he also speaks of wanting to add emotional content to the precise descriptive mode associated with New Topographics.*34

In Soth’s large-format photographs, wrinkles in a bedspread, photographs pinned to a wall, objects held by a sitter, and tools left in a yard are rendered with the same precision. The PÓS study places Sleeping by the Mississippi between immediacy and formalism because exact outward description and recurring emotional motifs coexist within the work.*28 The clarity of large-format photography that Soth learned from Shore and Sternfeld records the form of a place together with details that suggest the desires and dreams of the people who inhabit it. Those details acquire meaning through recurrence with objects and places elsewhere in the book, without claiming to explain a person’s psychology in a single image.

Arbus, Hujar, and Portraiture

Diane Arbus was both a precedent that gave Soth the courage to approach strangers and, later, a point of comparison for thinking about the risks of turning portrait subjects into narratives. Soth has referred to an “Arbus problem”: the possibility that a real person’s difference can be intensified for the sake of the photographer’s work until it obscures the person themselves.*12 In later years, Soth has referred more strongly to Peter Hujar, drawn to portraits that confront a sitter directly while reducing the sensational effect of spectacle.*12

The extended encounter produced by a large-format camera does not in itself resolve this ethical problem. As the National Portrait Gallery notes, the time required to prepare an 8×10 creates a kind of encounter distinct from the snapshot.*37 The PÓS study compares Charles, Vasa, MN with Arbus’s frontal portraiture while arguing that the meaning of “eccentricity” is not fixed by the portrait alone; it shifts according to surrounding objects, other photographs in the series, and the viewer’s judgment.*28 Within Soth’s sequences, preserving this uncertainty helps prevent a real person from being too firmly fixed into a predetermined role.

Larry Sultan and the Narrative Photobook

Larry Sultan’s Pictures from Home offers a precedent for Soth’s photobooks from a lineage outside road photography. In The Photographic Journal, Soth cites it as a major achievement of the narrative photobook.*48 According to MACK, Sultan spent a decade in the 1980s returning to his parents’ home, combining contemporary photographs, stills from home movies, conversations, his own writing, and memorabilia into a “narrative collage” in which the boundary between documentary and staging remains unstable.*54

In Pictures from Home, contemporary photographs, old family footage, conversations, and writing both supplement and contradict one another within the same book.*54 Soth uses letters in NIAGARA and fictional writing in Broken Manual, while Songbook removes true stories. Across these works he alternates between adding narrative information and reducing it so that relationships between photographs carry more of the meaning, adjusting how much fragmentariness remains from project to project.

Narrative and the Ethics of Portraiture

In Soth’s later work, a self-critical attitude emerges toward the very ability to create narratives between photographs. Fraenkel Gallery traces a movement from the open-ended long-term projects of his early career through Songbook to I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating, where attention narrows from the larger story of “America” to one-to-one encounters.*17 In an Aperture conversation, Soth acknowledges that viewers can project a degree of intimacy onto portraits that was not actually present, while also describing photography itself as a medium that produces distance.*52 The act of arranging photographs to create meaning overlaps with the act of incorporating real people into an author’s theme.

In the storyworld described by Brant, viewers supply relationships between photographs that the author leaves unresolved.*29 During the period of I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating, Soth himself expressed ethical discomfort with the photographer’s control over the shutter, selection, and presentation, and with treating a person as one element within a work.*45 In the later work, Soth loosens the strong thematic links between different people and spends more time with one person in one room. Here Soth continues to use storytelling while examining the point at which connecting photographs begins to determine the meaning of another person.

Reception and Historical Position

After Sleeping by the Mississippi was included in the 2004 Whitney Biennial, the Walker Art Center organized From Here to There: Alec Soth's America in 2010, the first major U.S. survey of his work, bringing together more than one hundred photographs made since 1994.*25 The Walker exhibition placed Soth’s research, chance encounters, large-format camera, and serial projects within a history of American road photography extending through Evans, Frank, Eggleston, and Shore.*3 The exhibition positioned Soth within the question of how forms developed in twentieth-century American photography were inherited and altered after 2000, beyond his reputation as a prominent photobook maker.*3

In Japan, the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura & Hayama presented Gathered Leaves in 2022, bringing together major series and reconfiguring work developed through photobooks within the exhibition space.*22 Tokyo Photographic Art Museum’s 2024–2025 exhibition A Room of Rooms traced the recurring motif of the interior from Soth’s early work through I Know How Furiously Your Heart Is Beating.*18 Soth’s place in photographic history rests on a method that begins from photography’s inability to fully narrate continuous time: he gathers fragments on the road, gives individual encounters time through the 8×10 camera, and creates relationships among distant fragments in the photobook. In later work, he also made the consequences of that narrativization—the extent to which it can determine the meaning of real people—a subject of his own work. Across successive projects, Soth has tested how much narrative photography can sustain and where its limits lie.

arata-dodo.html.title: Arata Dodo | Taigan and the Photobook as a Form of Travel | Photo Coordinates
arata-dodo.html.meta_description: Arata Dodo photographs places where people live, from rapidly changing Shanghai to the five countries bordering the Caspian Sea, Ulaanbaatar, and Kyoto. In books including Ways of Shanghai, Taigan, and White Map on the Silk Road, he records urban change, borders, religion, resource industries, and family life through photographs that keep people and their surroundings in the same frame. His travel photography treats each destination as an inhabited present and incorporates his own judgment about what needs to be seen now, without turning distant places into specimens of cultural difference.

arata-dodo.html.thesis_html: Dodo changed how travel photography could structure distant places. Working within the long tradition of the snapshot, he entered places unfamiliar to him, kept people and their surroundings within the same frame, and used photobook sequencing to compare photographs made across national borders. Ways of Shanghai records a city undergoing rapid change in the present tense. Taigan divides five countries into chapters while preserving recurring forms of everyday life that resist classification by nationality alone. The photobook preserves the distance between a traveling photographer and the places he encounters instead of turning those places into specimens of an “other culture.”

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Why Photography

Dodo studied photography at Osaka University of Arts, but he has described the starting point of his work as a desire to “see a world I do not know.” In a 2012 talk, he explained that, while thinking about how his work might differ from that of his photographer father, Shunji Dodo, he began looking toward “somewhere other than here” and making repeated trips to Shanghai, which he could reach by boat from Osaka’s Nanko port*19. As he repeatedly directed the camera toward unfamiliar environments, the question “What is happening in the world?” and his own position within it began to take form through the work*19.

Shanghai was changing quickly as older neighborhoods were demolished and replaced. Dodo has recalled that seeing buildings and ways of life that he felt could “only be seen now” made him newly conscious of photography’s capacity to record*3. In the same interview, he said that he did not want photographs to repeat what could already be explained in words; photography should carry scenes that cannot be fully accounted for verbally*3. Traveling to unfamiliar places and recording things caught in the midst of change became the link between travel and photography in his work.

Family and Photographic Education

Dodo’s father, Shunji Dodo, is also a photographer. Dream Boat, a three-person exhibition that also included his younger brother Takeshi Dodo, placed photographs made by the family across an extended span of time alongside one another.*8 Shunji Dodo is known for returning over long periods to places such as Osaka and the Kii Peninsula; Arata, by contrast, has moved through Shanghai, the Caspian coast, Mongolia, and Kyoto. In a text written around the three-person exhibition, Shunji likewise described photography as a way of leaving a record from within the course of a life.*18 Arata himself locates the beginning of his own work in his encounter with Shanghai and in the question of why he was taking photographs, rather than in photography as a family profession.*14

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
People and the City in the Same Frame

Ways of Shanghai repeatedly avoids extreme proximity to the face, keeping the body and the surrounding urban space together within the frame. In a text republished by AKAAKA with the later edition, Shomei Tomatsu noted that Dodo used few close-ups or medium shots and photographed Shanghai in full shots as though it were “his own city.”*4 At this distance, facial expression alone cannot stand in for cultural difference. Clothing, walls, signs, construction sites, and the width of roads enter the frame with the same visual weight as the people themselves.Ways of Shanghai earned Dodo the Photographic Society of Japan Newcomer’s Award in 2000.*7

Neighborhoods in Shanghai were being dismantled even while Dodo was photographing them, as the city was remade around him. He continued to work during a period in which old and new structures coexisted*3. Under those conditions, keeping people together with nearby shops, signs, roads, and construction sites recorded the changing environment more fully than isolating a symbolic person or building. Tomatsu’s emphasis on the full shot identifies this refusal to separate people from place as central to Dodo’s “way” of photographing Shanghai*4.

Travel as a Condition of Photography

Taigan was made while traveling through the five countries bordering the Caspian Sea: Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Iran. AKAAKA describes the work as a form of “witnessing” both the character of the land and the activities of the people who live there*1. Dodo has said that, alongside his desire to see unfamiliar countries beyond the Silk Road, he traveled far from home because of the question, “What is happening in the world?”*19. Travel became a working condition that removed him from familiar surroundings and required him to keep deciding, on location, what deserved to be photographed.

About a decade after Ways of Shanghai, while continuing to work in commercial photography, Dodo arrived at the question of “what should I make sure to see in the time I am living through?” and chose the Caspian Sea as one answer.*3 In Taigan, that question takes form in a sequence that places oil fields, roads, houses, religious dress, children at play, interiors, and night scenes alongside one another without organizing the work around the romance of travel.An exhibition at the Nikon Salon ran alongside the publication of the book, so Taigan was presented in both photobook and exhibition form.*10

Borders Within a Single Book

Taigan divides the five countries into separate chapters, yet gestures, clothing, roads, interiors, play, and rest recur within a shared photographic rhythm. AKAAKA links the title, meaning “opposite shore,” both to a geographical shore across the water and to the photographer’s own sense of distance. The chapters mark national borders, while the continuity of the pages preserves similarities in everyday life that are difficult to classify by country alone.*1 The book keeps national differences intact while placing recurring forms of daily life across those borders within a single sequence.

Connecting Places Through the Photobook

In Dodo’s work, the order in which photographs are placed matters as much as movement between locations. Taigan is a 176-page book organized by country across five chapters, with art direction by Bunpei Yorifuji*5. In a public conversation between Dodo and Yorifuji, the time accumulated in the book and the discoveries made through its construction became subjects in their own right*15. The photobook allows gestures, colors, and recurring forms of life from geographically distant places to connect across pages, holding national chapters and cross-border similarities in the same structure.

White Map on the Silk Road (2019) brought together work made at different times and in different regions, including Taigan, Ways of Shanghai, Ulaanbaatar, and Nara.*2 Case Publishing’s English text states that Dodo is not searching for an “elusive other,” but looking at the varied ways in which people organize their lives.*2 The book rearranges several journeys across the geographical divisions of earlier publications, allowing the identity of each series and recurring forms of life across them to appear at once. Genkosha’s account likewise records the relationship between the exhibition and the photobook across Shanghai, the Caspian Sea, and Ulaanbaatar.*9

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Ways of Shanghai

Ways of Shanghai, first published in 1999 and later reissued by AKAAKA, is a central early work.*4 Made amid Shanghai’s rapid redevelopment, the photographs repeatedly include people, construction, roads, shops, and interiors within a single frame. Dodo’s account of becoming more conscious of photography’s documentary capacity during this period frames the work as a record of the city while it was still changing. It preserves the density of a city in transition before that change could be organized retrospectively into a settled historical image.*3

Taigan

Taigan was published by AKAAKA in 2012 and received the 38th Kimura Ihei Award.*6 The photographs are organized by country, but as the pages accumulate, signs of political and religious difference intersect with shared activities such as eating, resting, family life, and play. Akiko Otake’s observation that a gaze searching for difference coexists with a sensation in which difference disappears is closely tied to the book’s editorial structure.*17 The National Research Institute for Cultural Properties, Tokyo, also records Dodo’s receipt of the 38th Kimura Ihei Award in 2013.*12

White Map

White Map on the Silk Road was published in conjunction with a 2019 exhibition at the Irie Taikichi Memorial Museum of Photography Nara City.*2 The 45-page publication rearranges different series made in Shanghai, around the Caspian Sea, in Ulaanbaatar, Nara, and elsewhere. Case Publishing describes local differences as appearing along a continuum, with everyday life in each place forming a many-sided world.*2 Where Taigan develops one region as a sustained series, White Map on the Silk Road makes the act of re-editing several earlier journeys across regions part of the work itself.

Kyoto and Film

Dodo also worked closer to home. In Oni ni mo Fuku ni mo: Mou Hitotsu no Kyoto, he photographed people, festivals, and daily life in Kyoto, focusing on layers of lived experience distinct from the city’s familiar image as a tourist destination.*13 AdverTimes. records that he photographed 26 municipalities across Kyoto Prefecture over parts of three years beginning in 2015.*11 Dodo worked as the still photographer on Naomi Kawase’s An, then served as director of photography for the first time on Hikari (2017) and again shot Vision (2018).*3 Across still photography and film, his work continues to depend on staying in a place long enough to register both human movement and the time unfolding around it.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Critical Responses to Taigan

Critical writing on Taigan has centered on the distance through which travel was translated into a photobook, rather than on the novelty of its locations. Dan Abbe distinguished Dodo’s work from travel photography that turns a destination into a stage for the photographer’s own fantasy, praising the way Dodo remains within the uncertainty of the journey itself*16. Akiko Otake argued that a gaze trying to identify the cultural signs of the five countries repeatedly reaches moments where those signs become impossible to distinguish within the photographic sequence*17. Kimi Himeno likewise explained that the book was edited as a work about distance between self and other, rather than as a straightforward travelogue*19. Together, these readings position Dodo’s travel photography as a record that preserves the distance between photographer and place instead of treating distant locations primarily as information to be delivered to the viewer.

Family Lineage and an Independent Direction

Arata Dodo is often introduced as the son of Shunji Dodo, and Dream Boat brought together photographs by father and brothers within a single exhibition.*8 Shunji’s best-known work is grounded in accumulated return to places such as Osaka and the Kii Peninsula. Arata moves from Shanghai to the Caspian Sea and Ulaanbaatar, recalibrating his distance each time the location changes. The family’s photographic culture remains an important background, while Arata’s own method was formed by his experience in Shanghai, the question of why he was photographing, and the travel series that followed.*14

Within Japanese Photobook Culture

Dodo’s major projects extend through the editing of the photobook, which functions as a unit of the work rather than as a secondary record of photographs already complete. Ways of Shanghai received the Photographic Society of Japan Newcomer’s Award, and Taigan received the Kimura Ihei Award.*6 For White Map on the Silk Road, Case Publishing rearranged several series within one volume, re-editing previously published work beyond its earlier regional groupings.*2 Editing photographs from different journeys into the time of a single book allows separate locations to function within one sustained work.

TOTEM POLE PHOTO WORKSHOP, directed by Shinya Arimoto, placed Dodo’s method within a tradition of travel snapshots “continuing for more than half a century,” making the question of how he formed his own work from this established method the subject of a public lecture.*20 Dodo’s contribution lies in bringing three elements into one sustained body of work: the distance that allows people and city to occupy the frame together, noted by Shomei Tomatsu in Ways of Shanghai; repeated movement across borders; and photobook editing that places different locations in relation to one another.*4

boris-mikhailov.html.lead_html: Boris Mikhailov is a Ukrainian photographer who has recorded Kharkiv from the Soviet period into the post-Soviet era through hand-coloring, double projection, rough snapshots, combinations of photographs and text, and staged bodies. Across Red, Yesterday’s Sandwich, Unfinished Dissertation, At Dusk, and Case History, he photographed forms of everyday life excluded from official imagery, rejected polished and “correct” photography, and mixed document with performance in ways that unsettled the ethics of documentary photography.
boris-mikhailov.html.thesis_html: In an environment where Soviet official photography circulated orderly images of health, labor, and public celebration, Mikhailov made work from failed everyday photographs, hand-coloring, double projection, private nudity, and handwritten text. After the collapse of the Soviet system, Case History included payment to homeless participants and incorporated posing and performance into the act of photographing. His work challenged the assumption that documentary photography shows facts by keeping the photographer’s intervention outside the frame. State-sanctioned images, the photographer’s decisions, and transactions with the people being photographed all became part of the work, making the construction of a social record inseparable from the record itself.

sections.title: Why Photography
sections.body_html:
The Factory Camera and a “Way Out”

Mikhailov worked as an electromechanical engineer and entered photography after being given a camera to document a state-run factory. He has described using the factory darkroom to develop private photographs as well, and losing his job in 1968 after the KGB discovered nude photographs of his wife, followed by interrogation and a search of his home*1.

The episode shaped Mikhailov’s understanding of photography as a personal means of escape. He later called photography his “way out,” explaining that it connected previously separate parts of his life—friendship, love, and everyday experience—and gave meaning to his own existence*1.

At the beginning of his work, a camera intended to document a factory for the state became a medium for private life and for preserving his own judgment. The Photographers’ Gallery likewise identifies the factory camera, his self-taught approach, and his dismissal over nude photographs as formative elements of his early work*2.

Censorship and the Kharkiv School of Photography

In the Soviet Union of the 1960s and 1970s, photographs of intoxicated people, naked bodies, failure, or poverty conflicted with the healthy, heroic image of society promoted by official photographic culture. Nadiia Bernard-Kovalchuk argues that photographers in Kharkiv in the early 1970s developed ways of deliberately intertwining documentation and subjectivity in response to the authoritative photographic discourse of the state*6.

Within the Kharkiv School of Photography, Yevgeniy Pavlov, Viktor Kochetov, and others also used hand-coloring, montage, and representations of the body to make images outside the norms of official photography. Igor Manko identifies Mikhailov’s idea of “bad photography for bad reality” as a crucial development, turning low-quality film and paper, blur, weak contrast, and scratches on film into forms of social criticism*7.

The Maison Européenne de la Photographie presents his more than fifty years of work as spanning documentary, conceptual art, painting, and performance, and describes an artist who unsettles established visual codes through changing techniques and formats.*3

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
“Bad Photography” as a Method

Mikhailov’s “bad photography” grew from the judgment that polished, technically accomplished photographs could not adequately convey the poverty and contradictions of Soviet everyday life. Cheap materials, narrow tonal range, blur, and scratches remained visible, producing a visual language at odds with the orderly social image of official photography.*7

Fotomuseum Winterthur calls him a “conceptual documentarist,” describing a body of work that moves between documentary photography and constructed images.*5 The Berlinische Galerie likewise describes his work since 1966 as a sustained intersection of conceptual methods and documentary photography.*4 From the beginning, documenting everyday life and finding forms that separated it from official idealization developed within the same body of work.

The question of the photographic “fact” also connects Mikhailov to the Soviet avant-garde of the 1920s, when Alexander Rodchenko and others sought to construct postrevolutionary facts through new angles and sequences. Writing on Unfinished Dissertation, Helen Petrovsky draws a line from the 1928 debates on photography, including Rodchenko, to Mikhailov, arguing that the conditions under which a photographic “fact” could be produced took a different form under late socialism*28.

Private Photographs and Official Images

Hand-coloring became a way to manipulate the social codes attached to photographs. Red places the red of flags, clothing, signs, and public celebrations in the same sequence as accidental reds found in private life. In May Day Parade, hand-coloring overlays the “compulsory masquerade” of public culture with the history of photographic alteration.*9

In Luriki, Mikhailov returned to the hand-colored family photographs he had produced as paid commissions. The series brings together the convention of ordinary people preserving respectable images of themselves and the semi-legal photographic retouching he undertook to earn a living, treating anonymous family pictures as a social portrait of Soviet life.*8

Yesterday’s Sandwich superimposes separate slides of streets, naked bodies, plants, food, and other subjects, forcing private life and public space—elements that cannot be resolved into a single coherent scene—into the same image.*10

Photographs and Text Side by Side

In Unfinished Dissertation, Mikhailov pasted everyday photographs onto the backs of discarded dissertation pages and added handwritten notes and quotations. He understood this combination as a new photographic object, not as a conventional “book layout.”*11

Michele Fabio Vangi describes the work as an “iconotext” in which private diary and photographic theory merge, emphasizing a relationship in which writing does not simply explain the photographs. Photographs, quotations, and private notes do not converge on a single conclusion; the pages preserve personal memory in an unfinished state.*12

Introducing Staging into the Document

Discussing the staging in Case History, Mikhailov has said that when he returned from Berlin to Kharkiv, conventional documentary photography could not express a society in which homelessness was rapidly increasing beneath the advertising surface of capitalism. He believed a “new method” was necessary.*14

He stated that “documentary cannot be truth” and asked real people to repeat gestures drawn from art history and everyday life. MoMA likewise notes that he paid the people he photographed and worked with them to construct poses recalling religious and history painting.*15

Through staging, prostitution, illness, unemployment, and social abandonment become sustained scenes instead of fleeting moments observed on the street. The photographer’s intervention remains part of the photographic situation. The series keeps the photographer visible as an active participant in the photographic encounter.*14

The Ethics of Case History

Writing on Case History, Frieze raised the possibility that contemporary art representing other people’s suffering could become “poornography,” asking where humanitarian concern ends and the pleasure of looking at misery begins.*18

Ingrid Nordgaard argues that payment intensifies the power imbalance between photographer and subject while agency remains in the participants’ posing and performance of their own bodies. She analyzes Case History as a work in which documentation and performance operate simultaneously.*16

In Afterall, Viktor Misiano, Anna Pilkington, and Walead Beshty approached the work from different angles, examining the ethics of looking at suffering and the ways bodily empathy resists being reduced to uncomplicated sympathy.*17

Olena Chervonik argues that reducing the debate to the ethics of payment obscures the continuity of Mikhailov’s work since the 1960s, when he photographed subjects that were considered unfit for display, including nudity, drinking, and leisure.*19

The ethical contradictions of Case History remain unresolved. The presentation of social facts, the transformation of nudity and wounds into artworks, paid photographic encounters, and the act of viewing them all collide within the same project.

sections.title: Major Works and Photobooks
sections.body_html:
Red and Double Projection

Red (1968–75) gathers red as it appears in flags, signs, clothing, and private life, placing the official symbolic color of communism alongside incidental red in everyday experience. Agata Pyzik argues that reducing the color to a political sign once again overlooks the picnics, relationships, sexuality, and other forms of ordinary life present in the series.*21

Yesterday’s Sandwich (late 1960s–1970s) overlays two slides to create a third scene from otherwise unrelated images. The New York Review of Books connects these doubled fields of vision to the experience of late Soviet life, in which surveillance and private existence occupied the same visual field.*23

Photographic Series with Text

Unfinished Dissertation (1984–85) places photographs, quotations from philosophy and science, private notes, and someone else’s dissertation paper on the same pages. Its deliberately “unfinished” structure refuses to make either photograph or text responsible for explaining the whole.*12

By the Ground and At Dusk

In By the Ground (1991), made immediately after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Mikhailov held the camera below waist level and framed pedestrians, roads, snow, and luggage in horizontal images taken close to the ground.In At Dusk (1993), figures and belongings moving through the street appear within blue-toned winter landscapes.*25 The Pinault Collection describes this blue as a color that overlays Mikhailov’s childhood memories of the Second World War with social conditions in Kharkiv during the 1990s.*31

Saim Demircan reads these series as images of Kharkiv made from “ground level” that lead toward Case History, emphasizing their attention to people overlooked by larger narratives of state and war*22.

Case History

Case History (1997–98) comprises roughly 400 photographs. It depicts the bodies, clothing, wounds, sexuality, families, and street lives of people who had lost work or housing, often through scenes that include deliberate posing.*14

The New Yorker presented the work through an open question: whether it amounted to an absurd “Theatre of the Ridiculous” or a contemporary form of the severe social criticism associated with George Grosz and Max Beckmann*30.

The photobook sequences a large number of images, repeatedly presenting both the new social class produced by post-Soviet conditions and the acts of photographing and viewing its members. MoMA places Case History among Mikhailov’s most challenging works dealing with the homeless population that emerged after the collapse of the Soviet Union.*14

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
Soviet Photography and Moscow Conceptualism

Mikhailov occupies several intersecting lines of photographic history beyond the problem of photographing “truth” under censorship. While the Kharkiv School of Photography challenged official socialist realism, research by MOKSOP shows that from the late 1970s Mikhailov was also in contact with Moscow Conceptualists including Ilya Kabakov and Erik Bulatov, deepening his use of text, appropriation, and repetition within photography*8.

In a 1994 Art Journal essay, Alla Efimova read Mikhailov’s work through the problems of fear and “truth,” describing a photographic ethics concerned with separating one’s own voice from the official chorus*29.

The “truth” at stake in Mikhailov’s work takes a form distinct from transparent objectivity. In Unfinished Dissertation and his “bad photography,” incompletion, accident, failure, and private language remain visible against a state culture that spoke about society through finished, authoritative images, allowing several voices to coexist within the photograph.

Western Reception and Misreading

From the 1990s onward, museums in Western Europe and the United States rapidly embraced Mikhailov as a photographer who revealed life inside the former Soviet Union. In 2004, the ICA Boston organized his first U.S. retrospective and presented his work as a record extending over more than thirty-five years through the Soviet Union’s height, decline, collapse, and aftermath*13. The 2000 Hasselblad Award recognized the collapse of the Soviet utopia as a major subject of his work while emphasizing the coexistence of criticism, humor, and emotion*24.

In a 2012 review of a retrospective, however, Pyzik criticized the institutional Western tendency to reduce the work to a contrast between an “oppressive Soviet Union” and a “free West.” She argued that the catastrophe visible in Case History intensified after the shift toward neoliberal capitalism*21.

Brian Dillon similarly noted in 2026 that when Mikhailov first became widely known in the West, Case History was often received as a “documentary revelation” of post-Soviet misery. That reading alone pushes into the background a much longer body of work, extending from the 1960s through underground humor, performance, conceptual manipulation, and the details of everyday life*20.

Reconsidering Mikhailov Through Ukrainian Photographic History

The large-scale retrospective Ukrainian Diary, shown from 2022 onward, repositioned Mikhailov as a Ukrainian artist who has photographed Kharkiv for more than half a century, correcting the narrower Western label of a “photographer of the former Soviet Union.” The MEP described him as one of Eastern Europe’s most influential contemporary artists and reorganized more than twenty series through both social and political history and formal experimentation*3. The 2019 Kyiv exhibition The Forbidden Image had already presented the trajectory from the risks of early censorship to Case History as one sustained effort to test the boundaries of political and social norms*26.

A research article from The Photographers’ Gallery examines the designation “Ukrainian” itself, placing the Kharkiv School of Photography across the Brezhnev-era stagnation, perestroika, and the difficult birth of an independent Ukrainian state*27.

Mikhailov incorporates into his work the conditions under which states, families, photographers, and museums each produce images of society, changing form as those conditions change. Hand-coloring, failed photographs, writing, performance, nudity, and extended photobook sequences connect as methods for resisting any single, correct image through which society might be explained.

related_annotations./en/photographers/zanele-muholi.html: Both make socially vulnerable bodies visible, but Muholi centers communal self-representation and the archive, while Mikhailov leaves the asymmetry between photographer and subject explicitly unresolved.
related_annotations./en/movements/documentary.html: An approach that does not merely photograph social reality but unsettles the ethics of the viewer.

edward-burtynsky.html.lead_html: Edward Burtynsky is a Canadian photographer who has photographed landscapes transformed by the extraction, processing, transport, and consumption of resources: mines, quarries, factories, shipbreaking yards, oil fields, water infrastructure, and farmland. In Manufactured Landscapes, Oil, Water, and Anthropocene, he links industrial sites dispersed across distant regions into long-term series, presenting environmental damage within compositions shaped by color, repetition, and topographic pattern. His upbringing in an industrial city, the legacy of New Topographics, debates over beauty and environmental crisis, and critiques concerning labor, consumption, and aerial vision are central to understanding his photographs.
edward-burtynsky.html.thesis_html: Burtynsky’s contribution to contemporary landscape photography was to photograph human-altered land as an industrial system extending from extraction and manufacturing through transport, consumption, and disposal. After New Topographics brought suburbs and industrial structures into landscape photography, he followed individual resources such as oil, water, and minerals, connecting geographically separated sites through long-term series. He avoided framing the work as an indictment of a single company or site, placing the resources on which daily life depends alongside the landscapes altered by their supply. The resulting landscape includes consumers as well as producers; environmental damage appears as part of industrial civilization itself. This is the central proposition of his work.

sections.title: Background and Era
sections.body_html:
Industrial City and Darkroom

Burtynsky was born in St. Catharines, Ontario, in 1955. His father worked at an automobile plant, and the city was shaped by factories and large ships moving through the Welland Canal*1. Around age eleven, his father acquired darkroom equipment, a camera, and film, giving him the freedom to experiment with shooting and developing. Burtynsky has recalled being fascinated by the way reality became another image on film*2.

As a child he also painted landscapes, while industry and agriculture existed side by side in St. Catharines. Photography allowed him to observe both directly while organizing terrain, infrastructure, color, and repetition within a single frame. His later industrial landscapes emerged where an interest in nature met an equally immediate awareness of production*2.

Evidence of Man

When Burtynsky began studying photography at Ryerson Polytechnical Institute in 1976, one of his early assignments was titled “Evidence of Man.” He photographed an old canal in his hometown and later explained that the assignment gave him a way to observe the marks humanity leaves on the land from a degree of remove*3. Around his student years he also worked in an automobile factory and in mining, encountering industry as a site of labor and material production as well as an artistic subject*3.

In 1981, near Frackville, Pennsylvania, he encountered land transformed by mining. Burtynsky has recalled recognizing it as a subject of his own time, then expanding from mines to railcuts, quarries, tailings, factories, and waste*2. It marked a shift toward treating the material origins of everyday life—and the landscapes from which those materials come—as subjects of landscape photography.

New Topographics

From his student years, Burtynsky looked to New Topographics: Photographs of a Man-Altered Landscape (1975) and photographers associated with it. He has cited Stephen Shore and Lewis Baltz, describing the exhibition as part of a shift from landscape photography centered on the celebration of nature toward a more restrained account of land shaped by human activity*3.

At the same time, Burtynsky has cited Albert Renger-Patzsch, Charles Sheeler’s industrial photography, Caspar David Friedrich, and Abstract Expressionism among his references*4. Art Canada Institute likewise notes the intersection of painting and photography in his early work*5. He inherited the New Topographics concern with the human-altered landscape while retaining color, repetition, and a scale that often evokes the sublime. Those elements became foundational to his industrial landscapes.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Beauty and Indictment in the Industrial Landscape

Burtynsky has explained that he did not set out to condemn corporations or specific actors; he wanted to “reconnect” viewers with the industrial world on which their lives depend*3. In an interview with National Geographic, he likewise said that beauty itself was not the goal. Color, texture, composition, and light were means of preserving a sense of astonishment at “what is happening” in the image*4. The National Gallery of Canada describes the work as “disturbingly sublime.” The orange of mine tailings, the repetition of quarries, and the geometry of irrigated land bring damage and visual order into the same image*6.

Jennifer Peeples terms this contradiction the “toxic sublime,” arguing that images in which beauty and ugliness, safety and danger, the immense and the minute coexist can direct attention toward contaminated sites that ordinarily remain distant*7. Their beauty also carries the risk of turning environmental damage into scenery available for aesthetic consumption. Burtynsky’s form does not make beauty synonymous with critique. It places dependence on industrial civilization and damage to land within the same visual experience, leaving that tension open to criticism.

Photographing Industry as a Chain

Burtynsky’s series rarely end with a single damaged site or factory. Joshua Schuster argues that by moving through extraction, commodification, and recycling, the photographs reveal how commodities connect corporations, labor, environmental costs, and consumers*8. Oil follows petroleum from oil fields through refining and transport to automobile culture, discarded tires, and shipbreaking*9. Water brings together sources, dams, irrigation, agriculture, salt pans, and depleted landscapes, tracing how water is gathered, controlled, and consumed*10.

Causal chains in industrial civilization often unfold across distant places and long periods, which makes them difficult to contain in a single emblematic environmental photograph. By placing extraction sites, manufacturing centers, transport networks, and post-consumer waste across multiple locations, the series links individual landscapes as stages in a supply chain. Serial form thus shows changes to land through the movement of resources and commodities.

Distance from the Human Figure

Burtynsky often photographs mines, factories, cities, and farmland as the results of collective activity, giving less emphasis to individual faces. He has said that he is interested in the cumulative mark that human effort and corporate activity leave on the land, more than in any one person*4. Distant and elevated viewpoints allow infrastructure, terrain, and accumulated labor to dominate the frame, emphasizing the scale of industrial systems.

That distance has also drawn criticism. From an environmental justice perspective, Sarah Jaquette Ray acknowledges the work’s ability to implicate viewers in global consumption while warning that “beautiful landscapes” can obscure the bodies of workers exposed to toxicity and the unequal concentration of harm in particular regions and classes*11. A form that surveys massive structures can disclose industrial scale while making the costs borne by individual workers and residents less legible.

sections.title: Major Works and Series
sections.body_html:
Railcuts / Mines / Tailings

In the 1980s, Railcuts and Mines focused on the marks left by railroad construction and mining as they cut through rock. In Railcuts #8 discussed by Art Canada Institute, the track and train traversing the mountainside place the railway tied to nation-building in the same frame as the altered land*5. In Nickel Tailings (1996), an orange stream of effluent from nickel processing makes the later tension between beauty and toxicity explicit*6.

Manufactured Landscapes / China

The 2003 book Manufactured Landscapes gathered quarries, mines, tailings, recycling, oil, and shipbreaking under the idea of the “manufactured landscape”*12. Beginning in 2002, Burtynsky photographed old factories, new manufacturing, coal, shipbuilding, recycling, urban redevelopment, and the Three Gorges Dam in China, developing a series around landscapes reshaped as China became a global center of production and around the supply networks attached to that transformation*13.

Jennifer Baichwal’s film Manufactured Landscapes presents the shooting locations and long durations of factory labor in moving images, restoring production time that the still photographs compress*14. Gerda Cammaer argues that the film combines aesthetic photography with social documentary, complicating the binary of the photographer as either a beautifying artist or an accusatory documentarian*15.

Oil / Water

Oil traces petroleum beyond extraction, through oil fields, refineries, highways, car culture, discarded tires, and the decommissioning of aircraft and ships. Burtynsky identifies the contradiction at the series’ origin: oil enabled freedom of movement and modern life, while dependence on it has generated environmental problems*9.

Water photographs natural sources as well as dams, agriculture, irrigation, aquaculture, salt pans, and depleted water systems*16. NOMA presents the series as moving across the supply, control, movement, and depletion of water, making more explicit Burtynsky’s tendency to treat a resource through its social uses across multiple sites*10.

Anthropocene

The 2018 project Anthropocene is a collaboration by Burtynsky, Jennifer Baichwal, and Nicholas de Pencier encompassing a book, touring exhibition, feature film, and educational website*17. At the AGO, photographs were combined with high-resolution film and augmented reality to present extraction, deforestation, extinction, and urbanization at different scales*18. The project moves beyond asking a single photograph to stand for planetary change, combining film and exhibition to address differences of time, scale, and place.

sections.title: Criticism and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Beauty and Environmental Crisis

The central debate around Burtynsky asks whether rendering environmental destruction visually compelling can function critically or turns destruction into consumable spectacle. Peeples’s “toxic sublime” describes beauty as a possible point of entry into contaminated sites while retaining the risk of aestheticizing crisis*7. Schuster further argues that the “industrial sublime,” when dominated by awe and anxiety, can weaken attention to concrete relations among commodities, corporations, labor, and environmental costs*8.

An early review in The Brooklyn Rail likewise observes that tailings, oil fields, factories, and shipbreaking can produce awe and guilt at the same time*19. In Burtynsky’s work, beauty remains part of the critical problem. Its capacity to hold attention on environmental crisis and its capacity to transform damage into an aesthetic object continue to divide assessments of the photographs.

China: Labor and Consumption

In the China series, questions of who produces, who consumes, and who bears environmental costs become especially pronounced. An interdisciplinary study by Patricia Ballamingie and others argues that Western viewers risk reproducing “othering” when they see huge factories and dams as signs of a modernization in China cast as alien, severing the connection between Chinese production and consumption in Europe, Canada, and the United States*20. The essay argues that this risk requires recognition that Western consumers themselves are implicated in the changes visible in China.

Manufactured Landscapes restores factory time and labor to moving images, supplementing social relations that still photography can push into the distance. Gerda Cammaer argues that the film joins the artist’s working process to social documentary and presents mass production and mass consumption as a problem in which viewers themselves participate*15.

Aerial Views and Land

Recent aerial work has prompted a different critique. A 2026 study of representations of the Athabasca Oil Sands argues that abstraction from above reveals the scale of extraction while potentially presenting land as an unpopulated resource space and pushing labor and Indigenous relationships to land into the background*21. This surveying viewpoint compresses enormous systems into a single image, but it can also leave the specific histories, ownership, and everyday life of a place outside the frame.

Position in Contemporary Landscape Photography

Burtynsky’s importance does not rest on being the first photographer to depict industrial landscapes. In the 1970s, New Topographics made the “man-altered landscape” central to landscape photography, and Burtynsky has acknowledged the influence of Shore and Baltz*3. Catherine Zuromskis compares the 1975 New Topographics exhibition with Oil (2009), arguing for a continuing problem in how landscape photography frames the petroleum industry and the petroleum-dependent daily life of the West—petroculture*22.

Michael Truscello likewise compares Oil with Mitch Epstein’s American Power as photographs of energy infrastructure after New Topographics. He reads extraction and transport sites as “sites of passage” where civilization and ecosystems come into contact, not as isolated scenes of environmental destruction*23. Within that lineage, Burtynsky has spent decades connecting mining, oil, water, agriculture, and waste as stages in a chain through which resources are extracted, processed, transported, consumed, and discarded. ICP’s The Great Acceleration reframes more than forty years of his work through interconnected global shifts in population, resource extraction, transportation, water use, and food production*24.

Burtynsky’s position in contemporary landscape photography lies in making the industrial systems that support modern life themselves into landscape subjects, and in placing their beauty, scale, labor, consumption, and land rights within the same field of debate.

fabian-marti.html.meta_description: Fabian Marti is a Swiss artist whose work moves across scanners, scratched negatives, photograms, appropriated images, ceramics, video, and installation. Dust and scratches on the scanning surface, drawing on negatives, and computer-generated forms returned to the darkroom leave visible traces of the machines and handwork through which the photographic image was made. Since the 2000s, Marti has used digital imagery as a meeting point for reproduction, chance, material processes, and mystical signs, retaining the residue that digital correction typically removes.

fabian-marti.html.thesis_html: Marti brought to photography a resistance to treating the digital image as a smooth, controlled, finished product. Using scanners, scratched negatives, and photograms, he preserves dust, damage, and accidental exposure within mechanical reproduction. At the same time, he flips, duplicates, cuts, and rescans symbols already loaded with meaning—skulls, masks, crosses, crystals, and the covers of science-fiction books. Neither the image’s physical traces nor the meanings of its symbols remain fixed; the movement between digital processes and the darkroom becomes part of the photograph itself.
