sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
Choosing Photography

Dijkstra initially enrolled in a teacher-training program in crafts and visual arts, but felt it did not suit her. Around age nineteen, using a camera borrowed from a friend prompted her to pursue photography. After taking a photography course, she entered the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam in 1981. She has recalled that she had been strongly drawn to observing people since childhood.*1 At the De Moor Cultural Centre, Hans Aarsman encouraged her to photograph people. A workshop in Rome taught by Corinne Noordenbos helped shift her from treating the figure as one element in the frame toward portraits built on a direct, face-to-face encounter with the sitter.*2 She later photographed young people at the Paradiso club. Dijkstra has described photography as a medium through which she can examine how people change. Comparing photographs revealed differences in gaze and expression that she had not noticed with the naked eye, an experience that informed her later long-term series.*1

Her graduation work reflected the staged photography that became prominent in the 1980s. She subsequently made commissioned portraits for magazines including Quote, Elle, and Elegance, as well as for corporate clients.*2 In commissioned work, sitters often arrived with a fixed idea of how they wanted to appear. Dijkstra came to feel constrained by the need to satisfy that expectation while also recording what she herself perceived in the person. Hripsimé Visser describes Beach Portraits as her first fully self-directed project, begun from the need to move beyond the limits of commissioned work.*2 Jennifer Eileen Quick’s 2008 study interprets Dijkstra’s shift from early professional portraiture to the independent work of the 1990s as a move away from constructing images that fit social roles and toward portraits in which self-presentation and bodily response do not fully coincide.*3 A photograph can hold, in the same frame, the pose chosen by the subject, the conditions established by the photographer, and glances, tension, balance, and gestures that neither fully controls. This capacity became the basis of Dijkstra’s independent portraiture.

The Turn of Self-Portrait

In 1990, Dijkstra fractured her hip in a bicycle accident. After a long recovery, she took up swimming as rehabilitation.*38 The following year, after swimming thirty laps, she photographed her exhausted body in Self-Portrait, Marnixbad, Amsterdam, Netherlands, June 19, 1991. She has explained that the intensity of her fatigue left little energy for thinking about a pose, allowing her posture to emerge more unconsciously.*5 The photograph did not expose a “true self.” It registered a mismatch between the effort to compose one’s appearance and a fatigued body that would not fully comply. Establishing that discrepancy within a single portrait led directly to the method of Beach Portraits.*6

The Frontal Portrait Tradition

By the early 1990s, when Beach Portraits began, frontal portraits made under consistent conditions and presented as a series already belonged to several photographic traditions. August Sander’s People of the Twentieth Century linked individuals to social structure through clothing, occupation, class, and gesture. In postwar Germany, the typologies of Bernd and Hilla Becher were followed by artists such as Thomas Struth and Thomas Ruff, who redirected objectivity, repetition, and large-scale photography toward different questions. Quick places Dijkstra’s clear realism at the intersection of the New Objectivity lineage and the languages of American portraiture associated with Richard Avedon and Diane Arbus.*3 Dijkstra inherited frontality and repetition and redirected them toward people in the process of acquiring a social image. Her portraits leave both social type and psychological certainty unresolved.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Dijkstra’s portraits are not premised on the idea that a person’s inner life appears transparently in a photograph. Sitters become aware of the camera and arrange themselves accordingly, but their gestures also carry patterns learned through age, clothing, gender, peers, occupation, and state institutions.*3 Fatigue, tension, a shifting stance, or a change in gaze can also resist that self-staging. Frontality, spare backgrounds, extended sitting times, serial work, and video allowed Dijkstra to record the mismatch between self-presentation and bodily or social pressures without reducing it to personality.

Self-Presentation and Pose

In Dijkstra’s frontal portraits, sitters choose their own stance and gaze. In a 1998 interview with Claire Bishop, discussed by Quick, Dijkstra described what she sought as a “natural portrait” and explained that she gave very few detailed instructions, allowing each person to decide how to pose.*3 The effort to appear natural itself becomes visible in posture and expression. Katy Siegel’s “Real People” argues that efforts at self-presentation reveal both social position and individual habits. Quick develops this point by describing a subject who is neither determined entirely by society nor free to invent any identity at will, but continually adjusts the image of the self between those forces.*3 A long sitting can encompass the initial pose, its revisions, the easing of tension, and renewed awareness of the camera. The waiting is not a strategy for exposing an unguarded “real face.” It gives photographic form to the instability of self-presentation.

Why She Photographs Young People

Dijkstra has repeatedly photographed people from adolescence into early adulthood. By her own account, youth was not a predetermined subject. An early Beach Portraits session with a thirteen-year-old girl deepened her interest in an age when emotions and self-image have not yet settled and their uncertainty is more likely to register in posture and expression.*7 Visser likewise explains that adults tend to be more conscious of pose and appearance when photographed, which helped direct Dijkstra’s attention toward children and young people.*2 In a 2020 Financial Times interview, Dijkstra cited the fact that young people are not yet fixed and still contain many possibilities as a reason she photographs them.*8

Her interest therefore centers on the formation of self-image through clothing, body culture, peer groups, gender norms, class, and regional difference, not on an idealized image of youth. In Beach Portraits, Dijkstra was attentive to differences between young people at affluent American resorts, where body culture and fashion magazines shaped self-presentation, and young people in Poland soon after the fall of the Berlin Wall.*7 Julian Stallabrass reads this comparison as a record of young people being socialized into commercial image culture.*9 Quick similarly argues that in Buzzclub, clothing, displays of sexual attractiveness, and peer pressure cannot be separated from the subjects’ understanding of themselves.*3 Adolescence and early adulthood are periods in which bodily development coincides with testing behaviors learned from others as one’s own. Dijkstra repeatedly photographed this stage because the incomplete fit between individual intention and socially learned codes remains especially legible in the body.

Spare Backgrounds

Spare backgrounds remove the sitter from a descriptive domestic or social setting and concentrate attention on posture and bodily detail. The Guggenheim retrospective transcript explains that Dijkstra isolates subjects from context to direct attention toward detail; indoors, she removes furniture, and in New Mothers she used the white walls of the women’s homes as backgrounds.*5 In Beach Portraits, sea and sky function as an almost constant stage, with few buildings or tourist markers to identify place. In a 1998 review, Jennifer Higgie argued that the repeated format intensifies small differences—a clenched fist, the tilt of a pelvis, skin, scars, and hair.*10 A study published online in 2025 and included in a 2026 journal issue places the series at an intersection of modernist photography, deadpan, seventeenth-century Dutch painting, and conceptual repetition through the idea of “non-specificity.”*11 Removing contextual information leaves posture, clothing, bodily detail, and the viewer’s own habit of judging people through those signs in sharper relief.

This reduction of information does not simply free the individual from context. Stallabrass calls the frontal, centered, repetitive format, sparse backgrounds, and large, highly detailed prints “quasi-ethnographic”: a form that can encourage empathy with individuals while also holding multiple bodies at a comparative distance.*9 A pared-down image intended to resist typology can become, on the museum wall, a format for inspecting people one by one. The tension between a portrait that insists on individual specificity and a gaze that compares and classifies is built into Dijkstra’s method.

Seriality and Time

From early in her career, Dijkstra favored series built through repeated conditions over selecting a single “definitive” image. She has said that when she began Beach Portraits, working serially gave her a firmer way to address the subject.*1 A single portrait can easily fix the clothing, posture, or social role of one moment as if it defined the person. Placing different people within the same format—or returning to the same person over years, as in Almerisa and Olivier—prevents any one moment from functioning as a final image of the subject.

Quick analyzes Almerisa and Dijkstra’s series on the soldier Evgenya as examples in which a person’s changing social role never resolves into a representative type.*3 Stallabrass likewise sees in Almerisa the passage of a refugee child adapting to the culture of her host country through clothing and body language.*9 Repeated conditions preserve what has changed alongside what has remained. In Dijkstra’s serial portraits, self-image never arrives at a single finished form; it continues to be revised as environments and roles change.

Time in Video

A still photograph fixes a single moment of self-presentation. Video can record, within the same duration, both the effort to maintain an appearance and the body’s changes over time. After making photographs for Buzzclub, Dijkstra reviewed the contact sheets and felt that the movement and sound that created the club’s atmosphere were missing from the still images; she returned the following year to work in video.*12 Video can include speech, music, and ambient sound, and can follow the periods when a person is conscious of the camera, becomes absorbed in music or movement, and then becomes aware of being filmed again.*12 Self-presentation appears as an action that changes through duration, not as a fixed pose.

Speaking about The Krazyhouse and The Gymschool, Dijkstra has said that she leaves key decisions open during filming, allowing improvisation and unexpected events to enter the work.*13 In The Gymschool, girls are arranged in age order from eight to twelve; as their technical skill increases, the work tracks simultaneous changes in bodily control and expressive freedom.*13 Jennifer Blessing’s decision to devote a separate essay to Dijkstra’s video work in the 2012 retrospective catalogue likewise positions moving-image work as a second form of portraiture concerned with self-presentation changing over time, not as an adjunct to the photographs.*14

sections.title: Major Works and Series
sections.body_html:
Beach Portraits

Beach Portraits began in 1992 and consists of full-length portraits, made on beaches in Europe and the United States, primarily of children and young people. One of its best-known works, Odessa, Ukraine, August 4, 1993, shows a boy standing full-length against sand, sea, and sky. MoMA notes that his effort to project adult confidence instead heightens his awkwardness.*15Kolobrzeg, Poland, July 26, 1992, the sitter’s hip-shifted stance has prompted comparisons with classical contrapposto and Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus.*16 Dijkstra, however, gave few detailed directions about posture or expression in the series. She photographed the process in which a pose took shape and then loosened over the course of waiting.*2 Jacques Rancière discusses the work as a social photograph of an age group in transition while also noting how its frontality and large exhibition scale give it an enigma akin to classical portrait painting.*17

The series also records regional differences in the early 1990s, shortly after the Cold War. Dijkstra has recalled seeing young people at Hilton Head Island in the United States who were highly conscious of their bodies under the influence of affluent resort culture and fashion magazines, while in Poland in 1992 she found less self-consciousness about fashion and felt the social differences of the period after the fall of the Berlin Wall.*7 The Städel Museum likewise situates Beach Portraits within the social changes of the 1990s, noting Dijkstra’s use of the same compositional structure for young people in different countries.*6 Higgie points to the individual differences that remain forceful within the repeated composition: clenched hands, the spread of the legs, wet swimsuits, hair, and gaze.*10 Recent scholarship describes this structure through “non-specificity”: the subjects carry information about place and generation without becoming representative examples of either.*11

New Mothers and Bullfighters

New Mothers (1994) and Bullfighters (1994, 2000) extend to adult portraiture the condition Dijkstra discovered in her post-accident self-portrait: photographing someone immediately after an intense bodily experience. Of the three mothers photographed in 1994, Julie was photographed one hour after giving birth, Tecla one day after, and Saskia one week after. The forcados in Bullfighters were photographed immediately after a bullfight, with blood and dirt still on their bodies.*18 Writing on New Mothers, Laurie Hurwitz notes that sweat, blood, postpartum underwear, and sanitary products remain in the frame, far removed from idealized images of mother and child.*19 The social roles of “mother” and “bullfighter” appear alongside the exhaustion, wounds, and dirt left by childbirth or the bullfight, preventing these recently assumed roles from settling into completed types.

Dijkstra photographed the women in their homes while excluding furniture, pictures, and other descriptive elements of their surroundings, concentrating the image on the body and the act of holding the child.*5 For Alison Dean, the issue extends beyond whether the photographs reveal the “truth” of the postpartum body to the forms of intimacy and distance produced among photographer, subject, and viewer when that body is publicly displayed as a photograph.*20 New Mothers therefore places a non-idealized image of the postpartum body alongside the question of how another person looks at it.

Almerisa and Soldiers

Almerisa began with a photograph made in 1994 of a girl who had arrived in the Netherlands from Bosnia, photographed in a refugee reception center, and continued through eleven images until 2008.*21 An interview with the National Portrait Gallery of Australia notes that Almerisa chose her own clothes for each sitting, while Dijkstra retained the chair as a recurring element that allowed photographs from different moments to be compared.*22 MoMA describes how growth and adaptation from Eastern European to Western European life register through changes in clothing, hairstyle, furniture, posture, and family structure.*23 Quick resists reading the series as a linear story in which adaptation entails the loss of an authentic self. She instead analyzes it as a process in which individual choices and external social conditions are reconfigured at each stage.*3 By photographing the same person in the same format over time, no single image becomes a final portrait that stands for her.

In the series on soldiers, bodily change is compounded by the institutions of the state and the military. Olivier (2000–2003) follows a young man who joined the French Foreign Legion, recording physical and psychological changes from enlistment through continued service.*24 Israel Portraits began with a 1999 commission from the Herzliya Museum of Art to photograph people in Israel; Dijkstra photographed young soldiers both in barracks and at home while on leave. Gil Pasternak treats the series as one of the works in Dijkstra’s oeuvre most directly conditioned by national politics, arguing that the photographs make visible the social position military service inscribes on the individual body.*25 Uniforms, training, and conscription alter bodies and behavior, yet the sitters never collapse into types that simply represent the institution.

Buzz Club and Night Watching

The Buzz Club, Liverpool, UK / Mystery World, Zaandam, NL 1996–97 is a two-channel video for which Dijkstra set up a temporary white-background studio inside clubs and filmed young people one at a time. MACBA describes the club as a social space where young people, away from parental supervision, try out clothing and bodily presentation and test their sexual attractiveness.*26 Small actions—smoking a cigarette, drinking beer, dancing to music—continue through the videos. Against the white background, each person’s behavior is sustained in isolation from the club crowd.*12 In The Krazyhouse, each subject chooses a favorite song and dances alone, allowing gestures shaped by awareness of the camera to coexist with immersion in the music.*13

In later videos, Dijkstra extended her attention from bodily self-presentation to the act of looking at art. I See a Woman Crying (Weeping Woman) (2009) films children looking at Picasso’s Weeping Woman, kept outside the frame, as they use words to infer the woman’s emotions and circumstances.*27 Night Watching (2019) is a three-channel video of fourteen groups of museum visitors responding to Rembrandt’s The Night Watch; the painting itself never appears on screen.*28 Since the late 1980s, Thomas Struth’s Museum Photographs has placed historical works of art and the visitors who look at them within the same photographic frame.*29 Dijkstra leaves only the viewers’ words and reactions in the video, so the act of looking unfolds through multiple interpretations that continue over time.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Historical Position
sections.body_html:
Sander and Arbus

Dijkstra and August Sander share frontality and serial form, but differ in how they relate the individual to social type. Sander’s People of the Twentieth Century organized sitters by occupation and class, linking individual portraits to the structure of German society in his time. Quick argues that while Sander’s subjects are comparatively legible as representatives of occupations and classes, Dijkstra uses a similarly clear realism to expose the unstable fit between social position and individual.*3 Dijkstra herself has praised Sander’s The Student for the way its focus on the sitter’s eyes preserves individual character and dignity within a social type.*30 Dijkstra inherited the problem of holding individual presence and social code within the same photographic conditions while leaving classification unresolved.

Comparison with Diane Arbus shifts the emphasis to the subject’s self-presentation. Katy Siegel’s “Real People,” published in a 2001 exhibition catalogue, became an important early essay that approached Dijkstra through both Sander and Arbus.*31 Drawing on Siegel, Quick places Dijkstra’s portraits between Sander’s sociological legibility and the psychologically unsettling portraiture associated with Arbus.*3 An effort to appear as oneself reveals both socially learned gestures and individual habits.*3 SFMOMA describes Arbus’s portraiture as an exploration of appearance and identity, performance and reality.*32 Dijkstra repeatedly worked through this discrepancy between self-presentation and the photographic image in controlled settings such as beaches, white walls, barracks, and clubs.

Ruff and Deadpan

Thomas Ruff’s Porträts and Dijkstra’s portraits share frontality, repetition, and large-scale color, but diverge in how they treat the possibility of reading psychology from a person’s surface. Ruff systematically used everyday clothing, frontal orientation, even lighting, and neutral expression to make enormous, highly detailed faces while refusing the expectation that such detail would reveal inner character. MoMA identifies this failure of psychological access despite technical precision as central to the series.*33 Stallabrass treats Ruff as an extreme case in which increased visual information does not stabilize meaning, and argues that Dijkstra shares a “quasi-ethnographic” format of frontality, repetition, and large, high-resolution photographs.*9

In Dijkstra’s work, surface information does more than block psychological interpretation. The effort to hold a posture, the placement of hands, the way a uniform sits on the body, or clothing learned from peers all provide information about the sitter, but none functions as proof of character. As Stallabrass notes, the format can create both a sense of proximity to the subject and the distance of examining a specimen.*9 The contradiction between an image that respects individual specificity and a museum display that makes bodies available for comparison is one of the critical tensions in Dijkstra’s portraiture.

Goldin and Intimacy

Comparison with Nan Goldin turns on how intimacy is produced through the photographic relationship. MoMA describes The Ballad of Sexual Dependency as an installation of 35mm slides and a soundtrack assembled from years of photographs of private relationships, conflicts, and living environments within Goldin’s own social circle.*34 When ICA Boston placed the two artists in dialogue, it contrasted Goldin’s photographs of intimates in the midst of lived events with Dijkstra’s stripped-down settings, still poses, and extended observation of people at turning points in their lives.*35

Alison Dean complicates any simple opposition between Goldin as insider and Dijkstra as outsider. Instead of reducing the photographer-subject relation to empathy versus voyeurism, she asks what kinds of intimacy photographer, subject, and viewer form through the photograph.*20 In New Mothers, the removal of domestic surroundings and the frontal presentation of the nude postpartum body bring a private bodily experience into a public exhibition space. Goldin built her portraits through the shared experience and memory of a community; Dijkstra maintains distance from the sitter and makes the relationship established during the session part of the photograph. Their difference lies less in the degree of intimacy than in the time and photographic relationship through which it is produced.

Critical Reception and Current Position

From the earliest criticism, Dijkstra’s photographs have resisted being reduced to images that simply “capture an unguarded moment.” A 1998 conversation with Claire Bishop, cited by Quick, already addressed the simultaneous presence of staging and naturalness.*3 That same year, Jennifer Higgie described the work as retaining the artifice produced by photography itself instead of claiming to expose the subject’s secrets.*10 In 2001, Katy Siegel read the work through the intersection of social type and psychological portraiture; in 2007, Stallabrass added a critique of ethnographic classification and the power of observation in the museum.*9 Quick’s 2008 study systematized these debates through the problem of contemporary subjectivity, in which individual choice and social conditions continue to be negotiated within a single portrait.*3

Around the same period, Michael Fried’s Why Photography Matters as Art as Never Before discussed Dijkstra alongside Thomas Ruff and Thomas Struth as key artists in his account of large-scale photography and its relation to the viewer.*36 From another direction, Jacques Rancière described Dijkstra’s young people, mothers, and bullfighters as records of changing social types that, through frontality and exhibition scale, also acquire the enigma of classical portrait painting.*17 Together, these accounts move discussion beyond the psychology of the sitter toward the kind of figure a photograph produces in an exhibition space and the distance it establishes between viewer and subject.

In the 2012 SFMOMA/Guggenheim retrospective, Sandra S. Phillips discussed roughly two decades of portraits as work that extracts temporary states—especially those of young people—from the flow of time, while Jennifer Blessing considered the video works in a separate essay.*14 Phillips argues that the scale and physical proximity of Dijkstra’s photographs make these temporary states particularly memorable.*4 In 2017, Dijkstra received the Hasselblad Foundation International Award in Photography.*24 Berlinische Galerie’s 2024–25 exhibition Still — Moving surveyed photographs and videos from 1992 to 2024 as a sustained portrait project.*37 Dijkstra’s place in photographic history rests on her sustained examination of the points at which self-presentation, social role, bodily response, the photographer’s conditions, and the viewer’s interpretation fail to align, across frontal portraiture, serial work, and video.

thomas-struth.html.lead_html: Thomas Struth is a German photographer whose subjects have ranged from unpeopled city streets and family portraits to museum visitors, tropical rainforests, and scientific and technological facilities such as NASA and CERN. Across Unconscious Places, Family Portraits, Museum Photographs, New Pictures from Paradise, and Nature & Politics, he has used large-format photography and sustained serial work to examine how human history and acts of judgment remain embedded in streets, families, cultural institutions, and technological systems. The central questions here are why he moved from painting to photography, what he absorbed from the Bechers, and where his method departed from theirs.
thomas-struth.html.thesis_html: Bernd and Hilla Becher photographed the same types of industrial structures under nearly identical conditions, then placed multiple images together so that differences in form could be compared. Struth carried forward this comparative logic without imposing one photographic rule on streets, families, museums, and scientific facilities. In his unpeopled street photographs, buildings and roads register the effects of wartime destruction, reconstruction, and urban planning. In the family portraits, the families determine how they sit and how much space separates one person from another. Museum Photographs places historical paintings and contemporary viewers in a single frame. In Nature & Politics, Struth avoids portraits of individual researchers and photographs the research apparatus itself—the material result of many specialists, budgets, and policy decisions. For each subject, he asks what must share the frame for the human decisions that produced a place or group to become comparable, then reconsiders camera position, the treatment of figures, and the scale of the image. This continual redesign of the photographic rules is Struth’s specific contribution.

sections.title: Background and Historical Context
sections.body_html:
From Painting to Photography

Struth entered the Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in 1973 and began studying with Gerhard Richter the following year. At first, photography served as source material for realist paintings: he used a 35mm camera to photograph passersby and city streets*1. He later recalled realizing that his interest lay less in handling paint than in “making pictures,” and that the photograph itself already contained the image he needed*13. He also said that he was drawn to observing things that existed in the world and thinking through social and political questions, instead of projecting his own psychology onto the picture*14. In 2015, he described himself first as a “picture-maker” and explained that he uses a camera because painting the complicated reality before him would require an enormous amount of time*19.

The compositional concerns Struth had learned through painting remained active after he chose photography. A MoMA exhibition catalogue describes Struth’s aims as investigative and reportorial while characterizing his organization of the picture as “painterly”; it compares his early empty streets with Richter’s gray urban paintings of the 1960s*29. Richter blurred photographic source images as he translated them into painted surfaces. Struth kept buildings, pavement, signs, vacant lots, and other elements already present in the world together within the photographic frame. Photography suited his desire to register many existing pieces of information at once and to think about society through their arrangement.

Postwar Germany and the Street

Assisting Richter with Atlas and encountering its accumulation of private and press photographs gave Struth experience of comparing images and considering how meaning changes across a group, instead of approaching each photograph in isolation*1. Michael Asher, Daniel Buren, Richard Serra, and others also visited the academy. Their presence brought him close to art that treated the site, institution, and social setting of a work as part of the work itself*3.

At the same time, the West Germany in which Struth grew up was rebuilding its cities while pushing the crimes and destruction of the war into the past and trying to establish the appearance of a “normal society”*18. His turn to streets did not depend on using politicians or citizens as representative figures. A single street could contain prewar buildings, postwar reconstruction, the width of roads, vacant lots, and new commercial architecture. Struth understood these physical layers as evidence of what a society had preserved, demolished, and chosen to build over a long span of time*2. Here he developed a method of reading human choices through the places left by those choices, without photographing the decision-makers themselves.

The Bechers’ Class

In 1976, on Richter’s recommendation, Struth transferred to Bernd Becher’s photography class. He had not previously known the work of Bernd and Hilla Becher and later recalled worrying that the street photographs he had already made might look similar to theirs*13. The chronology rules out a simple account of his empty streets as an imitation of the Bechers’ style. What the class offered was an environment in which photographic history could be discussed alongside literature, politics, economics, and film, and in which photography became a means of thinking about society*1.

The Bechers photographed disappearing blast furnaces, water towers, and other industrial structures under controlled conditions—uniform light, frontal viewpoints, and consistent distance—and arranged multiple photographs in grids. This made it possible to compare shared structural features with individual differences among buildings serving the same purpose*17. Struth inherited this rigor of comparison. Yet, as the Museo del Prado has noted, he resisted organizing cities into a strict typology or “inventory”*16. His concern was the way different periods, uses, and judgments accumulated within a single street.

Monika Perenyei places this formation alongside Struth’s experience classifying and arranging photographs for Richter’s Atlas, giving the Bechers only one part of the account*26. From the Bechers came a method of controlling photographic conditions so that differences could be compared; from Richter came the experience of seeing meanings shift when unlike images were placed together. Struth later changed composition, the presence or absence of figures, and the scale of the image as he moved among streets, families, museums, forests, and scientific facilities. The governing question became what kind of comparison would make each subject intelligible; preserving a single visual style was secondary.

sections.title: Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
From Streets to Scientific Facilities

Across Struth’s work, human decisions repeatedly appear as forms embedded in objects and spaces. On the street, replaced buildings, roads, signs, and vacant lots carry the results of urban planning and economic activity. In the family portraits, where people sit, how far apart they are, and how they face the camera register how a family chooses to present itself. In museums, the placement of paintings and the positions assumed by viewers record habits of looking. In scientific facilities, researchers and politicians may be absent, yet their decisions remain materialized in machines, pipes, and technical layouts. The subjects change from series to series, but the question persists: what can close observation of a human-made situation tell us about the society that produced it?*14

In the early street photographs, Struth placed the camera near the center of the road and used one-point perspective so that the buildings on either side could be examined under comparable conditions. Perenyei describes this central perspective as a prototype for what Struth identified as an “impersonal interest,” while also noting that it creates a theatrical space that carries the eye deep into the picture*26. The centered composition helped make differences in architectural age, function, and alteration legible within the frame.

His compositions changed over time. Nana Last argues that the later street photographs changed by incorporating what Struth had learned from photographing people in portraits and from constructing denser pictorial fields in the museum photographs*32. Families called for frontality; museums required relations between paintings and viewers; rainforests demanded dense, nearly undifferentiated detail; technological sites required a legible view of elaborate apparatus. Central perspective and frontal presentation therefore remained tools, not a fixed signature style.

Family Portraits and Family Arrangement

Family Portraits began with a collaborative project with psychoanalyst Ingo Hartmann. Family photographs brought by patients were copied at the same size so that arrangement, generation, and physical distance among figures could be compared*5. In the portraits that followed, the families themselves discussed the location and arrangement, and every sitter looked toward the lens. The 1986 The Shimada Family, Yamaguchi, in the collection of the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum, is an early example*6. Struth’s aim was narrower than a classification of society by occupation or class. He was examining what becomes visible when one family constructs a public image of “this is who we are” before the camera.

Struth avoids both the stolen “natural” instant and a staged psychological drama in which sitters are assigned roles. A CAA Reviews discussion of Michael Fried emphasizes that the subjects are fully aware of being photographed, yet cannot control every resemblance of face and body, posture, proximity, or culturally specific family gesture that enters the image*28. Clothing and seating positions record the self-image the family consciously constructs; bodily resemblance, gaze, and distance record features that cannot be completely staged. The photograph becomes a place to compare the image the family intends to present with the arrangement actually recorded by the camera. The 1997 volume Thomas Struth: Portraits, with essays by Thomas Weski, Norman Bryson, and Benjamin H. D. Buchloh, also shows how the series has been considered through the histories of portraiture and painting as well as questions of representation and viewing*33.

Museum Photographs and the Viewer

The origins of Museum Photographs lie partly in Struth’s time living in Rome and Naples in the late 1980s. He became attentive to the difference between settings where religious paintings remained connected to church architecture and everyday belief and secular museums where works had been separated from their original use and history and displayed as “masterpieces”*7. When he photographed the art historian Giles Robertson in front of an old painting in 1987, Struth later recalled recognizing the possibility of placing “a present moment and a historical moment in one photographic plane”*7. The museum thus became a site where he could observe how paintings from the past are seen by people in the present.

The 2005 volume Thomas Struth: Museum Photographs includes Hans Belting’s “Photography and Painting” and Walter Grasskamp’s “Observing the Observer,” among other texts*27. The book addresses the meaning of the paintings themselves and the way works are presented within museum architecture and perceived by viewers*27. Struth’s photographs bring figures in old paintings, frames, walls, floors, and contemporary visitors into the same picture. Several temporal layers coexist: the past in which the painting was made, the present in which museum visitors encounter it, and the later present in which another viewer confronts Struth’s finished photograph. Museum Photographs makes those layers comparable within a single frame, asking how images from the past continue to live through present-day exhibition spaces and habits of viewing.

That relationship depends on exact composition. According to Struth’s archive, visitors in most of the series were not staged. He established the camera position and frame first, then waited for a configuration in which the painting and the people cohered within it*7. Perenyei draws a continuity between the central perspective of the early street photographs and the central or oblique camera positions used in the museum pictures*26. Perspective that had helped compare buildings in the streets now linked the perspectival space contained within a painting to the real space occupied by museum visitors.

San Zaccaria, Venice (1995) makes this structure especially clear. The Met explains that Bellini’s altarpiece uses light and perspective to create an imagined space beyond the wall, while Struth’s photograph places that painted space and the tourists in front of it within a single photographic field*30. The saints in the altarpiece, the church architecture, and the seated and standing visitors occupy a continuous depth. A pictorial space composed roughly five centuries earlier therefore appears contiguous with the present space of viewing. The painting itself becomes another spatial system within the photograph’s composition.

New Pictures from Paradise and the Rainforest

In New Pictures from Paradise, begun in 1998, many of the social clues present in earlier works—architecture, signs, clothing, furniture—largely disappear. Struth said that in a Walker Evans photograph, or in his own street photographs, he could move from cars to houses to terrain and analyze how a place had been made. In the forest, he sought such a density of detail that the viewer could no longer decide which information should count as primary*14. Guggenheim Bilbao also notes that Struth described these as his most intuitive pictures*9.

The series tests the limits of the analytic method that had guided much of his earlier work. In the streets, differences among buildings offered points of comparison; in museums, the positions of viewers and paintings could be read against one another. The forest does not easily separate foreground from background or significant detail from incidental detail. Greater resolution produces more information without guaranteeing a direct path to understanding. Looking therefore takes longer, and the gap between seeing and comprehending becomes part of the work itself.

sections.title: Key Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Leonard Street

The 1978 Leonard Street, Tribeca, New York is a key example of Struth’s early street photographs. The camera is positioned near the center of the road, with façades, pavement, parked cars, and signs organized around a vanishing point. The Met places the work at an intersection of the Bechers’ comparative method, the urban architectural photography of Charles Marville and Eugène Atget, and Minimal and Conceptual art*4. New York streets brought buildings of different periods and functions into the same view. Photographing multiple streets from a consistent position made the accumulated choices that had produced a street comparable; individual buildings became evidence within that larger structure*16.

Museum Photographs

In the 1989 Louvre 2, Paris, adults standing before paintings, children seated on the floor, and the architecture of the gallery all occupy the same frame*8. Struth set up a large-format camera and waited, without staging the crowd, until the painting and the viewers formed a workable configuration. The subject therefore includes the present-day act of looking, not just the isolated masterpiece*7. The museum visitor is both a viewer within the photograph and, for us, a figure whose behavior as a viewer can itself be observed.

In the 1999 National Museum of Art, Tokyo, Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People is brightly illuminated before a darkened audience, giving the exhibition a structure close to that of a cinema screen. The Met notes the contrast between figures advancing through revolutionary history inside the painting and late-twentieth-century viewers standing still before the luminous image*25. The photograph asks how a history painting centered on collective action is encountered by contemporary bodies within an exhibition shaped by tourism and international cultural exchange.

At the Museo del Prado in 2005, Struth revised the method of the series itself. His longstanding interest in Las Meninas brought him to the museum, but after making Audiences he felt he could no longer photograph “the backs of people standing before a painting” in the same way. He moved into the center of the room and framed the scene so that painted figures and actual visitors overlapped more closely*36. To keep both paintings and crowds in focus with an 8×10 camera, he installed roughly fifteen flash units across the ceilings of several rooms*36. The large format and flash made it possible to keep painted figures, contemporary viewers, and details of the galleries equally available for comparison within one photograph.

Nature & Politics

From 2007 onward, NASA facilities, shipyards, nuclear-fusion research sites, and pharmaceutical plants became major subjects. Work at the Kennedy Space Center helped direct Struth toward places where science, politics, money, and power converge and where “technology and ambition” take material form*10. Nature & Politics includes research and industrial sites such as CERN and addresses expectations placed on science and technology, the desire to intervene in nature, and the limits of knowledge*11. The near-absence of people directs attention to the material outcome of decisions made by researchers, corporations, and states—enormous machines, pipes, cables, and controlled environments—rather than to individual personalities or the spectacle of machinery*12.

In this sense, the empty streets and the scientific facilities remain methodologically connected across several decades. In the early streets, Struth did not photograph the politicians or architects who made the city; he photographed the condition in which their decisions remained visible as buildings and roads. In Nature & Politics, he again avoids portraits of individual scientists or executives and brings into one picture apparatus built from the work of many specialists, budgets, and research goals. Michael Fried argues that the technology photographs are extraordinarily dense with traces of human purpose and design, inviting viewers to understand their details while withholding a complete grasp of the whole*35. In the early streets, visual clarity assisted comparison. Here, comparable resolution also reveals how contemporary technological systems can exceed the understanding of any single person.

Large-Format Color Photography and Exhibition Space

The large color photographs Struth adopted from the late 1980s onward do more than display abundant detail. Perenyei analyzes Museum Photographs within the development of the “photographic tableau” in contemporary art from the late 1970s onward, arguing that photography became an autonomous “picture-object” as it intersected with film, performance, sculpture, and the Western tradition of the single pictorial field*26. A small print can be examined at close range. A photograph that occupies a large section of wall asks the viewer to move physically—stepping back to take in the whole, then approaching to follow details.

Michael Fried’s Why Photography Matters as Art as Never Before discusses large-scale photographs by Struth, Jeff Wall, Thomas Ruff, Andreas Gursky, and others as works encountered on the wall in a manner historically associated with painting*28. For Struth, this scale is especially consequential in Museum Photographs. People are already looking at art inside the photograph; when an actual viewer stands before the large print, his or her own posture of looking can be measured against theirs. Scale directs attention toward the act of viewing itself.

Discussing Times Square, New York (2000), The Met argues that the scale and pictorial complexity of Struth’s work helped bring to photography the kind of sustained attention historically directed toward painting*31. From a distance, the city and crowd can be read as a single composition. At close range, attention moves among advertisements, stock-market displays, architectural surfaces, and individual bodies. Enlargement turns the quantity of information in a photograph into time actually spent looking.

sections.title: Critical Reception and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
How Struth Differs from the Bechers

For roughly half a century, the Bechers concentrated on a single field of disappearing industrial architecture. They standardized weather, distance, and viewpoint, then placed multiple photographs together so that individual variations could be understood through a common type*17. By the 1970s, this impersonal serial form had also been received within Minimal and Conceptual art*3. Struth learned this discipline of comparison while keeping both his subjects and his photographic rules open to change. His 1976 street grid preceded his knowledge of the Bechers’ work, and he later said that although their comparative method interested him, blast furnaces and water towers were not his subject*14. This helps explain why the Museo del Prado acknowledges the influence of typological procedure while distinguishing Struth’s work from a strict, inventory-like Conceptual system*16.

The distinction lies in how photographic rules function. The Bechers maintained a consistent rule so that many industrial structures could be compared. Struth changes the rule according to the question: an empty, centered street; a frontal family portrait; a large museum picture containing painting and viewer at once; a scientific facility rendered with enough precision to preserve the dense apparatus. What he inherited was less the Bechers’ appearance than the habit of designing photographic conditions for comparative thought. The Städel Museum’s reconsideration of the “Becher school” as something more diverse than a single shared style reinforces this distinction*15.

Atget, Evans, and Urban Photography

The Met explicitly connects Leonard Street to the urban architectural photography of Charles Marville and Eugène Atget, predecessors who long predate the Bechers*4. Marville worked on a municipal commission to record Haussmann’s transformation of Paris, photographing both the old city slated for demolition and new urban infrastructure*24. Over more than thirty years, Atget accumulated photographs of Parisian buildings, streets, shops, and gardens as “old Paris” changed under modernization*21. From this lineage, Struth drew a method of registering historical change through specific architecture and streets, treating the city as an accumulation of material evidence.

The connection to Walker Evans is more direct. Struth has said that in an Evans photograph he could examine cars, houses, and terrain in sequence and analyze a place by relating those details to his own experience*14. Evans described American society through roadside architecture, signs, inexpensive shops, houses, and other vernacular environments; his clear photographic language later influenced the Bechers as well*22. Struth was also studying Ed Ruscha and Stephen Shore on his own during the 1970s, so the Bechers were not his only route into urban photography*18.

In its account of Times Square, New York, The Met names Atget, Marville, Sander, and Evans as part of Struth’s historical lineage. It also distinguishes their records of modernization within particular cities or nations from Struth’s attention to cities whose cultural boundaries have become more complicated through globalization*31. Perenyei further argues that the one-point perspective of the early streets does more than inventory buildings: it carries the eye into depth and anticipates compositional strategies used later in the museum photographs*26. Struth’s street pictures therefore join a photographic history of reading society through the surfaces of places with a perspectival organization of the frame rooted in his training as a painter.

Sander and Family Portraits

August Sander was an important precedent in New Objectivity for the Bechers*3. Family Portraits sets a different problem from Sander’s social types. Recent criticism distinguishes Sander’s effort to organize society through occupations and classes from Struth’s lack of an encyclopedic classificatory plan; Struth concentrates on the way a particular family presents itself in a public image*20. The High Museum’s account of The Richter Family 1 likewise recalls the frontality of Sander and the Bechers while drawing attention to the parents’ and children’s postures and to paintings in the room as signs specific to this family*23. Guggenheim Bilbao describes Struth’s family portraits as the result of formal sessions in which subjects knowingly face the camera, recording both individual characteristics and the structure of the family as a group*38.

Through Fried’s argument, the distinction also concerns what posing means. Struth’s families know they are being photographed, face forward, and collectively participate in how they will appear. Yet resemblances of face and body, degrees of physical closeness, differences in seated height, and interpersonal distance contain features that exceed the self-image they intend to construct*28. Because the photographer does not stage a psychological narrative, the consciously arranged family image can be compared with what the camera records through bodies and placement. A similar attitude carries into the museum photographs: Struth records how viewers actually stand and look instead of inventing motives for their behavior.

Museum Photographs and Contemporary Art

Struth’s significance within contemporary art is tied to a change in how photographs were exhibited. During the 1970s, Conceptual art frequently used photography for documentation, information, and classification. From the late 1970s through the 1980s and after, works by Jeff Wall, Thomas Ruff, Andreas Gursky, Struth, and others increasingly occupied large sections of museum and gallery walls and invited prolonged attention as single pictures. Fried discusses this development in terms of tableau photography*28. Perenyei likewise places Struth within the process through which photography entered contemporary art as an autonomous pictorial field while intersecting with film, performance, sculpture, and painting*26.

When Struth stayed in New York in 1978, this shift in photography coincided with active debates about museums, authorship, and representation. Perenyei identifies the institutional critique associated with Rosalind Krauss, Douglas Crimp, and the circle around October as part of this historical setting*26. Having learned in Düsseldorf to compare and analyze photographs, Struth photographed New York streets in an environment where questions about what photographs record were increasingly joined by questions about where and how they are seen.

Museum Photographs brings these two developments together. Its subject is the museum that displays old paintings as “masterpieces” before large numbers of visitors. The finished photographs, meanwhile, approach two meters in scale and return to museum and gallery walls to be viewed in a manner associated with painting. A photograph of people looking in a museum thus returns to the museum, where a new audience stands before it. MoMA’s On the Edge catalogue explains that viewers of Struth’s photographs may recognize their own activity in the visitors depicted within the frame and become conscious of what they themselves are doing there*29.

The relation to painting is equally concrete. MoMA characterizes Struth’s aims as investigative while describing his compositional organization as “painterly”*29. Their relation to painting lies in Struth’s understanding of perspective, figure placement, and the organization of the whole pictorial field, which he applies to configurations produced by actual streets and viewers. In Museum Photographs, the calculated placement of figures inside a history painting shares a plane with contemporary visitors who have gathered before it. The story composed in the painting’s past can therefore be compared directly with present-day acts of viewing.

For its 2002 retrospective, The Met introduced Struth as an important artist in bringing photography into the mainstream of contemporary art and giving it a scale and ambition comparable to major art of the past*37. The point extends beyond the physical size of the print. Struth demonstrated that photography could retain its capacity to record while addressing the history of painting, the museum as an institution, the viewer’s body, and contemporary society within a single work. At the moment when photography came to share exhibition space with painting and sculpture, Museum Photographs made that new position of photography one of its own subjects.

How Struth Differs from Gursky, Ruff, and Höfer

The Düsseldorf School is often treated as a shared style, but The Met cautions against simply equating Struth with Andreas Gursky. Both work at large scale and photograph social spaces around the world; Struth emphasizes how history and individual lives are joined within places, while Gursky places greater weight on the collectives and systems that organize production and consumption*3. Thomas Ruff turned more directly toward the systems and technologies through which photographs become images, while Candida Höfer pursued sustained observation of public interiors. The Städel Museum’s reconsideration of the Becher class as a setting from which markedly different forms of photography emerged makes the same point*15.

Nana Last reads Struth’s work from 1978 to 2018 through three stages—“archive / matrix / assembly”—and treats the series as a development in which methods learned in one body of work alter what becomes possible in the next*32. From this perspective, the abstract word “institution” is not enough to connect the empty streets, families, museums, forests, and technological sites. To learn about society, Struth compares architecture in the streets, studies the placement of people within families, brings paintings and viewers into one museum image, creates forests in which analysis itself becomes difficult, and photographs the technological apparatus in which human decisions have taken material form. Each time he reconsiders where to place the camera, whether to include people, how much detail to preserve, and how large the photograph should be. The 2002 retrospective catalogue similarly includes Charles Wylie’s “A History of Now,” Maria Morris Hambourg and Douglas Eklund’s “The Space of History,” and Ann Goldstein’s “Portraits of Self-Reflection,” examining urban photographic history, history and space, and portraiture across Struth’s work*34.

related_annotations./en/photographers/becher.html: Teachers whose typological method compared structures of the same kind under fixed conditions. Struth kept the classificatory format open, redesigning the photographic method for cities, families, museums, and scientific facilities.
related_annotations./en/photographers/thomas-ruff.html: A contemporary from the same class who turned toward the systems and imaging technologies of photography itself. His direction clarifies Struth 's greater emphasis on social history.
related_annotations./en/photographers/gursky.html: A contemporary who likewise works with large-format color photography. Gursky often surveys crowds and the systems of production and consumption from an elevated viewpoint; Struth follows the positions of individuals within historical places.
related_annotations./en/photographers/wall.html: A useful comparison for the move of large color photographs into the exhibition scale of contemporary art, while staged scenes distinguish Wall's method from Struth's observational approach.
related_annotations./en/photographers/eugene-atget.html: A predecessor who recorded a changing Paris through extensive photographs of streets and architecture. Struth places less emphasis on preservation than on the coexistence of different historical periods within the present city.
related_annotations./en/photographers/evans.html: A predecessor who read society through everyday environments such as architecture, signs, and roads. Struth refers to Evans when explaining the legibility of his own early street photographs.
related_annotations./en/photographers/sander.html: A predecessor who organized society through human types. Family Portraits compares arrangements that individual families construct for themselves instead of building a classificatory system.
related_annotations./en/movements/dusseldorf-school.html: Photographers who emerged from the Bechers' class. The important question is how each transformed a comparative method, not whether they shared one style.
related_annotations./en/movements/large-format-color.html: An exhibition format that presents museums, families, and technological facilities at a scale that engages the viewer's body.
related_annotations./en/movements/conceptual-art.html: A historical background for understanding the early grids, controlled conditions, and comparative method.

zanele-muholi.html.title: Zanele Muholi | Faces and Phases and Visual Activism | Photo Coordinates
zanele-muholi.html.meta_description: Zanele Muholi, who describes themself as a “visual activist,” has photographed Black LGBTQIA+ communities in South Africa as well as themself over an extended period. Across Only Half the Picture, Faces and Phases, Being, Brave Beauties, and Somnyama Ngonyama, Muholi moves among records of violence, frontal portraiture, intimate daily life, and self-portraiture. Their photography turns legal equality alongside continuing discrimination and violence in post-apartheid South Africa into an archive that preserves participants’ names and images.

zanele-muholi.html.lead_html: Zanele Muholi, who describes themself as a “visual activist,” has photographed Black LGBTQIA+ communities in South Africa as well as themself over an extended period. Across Only Half the Picture, Faces and Phases, Being, Brave Beauties, and Somnyama Ngonyama, Muholi moves among records of violence, frontal portraiture, intimate daily life, and self-portraiture. Their photography turns legal equality alongside continuing discrimination and violence in post-apartheid South Africa into an archive that preserves participants’ names and images.
zanele-muholi.html.thesis_html: Muholi made portraiture into a long-term archive in which Black LGBTQIA+ participants preserve their own names and images. Faces and Phases records participants with names, locations, and dates, often photographing the same person again after years have passed. Being preserves lovers’ everyday lives alongside the history of violence, while Somnyama Ngonyama turns the camera on Muholi themself. Moving among portraiture, intimate photography, and self-portraiture, Muholi builds the record around who appears, who names themself, and which images enter history, keeping Black LGBTQIA+ lives from being collapsed into an anonymous “social issue.”

sections.title: Background and Historical Setting
sections.body_html:
Why Photography

Muholi’s turn to photography grew from both activist experience and a personal need for images. In an interview with The Brooklyn Rail, Muholi recalled receiving a compact camera from a first lover and finding in photography a way to recover a sense of freedom and connection to themself.*17 Muholi entered the Market Photo Workshop at age twenty-nine to study photography professionally and has said that there was a period when images communicated their experience more readily than words and photography helped save them.*17 Photography became a means of reclaiming personal experience and leaving a visible record that people from the same community had lived.

Beginning around 2002, Muholi documented the lives of Black lesbians in South Africa who had experienced hate crimes, developing this work into Only Half the Picture. The Guardian contrasts this early series with the later Being, which photographs everyday intimacy.*18 Legal rights coexisted with a continuing threat of violence in daily life, bringing activism and photography into the same work. Stevenson’s biography likewise describes Muholi’s work as a sustained record of Black LGBTQIA+ life, violence, and self-representation.*1

Photographic Education in South Africa

The Market Photo Workshop, founded by David Goldblatt, became an important site of training for Muholi. In an interview with The Guardian, Muholi explained that the workshop helped formalize concerns they were already pursuing as photography and sharpened their method through discussion with other photographers.*18 Muholi also names Goldblatt as an important mentor in The Brooklyn Rail, describing him as someone who offered an opportunity to learn when university education was financially difficult to access.*17

At the same time, Muholi has remained attentive to the question of who has historically made photographs in South Africa. In Aperture’s feature on Faces & Phases, Muholi describes learning apartheid-era photographic history through the work of male photographers such as Ernest Cole, Alf Kumalo, and Goldblatt, and only later encountering the history of Black women photographers.*10 That absence contributed to Muholi’s decision to make images from within the community and to challenge photographs that explained Black queer people from the outside.

sections.title: The Core of the Work
sections.body_html:
Turning Portraiture into an Archive

Faces and Phases began in 2006 and is an ongoing project portraying Black lesbians, trans people, and gender-nonconforming participants together with their names, locations, and dates. Yancey Richardson describes it as an effort to rewrite a Black queer and trans visual history erased by discrimination and violence.*3 Because the same participants reappear after intervals of time, a single portrait does not become a fixed “type.” Changes in hairstyle, clothing, age, and expression enter the archive as well. The Walther Collection likewise holds the series as a long-term visual record of a community.*11

Kylie Thomas discusses Faces and Phases as an “intimate archive,” arguing that lesbian experiences made difficult to speak publicly enter established forms of memorial and portrait photography while changing those forms in the process*19. By placing portraits of living and deceased participants within the same sequence, deaths caused by violence do not disappear into anonymous statistics but remain located within communal memory. The archive becomes both a repository and an active intervention into whose lives and deaths enter the public record.

Frontal Portraiture and the Returned Gaze

Many Faces and Phases portraits are strongly frontal, with participants looking back into the camera. In MoMA’s Anele “Anza” Khaba, the face, clothing, and posture remain connected to a restrained background while the gaze is returned outward from the image.*5 This composition prevents the viewer from settling comfortably into a position of one-way observation. In The Brooklyn Rail, Muholi also distinguishes between the experience of participants being “othered” by an unfamiliar photographer and being photographed by someone from the same community.*17

For Muholi, “visibility” centers on who controls the image as well as on who is seen. In an interview with the Pew Center, Muholi explains a preference for the term visual activist over visual artist, placing human rights, self-representation, and ownership of one’s own voice at the center of the work*21. The portrait therefore functions as a site where participants determine how they appear, how they name themselves, and which image is carried forward, instead of presenting them as subjects already understood from the outside.

Photographing Intimate Daily Life

Being photographs lovers’ bodies, bedrooms, embraces, and moments of rest. Katlego Mashiloane and Nosipho Lavuta, held by the National Museum of Women in the Arts, exemplifies the series’ effort to record Black lesbian life through intimate daily experience instead of only through scenes of violence or crisis.*12 As Muholi tells The Guardian, “existing every day is political.” Making only the damage of violence visible would define communal life primarily through victimhood.*18 The quiet scenes in Being were necessary to counter that imbalance.

Self-Portraiture and Black Representation

In Somnyama Ngonyama, Muholi turns the camera on themself, using familiar materials—clothespins, rubber gloves, tires, cables, fabric—as clothing and headpieces. In the artist statement published by Stevenson, the turn from photographing others to photographing themself marks a shift toward personally performing histories and present conditions surrounding the Black body.*2 Aperture’s photobook connects each self-portrait to different circumstances of place, event, labor, colonialism, and racial representation.*9

In the prints, Muholi deepens the black tones of the skin and heightens contrast with the whites of the eyes and everyday objects. Autograph describes this manipulation as a form of self-representation that questions the historical ways Black bodies have been seen.*8 The New Yorker compares Muholi with staged self-portraiture by Cindy Sherman, Claude Cahun, and Carrie Mae Weems, while cautioning that locating the work only within that lineage risks weakening its protest against the historical representation of Black people and its effort to reclaim those images.*22

Photobooks and the Long-Term Archive

Muholi’s portraits are exhibited individually, but grids, photobooks, and long-running series give them another function. The Faces and Phases photobook combines numerous portraits and testimonies, connecting individual faces to the duration of a community. Aperture presents the series as an ongoing publication of Black queer history in South Africa.*10 In an interview with TIME, Muholi also describes the archive as a way for people to “be counted,” emphasizing that participants’ existence should not disappear from the record.*23

sections.title: Major Works, Methods, and Media
sections.body_html:
Early Work and Being

Only Half the Picture is an early series combining hate crimes, traces of violence, bodies, and everyday life. It was presented as a solo exhibition at the Johannesburg Art Gallery in 2004. The Guardian identifies Muholi’s documentation of victims beginning around 2002 as an origin point for the work.*18 The subsequent Being photographs intimate scenes between lovers, placing everyday affection alongside the record of violence.*12

Faces and Phases

Faces and Phases is one of Muholi’s longest-running projects, with works held by institutions including MoMA, the Brooklyn Museum, and the Walther Collection.MoMA’s Sunday Francis Mdlankomo likewise shows the series’ characteristic structure of a frontal portrait against a restrained background.*6 Works in the Brooklyn Museum collection further show the series’ incorporation into international museum collections.*14 As the number of works grows, differences within the community become more pronounced than any single representative image. This accumulation is one of the series’ formal strengths.

Brave Beauties

Brave Beauties portrays trans women and gender-nonconforming participants through the self-staging of pageantry and fashion. SFMOMA’s Eye Me brought together Faces and Phases, Brave Beauties, and Somnyama Ngonyama, showing the continuity between portraiture, fashion, self-presentation, and Muholi’s activism.*7 Here, beauty becomes a field in which participants use clothing, posture, and gaze to shape how they appear, creating a form of self-representation distinct from the archival structure of Faces and Phases.

Somnyama Ngonyama

Somnyama Ngonyama, a Zulu title translated as “Hail the Dark Lioness,” accumulates self-portraits made in different locations. Aperture’s photobook brings the series together in sequence and connects everyday materials used as costume, as well as the places of production, to specific histories.*9 Works made before the self-portrait series, including the Guggenheim’s TK, 2010, show that the body and self-representation were already central concerns.*15 Somnyama Ngonyama concentrates those questions on Muholi’s own face, placing the photographer’s body inside the same histories of gaze and self-representation.

sections.title: Criticism and Place in Photographic History
sections.body_html:
After South African Documentary Photography

Muholi was trained within Goldblatt’s educational legacy and inherits a history in which South African photography documented social inequality during apartheid.*17 Muholi also addresses how their own community was missing from historical photographic archives, placing the relationship between photographer and participant at the center of the work. In an Aperture interview, Muholi describes discovering earlier Black women photographers only later and links the scarcity of images like their own within established photographic history to the urgency of making new ones.*10

Critiques of Visibility

Muholi gives social “visibility” different formal structures across the series. The frontal portraits of Faces and Phases, intimate scenes of Being, performances of Brave Beauties, and self-portraits of Somnyama Ngonyama each change who makes the image, how a person is recorded, and the unit through which the work is preserved, as well as who appears before the camera. Z'étoile Imma and Kylie Thomas interpret these differences in form as ways of resisting the reduction of Black queer and trans life to a single image of a social problem.*20

The work has also met political hostility within South Africa. Thomas discusses a 2009 incident in which the minister of arts and culture at the time condemned an exhibition including Muholi’s work as “immoral” and walked out, arguing that the incident itself exposed a struggle over who is permitted to recognize queer bodies within public representation*19. Within this political conflict, frontal portraiture and archival accumulation become concrete forms for preserving lives that state and society had pushed outside the record as named, imaged presences.

Museums and Activism

Muholi’s work has been collected and exhibited by institutions including MoMA, SFMOMA, the Brooklyn Museum, and the Guggenheim, and has received broad recognition within the art museum system.MoMA’s artist page lists collection works including Faces and Phases alongside the artist’s exhibition history.*4 In 2026, Muholi was named the recipient of the Hasselblad Award, with the foundation recognizing their sustained visual activism and contribution to photographic history.*16

Muholi’s own definition of the work keeps activism and art continuous despite this institutional recognition. In Art21, Muholi discusses image-making and community-building as part of the same activity and treats photography as a means of preserving people’s voices and existence*13. At the Pew Center, Muholi likewise explains the self-description visual activist as a term that gives priority to human rights and self-representation*21. Even as museum recognition has expanded, the questions of who makes an image and for whom it is preserved remain criteria within the work.
